title: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து
theme: An unnamed First One, known only through epithets, is made the ground of learning, freedom from anxiety and the crossing of the sea. The chapter's recurring claim is exclusive: without reaching those feet, these things are out of reach.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the First One's existence (1), learning's fruit (2), those who think of, praise and follow him reach release (3-6), the fault of not doing so (7-9), and both outcomes stated together (10).
source_issues: Manakkudavar's comment on verse 9 ends with a stray '10', apparently a verse or page number.
Parimelazhagar's comment on verse 10 has spelling slips: இரைவன் for இறைவன் and பிரவி for பிறவி.

couplet: A, as its first of letters, every speech maintains;
The "Primal Deity" is first through all the world's domains.
pope.gloss: As the letter A is the first of all letters, so the eternal God is first in the world.

reading: As all letters have 'a' as their first, the world has the Primal Lord as its first.
nuance: The verse gives a simile of being first and says nothing of creating. Parimelazhagar reads it as establishing that the unseen deity exists, arguing from the visible world, which is more than the couplet states.

couplet: No fruit have men of all their studied lore,
Save they the 'Purely Wise One's' feet adore.
pope.gloss: What Profit have those derived from learning, who worship not the good feet of Him who is possessed of pure knowledge ?

reading: What has learning achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the one of pure knowledge?
nuance: The question assumes that learning has a purpose beyond itself. It is the chapter's first conditional, and it is put to the learned, not to the ignorant.

couplet: His feet, 'Who o'er the full-blown flower hath past,' who gain
In bliss long time shall dwell above this earthly plain.
pope.gloss: They who are united to the glorious feet of Him who passes swiftly over the flower of the mind, shall flourish long above all worlds.

reading: Those who reach the noble feet of the one who walked upon the flower will live long upon the earth.
nuance: The Tamil says நிலமிசை, on the earth, so reading it as a world above is an interpretation. Parimelazhagar also rejects an identification of 'the one who walked on the flower' with another deity, which shows the epithet was already disputed.

couplet: His foot, 'Whom want affects not, irks not grief,' who gain
Shall not, through every time, of any woes complain.
pope.gloss: To those who meditate the feet of Him who is void of desire or aversion, evil shall never come.

reading: Those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering, anywhere or at any time.
nuance: The one sought is defined by what he lacks. Parimelazhagar's explanation makes the benefit mimetic: those who reach him also lose liking and aversion, and so lose the suffering these cause.

couplet: The men, who on the 'King's' true praised delight to dwell,
Affects not them the fruit of deeds done ill or well.
pope.gloss: The two-fold deeds that spring from darkness shall not adhere to those who delight in the true praise of God.

reading: The two kinds of deed born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
nuance: The verse says both kinds, so good deeds are also among what must not cling. That is a stronger claim than 'worship removes sin'.

couplet: Long live they blest, who 've stood in path from falsehood freed;
His, 'Who quenched lusts that from the sense-gates five proceed'.
pope.gloss: Those shall long proposer who abide in the faultless way of Him who has destroyed the five desires of the senses.

reading: Those who stand firm on the truthful path of conduct of the one who quenched the five senses' desires will live long.
nuance: This is the only verse in the chapter that asks for a way of living instead of reaching or praising. Parimelazhagar says the path was taught by the one who quenched the five, as a poem belongs to its poet, which makes him a teacher and not only an object of worship.

couplet: Unless His foot, 'to Whom none can compare,' men gain,
'Tis hard for mind to find relief from anxious pain.
pope.gloss: Anxiety of mind cannot be removed, except from those who are united to the feet of Him who is incomparable.

reading: Except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one, it is hard to remove the mind's anxiety.
nuance: The verse says அரிது, hard. Parimelazhagar explicitly takes this as impossibility, which hardens the claim beyond its plain wording.

couplet: Unless His feet 'the Sea of Good, the Fair and Bountiful,' men gain,
'Tis hard the further bank of being's changeful sea to attain.
pope.gloss: None can swim the sea of vice, but those who are united to the feet of that gracious Being who is a sea of virtue.

reading: Except for those who reach the feet of the gracious one who is a sea of virtue, the other seas are hard to swim.
nuance: The sea of virtue set against 'other seas' is the image's whole point. Pope's gloss, 'sea of vice', is not in the Tamil.

couplet: Before His foot, 'the Eight-fold Excellence,' with unbent head,
Who stands, like palsied sense, is to all living functions dead.
pope.gloss: The head that worships not the feet of Him who is possessed of eight attributes, is as useless as a sense without the power of sensation.

reading: A head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is as useless as a sense organ that cannot sense.
nuance: The verse never lists the eight. Parimelazhagar gives a list from Saiva scripture and records rival lists, so any particular list is the commentator's. Manakkudavar goes further and says such bodies lack life.

couplet: They swim the sea of births, the 'Monarch's ' foot who gain;
None others reach the shore of being's mighty main.
pope.gloss: None can swim the great sea of births but those who are united to the feet of God.

reading: Those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births, and those who do not reach them cannot.
nuance: The chapter closes with both outcomes in one couplet. Verses 7 and 8 hedge with 'hard', and this one drops the hedge. Parimelazhagar's 'reach' comes from the verse's own closing negative, since the positive verb is left implied.

title: வான்சிறப்பு
theme: Rain is the unacknowledged condition of everything: food, farming, the sea's life, worship, giving, austerity and conduct. The chapter makes virtue and the gods depend on a natural cause.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: rain as the cause of the world's going on (11-17), and as the cause of virtue, wealth and pleasure (18-20).
source_issues: Kalaignar's entry for verse 17 ends with an unrelated sentence beginning 'இ. அடைநலம் அடைமொழிகளைச்', apparently from a different text. It is not part of his comment on this verse.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 16 and 20.

couplet: The world its course maintains through life that rain unfailing gives;
Thus rain is known the true ambrosial food of all that lives.
pope.gloss: By the continuance of rain the world is preserved in existence; it is therefore worthy to be called ambrosia.

reading: Because the world keeps going through the rain's constancy, rain deserves to be understood as amrita.
nuance: The word உணரற்பாற்று makes this a matter of recognition, since rain is ordinary and easily taken for granted. Manakkudavar draws this out by saying it should not be thought of as a mere element.

couplet: The rain makes pleasant food for eaters rise;
As food itself, thirst-quenching draught supplies.
pope.gloss: Rain produces good food, and is itself food.

reading: Rain produces the food that eaters eat, and rain is itself food to those who drink it.
nuance: Five uses of துப்பு pack the couplet, and the wordplay enacts the idea: the same substance is the maker, the made and the eater's need.

couplet: If clouds, that promised rain, deceive, and in the sky remain,
Famine, sore torment, stalks o'er earth's vast ocean-girdled plain.
pope.gloss: If the cloud, withholding rain, deceive (our hopes) hunger will long distress the sea-girt spacious world.

reading: If the sky fails, hunger stays and torments this wide world, though it is surrounded by spreading water.
nuance: The irony is in விரிநீர்: the world is ringed by water and still starves. Parimelazhagar makes this explicit. பொய்ப்பின் also treats the sky as something that can break its word.

couplet: If clouds their wealth of waters fail on earth to pour,
The ploughers plough with oxen's sturdy team no more.
pope.gloss: If the abundance of wealth imparting rain diminish, the labour of the plough must cease.

reading: If the bounty of the rains declines, ploughmen will not plough.
nuance: Parimelazhagar takes the verse as explaining why food runs out. The human labour is real but placed downstream of a yield the farmer doesn't control.

couplet: 'Tis rain works all: it ruin spreads, then timely aid supplies;
As, in the happy days before, it bids the ruined rise.
pope.gloss: Rain by its absence ruins men; and by its existence restores them to fortune.

reading: Rain is what ruins, and then it is rain again that supports and lifts up the ruined.
nuance: The verse says only that rain ruins. The commentators here take the ruin as failure to fall, though a reader might expect flood too. The power to destroy and restore belongs to one impersonal agent, with no moral reason given.

couplet: If from the clouds no drops of rain are shed.
'Tis rare to see green herb lift up its head.
pope.gloss: If no drop falls from the clouds, not even the green blade of grass will be seen.

reading: Unless drops fall from the sky, it is hard to see even the head of a green blade of grass.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the implied 'even': if the grass is gone, not even a life with one sense remains. The argument descends to the smallest thing that lives.

couplet: If clouds restrain their gifts and grant no rain,
The treasures fail in ocean's wide domain.
pope.gloss: Even the wealth of the wide sea will be diminished, if the cloud that has drawn (its waters) up gives them not back again (in rain).

reading: Even the vast sea would lose its nature if the cloud held back after taking from it.
nuance: The source of rain needs rain, so the dependence runs in a circle. Parimelazhagar makes this the point, and Kalaignar turns the same cycle into a social lesson.

couplet: If heaven grow dry, with feast and offering never more,
Will men on earth the heavenly ones adore.
pope.gloss: If the heaven dry up, neither yearly festivals, nor daily worship will be offered in this world, to the celestials.

reading: If the sky dries up, festival and worship will cease here, even for the gods.
nuance: The word 'even' reverses the usual order: the celestials depend on what the sky provides through human offering. Kalaignar's comment adds scepticism with 'those said to live in the sky', which the verse does not express.

couplet: If heaven its watery treasures ceases to dispense,
Through the wide world cease gifts, and deeds of 'penitence'.
pope.gloss: If rain fall not, penance and alms-deeds will not dwell within this spacious world.

reading: If the sky does not give, neither giving nor austerity will last in this wide world.
nuance: Parimelazhagar maps giving broadly to the householder and austerity to the renunciant, so this verse quietly announces the two paths that chapters 3 and 5 go on to compare. Even austerity, which might seem independent of plenty, is included.

couplet: When water fails, functions of nature cease, you say;
Thus when rain fails, no men can walk in 'duty's ordered way'.
pope.gloss: If it be said that the duties of life cannot be discharged by any person without water, so without rain there cannot be the flowing of water.

reading: If no one's world can do without water, then its flow can't exist without the sky.
nuance: The whole dispute rests on ஒழுக்கு, which can mean a flow or conduct. On the second reading, the chapter ends by saying morality depends on rain.

title: நீத்தார் பெருமை
theme: The greatness of those who have renounced: immeasurable, grounded in mastery of the senses, and shown in the force of their word and anger. It ends by saying that the name அந்தணர் belongs to those whose conduct is cool grace toward all beings.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: their greatness exceeds all others (21-23), its causes are quenching the five, yoga and knowledge of the principles (24-27), their authority (28-29), and their grace despite that authority (30).
source_issues: Manakkudavar is not aligned for verse 27. His comment on verse 30 says 'these eight', which suggests his grouping of this chapter differs from the running order here.

couplet: The settled rule of every code requires, as highest good,
Their greatness who, renouncing all, true to their rule have stood.
pope.gloss: The end and aim of all treatise is to extol beyond all other excellence, the greatness of those who, while abiding in the rule of conduct peculiar to their state, have abandoned all desire.

reading: The settled view of the texts is to place the greatness of those who renounce within their discipline above all other excellence.
nuance: The verse says only ஒழுக்கத்து, in discipline. Parimelazhagar's ladder from duties of varna to release is his own construction. The commentators also give very different reasons for the agreement among texts.

couplet: As counting those that from the earth have passed away,
'Tis vain attempt the might of holy men to say.
pope.gloss: To describe the measure of the greatness of those who have forsaken the two-fold desires, is like counting the dead.

reading: Trying to state the measure of renouncers' greatness is like counting all the dead who have ever lived.
nuance: It's a strange image of praise. The dead aren't only numerous but past counting in principle. My reading, offered tentatively, is that comparing renouncers to the dead also suits people who have left the world.

couplet: Their greatness earth transcends, who, way of both worlds weighed,
In this world take their stand, in virtue's robe arrayed.
pope.gloss: The greatness of those who have discovered the properties of both states of being, and renounced the world, shines forth on earth (beyond all others).

reading: The greatness of those who discern the two ways and take on virtue here stands highest in the world.
nuance: ஈண்டு, here, is important: this choice is made in this life. Parimelazhagar uses an implied 'only' to place them above even emperors.

couplet: He, who with firmness, curb the five restrains,
Is seed for soil of yonder happy plains.
pope.gloss: He who guides his five senses by the hook of wisdom will be a seed in the world of heaven.

reading: One who guards the five with the goad of firmness is a seed for the finest ground.
nuance: The goad implies the elephants, which the verse doesn't mention, and then the image shifts to farming. வரன் leaves the 'field' open: Parimelazhagar makes it release, while Kalaignar makes it renunciation itself. The word உரன் suggests strength, though Parimelazhagar says it refers here to understanding.

couplet: Their might who have destroyed 'the five', shall soothly tell
Indra, the lord of those in heaven's wide realms that dwell.
pope.gloss: Indra, the king of the inhabitants of the spacious heaven, is himself, a sufficient proof of the strength of him who has subdued his five senses.

reading: Of the strength of one who has quenched the five, Indra, lord of the wide heavens, is witness enough.
nuance: The verse does not say how Indra testifies. The commentators supply two opposed stories, one in which Indra failed and another in which he fears.

couplet: Things hard in the doing will great men do;
Things hard in the doing the mean eschew.
pope.gloss: The great will do those things which is difficult to be done; but the mean cannot do them.

reading: Those who do what is hard to do are great, and those who can't do it are small.
nuance: The verse doesn't say what is hard, so it reads as general. In its context the commentators narrow it to yoga. Manakkudavar turns it into a warning within the chapter: renouncing alone does not make one great.

couplet: Taste, light, touch, sound, and smell: who knows the way
Of all the five,- the world submissive owns his sway.
pope.gloss: The world is within the knowledge of him who knows the properties of taste, sight, touch, hearing and smell.

reading: The world lies within the one who discerns the kinds of the five: taste, light, touch, sound and smell.
nuance: கட்டே is the crux. Pope's 'owns his sway' and Parimelazhagar's 'within his knowledge' suggest different kinds of mastery. Parimelazhagar's whole twenty-five principles are not in the couplet, which names only the five.

couplet: The might of men whose word is never vain,
The 'secret word' shall to the earth proclaim.
pope.gloss: The hidden words of the men whose words are full of effect, will shew their greatness to the world.

reading: The greatness of those whose word is full is shown on earth by their hidden words.
nuance: நிறைமொழி and மறைமொழி echo each other: a complete word and a concealed one. The verse doesn't say whether the proof is what the words do or what they teach.

couplet: The wrath 'tis hard e'en for an instant to endure,
Of those who virtue's hill have scaled, and stand secure.
pope.gloss: The anger of those who have ascended the mountain of goodness, though it continue but for a moment, cannot be resisted.

reading: The anger of those who have climbed the hill of good qualities, even for a moment, is hard to withstand.
nuance: The crux is whose capacity காத்தல் refers to, and the commentators turn the verse in opposite directions. Pope sides with the threatening reading.

couplet: Towards all that breathe, with seemly graciousness adorned they live;
And thus to virtue's sons the name of 'Anthanar' men give.
pope.gloss: The virtuous are truly called Anthanar; because in their conduct towards all creatures they are clothed in kindness.

reading: Those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, because they live clothed in cool kindness toward every living being.
nuance: The verse defines a status word by conduct, and its logic is a reason (ஒழுகலான்), so the name follows from the behaviour. Placed right after 29, its coolness is the counterweight to the sage's terrifying anger.

title: அறன்வலியுறுத்தல்
theme: Virtue's power: nothing brings more gain, and forgetting it is the worst loss. The chapter defines it inwardly, as a clean mind free of four faults, and presses that it must be practised now and continually.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: nothing surpasses it (31), the harm of neglect (32), how it is practised (33), its nature (34-35), practising it while the body lasts (36), proof (37), its fruit of release (38), its fruit of joy and renown (39), and what must be done and avoided (40).
source_issues: Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 32, 33, 35 and 37. His comment on verse 34 refers to the four faults as already stated, which suggests a different verse order in his text.

couplet: It yields distinction, yields prosperity; what gain
Greater than virtue can a living man obtain?
pope.gloss: Virtue will confer heaven and wealth; what greater source of happiness can man possess ?

reading: It yields distinction and it yields wealth: what gain is greater for a living being than virtue?
nuance: The appeal is to self-interest, as virtue is praised for what it brings. Parimelazhagar takes சிறப்பு as release and செல்வம் as heaven, while Manakkudavar takes the second more plainly as wealth and sees the verse as answering those who say prosperity comes from wealth.

couplet: No greater gain than virtue aught can cause;
No greater loss than life oblivious of her laws.
pope.gloss: There can be no greater source of good than (the practice of) virtue; there can be no greater source of evil than the forgetfulness of it.

reading: No gain surpasses virtue, and no ruin surpasses forgetting it.
nuance: The opposite of virtue here is மறத்தல், forgetting, not doing wrong. Ruin comes through inattention, so the danger is ordinary.

couplet: To finish virtue's work with ceaseless effort strive,
What way thou may'st, where'er thou see'st the work may thrive.
pope.gloss: As much as possible, in every way, incessantly practise virtue.

reading: As far as you are able, without stopping, do the work of virtue wherever it can go.
nuance: ஒல்லும் வகையான் sets the measure by capacity, so the demand is relentless in duration but not impossible in scale. Parimelazhagar gives 'wherever' as mind, speech and body, while Kalaignar turns it into a requirement that all one's acts be virtuous.

couplet: Spotless be thou in mind! This only merits virtue's name;
All else, mere pomp of idle sound, no real worth can claim.
pope.gloss: Let him who does virtuous deeds be of spotless mind; to that extent is virtue; all else is vain show.

reading: To be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue, and everything else is noisy show.
nuance: ஆகுல means clamour, so the charge against outward virtue is that it wants an audience. Parimelazhagar reads the verse with 33, so it concerns the mind of someone already doing good, not the mind in place of deeds. Manakkudavar's comment says the four faults were named earlier, which implies his text placed 35 before this verse.

couplet: 'Tis virtue when, his footsteps sliding not through envy, wrath,
Lust, evil speech-these four, man onwards moves in ordered path.
pope.gloss: That conduct is virtue which is free from these four things, viz, malice, desire, anger and bitter speech.

reading: Virtue is what proceeds without slipping into these four: envy, craving, anger and harsh speech.
nuance: Virtue is defined by exclusion. The verse only lists the faults, and Parimelazhagar supplies a causal chain in which craving leads to anger and anger to harsh speech. Three of the four are inward and one is spoken.

couplet: Do deeds of virtue now. Say not, 'To-morrow we'll be wise';
Thus, when thou diest, shalt thou find a help that never dies.
pope.gloss: Defer not virtue to another day; receive her now; and at the dying hour she will be your undying friend.

reading: Do virtue without saying 'we'll see to it later': when you perish, it is a companion that doesn't perish.
nuance: The pun பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றா turns on one verb: you perish and it doesn't. The verse doesn't say how virtue survives, and that is where the commentators part.

couplet: Needs not in words to dwell on virtue's fruits: compare
The man in litter borne with them that toiling bear!
pope.gloss: The fruit of virtue need not be described in books; it may be inferred from seeing the bearer of a palanquin and the rider therein.

reading: There is no need to say 'this is the way of virtue': look between the one who bears the palanquin and the one who rides in it.
nuance: The couplet is very compressed, and it never says what difference we are to see. Taken at face value, it treats social rank as visible evidence of moral merit, which is one of the harder claims in the book.

couplet: If no day passing idly, good to do each day you toil,
A stone it will be to block the way of future days of moil.
pope.gloss: If one allows no day to pass without some good being done, his conduct will be a stone to block up the passage to other births.

reading: If you do good so that no day falls away unused, that is a stone blocking the road of your days.
nuance: வீழ்நாள் and வாழ்நாள் are set against each other, so fallen days are contrasted with living days. The stone's job depends entirely on what வாழ்நாள் means here.

couplet: What from virtue floweth, yieldeth dear delight;
All else extern, is void of glory's light.
pope.gloss: Only that pleasure which flows from domestic virtue is pleasure; all else is not pleasure, and it is without praise.

reading: Only what comes through virtue is joy; everything else lies outside it and has no renown either.
nuance: Pope's gloss restricts this to 'domestic virtue', which follows Parimelazhagar and is not in the Tamil. The verse has a strong implication: joy is not separate from virtue and can't be got apart from it.

couplet: 'Virtue' sums the things that should be done;
'Vice' sums the things that man should shun.
pope.gloss: That is virtue which each ought to do, and that is vice which each should shun.

reading: What a person should do is virtue, and what a person should escape is blame.
nuance: Virtue's counterpart here is பழி, blame, not sin. Parimelazhagar explains it as what is blamed, and takes it to mean bad deeds. The term gives virtue a social measure as well as a cosmic one.

title: இல்வாழ்க்கை
theme: The household life as the support of everyone else and as the fullest form of virtue. Having just exalted renunciants in chapter 3, the book now asks what they could gain by leaving home, and the commentators work hard to limit that challenge.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the household's service to all (41-42), how the householder does virtue (43-45), its superiority (46-49), and its fruit in the next life (50). He holds its fruit in this life, renown, for the end of the section.
source_issues: The Tamil of verse 50 in kg/core reads வான்உநற்யும், a typo for வான்உறையும் as Parimelazhagar's own text shows.
Manakkudavar's comment on verse 45 has OCR damage ('அவ் > ரண்டினையு', 'கொடுக்கவேண்டுமெ தும்'), and his comment on verse 49 ends with a stray '10'.

couplet: The men of household virtue, firm in way of good, sustain
The other orders three that rule professed maintain.
pope.gloss: He will be called a (true) householder, who is a firm support to the virtuous of the three orders in their good path.

reading: The one called a householder is the steady support, on their good path, of the three who keep their proper way.
nuance: The verse doesn't name the three, and what is meant by இயல்புடைய decides who is included.

couplet: To anchorites, to indigent, to those who've passed away,
The man for household virtue famed is needful held and stay.
pope.gloss: He will be said to flourish in domestic virtue who aids the forsaken, the poor, and the dead.

reading: The householder is the support of those who have let go, those who have nothing and those who have died.
nuance: A single support reaches even the dead. Chapter 3 uses துறந்தார் for renouncers, so Parimelazhagar's different reading here gives the same word a very different sense.

couplet: The manes, God, guests kindred, self, in due degree,
These five to cherish well is chiefest charity.
pope.gloss: The chief (duty of the householder) is to preserve the five-fold rule (of conduct) towards the manes, the Gods, his guests, his relations and himself.

reading: To tend properly the five, namely ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself, is the chief duty.
nuance: The self is last on a list of duties. Parimelazhagar's reason is that one must exist in order to do any virtue, so self-care is a moral requirement. Kalaignar replaces ancestors and gods with memory of the dead and honour for those who live well.

couplet: Who shares his meal with other, while all guilt he shuns,
His virtuous line unbroken though the ages runs.
pope.gloss: His descendants shall never fail who, living in the domestic state, fears vice (in the acquisition of property) and shares his food (with others).

reading: If a life fears blame and shares its food, its line never fails at any time.
nuance: Fear of blame comes before sharing because generosity can't launder what was wrongly got. Parimelazhagar gives a striking account of how merit and fault split in that case.

couplet: If love and virtue in the household reign,
This is of life the perfect grace and gain.
pope.gloss: If the married life possess love and virtue, these will be both its duty and reward.

reading: If household life has love and virtue, these are its character and its fruit.
nuance: The verse makes the reward internal: the fruit of having love and virtue is having them. Parimelazhagar directs love to the wife and virtue to sharing, whereas Manakkudavar directs love to everyone and says no further reward is needed.

couplet: If man in active household life a virtuous soul retain,
What fruit from other modes of virtue can he gain?
pope.gloss: What will he who lives virtuously in the domestic state gain by going into the other, (ascetic) state ?

reading: If one conducts household life in the way of virtue, what would one gain by going off along the outside way?
nuance: The rhetorical question challenges chapter 3 directly. Everything depends on how far 'outside way' reaches.

couplet: In nature's way who spends his calm domestic days,
'Mid all that strive for virtue's crown hath foremost place.
pope.gloss: Among all those who labour (for future happiness) he is greatest who lives well in the household state.

reading: One who lives the household life according to its nature stands first among all who strive.
nuance: The verse doesn't say what they strive for, so the comparison group changes with each commentator.

tamil: ஆற்றின் ஒழுக் கி அறனிழுக்கா இல்வாழ் க்கை

couplet: Others it sets upon their way, itself from virtue ne'er declines;
Than stern ascetics' pains such life domestic brighter shines.
pope.gloss: The householder who, not swerving from virtue, helps the ascetic in his way, endures more than those who endure penance.

reading: A household life that keeps others on their way and doesn't itself slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance.
nuance: The word chosen, நோன்மை, is the ascetic's own virtue claimed for the householder. Parimelazhagar's reason is that the ascetic bears only their own pain, while the householder also bears that of others.

couplet: The life domestic rightly bears true virtue's name;
That other too, if blameless found, due praise may claim.
pope.gloss: The marriage state is truly called virtue. The other state is also good, if others do not reproach it.

reading: What is called virtue is household life, and that too is good if there is nothing in it others can blame.
nuance: The whole verse turns on what அஃதும் points to. On one reading it is a rebuke to renunciants, and on another it is a condition on householders. Manakkudavar's explanation also shows a caste assumption of his own.

couplet: Who shares domestic life, by household virtues graced,
Shall, mid the Gods, in heaven who dwell, be placed.
pope.gloss: He who on earth has lived in the conjugal state as he should live, will be placed among the Gods who dwell in heaven.

reading: One who lives on earth as life should be lived will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky.
nuance: வைக்கப்படும், 'will be placed', could mean a destiny or an estimation. Manakkudavar treats it as being honoured by all, while Parimelazhagar also expects actual godhood later on. The Tamil word for how to live, வாழ்வாங்கு, is left undefined.

title: வாழ்க்கைத் துணைநலம்
theme: The wife as the household's real wealth. The chapter praises her steadfastness and even grants her power over the rain, yet it is told largely from the husband's side, and it measures her by what she makes possible for his life.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's notes divide it: her qualities and fit with his income (51), that only her worth matters to household life (52-53), steadfastness and its power (54-55), steadfastness and its protection (56-57), her reward (58), the husband's shame without it (59), and a bridge to children (60).
source_issues: Kalaignar's entry for verse 55 continues with text about his commentary ('கலைஞரின் நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலத்துக்கு'), so it appears to be taken from a secondary essay. Only its first sentence is used here, and it should be checked against his own commentary.
The Tamil of verse 51 in kg/core reads மனைக்தக்க, a typo for மனைத்தக்க.
Manakkudavar's entry for verse 60 opens with a fragment of the verse and ends with a stray '10'.

couplet: As doth the house beseem, she shows her wifely dignity;
As doth her husband's wealth befit, she spends: help - meet is she.
pope.gloss: She who has the excellence of home virtues, and can expend within the means of her husband, is a help in the domestic state.

reading: She who has the excellence the home needs, and lives within the means of the man who took her, is the companion of life.
nuance: Income literacy is half the definition, and it comes before chastity is mentioned. Parimelazhagar makes her skills concrete: knowing what is needed, cooking and neighbourly help. Manakkudavar instead reads மனை as her birth family, which shifts the standard from her work to where she comes from.

couplet: If household excellence be wanting in the wife,
Howe'er with splendour lived, all worthless is the life.
pope.gloss: If the wife be devoid of domestic excellence, whatever (other) greatness be possessed, the conjugal state, is nothing.

reading: If the wife lacks household excellence, the life has nothing, whatever other distinction it may have.
nuance: The final word இல், nothing, is blunt. The verse doesn't say the life is worse, it says the life isn't there at all, and Parimelazhagar says this is because it bears no fruit.

couplet: There is no lack within the house, where wife in worth excels,
There is no luck within the house, where wife dishonoured dwells.
pope.gloss: If his wife be eminent (in virtue), what does (that man) not possess ? If she be without excellence, what does (he) possess ?

reading: What is lacking if the wife has worth, and what is present if she does not?
nuance: Two questions with no answers given. Manakkudavar supplies the sharp version: though the man has nothing, nothing is lacking, and though he has everything, nothing is there.

couplet: If woman might of chastity retain,
What choicer treasure doth the world contain?
pope.gloss: What is more excellent than a wife, if she possess the stability of chastity ?

reading: What is greater than a woman, if she has the firmness called கற்பு?
nuance: The word திண்மை presents கற்பு as a strength, not as mere purity. Whether the verse is ranking a possession or a form of life is what divides the commentators.

couplet: No God adoring, low she bends before her lord;
Then rising, serves: the rain falls instant at her word!
pope.gloss: If she, who does not worship God, but who rising worships her husband, say, "let it rain," it will rain.

reading: She who rises worshipping her husband and not a god: if she says 'rain', it rains.
nuance: The verse says flatly that she doesn't worship a god. Parimelazhagar softens this by adding 'other' gods. The line is both the strongest claim of a woman's power in the book and the most troubling, and Kalaignar's entry reads the rain as an image of fearful servitude, not of power.

couplet: Who guards herself, for husband's comfort cares, her household's fame,
In perfect wise with sleepless soul preserves, -give her a woman's name.
pope.gloss: She is a wife who unweariedly guards herself, takes care of her husband, and preserves an unsullied fame.

reading: She is a woman who guards herself, cares for the man who took her, keeps their good name and does not flag.
nuance: பெண் here is a title that has to be earned, as the verse defines who counts as a woman. Parimelazhagar takes சொல் as a shared reputation for wife and husband, which means she is responsible for both.

couplet: Of what avail is wat ch and ward?
Honour's woman's safest guard.
pope.gloss: What avails the guard of a prison ? The chief guard of a woman is her chastity.

reading: What use is the guarding of women by confinement? The guard that their own steadfastness keeps is the best.
nuance: The verse rejects confinement because it does not work, and it doesn't speak of the woman's rights. It leaves in place the assumption that she needs guarding, but it moves that guard inside her.

couplet: If wife be wholly true to him who gained her as his bride,
Great glory gains she in the world where gods bliss abide.
pope.gloss: If women shew reverence to their husbands, they will obtain great excellence in the world where the gods flourish.

reading: If women obtain the one who obtained them, they will gain great distinction in the world where the gods live.
nuance: The word play பெற்றாற் பெறின் leaves open what 'obtaining' a husband means. Who has to be worthy depends on how the gap is filled.

couplet: Who have not spouses that in virtue's praise delight,
They lion-like can never walk in scorner's sight.
pope.gloss: The man whose wife seeks not the praise (of chastity) cannot walk with lion-like stately step, before those who revile them.

reading: Those whose home does not seek renown cannot walk with a great beast's proud gait before those who deride them.
nuance: The man's public bearing is said to depend on his wife's conduct. ஏறு needn't mean a lion as Pope and Parimelazhagar have it, since the word covers male animals generally, and Manakkudavar describes the gait without naming an animal.

couplet: The house's 'blessing', men pronounce the house-wife excellent;
The gain of blessed children is its goodly ornament.
pope.gloss: The excellence of a wife is the good of her husband; and good children are the jewels of that goodness.

reading: They call a home's excellence its blessing, and good children its fine ornament.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says this verse prepares for the next chapter by naming the wife's ornament. Children are ornaments here and do not yet have the value they get in chapter 7. Kalaignar takes மனைமாட்சி as the family's culture and not specifically the wife's.

title: புதல்வரைப் பெறுதல்
theme: Children are the greatest thing one can obtain: first for the fruit they bring beyond this life, then for sensuous joy in them, and finally for their worth in the world. It moves from possessing them to being known by them, and the last verse has the father judged by the son.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of having sons (61), the next-world fruit (62-63), the joys in this life (64-66), the father's duty (67), others' delight (68), the mother's joy (69), and the son's duty (70). Verses 67 and 70 frame the final group as a pair of debts.
source_issues: Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 62 is a duplicate of his comment on verse 61, so it is misaligned and hasn't been used. His note at 63 does say that verses 62-63 concern the next-world fruit.
Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 66 begins at the விளக்கம், without the word-by-word gloss. His entry for verse 69 starts with a stray '>'.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 62, 67 and 70. His entry for verse 66 ends with a stray '6'.
Kalaignar's entry for verse 64 ends with a stray '65.'.

couplet: Of all that men acquire, we know not any greater gain,
Than that which by the birth of learned children men obtain.
pope.gloss: Among all the benefits that may be acquired, we know no greater benefit than the acquisition of intelligent children.

reading: Of all that can be gained, we know of nothing else like children who come to know what should be known.
nuance: The first-person யாம் அறிவது is unusual and it sounds personal. The word அறிவறிந்த makes this a conditional praise: not children as such, but children who come to understand.

couplet: Who children gain, that none reproach, of virtuous worth,
No evils touch them, through the sev'n-fold maze of birth.
pope.gloss: The evils of the seven births shall not touch those who abtain children of a good disposition, free from vice.

reading: Evils will not touch one for seven births, if one has children of good character who bring no blame.
nuance: The verse assumes a child's character can protect a parent across births. Kalaignar's reading turns seven births into seven generations, which reverses the direction from the parent's future to the descendants', but no aligned Parimelazhagar or Manakkudavar comment is available to set against it here.

couplet: 'Man's children are his fortune,' say the wise;
From each one's deeds his varied fortunes rise.
pope.gloss: Men will call their sons their wealth, because it flows to them through the deeds which they (sons) perform on their behalf.

reading: People call their children their wealth, because the wealth of those children comes by way of their own deeds.
nuance: தம்தம் வினை is the crux: whose deeds, and whose wealth? Pope's couplet and his own gloss take opposite sides of this.

couplet: Than God's ambrosia sweeter far the food before men laid,
In which the little hands of children of their own have play'd.
pope.gloss: The rice in which the little hand of their children has dabbled will be far sweeter (to the parent) than ambrosia.

reading: Far sweeter than amrita is the plain gruel stirred by the small hands of one's own children.
nuance: The food is கூழ், a humble gruel, and it is sweet because of the mess. Parimelazhagar illustrates the mess by citing Purananuru 188, which makes this verse a real thread across books.

couplet: To patent sweet the touch of children dear;
Their voice is sweetest music to his ear.
pope.gloss: The touch of children gives pleasure to the body, and the hearing of their words, pleasure to the ear.

reading: Touching one's children is joy to the body, and hearing their words is joy to the ear.
nuance: The chapter dwells on the senses here, after verses that praise restraining them. Parimelazhagar notes that சொல் is deliberately general, so it covers grown learned speech as well as baby talk.

couplet: 'The pipe is sweet,' 'the lute is sweet,' by them't will be averred,
Who music of their infants' lisping lips have never heard.
pope.gloss: "The pipe is sweet, the lute is sweet," say those who have not heard the prattle of their own children.

reading: 'The flute is sweet, the lute is sweet', say those who haven't heard their own children's prattle.
nuance: The verse never actually says prattle is sweeter. It leaves that to be inferred, and Parimelazhagar notes this implied ending. Such praise comes in the form of mild scorn for the musically refined.

couplet: Sire greatest boon on son confers, who makes him meet,
In councils of the wise to fill the highest seat.
pope.gloss: The benefit which a father should confer on his son is to give him precedence in the assembly of the learned.

reading: The good a father does for a son is to make him sit at the front in the assembly.
nuance: Parimelazhagar rules out nepotism: the son must actually surpass the assembly in learning. He adds that making him rich is no real good, since wealth brings pain.

couplet: Their children's wisdom greater than their own confessed,
Through the wide world is sweet to every human breast.
pope.gloss: That their children should possess knowledge is more pleasing to all men of this great earth than to themselves.

reading: Their children's understanding is sweet to all beings on the great earth, more than to themselves.
nuance: தம்மின், than themselves, can attach to two different things. Pope's couplet and gloss again split, one on each side.

couplet: When mother hears him named 'fulfill'd of wisdom's lore,'
Far greater joy she feels, than when her son she bore.
pope.gloss: The mother who hears her son called "a wise man" will rejoice more than she did at his birth.

reading: A mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than at the hour she bore him.
nuance: The verse says she hears. Parimelazhagar's explanation is his own and is telling: he says women cannot know this for themselves. The verse may simply show that public recognition is what is wanted. It sets the birth's joy as the baseline and goes beyond it.

couplet: To sire, what best requital can by grateful child be done?
To make men say, 'What merit gained the father such a son?'
pope.gloss: (So to act) that it may be said "by what great penance did his father beget him," is the benefit which a son should render to his father.

reading: The help a son gives his father is the saying, 'What penance did this one's father do?'
nuance: The repayment is a sentence spoken by others. The son can't deliver it directly, only live so that others say it. The verse uses the language of austerity (நோற்றான்), so fatherhood is framed as a kind of penance.

title: அன்புடைமை
theme: Love cannot be hidden, gives itself away to the bone, and is what makes a body alive. Without it, virtue burns a person and a life is a withered tree.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: love's reality (71), its excellence (72-76), and the fault of lacking it (77-80). The verses also keep rhyming அன்பு with என்பு, love with bone (72, 73, 77, 80), and this runs through the chapter as its sound and argument.
source_issues: Pope's couplet for verse 77 in kg/core begins with the stray text '77,', and the couplet and gloss fields appear to be split wrongly.
The Tamil of verse 79 in kg/core has a stray space: எவன்செய்பு ம் for எவன்செய்யும்.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verse 74, and his entry for verse 71 ends with a stray '10'.
Kalaignar's entry for verse 79 ends with a stray '80.'.

couplet: And is there bar that can even love restrain?
The tiny tear shall make the lover's secret plain.
pope.gloss: Is there any fastening that can shut in love ? Tears of the affectionate will publish the love that is within.

reading: Is there any bolt that can shut in even love? The small tears of the loving will proclaim it.
nuance: A tiny tear (புன்கணீர்) produces an uproar (பூசல்), and the contrast in scale is the point. Parimelazhagar specifies that the tears fall at the beloved's pain, and he treats them as logical inference: love is unseen but can be inferred.

couplet: The loveless to themselves belong alone;
The loving men are others' to the very bone.
pope.gloss: Those who are destitute of love appropriate all they have to themselves; but those who possess love cons ider even their bones to belong to others.

reading: The loveless belong to themselves in everything, and the loving belong to others even to their bones.
nuance: Love is framed as a question of ownership. Parimelazhagar glosses the bones by citing Purananuru 43, on the king who gave his own flesh for a dove, which is a direct thread to the Sangam corpus.

couplet: Of precious soul with body's flesh and bone,
The union yields one fruit, the life of love alone.
pope.gloss: They say that the union of soul and body in man is the fruit of the union of love and virtue (in a former birth).

reading: They say the bond of the precious life with the bone is the way that came to be joined with love.
nuance: The syntax is compressed, and the verse could give embodiment a purpose or a past cause. On Parimelazhagar's reading, the body exists for loving, which is an unusually positive view of embodiment. Pope's gloss follows the past-birth view.

couplet: From love fond yearning springs for union sweet of minds;
And that the bond of rare excelling friendship binds.
pope.gloss: Love begets desire: and that (desire) begets the immeasureable excellence of friendship.

reading: Love gives rise to eagerness for others, and that gives rise to the unsought distinction called friendship.
nuance: Love is a seed with a sequence. Parimelazhagar widens the final term a great deal: love for one's own extends to everyone, until the person has neither enemies nor neutrals. நாடா, unsought, suggests this distinction arrives without being chased.

couplet: Sweetness on earth and rarest bliss above,
These are the fruits of tranquil life of love.
pope.gloss: They say that the felicity which those who, after enjoying the pleasure (of the conjugal state) in this world, obtain in heaven is the result of their domestic state imbued with love.

reading: They say that the distinction won by those who have known joy in this world is the outcome of a life settled in love.
nuance: The commentators disagree about the timeline. Manakkudavar puts the love in a past birth, Parimelazhagar puts the distinction in heaven after this life, and Kalaignar keeps both in this life. Parimelazhagar's contrast is a pointed one: ascetics reach heaven through pain, while householders reach it through joy.

couplet: The unwise deem love virtue only can sustain,
It also helps the man who evil would restrain.
pope.gloss: The ignorant say that love is an ally to virtue only, but it is also a help to get out of vice.

reading: The ignorant say that love supports only virtue, but it is also the ally against, or of, மறம்.
nuance: The word மறம் is the problem. It can mean sin or valour, and the ambiguous dative 'for மறம்' leaves open whether love helps to remove it or to do it.

couplet: As sun's fierce ray dries up the boneless things,
pope.gloss: So loveless beings virtue's power to nothing brings.

reading: Virtue burns what has no love, as the sun burns what has no bones.
nuance: It is a chilling image, and on Parimelazhagar's explanation the sun bears no malice: it shines equally, and the boneless creature perishes by its own nature. Virtue is thus not vindictive, which makes this verse more unsettling.

couplet: The loveless soul, the very joys of life may know,
When flowers, in barren soil, on sapless trees, shall blow.
pope.gloss: The domestic state of that man whose mind is without love is like the flourishing of a withered tree upon the parched desert.

reading: A life without love inside is like a dried tree putting forth shoots on hard ground.
nuance: The image is an impossibility, as Parimelazhagar says and as Manakkudavar explains: there is nothing in the tree to cause sprouting. The verse says உயிர்வாழ்க்கை, a living being's life, and Parimelazhagar and Pope narrow it to household life.

couplet: Though every outward part complete, the body's fitly framed;
What good, when soul within, of love devoid, lies halt and maimed?
pope.gloss: Of what avail are all the external members (of the body) to those who are destitute of love, the internal member.

reading: What use are all the outer parts to those without love, the inner part of the body?
nuance: Love is classed as an organ, which is a striking way to make it non-optional. Parimelazhagar explicitly refutes the bodily-organs reading that Kalaignar's comment follows.

couplet: Bodies of loveless men are bony framework clad with skin;
Then is the body seat of life, when love resides within.
pope.gloss: That body alone which is inspired with love contains a living soul: if void of it, (the body) is bone overlaid with skin.

reading: The seat of life goes by way of love; for those without it, a body is bones wrapped in skin.
nuance: The final verse is about what counts as alive, and it isn't an exaggeration about ethics. Manakkudavar connects உயிர்நிலை to release, whereas Parimelazhagar connects it to the household virtue that makes a body live.

title: விருந்தோம்பல்
theme: Hospitality is the reason for having a home and wealth at all. Hosting does not impoverish, refusing it makes a rich person poor, and it depends finally on the face with which a guest is met.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (81-82), its fruit in this life (83-85), its fruit in the next (86), the reason for both (87), the fault of neglecting it (88-89), and the need for a pleasant face (90).
source_issues: Pope's couplet for verse 88 in kg/core begins with stray markup, '< br> 88.', and the couplet and gloss fields are split wrongly.
The Tamil of verse 90 in kg/core reads குநழ்யும், a typo for குழையும். The Tamil of verse 82 has a stray space in வேண் டற்பாற் றன்று.
Manakkudavar's entry for verse 82 opens with a fragment of the verse.

couplet: All household cares and course of daily life have this in view.
Guests to receive with courtesy, and kindly acts to do.
pope.gloss: The whole design of living in the domestic state and laying up (property) is (to be able) to exercise the

reading: All of staying at home and living by guarding one's goods is for the purpose of caring for guests and doing them good.
nuance: The verse gives household life a purpose outside itself. Parimelazhagar draws the consequence: without this, the toil of home and earning has no fruit.

couplet: Though food of immortality should crown the board,
Feasting alone, the guests without unfed, is thing abhorred.
pope.gloss: It is not fit that one should wish his guests to be outside (his house) even though he were eating the food of immortality.

reading: Even if it were the medicine of immortality, eating it alone while the guest stays outside is not to be desired.
nuance: Parimelazhagar offers a second, sharper reading as acceptable: if someone calls even one meal eaten without a guest a medicine of immortality, reject it. Either way, the argument sets a refusal to eat alone over the prospect of not dying.

couplet: Each day he tends the coming guest with kindly care;
Painless, unfailing plenty shall his household share.
pope.gloss: The domestic life of the man that daily entertains the guests who come to him shall not be laid waste by poverty.

reading: The life of one who daily tends the guest who comes will not suffer and fall into ruin.
nuance: It answers the obvious worry that hosting every day would be ruinous. Parimelazhagar goes further than the verse's 'not ruined': he says wealth will keep branching out.

couplet: With smiling face he entertains each virtuous guest,
'Fortune' with gladsome mind shall in his dwelling rest.
pope.gloss: Lakshmi with joyous mind shall dwell in the house of that man who, with cheerful countenance, entertains the good as guests.

reading: The fair goddess dwells with a glad heart in the home of one who tends good guests with a glad face.
nuance: A chiasm links the two gladnesses: the host's face and the goddess's heart. Parimelazhagar's reason is that she's pleased when her wealth goes the right way. He also takes நல், 'good', to limit the guests to those of high knowledge and conduct.

couplet: Who first regales his guest, and then himself supplies,
O'er all his fields, unsown, shall plenteous harvests rise.
pope.gloss: Is it necessary to sow the field of the man who, having feasted his guests, eats what may remain ?

reading: Must one even sow the field of the person who feeds guests and then eats what's left?
nuance: மிச்சில், leftovers, is a low word for the host's own food, as if the guest's plate comes first. The rhetorical question doesn't say what the answer is, and the commentators answer it in opposite ways.

couplet: The guest arrived he tends, the coming guest expects to see;
To those in heavenly homes that dwell a welcome guest is he.
pope.gloss: He who, having entertained the guests that have come, looks out for others who may yet come, will be a welcome guest to the inhabitants of heaven.

reading: One who tends the guest who is leaving and watches for the guest to come will be a good guest to those in the sky.
nuance: The host becomes the guest in heaven, and the verse has an elegant reciprocity. Manakkudavar gives 'watching' a concrete rule: not eating without a guest. Kalaignar's 'those in the sky of renown' removes the literal heaven that Parimelazhagar assumes.

couplet: To reckon up the fruit of kindly deeds were all in vain;
Their worth is as the worth of guests you entertain.
pope.gloss: The advantages of benevolence cannot be measured; the measure (of the virtue) of the guests (entertained) is the only measure.

reading: The fruit of this sacrifice has no set measure: it is as great as the guest's worth.
nuance: Calling hospitality வேள்வி claims the language of ritual for a household meal. The measure is the guest and not the cost, and Parimelazhagar supports this with a Naladiyar verse. This also introduces a hierarchy among guests, which sits awkwardly with welcoming whoever comes.

couplet: With pain they guard their stores, yet 'All forlorn are we,' they'll cry,
pope.gloss: Who cherish not their guests, nor kindly help supply.

reading: Those who don't take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods anxiously and then say 'we have no support'.
nuance: It is a late regret: the wealth they guarded with such pain is gone. பற்றற்றேம் can also be read as the renouncer's boast, 'we're without attachment', and that echo seems to me to sharpen the irony, though no commentator here says so.

couplet: To turn from guests is penury, though worldly goods abound;
'Tis senseless folly, only with the senseless found.
pope.gloss: That stupidity which excercises no hospitality is poverty in the midst of wealth. It is the property of the stupid.

reading: Poverty in the midst of having is the folly that neglects hospitality, and it is found only among fools.
nuance: The verse redefines poverty as a failure of use, not a lack of goods. Parimelazhagar explains: since folly takes away the benefit one gets from wealth, it makes having into not having.

couplet: The flower of 'Anicha' withers away, If you do but its fragrance inhale;
If the face of the host cold welcome convey, The guest's heart within him will fail.
pope.gloss: As the Anicham flower fades in smelling, so fades the guest when the face is turned away.

reading: The anicham flower wilts when smelled, and a guest wilts when the host's face changes on seeing them.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's analysis has the guest more delicate than the flower, as the flower needs to be touched but the guest wilts at a distance. He gives a sequence of pleasant face, pleasant word and good deed, which leads directly into the next chapter.

title: இனியவைகூறல்
theme: Sweet speech is defined as loving, guileless and true, then ranked above generous giving. Its closing argument is almost one of common sense: why would anyone choose the unripe fruit?
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: what sweet speech is (91), its value especially in hospitality (92-93), its fruit in this life (94-95), in the next (96), in both (97-98), and the fault of harsh speech (99-100).
source_issues: The Tamil of verse 98 in kg/core reads சிறுமையுவு, a typo for சிறுமையுள் as Parimelazhagar's text shows.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 92, 93, 94, 95 and 98.

couplet: Pleasant words are words with all pervading love that burn;
Words from his guileless mouth who can the very truth discern.
pope.gloss: Sweet words are those which imbued with love and free from deceit flow from the mouth of the virtuous.

reading: Sweet words are those from the mouths of people who see the true thing, moist with love and free of deceit.
nuance: The definition rules out flattery. Sweetness needs truthfulness and love, and ஈரம், moisture, makes love a physical quality of the words. Whether it allows rebuke is what the commentators bring out.

couplet: A pleasant word with beaming smile's preferred,
Even to gifts with liberal heart conferred.
pope.gloss: Sweet speech, with a cheerful countenance is better than a gift made with a joyous mind.

reading: Better than giving with a glad heart is to be, with a glad face, a person of sweet speech.
nuance: This is a surprising ranking in a book so committed to giving. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is that sweet speech is in one's own power, where a gift depends on wealth, yet it comes naturally only to a virtuous heart, so it's the rarer thing.

couplet: With brightly beaming smile, and kindly light of loving eye,
And heart sincere, to utter pleasant words is charity.
pope.gloss: Sweet speech, flowing from the heart (uttered) with a cheerful countenance and a sweet look, is true virtue.

reading: Virtue lies in sweet words from the heart, after looking kindly with a glad face.
nuance: The sequence is face, then eye, then heart, then word, and அகத்தானாம் is what keeps it from being mere manners. Parimelazhagar takes the emphatic ending as 'not in giving'. That's a strong inference: the verse may only be emphasizing speech.

couplet: The men of pleasant speech that gladness breathe around,
Through indigence shall never sorrow's prey be found.
pope.gloss: Sorrow-increasing poverty shall not come upon those who use towards all, pleasure-increasing sweetness of speech.

reading: Grievous want won't come to those whose sweet speech gives everyone joy.
nuance: The two forms உறூஉம் balance grief and joy in matching words. The promise seems to be social, not magical: Parimelazhagar reasons that one who has only friends comes to all wealth.

couplet: Humility with pleasant speech to man on earth,
Is choice adornment; all besides is nothing worth.
pope.gloss: Humility and sweetness of speech are the ornaments of man; all others are not (ornaments).

reading: Being humble and sweet-spoken is a person's ornament, and nothing else is.
nuance: The verse states humility without limit. Parimelazhagar limits it: one is to be humble toward those who deserve deference and sweet-spoken toward everybody. That's a notable narrowing by the commentator.

couplet: Who seeks out good, words from his lips of sweetness flow;
In him the power of vice declines, and virtues grow.
pope.gloss: If a man, while seeking to speak usefully, speaks also sweetly, his sins will diminish and his virtue increase.

reading: If one seeks out good things and speaks them sweetly, what is not virtue wears away and virtue grows.
nuance: நாடி, having sought out, makes sweetness conditional on content. Parimelazhagar adds the converse: good counsel spoken harshly isn't virtue. For him the effect is on the speaker's own merit, whereas Kalaignar makes it a method of guiding others.

couplet: The words of sterling sense, to rule of right that strict adhere,
To virtuous action prompting, blessings yield in every sphere.
pope.gloss: That speech which, while imparting benefits ceases not to please, will yield righteousness (for this world) and merit (for the next world).

reading: Speech that yields benefit and never parts from gentleness produces justice and brings forth good.
nuance: பயன் and பண்பு are held together, so usefulness alone doesn't suffice and neither does charm. Parimelazhagar defines நயன் strikingly as being in accord with the world.

couplet: Sweet kindly words, from meanness free, delight of heart,
In world to come and in this world impart.
pope.gloss: Sweet speech, free from harm to others, will give pleasure both in this world and in the next.

reading: Sweet speech free of pettiness gives joy in the next life and in this one.
nuance: The next life is named first, and Parimelazhagar says this is because its joy is greater. Kalaignar reads this as renown during and after life, which removes the afterlife. Pope's and Parimelazhagar's 'harm to others' is more specific than சிறுமை, smallness.

couplet: Who sees the pleasure kindly speech affords,
Why makes he use of harsh, repellant words?
pope.gloss: Why does he use harsh words, who sees the pleasure which sweet speech yields ?

reading: Why would one who sees how sweetly sweet speech yields use harsh words?
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes this an argument from experience: you know how others' sweet words feel to you, and harsh words are just as painful to them. The verse doesn't command, it only asks what the point is.

couplet: When pleasant words are easy, bitter words to use,
Is, leaving sweet ripe fruit, the sour unripe to choose.
pope.gloss: To say disagreeable things when agreeable are at hand is like eating unripe fruit when there is ripe.

reading: Speaking unpleasant things when pleasant ones are there is like grabbing raw fruit when ripe fruit is at hand.
nuance: The final charge is stupidity, not wickedness. Parimelazhagar makes the stakes much higher by reading the fruit as Avvai's nelli, which is like amrita, and the raw one as poison. He adds that harsh speech ends up hurting the speaker, and this allusion is a thread to the Sangam story of Avvai and the king.

title: செய்ந்நன்றி அறிதல்
theme: Gratitude: help is measured by its timing, its motive and the worth of the one who receives it, not by its size. Memory is ordered accordingly, so that good is kept and harm is let go, and ingratitude is called the one sin with no escape.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: help given without cause, in time or without calculation is immeasurable (101-103), any help grows with those who understand (104-105), do not abandon those who helped (106-107), forget harm (108-109), and the gravity of ingratitude (110).
source_issues: Parimelazhagar's comment on verse 107 refers to an explanation of the seven kinds of birth at verse 62, but his entry for 62 here is a duplicate of 61 (see ch007).
Parimelazhagar's comment on verse 110 is scrambled: its last sentences are out of order ('இதனால் செய்ந்நன்றி கோறலின் கொடுமை கூறப்பட்டது. முதலிய பாதகங்களைச் செய்தல்.').
Kalaignar's entry for verse 103 ends with a stray '104.'. Manakkudavar's entry for verse 107 ends with empty brackets.

couplet: Assistance given by those who ne'er received our aid,
Is debt by gift of heaven and earth but poorly paid.
pope.gloss: (The gift of) heaven and earth is not an equivalent for a benefit which is conferred where none had been received.

reading: For help given when no help was given first, earth and heaven together are hardly repayment.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives the reason: all repayment has a cause, and this help has none, so nothing can match it. He also records a variant reading, in which the helped person could not return it, which changes the focus from the giver's freedom to the receiver's helplessness.

couplet: A timely benefit, -though thing of little worth,
The gift itself, -in excellence transcends the earth.
pope.gloss: A favour conferred in the time of need, though it be small (in itself), is (in value) much larger than the world.

reading: Help given in its time, though small, is far greater than the earth.
nuance: Value here is relative to the need of the moment. Parimelazhagar's phrase is striking: it's the moment of mortal crisis that is being weighed, not the gift.

couplet: Kindness shown by those who weigh not what the return may be:
When you ponder right its merit, 'T is vaster than the sea.
pope.gloss: If we weigh the excellence of a benefit which is conferred without weighing the return, it is larger than the sea.

reading: If you weigh the good of help given by those who don't weigh the return, it is greater than the sea.
nuance: The verb தூக்கு is used twice: the giver doesn't weigh, and the recipient should. The three opening comparisons go from earth and heaven to earth to sea, and the verses seem interested in measure as such.

couplet: Each benefit to those of actions' fruit who rightly deem,
Though small as millet-seed, as palm-tree vast will seem.
pope.gloss: Though the benefit conferred be as small as a millet seed, those who know its advantage will consider it as large as a palmyra fruit.

reading: Though the good done is only as much as a millet, those who understand its fruit take it as a palm.
nuance: The enlargement happens in the recipient's mind, and it isn't an error, it's a discipline. Parimelazhagar says the fruit in question is what comes to the one who regards it this way, so gratitude also benefits the grateful.

couplet: The kindly aid's extent is of its worth no measure true;
Its worth is as the worth of him to whom the act you do.
pope.gloss: The benefit itself is not the measure of the benefit; the worth of those who have received it is its measure.

reading: Help is not bounded by the help given: its measure is the worth of those to whom it was done.
nuance: The verse repeats உதவி three times and it isn't clear which help is being measured.

couplet: Kindness of men of stainless soul remember evermore!
Forsake thou never friends who were thy stay in sorrow sore!
pope.gloss: Forsake not the friendship of those who have been your staff in adversity. Forget not be benevolence of the blameless.

reading: Do not forget the bond of the stainless, and do not abandon the friendship of those who were your strength in sorrow.
nuance: Two different people are owed loyalty: those of good character and those who helped when it was needed. Parimelazhagar says the first serves the next life and the second this one. The second debt holds whatever the helper's character is.

couplet: Through all seven worlds, in seven-fold birth, Remains in mem'ry of the wise.
Friendship of those who wiped on earth, The tears of sorrow from their eyes.
pope.gloss: (The wise) will remember throughout their seven-fold births the love of those who have wiped away their affliction.

reading: For all seven births they will remember the friendship of those who wiped away their sorrow.
nuance: துடைத்தவர், those who wiped, has a physical sense of wiping tears away. Parimelazhagar notes the past tense conveys speed, and he cites the lost Valaiyapathi for the phrase, which is a valuable thread.

couplet: 'Tis never good to let the thought of good things done thee pass away;
Of things not good, 'tis good to rid thy memory that very day.
pope.gloss: It is not good to forget a benefit; it is good to forget an injury even in the very moment (in which it is inflicted).

reading: It's not good to forget a good done; what's good is to forget, that very day, what isn't good.
nuance: நன்று repeats through the verse, so 'good' is both the thing remembered and the act of letting go. Parimelazhagar says this is about one person who has done both good and harm, which is narrower than a general call to forget all wrongs.

couplet: Effaced straightway is deadliest injury,
By thought of one kind act in days gone by.
pope.gloss: Though one inflict an injury great as murder, it will perish before the thought of one benefit (formerly) conferred.

reading: Even if they do something as painful as killing, it vanishes when one thinks of a single good they did.
nuance: This is a hard saying, as it places the burden on the injured person. Parimelazhagar explains it through 104: the millet taken as a palm outweighs everything. Kalaignar makes it more therapeutic, a way to keep from being wounded inside.

couplet: Who every good have killed, may yet destruction flee;
Who 'benefit' has killed, that man shall ne'er 'scape free!
pope.gloss: He who has killed every virtue may yet escape; there is no escape for him who has killed a benefit.

reading: Those who kill any good may have an escape, but there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him.
nuance: Ingratitude is ranked as the sin with no remedy. Parimelazhagar's list of lesser crimes comes from Purananuru 34, whose speaker makes the same comparison, so this verse is a direct thread to that poem.

title: நடுவு நிலைமை
theme: Impartiality: holding to what is due, whoever is involved, and giving up any gain that requires leaving it. The chapter's central image is the balance, and it treats loss incurred by being fair as no real loss.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (111), wealth got with and without it (112-113), how to recognise it (114), gain and loss don't come through bias (115-117), and then it speaks to those in assemblies (118-119) and to merchants (120).
source_issues: Manakkudavar's entry for verse 114 glosses a different text ('ஆரவாரத் தொழிலினானே') and includes an editor's parenthesis about a reading அச்சத்தால். It isn't used as a position here, but the variant deserves checking.
Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 117 repeats his word gloss inside the விளக்கம்.
The Tamil of verse 114 in kg/core reads காணப்ப படும், a typo for காணப் படும். Pope's gloss on verse 119 has a stray space, 'F reedom'.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verse 116.

couplet: If justice, failing not, its quality maintain,
Giving to each his due, -'tis man's one highest gain.
pope.gloss: That equity which consists in acting with equal regard to each of (the three) divisions of men [enemies, strangers and friends] is a pre-eminent virtue.

reading: That one thing called rightness is good if one can keep to it, part by part, in what is due.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says பெறின் conveys how rare this is. The whole verse depends on what பகுதி divides.

couplet: The just man's wealth unwasting shall endure,
And to his race a lasting joy ensure.
pope.gloss: The wealth of the man of rectitude will not perish, but will bring happiness also to his posterity.

reading: The wealth of a person of rectitude doesn't decay and is a strength to those who come after.
nuance: The claim concerns durability, not amount. Parimelazhagar explains that it lasts because it comes together with virtue.

couplet: Though only good it seem to give, yet gain
By wrong acquired, not e'en one day retain!
pope.gloss: Forsake in the very moment (of acquisition) that gain which, though it should bring advantage, is without equity.

reading: Even if it brings nothing but good, let go that very day of gain that comes from leaving what is fair.
nuance: The commentators differ on the force of 'even if'. For Parimelazhagar it's only a concession, because such gain can't really bring good. Kalaignar's wording allows that it may, which makes giving it up a costlier demand.

couplet: Who just or unjust lived shall soon appear:
By each one's offspring shall the truth be clear.
pope.gloss: The worthy and unworthy may be known by the existence or otherwise of good offsprings.

reading: Whether people are worthy or unworthy will be seen from what each leaves behind.
nuance: எச்சம், what remains, is left unspecified, and the choice has large consequences. Parimelazhagar's claim that the unworthy have no good children is a very confident generalisation, and it isn't in the verse.

couplet: The gain and loss in life are not mere accident;
Just mind inflexible is sages' ornament.
pope.gloss: Loss and gain come not without cause; it is the ornament of the wise to preserve evenness of mind (under both).

reading: Loss and increase are not absent from life; not letting the heart bend is the ornament of the worthy.
nuance: The verse doesn't explain where loss and gain come from, and Pope's 'not mere accident' assumes one view. The important move is that bias is presented as useless as well as wrong.

couplet: If, right deserting, heart to evil turn,
Let man impending ruin's sign discern!
pope.gloss: Let him whose mind departing from equity commits sin well consider thus within himself, "I shall perish."

reading: If one's heart leaves what is fair and does wrong, let one know: 'I will perish'.
nuance: The subject is the heart, so the act is inward. Parimelazhagar draws this out: thinking is the same as doing, and the very thought is an omen to be read. The first-person கெடுவல் யான் makes the warning a sentence one says to oneself.

couplet: The man who justly lives, tenacious of the right,
In low estate is never low to wise man's sight.
pope.gloss: The great will not regard as poverty the low estate of that man who dwells in the virtue of equity.

reading: The world won't count as ruin the low state of one who remains in virtue by standing fair.
nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses உலகம் as the noble, as commentators often do, and adds that they regard such poverty as wealth. That's a real narrowing, since the actual world may well despise it.

couplet: To stand, like balance-rod that level hangs and rightly weighs,
With calm unbiassed equity of soul, is sages' praise.
pope.gloss: To incline to neither side, but to rest impartial as the even-fixed scale is the ornament of the wise.

reading: To be settled and lean to no side, like the balance that first makes itself level and then weighs, is the ornament of the worthy.
nuance: A balance isn't indifferent: it first levels itself, then registers exactly what's put on it. Fairness here is a precise response, not neutrality. Parimelazhagar carries the image into assembly practice, with weighing as hearing both sides and not leaning as stating the result equally to all.

couplet: Inflexibility in word is righteousness,
If men inflexibility of soul possess.
pope.gloss: F reedom from obliquity of speech is rectitude, if there be (corresponding) freedom from bias of mind.

reading: Rectitude is speech without bend, provided one surely has no bend within.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's corollary is subtle: a correct statement made from a biased mind isn't impartiality. Manakkudavar adds that it excludes clever words which suit both sides.

couplet: As thriving trader is the trader known,
Who guards another's interests as his own.
pope.gloss: The true merchandize of merchants is to guard and do by the things of others as they do by their own.

reading: For traders, true trade is caring for others' goods as if they were their own.
nuance: Manakkudavar glosses வாணிகம் as profit, so honesty is what actually pays. Parimelazhagar's phrasing, taking no more and giving no less, closely resembles a description of merchants in Pattinappalai, as I recall it. That is my own observation, and it should be checked.

title: அடக்கமுடைமை
theme: Self-restraint is the treasure that decides one's end. It works through body, speech and mind, and the chapter is most vivid on the tongue, whose burn alone never heals.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: restraint's excellence in general (121-125), restraint of body (126), of speech (127-129), and of mind (130).
source_issues: Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 130 has apparent slips: செல்வி for செவ்வி and நெற்றியின்கண் for நெறியின்கண்.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 122 and 126.

couplet: Control of self does man conduct to bliss th' immortals share;
Indulgence leads to deepest night, and leaves him there.
pope.gloss: Self-control will place (a man) among the Gods; the want of it will drive (him) into the thickest darkness (of hell).

reading: Restraint leads one among the immortals, and lack of restraint drives one into thick darkness.
nuance: Both verbs are of driving, so restraint is itself a force that carries a person. The final உய்த்துவிடும் has a sense of finality.

couplet: Guard thou as wealth the power of self-control;
Than this no greater gain to living soul!
pope.gloss: Let self-control be guarded as a treasure; there is no greater source of good for man than that.

reading: Guard restraint as your wealth, for life has no greater gain than it.
nuance: Restraint is pictured as something to guard, as misers guard money, so the language of acquisition is turned to its opposite. Parimelazhagar notes this concerns humans, who can understand it and benefit.

couplet: If versed in wisdom's lore by virtue's law you self restrain.
Your self-repression known will yield you glory's gain.
pope.gloss: Knowing that self-control is knowledge, if a man should control himself, in the prescribed course, such self-control will bring him distinction among the wise.

reading: If one understands and keeps restrained in the right way, the restraint, recognised, will yield distinction.
nuance: The syntax is knotted, and the commentators parse the repeated அறிந்து differently: Parimelazhagar says one learns that restraint is itself knowledge, and Manakkudavar says one learns the five objects and the five organs. I'm unsure which is closest.

couplet: In his station, all unswerving, if man self subdue,
Greater he than mountain proudly rising to the view.
pope.gloss: More lofty than a mountain will be the greatness of that man who without swerving from his domestic state, controls himself.

reading: The stature of one who is restrained and doesn't stray from his station is much greater than a mountain's.
nuance: தோற்றம், how one looks or appears, makes this a visual comparison. The dispute over நிலை decides whether the verse has a social hierarchy in it.

couplet: To all humility is goodly grace; but chief to them
With fortune blessed, -'tis fortune's diadem.
pope.gloss: Humility is good in all; but especially in the rich it is (the excellence of) higher riches.
