reading: Bowing is good for all, and among them, for the rich it is a further wealth.
nuance: Parimelazhagar asks why the rich are singled out. Those with learning or birth may be humble without it being notable, but for the rich it stands out. Manakkudavar reads செல்வம் simply as abundance, which weakens the pun.

couplet: Like tortoise, who the five restrains
In one, through seven world bliss obtains.
pope.gloss: Should one throughout a single birth, like a tortoise keep in his five senses, the fruit of it will prove a safe-guard to him throughout the seven-fold births.

reading: If in one birth one can draw in the five like a tortoise, it is a protection for seven births.
nuance: The tortoise withdraws out of self-protection, and the image suggests retreat from danger, not conquest. The numbers one and seven make for an argument about return on effort. Kalaignar translates the seven births as all time.

couplet: Whate'er they fail to guard, o'er lips men guard should keep;
If not, through fault of tongue, they bitter tears shall weep.
pope.gloss: Whatever besides you leave unguarded, guard your tongue; otherwise errors of speech and the consequent misery will ensue.

reading: Whatever else they fail to guard, let them guard the tongue; if they don't, they'll suffer from the fault of their words.
nuance: This is a rare concession in a demanding chapter: it sets priorities for someone who cannot do everything. The opening யாகாவாராயினும் accepts failure in advance.

couplet: Though some small gain of good it seem to bring,
The evil word is parent still of evil thing.
pope.gloss: If a man's speech be productive of a single evil, all the good by him will be turned into evil.

reading: If even one bad word has its effect, it turns out that nothing is good.
nuance: The verse doesn't say what stops being good, and the commentators offer three scopes, from one's speech to one's whole moral record.

couplet: In flesh by fire inflamed, nature may thoroughly heal the sore;
In soul by tongue inflamed, the ulcer healeth never more.
pope.gloss: The wound which has been burnt in by fire may heal, but a wound burnt in by the tongue will never heal.

reading: A wound burned by fire heals inside, but a scar burned by the tongue doesn't heal.
nuance: புண் and வடு are carefully chosen: Parimelazhagar notes the first heals and is a wound, while the second stays and is a scar. For him the fire's mark may stay on the body but is healed in the mind, which reverses what one expects to be permanent.

couplet: Who learns restraint, and guards his soul from wrath,
Virtue, a timely aid, attends his path.
pope.gloss: Virtue, seeking for an opportunity, will come into the path of that man who, possessed of learning and self-control, guards himself against anger.

reading: Virtue itself looks for its moment and enters by the path to the one who has guarded against anger and has learned restraint.
nuance: The usual relation is reversed: virtue is a seeker waiting on a person. Parimelazhagar's gloss of செவ்வி pictures virtue as a petitioner awaiting a good moment to present its plea. Manakkudavar adds what must be restrained: the pride that comes from learning.

title: ஒழுக்கமுடைமை
theme: Conduct is to be guarded above life itself. It is what high birth really consists of, it outranks study, and its final test is living in accord with the world.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: conduct's excellence (131-132), the good that comes with it and the harm of its absence (133-137), its later results (138), and all conduct in speech and action summarised (139-140).
source_issues: The Tamil of verse 134 in kg/core has a stray space, பார் ப்பான், and Pope's gloss there has 'bi rth'.

couplet: 'Decorum' gives especial excellence; with greater care
'Decorum' should men guard than life, which all men share.
pope.gloss: Propriety of conduct leads to eminence, it should therefore be preserved more carefully than life.

reading: Since conduct gives excellence, conduct is to be guarded more than life.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reasoning is careful: life is the best of all things, but it doesn't confer distinction the way conduct does, so conduct gets greater care. He adds that this holds for high and low alike.

couplet: Searching, duly watching, learning, 'decorum' still we find;
Man's only aid; toiling, guard thou this with watchful mind.
pope.gloss: Let propriety of conduct be laboriously preserved and guarded; though one know and practise and excel in many virtues, that will be an eminent aid.

reading: Guard conduct with great effort; however much you search and weigh, it alone is the help.
nuance: The three forms of ஓம்பி, தெரிந்து and தேர்ந்து make it sound like a long investigation with one result. Parimelazhagar makes it a survey of all virtues, of which only this one helps in both lives.

couplet: 'Decorum's' true nobility on earth;
'Indecorum's' issue is ignoble birth.
pope.gloss: Propriety of conduct is true greatness of birth, and impropriety will sink into a mean birth.

reading: Having conduct is what noble birth is, and failing in it becomes low birth.
nuance: The verse redefines birth by behaviour. Even the conservative commentators allow that one's status can really change, though for Parimelazhagar it is within a varna frame that the verse doesn't state.

couplet: Though he forget, the Brahman may regain his Vedic lore;
Failing in 'decorum due,' birthright's gone for evermore.
pope.gloss: A Brahman though he should forget the Vedas may recover it by reading; but, if he fail in propriety of conduct even his high bi rth will be destroyed.

reading: Even if forgotten, the Veda can be learned again, but a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct declines.
nuance: This is a pointed ranking, because study is what the Brahmin is supposed to be defined by. It makes birth a thing that can be lost. Parimelazhagar says the rule extends from this high example to the other varnas.

couplet: The envious soul in life no rich increase of blessing gains,
So man of 'due decorum' void no dignity obtains.
pope.gloss: Just as the envious man will be without wealth, so will the man of destitute of propriety of conduct be without greatness.

reading: As there is no prosperity in the envious, so there is no elevation in one who lacks conduct.
nuance: The simile takes as given what chapter 17 has yet to argue, that envy destroys wealth. Parimelazhagar uses verse 166 to extend it: as an envious man's kin suffer, so do a person's kin when conduct fails.

couplet: The strong of soul no jot abate of 'strict decorum's' laws,
Knowing that 'due decorum's' breach foulest disgrace will cause.
pope.gloss: Those firm in mind will not slacken in their observance of the proprieties of life, knowing, as they do, the misery that flows from the transgression from them.

reading: The strong don't slacken in conduct, knowing what harm arises from a lapse.
nuance: The motive given is prudence, not love of virtue. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar differ a little on உரவோர், as strength of mind and understanding respectively, the same question raised by உரன் in verse 24.

couplet: 'Tis source of dignity when 'true decorum' is preserved;
Who break 'decorum's' rules endure e'en censures undeserved.
pope.gloss: From propriety of conduct men obtain greatness; from impropriety comes insufferable disgrace.

reading: From conduct people attain high standing, and from lapses they attain blame not properly theirs.
nuance: எய்தாப் பழி is the sharp part. Parimelazhagar sees that after one slip, even a false charge from an enemy is believed. Conduct is therefore a shield as well as a good.

couplet: 'Decorum true' observed a seed of good will be;
'Decorum's breach' will sorrow yield eternally.
pope.gloss: Propriety of conduct is the seed of virtue; impropriety will ever cause sorrow.

reading: Good conduct is a seed of good, and bad conduct always gives suffering.
nuance: The two halves are asymmetrical: one is a seed with a future harvest, the other suffers 'always'. Parimelazhagar shows each half implies what the other leaves out. Manakkudavar makes the seed one of release, which the verse doesn't say.

couplet: It cannot be that they who 'strict decorum's' law fulfil,
E'en in forgetful mood, should utter words of ill.
pope.gloss: Those who study propriety of conduct will not speak evil, even forgetfully.

reading: Speaking evil with their mouths, even by a slip, is not possible for those who have conduct.
nuance: It's a strong claim: conduct has become so ingrained that the slip itself can't occur. Parimelazhagar adds speech improper to one's varna to the list of evil words, which is his addition. He also says the redundant 'with the mouth' implies that it's a mouth used to good words.

couplet: Who know not with the world in harmony to dwell,
May many things have learned, but nothing well.
pope.gloss: Those who know not how to act agreeably to the world, though they have learnt many things, are still ignorant.

reading: Those who haven't learned to live in accord with the world have studied much and still lack understanding.
nuance: All three commentators narrow உலகம் to the noble. Yet Parimelazhagar makes an unusual concession in explaining why the verse says 'world': scripture contains things that no longer suit the present, and it omits things that do.

title: பிறனில் விழையாமை
theme: Desire for another man's wife is the height of folly and a loss in every register at once. The chapter speaks to men, frames the woman as belonging to another, and calls restraint here the greatest manhood.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the faults of one who desires another's wife (141-146) and the virtues of one who doesn't (147-150). The verses also trace the act through its stages: desiring, standing at the door, entering, looking and touching.
source_issues: The Tamil of verse 143 in kg/core has corrupted characters in விளிந்தா஡஢ன், which should read விளிந்தாரின் as Parimelazhagar's text shows.
Pope's text has typos in verse 145 ('triflel'), verse 146 ('ivades') and verse 150 ('dee ds').

couplet: Who laws of virtue and possession's rights have known,
Indulge no foolish love of her by right another's own.
pope.gloss: The folly of desiring her who is the property of another will not be found in those who know (the attributes of) virtue and (the rights of) property.

reading: The folly of desiring a woman who is another's possession doesn't exist in those who have seen virtue and wealth in this world.
nuance: பிறன்பொருளாள், the verse's own word, treats the woman as property. Parimelazhagar explains why only two of the three aims are named: the science of pleasure has a term for this very act, so its experts can't be cited against it.

couplet: No fools, of all that stand from virtue's pale shut out,
Like those who longing lurk their neighbour's gate without.
pope.gloss: Among all those who stand on the outside of virtue, there are no greater fools than those who stand outside their neighbour's door.

reading: Among all who stand outside virtue, none is a greater fool than those who stand outside another man's door.
nuance: The repeated கடை sets one threshold on another: outside virtue and outside the door. Parimelazhagar's reason is telling: other sinners at least get their pleasure, whereas this man is too afraid even for that. So the charge is stupidity, and even pleasure is lost.

couplet: They're numbered with the dead, e'en while they live, -how otherwise?
With wife of sure confiding friend who evil things devise.
pope.gloss: Certainly they are no better than dead men who desire evil towards the wife of those who undoubtingly confide in them.

reading: Those who take to evil in the home of people who trust them are surely no different from the dead.
nuance: The wrong here is defined by trust, as தெளிந்தார் shows: Parimelazhagar points out that the act is only possible because the husband trusts him. It's betrayal of a friend as much as sexual wrongdoing.

couplet: How great soe'er they be, what gain have they of life,
Who, not a whit reflecting, seek a neighbour's wife.
pope.gloss: However great one may be, what does it avail if, without at all considering his guilt, he goes unto the wife of another ?

reading: However great they are, what does it come to, when one enters another's home without weighing it even a millet's worth?
nuance: A millet's worth of thought would be enough to stop it. Parimelazhagar names Indra as the example of greatness lost. He also reports a reading of தேரான் பிறன் as 'the unsuspecting husband'.

couplet: 'Mere triflel' saying thus, invades the home, so he ensures.
A gain of guilt that deathless aye endures.
pope.gloss: He who thinks lightly of going into the wife of another acquires guilt that will abide with him imperishably and for ever.

reading: One who crosses into a home thinking it easy gets blame that never dies.
nuance: The contrast is in timescale: 'easy' describes one moment and the blame lasts forever. Parimelazhagar makes it the family's blame, so the cost falls on others too.

couplet: Who home ivades, from him pass nevermore,
Hatred and sin, fear, foul disgrace; these four.
pope.gloss: Hatred, sin, fear, disgrace; these four will never leave him who goes in to his neighbour's wife.

reading: Enmity, sin, fear and blame: these four never leave one who crosses into a home.
nuance: The four cover different kinds of consequence: social, moral, psychological and reputational. 'Home' throughout this chapter stands for the wife, an equation that the Tamil title itself makes.

couplet: Who sees the wife, another's own, with no desiring eye
In sure domestic bliss he dwelleth ever virtuously.
pope.gloss: He who desires not the womanhood of her who should walk according to the will of another will be praised as a virtuous house-holder.

reading: The one called a householder in the way of virtue is he who doesn't desire the womanhood of the one who belongs to another's way.
nuance: It's a negative definition of the householder, after chapter 5's positive ones. Parimelazhagar makes it exclusive: he alone is such a householder.

couplet: Manly excellence, that looks not on another's wife,
Is not virtue merely, 'tis full 'propriety' of life.
pope.gloss: That noble manliness which looks not at the wife of another is the virtue and dignity of the great.

reading: The great manhood that doesn't look at another's wife is, for the worthy, both virtue and complete conduct.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's explanation is a fine one: those who can subdue outer enemies can still find this inner enemy hard, so this is the greater manhood. He takes நோக்காத beyond looking, to not holding her in mind.

couplet: Who 're good indeed, on earth begirt by ocean's gruesome tide?
The men who touch not her that is another's bride.
pope.gloss: Is it asked, "who are those who shall obtain good in this world surrounded by the terror-producing sea ?" Those who touch not the shoulder of her who belongs to another.

reading: Who deserve good on this world ringed by the awesome sea? Those who don't touch the shoulders of a woman belonging to another.
nuance: The question-and-answer form and the immense sea are grand for such a plain answer. தோள் is the vocabulary of love poetry. The commentators differ on நாமநீர், as Parimelazhagar has fearful water and Manakkudavar has water that grants wishes.

couplet: Though virtue's bounds he pass, and evil dee ds hath wrought;
At least, 'tis good if neighbour's wife he covet not.
pope.gloss: Though a man perform no virtuous deeds and commit (every) vice, it will be well if he desire not the womanhood of her who is within the limit (of the house) of another.

reading: Even if one doesn't practise virtue and does what is wrong, it's good not to desire the womanhood of one within another's bounds.
nuance: The verse sets a minimum for someone who has failed at everything else. Parimelazhagar says this quality alone stands out, and Manakkudavar says that it brings good even with no other virtue. It doesn't say the person is thereby virtuous.

title: பொறையுடைமை
theme: Forbearance as strength: it wins the victory, it outlasts revenge's one day of pleasure, and for those who can bear harsh words it outranks fasting. Beyond it lies forgetting the wrong entirely.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: forbearance's excellence (151-154), bearing what others do (155-158), and bearing what others say (159-160).
source_issues: The Tamil of verse 153 in kg/core reads இன்நம்யுள், a typo for இன்மையுள். The Tamil of verse 154 reads பொநற்யுடைமை, a typo for பொறையுடைமை.
Manakkudavar's gloss on verse 153 ('புதுமையை நீக் காமை') may reflect a different understanding of விருந்தொரால், and is worth checking.
Manakkudavar is not aligned for verses 152 and 159.

couplet: As earth bears up the men who delve into her breast,
To bear with scornful men of virtues is the best.
pope.gloss: To bear with those who revile us, just as the earth bears up those who dig it, is the first of virtues.

reading: Like the earth that holds up those who dig into it, bearing with those who scorn you is the highest thing.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss brings out the image: the earth keeps the digger from falling, so the one injured is still supporting the one who injures. Forbearance here is more than not responding.

couplet: Forgiving trespasses is good always;
Forgetting them hath even higher praise;
pope.gloss: Bear with reproach even when you can retaliate; but to forget it will be still better than that.

reading: Always bear with excess against you; forgetting it is better still.
nuance: Parimelazhagar explains why forgetting ranks higher: to forbear, one must still hold the wrong in mind. He adds that one should forbear even when one has the power to punish, which is what makes this more than helplessness.

couplet: The sorest poverty is bidding guest unfed depart;
The mightiest might to bear with men of foolish heart.
pope.gloss: To neglect hospitality is poverty of poverty. To bear with the ignorant is might of might.

reading: The poverty of poverties is turning away a guest, and the strength of strengths is forbearance toward fools.
nuance: The verse is an analogy, as Parimelazhagar notes: just as turning a guest away isn't wealth, bearing with fools isn't weakness. The first half is there to change what we think the second half means.

couplet: Seek'st thou honour never tarnished to retain;
So must thou patience, guarding evermore, maintain.
pope.gloss: If you desire that greatness should never leave, you preserve in your conduct the exercise of patience.

reading: If you want நிறை never to leave you, keep and live by forbearance.
nuance: Forbearance is presented as the means, and நிறை is what is at stake. Parimelazhagar takes the latter as worth of character, and Manakkudavar as a guarded discipline: keeping what should be kept and rejecting what should be rejected.

couplet: Who wreak their wrath as worthless are despised;
Who patiently forbear as gold are prized.
pope.gloss: (The wise) will not at all esteem the resentful. They will esteem the patient just as the gold which they lay up with care.

reading: They don't count at all those who retaliate, but those who forbear they keep wrapped up like gold.
nuance: It's a claim about social estimation, which is why the motive is reputational. Parimelazhagar gives the reason: the person who retaliates has become the wrongdoer's equal. He reads 'wrapping up' as constantly bearing them in mind.

couplet: Who wreak their wrath have pleasure for a day;
Who bear have praise till earth shall pass away.
pope.gloss: The pleasure of the resentful continues for a day. The praise of the patient will continue until (the final destruction of) the world.

reading: Those who retaliate have one day's joy, and those who forbear have renown until they perish.
nuance: The verse honestly concedes that revenge is a pleasure. Parimelazhagar plays this down with 'false joy'.

couplet: Though others work thee ill, thus shalt thou blessing reap;
Grieve for their sin, thyself from vicious action keep!
pope.gloss: Though others inflict injuries on you, yet compassionating the evil (that will come upon them) it will be well not to do them anything contrary to virtue.

reading: Though others do you wrong, it's good to feel the pain of it and not do what is contrary to virtue.
nuance: நோநொந்து, grieving at the pain, doesn't say whose pain. On the first reading below, the wronged person pities the wrongdoer, which is a remarkable demand.

couplet: With overweening pride when men with injuries assail,
By thine own righteous dealing shalt thou mightily prevail.
pope.gloss: Let a man by patience overcome those who through pride commit excesses.

reading: Those who do wrong out of their excess, defeat them by your own rightness.
nuance: The language is of winning. Manakkudavar says it most directly: forbearing isn't defeat, it is victory. மிகுதி and தகுதி, excess and fitness, are set against each other as rival kinds of power.

couplet: They who transgressors' evil words endure
With patience, are as stern ascetics pure.
pope.gloss: Those who bear with the uncourteous speech of the insolent are as pure as the ascetics.

reading: Those who bear the harsh words from the mouths of those who go beyond bounds are as pure as those who have renounced.
nuance: Parimelazhagar spells out the implication: this is someone still in household life. The purity of renunciation can therefore be reached without renouncing. Here இறந்தார் means those who overstep, not the dead.

couplet: Though 'great' we deem the men that fast and suffer pain,
Who others' bitter words endure, the foremost place obtain.
pope.gloss: Those who endure abstinence from food are great, next to those who endure the uncourteous speech of others.

reading: Those who fast are great, but only after those who bear what others say in harshness.
nuance: The verse first grants greatness and then takes the top rank away. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is subtle: bearing insult is done while one's sense of 'I' and 'mine' is still in place, the very things that make it hard.

title: அழுக்காறாமை
theme: Envy is a self-inflicted ruin that needs no enemy. The chapter insists that the envious never rise and the unenvious never fall, and yet it admits the world sometimes shows otherwise, which it says is to be pondered.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the good of being without envy (161-162), the faults of envy (163-168), and the cause of ruin and of gain (169-170).
source_issues: Pope's couplet for verse 166 has a stray space ('f eed'). Manakkudavar's entry for verse 170 begins with a stray '[#]'.

couplet: As 'strict decorum's' laws, that all men bind,
Let each regard unenvying grace of mind.
pope.gloss: Let a man esteem that disposition which is free from envy in the same manner as propriety of conduct.

reading: Let one take as one's rule of conduct a nature whose heart has no envy.
nuance: ஒழுக்காறு and அழுக்காறு differ by one sound, so the sound of the verse sets conduct and envy against each other. Coming right after chapter 14, it makes an inner state into a rule of conduct.

couplet: If man can learn to envy none on earth,
'Tis richest gift, -beyond compare its worth.
pope.gloss: Amongst all attainable excellences there is none equal to that of being free from envy towords others.

reading: Among choice gains nothing equals it, if one can be free of envy toward anyone at all.
nuance: யார்மாட்டும், toward anyone at all, is what makes it hard. Parimelazhagar says this includes one's enemies. It's a further 'nothing greater' claim to be read along with those for virtue, restraint and children.

couplet: Nor wealth nor virtue does that man desire 'tis plain,
Whom others' wealth delights not, feeling envious pain.
pope.gloss: Of him who instead of rejoicing in the wealth of others, envies it, it will be said "he neither desires virtue not wealth."

reading: He who doesn't care for another's prosperity and envies it is called one who wants neither virtue nor gain.
nuance: The verse argues that envy works against what the envier wants. பேணாது goes beyond 'not envying': Parimelazhagar glosses it as failing to help, so what's required is positive support for another's prosperity.

couplet: The wise through envy break not virtue's laws,
Knowing ill-deeds of foul disgrace the cause.
pope.gloss: (The wise) knowing the misery that comes from transgression will not through envy commit unrighteous deeds.

reading: They do no wrong out of envy, because they know the harm that arises from a wrong path.
nuance: The second line nearly repeats verse 136, and here too the motive is prudence. Parimelazhagar's list of wrongs from envy covers thought, speech and action against those with wealth or learning.

couplet: Envy they have within! Enough to seat their fate!
Though foemen fail, envy can ruin consummate.
pope.gloss: To those who cherish envy that is enough. Though free from enemies that (envy) will bring destruction.

reading: For the envious that's enough: even without enemies, it brings about their ruin.
nuance: The verse is sardonic, and அதுசாலும், 'that is enough', sounds almost like a verdict. The envious person's enemy is within, and no outside enemy is needed.

couplet: Who scans good gifts to others given with envious eye,
His kin, with none to clothe or f eed them, surely die.
pope.gloss: He who is envious at a gift (made to another) will with his relations utterly perish destitute of food and rainment.

reading: The kin of one who envies what is given will perish, with nothing to wear or eat.
nuance: The cost falls on those near him. Parimelazhagar says his own ruin needn't be stated. Manakkudavar makes the fault active, that he stops another's giving, whereas Parimelazhagar makes it the feeling itself. Either way, the verse punishes innocents, and it doesn't address this.

couplet: From envious man good fortune's goddess turns away,
Grudging him good, and points him out misfortune's prey.
pope.gloss: Lakshmi envying (the prosperity) of the envious man will depart and introduce him to her sister.

reading: The fair goddess, grudging the envious man, will show him to her elder sister.
nuance: The verse describes the goddess's act with the word for envy's own attitude, அவ்வித்து, so the envier gets what he gives. The elder sister is misfortune. Kalaignar distances himself by saying this is how people describe it. Parimelazhagar also records a different reading of the verb.

couplet: Envy, embodied ill, incomparable bane,
Good fortune slays, and soul consigns to fiery pain.
pope.gloss: Envy will destroy (a man's) wealth (in his world) and drive him into the pit of fire (in the world to come.)

reading: The one evil called envy destroys good fortune and drives one to the bad place.
nuance: பாவி personifies a quality as a villain. Parimelazhagar acknowledges it's a figure of speech: a quality isn't a person, but this one is so cruel to its maker that it's called one. Kalaignar has 'evil path' where the older commentators have hell.

couplet: To men of envious heart, when comes increase of joy,
Or loss to blameless men, the 'why' will thoughtful hearts employ.
pope.gloss: The wealth of a man of envious mind and the poverty of the righteous will be pondered.

reading: The prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are matters to be pondered.
nuance: This verse admits what the next one denies. It doesn't state a resolution, only that it must be thought about. Parimelazhagar cites Silappatikaram 15.91-93 as an example of someone pondering this in the story of Kovalan's suffering, a direct thread between the two works.

couplet: No envious men to large and full felicity attain;
No men from envy free have failed a sure increase to gain.
pope.gloss: Never have the envious become great; never have those who are free from envy been without greatness.

reading: None have grown great through envy, and none free of it have lost out on increase.
nuance: It's an absolute claim, with 'none' twice. Parimelazhagar takes this as the moral cause of gain and ruin, immediately after his past-deeds reading of 169, without explaining how the two fit.

title: வெஃகாமை
theme: Coveting another's goods destroys one even in the wanting. Not wanting is presented as the real security of wealth, and it ends as a kind of pride and victory.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the faults of coveting (171-177), the good of not coveting (178-179), and both together (180). Many verses play on the sound of வெஃகு against அஃகு, to covet against to shrink.
source_issues: Manakkudavar is not aligned for verse 175. His entry for verse 177 opens with a fragment of the verse.

couplet: With soul unjust to covet others' well-earned store,
Brings ruin to the home, to evil opes the door.
pope.gloss: If a man departing from equity covet the property (of others), at that very time will his family be destroyed and guilt be incurred.

reading: If one covets another's good things and leaves aside fairness, the family perishes, and faults come at once.
nuance: The condition is only வெஃகின், if one covets, and ஆங்கே, right then, makes the penalty immediate. Parimelazhagar gives நடுவு a specific meaning: the recognition that what belongs to others isn't ours to take.

couplet: Through lust of gain, no deeds that retribution bring,
Do they, who shrink with shame from every unjust thing.
pope.gloss: Those who blush at the want of equity will not commit disgraceful acts through desire of the profit that may be gained.

reading: Those ashamed of unfairness won't do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain to be had.
nuance: நாணு, shame, is the operative word and it means this person is restrained from inside. Parimelazhagar glosses it with fear, which is a less interior motive than the verse's word.

couplet: No deeds of ill, misled by base desire,
Do they, whose souls to other joys aspire.
pope.gloss: Those who desire the higher pleasures (of heaven) will not act unjustly through desire of the trifling joy. (in this life.)

reading: Those who want the other joy won't do what's contrary to virtue out of desire for a small joy.
nuance: சிற்றின்பம் here refers to pleasure from taking others' goods, which isn't its common later meaning of sexual pleasure. The verse leaves 'the other joy' unnamed.

couplet: Men who have conquered sense, with sight from sordid vision freed,
Desire not other's goods, e'en in the hour of sorest need.
pope.gloss: The wise who have conquered their senses and are free from crime, will not covet (the things of others), with the thought "we are destitute."

reading: Those of faultless sight, who have conquered the senses, won't covet at the thought 'we have nothing'.
nuance: Need is the hardest case, and the verse rules out that excuse. Parimelazhagar goes a step further and says that such people don't count as poor at all, which removes the case instead of answering it.

couplet: What gain, though lore refined of amplest reach he learn,
His acts towards all mankind if covetous desire to folly turn?
pope.gloss: What is the advantage of extensive and accurate knowledge if a man through covetousness act senselessly towards all ?

reading: What is the use of fine and wide understanding if, coveting, one acts senselessly toward everyone?
nuance: The sound of அஃகி, to be fine, is played against வெஃகி, to covet, and a learned mind is shown undone by the same sound. Parimelazhagar repeats a principle from 140: the purpose of understanding is what one refrains from.

couplet: Though, grace desiring, he in virtue's way stand strong,
He's lost who wealth desires, and ponders deeds of wrong.
pope.gloss: If he, who through desire of the virtue of kindness abides in the domestic state i.e., the path in which it may be obtained, covet (the property of others) and think of evil methods (to obtain it), he will perish.

reading: One standing on the path out of desire for grace will perish if, desiring wealth, he plots wrongs.
nuance: வெஃகி is used twice: he desires grace and he desires wealth, in the one verb. The other notable word is சூழ, to plot: Parimelazhagar notes that it says the plotting alone destroys him, let alone the doing.

couplet: Seek not increase by greed of gain acquired;
That fruit matured yields never good desired.
pope.gloss: Desire not the gain of covetousness. In the enjoyment of its fruits there is no glory.

reading: Don't seek gain that comes by coveting: when it ripens, its fruit is hard to make good.
nuance: The word விளைவயின் brings in a harvest image: the wrong shows only when the crop comes in, so the problem is one of delayed consequences.

couplet: What saves prosperity from swift decline?
Absence of lust to make another's cherished riches thine!
pope.gloss: If it is weighed, "what is the indestructibility of wealth," it is freedom from covetousness.

reading: What keeps wealth from shrinking? Not coveting what's in another's hand, which that person wants.
nuance: The chapter's sound play, அஃகாமை and வெஃகாமை, is itself the answer. It offers a security for wealth that the wealthy might not expect: leaving others' goods alone.

couplet: Good fortune draws anigh in helpful time of need,
To him who, schooled in virtue, guards his soul from greed.
pope.gloss: Lakshmi, knowing the manner (in which she may approach) will immediately come to those wise men who, knowing that it is virtue, covet not the property of others.

reading: Fortune, knowing the way to come, approaches those who understand virtue and do not covet.
nuance: Here the goddess has to work out the right way to approach, as if she were the supplicant. Parimelazhagar's gloss explains the 'way' as time, place and the right moment.

couplet: From thoughtless lust of other's goods springs fatal ill,
Greatness of soul that covets not shall triumph still.
pope.gloss: To covet (the wealth of another) regardless of consequences will bring destruction. That greatness (of mind) which covets not will give victory.

reading: Coveting without thought yields destruction, and the pride called not-wanting yields victory.
nuance: செருக்கு normally means arrogance, and here it's a virtue. Parimelazhagar explains why it's a victory: it puts beneath it all those who scramble after wealth. Not wanting is a form of power.

title: புறங்கூறாமை
theme: Backbiting is placed below open wrongdoing because it adds falsity to harm: the smile to the face after the slander behind the back. The remedy is simple and hard: to see one's own faults as one sees a stranger's.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the good of not backbiting (181), the cruelty of backbiting (182-184), the faults that follow (185-189), and the way to stop (190).
source_issues: Parimelazhagar's entry for verse 185 opens with a fragment of the verse and stray markup ('br>'). His entry for verse 190 repeats a clause, and his entry for verse 187 has a stray space in 'கரு ததான்'.
Pope's couplet for verse 181 has a stray space ('wit hin').

couplet: Though virtuous words his lips speak not, and all his deeds are ill.
If neighbour he defame not, there's good wit hin him still.
pope.gloss: Though one do not even speak of virtue and live in sin, it will be well if it be said of him "he does not backbite."

reading: Though one doesn't speak of virtue and does wrong, it's pleasing if it is said, 'he doesn't backbite'.
nuance: The merit here is what's said about a person, which fits the chapter: a backbiter is judged by talk, and this man is praised by it. Virtue need not even be spoken of, which sets a very low floor.

couplet: Than he who virtue scorns, and evil deeds performs, more vile,
Is he that slanders friend, then meets him with false smile.
pope.gloss: To smile deceitfully (in another's presence) after having reviled him to his destruction (behind his back) is a greater evil than the commission of (every other) sin and the destruction of (every) virtue.

reading: Worse than denying virtue and doing wrong is destroying someone behind their back and then smiling falsely.
nuance: The ranking is what's striking. Parimelazhagar takes அறனழீஇ as openly saying there's no such thing as virtue, so the moral denier is rated above the smiling gossip. Honest wickedness is treated as less bad than a hidden betrayal.

couplet: 'Tis greater gain of virtuous good for man to die,
Than live to slander absent friend, and falsely praise when nigh.
pope.gloss: Death rather than life will confer upon the deceitful backbiter the profit which (the treatises on) virtue point out.

reading: Dying brings more of the gain that virtue speaks of than living on by backbiting and falsehood.
nuance: Death is compared favourably here, and the terms are moral accounting. Parimelazhagar's reason is that death at least stops the backbiting. Manakkudavar pictures a person who refuses to gossip and dies poor, which suggests that gossip may be a livelihood.

couplet: In presence though unkindly words you speak, say not
In absence words whose ill result exceeds your thought.
pope.gloss: Though you speak without kindness before another's face speak not in his absence words which regard not the evil subsequently resulting from it.

reading: Though you speak harshly to a person's face, do not speak words that have no regard for what follows, when they are not there.
nuance: The verse is a concession, as open harshness is the lesser evil, and it goes against chapter 10's standards. Manakkudavar takes care to add that this isn't permission for harsh speech.

couplet: The slanderous meanness that an absent friend defames,
'This man in words owns virtue, not in heart,' proclaims.
pope.gloss: The emptiness of that man's mind who (merely) praises virtue will be seen from the meanness of reviling another behind his back.

reading: That someone's heart doesn't really speak virtue will be seen from the meanness of their backbiting.
nuance: It's a test: talk about virtue is checked against talk about others. Parimelazhagar makes it specific: a backbiter can praise virtue, but because his mind is bad, what he says shouldn't be accepted.

couplet: Who on his neighbours' sins delights to dwell,
The story of his sins, culled out with care, the world will tell.
pope.gloss: The character of the faults of that man who publishes abroad the faults of others will be sought out and published.

reading: One who talks of another's faults will have his own faults picked out and talked about.
nuance: The passive voice doesn't say who will do the talking. Parimelazhagar makes it the injured party, who picks out from the speaker's many faults the ones that would hurt most, and says them to his face.

couplet: With friendly art who know not pleasant words to say,
Speak words that sever hearts, and drive choice friends away.
pope.gloss: Those who know not to live in friendship with amusing conversation will by back-biting estrange even their relatives.

reading: Those who don't know how to make friends through words that delight will divide even their own people with words that divide.
nuance: பகச்சொல்லி and நகச்சொல்லி are one sound apart, like divide and delight. The verse gives a diagnosis, that gossip is a social failure: those who can't please must separate. Parimelazhagar says even kin are affected, and strangers all the more.

couplet: Whose nature bids them faults of closest friends proclaim
What mercy will they show to other men's good name?
pope.gloss: What will those not do to strangers whose nature leads them to publish abroad the faults of their intimate friends ?

reading: Those whose way is to spread abroad even the faults of those closest to them, what would they do to strangers?
nuance: மரபினார் suggests a settled habit or even a family tradition, not a lapse. Parimelazhagar reports a variant reading, 'what sort of people are they?'

couplet: 'Tis charity, I ween, that makes the earth sustain their load.
Who, neighbours' absence watching, tales or slander tell abroad.
pope.gloss: The world through charity supports the weight of those who reproach others observing their absence.

reading: Is it out of regard for virtue that the earth bears the weight of one who watches for a person's back and speaks mean words?
nuance: The earth, the model of forbearance, finds this one hard. Parimelazhagar imagines the earth telling itself that bearing this is its duty. Manakkudavar adds darkly that otherwise it would shake him off.

couplet: If each his own, as neighbours' faults would scan,
Could any evil hap to living man?
pope.gloss: If they observed their own faults as they observe the faults of others, would any evil happen to men ?

reading: If people could see their own faults as they see strangers' faults, what harm would come to any living being?
nuance: The whole chapter resolves into a problem of seeing. காண்கிற்பின் means 'if they were able', and Parimelazhagar notes that this impartial comparison is rare.

title: பயனில சொல்லாமை
theme: Empty speech, especially before many, ruins the speaker's standing and even his claim to being fully human. The chapter ranks uselessness of speech as a graver failing than unkindness or lack of grace, and ends with a bare rule.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the fault of useless speech (191-196), the merit of refraining from it (197-199), and the rule of what to say and not say (200).
source_issues: 191: Manakkudavar's text begins mid-verse with a corrupted fragment (னேல்லாரு மெள்ளப் படும்), but its gloss is usable.
196: the verse text reads பராட்டு வானை, with a short first vowel, while Parimelazhagar reads பாராட்டுவான்.

couplet: Words without sense, while chafe the wise,
Who babbles, him will all despise.
pope.gloss: He who to the disgust of many speaks useless things will be despised by all.

reading: A person who talks emptily to the irritation of many ends up despised by all.
nuance: The verse says only 'many'. Parimelazhagar narrows them to the discerning, which turns the move from 'many' to 'all' into a causal chain: once the wise are repelled, everyone else follows.

couplet: Words without sense, where many wise men hear, to pour
Than deeds to friends ungracious done offendeth more.
pope.gloss: To speak useless things in the presence of many is a greater evil than to do unkind things towards friends.

reading: Saying useless things before many is worse than doing what is unwelcome to one's friends.
nuance: The ranking is startling: a word to an audience outweighs a deed against a friend. Parimelazhagar's explanation is that the talk brings more disgrace, so his measure is the speaker's standing and not the harm done.

couplet: Diffusive speech of useless words proclaims
A man who never righteous wisdom gains.
pope.gloss: That conversation in which a man utters forth useless things will say of him "he is without virtue."

reading: Expansive talk about useless things itself declares that the speaker is one without நயன்.
nuance: No one needs to accuse the talker, because the speech testifies against him. நயன் shifts through this chapter: Parimelazhagar takes it as liking in 192 and as justice here, so the word should not be given a single translation.

couplet: Unmeaning, worthless words, said to the multitude,
To none delight afford, and sever men from good.
pope.gloss: The words devoid of profit or pleasure which a man speaks will, being inconsistent with virtue, remove him from goodness.

reading: Graceless words that serve no purpose, spoken among many, lack நயன் and take a person away from what is good.

couplet: Gone are both fame and boasted excellence,
When men of worth speak of words devoid of sense.
pope.gloss: If the good speak vain words their eminence and excellence will leave them.

reading: If those of gentle nature speak useless things, their worth departs and the regard it earned goes with it.
nuance: The verse aims at the good, not the habitual babbler of 196. Standing already earned is not secure against this one lapse.

couplet: Who makes display of idle words' inanity,
Call him not man, -chaff of humanity!
pope.gloss: Call not him a man who parades forth his empty words. Call him the chaff of men.

reading: Don't call a person who keeps up useless talk a man; call him chaff among people.
nuance: For Parimelazhagar the image means a husk without the kernel of understanding, so the talk reveals emptiness and doesn't merely offend.

couplet: Let those who list speak things that no delight afford,
'Tis good for men of worth to speak no idle word.
pope.gloss: Let the wise if they will, speak things without excellence; it will be well for them not to speak useless things.

reading: Let the worthy say what lacks நயன் if they must; it is good that they not say what lacks use.
nuance: The concession is rhetorical, as Parimelazhagar observes: 'even if they say it' implies they should not. Its force is the comparison, which keeps the sting whichever sense of நயன் is taken.

couplet: The wise who weigh the worth of every utterance,
Speak none but words of deep significance.
pope.gloss: The wise who seek after rare pleasures will not speak words that have not much weight in them.

reading: Those whose understanding searches out rare ends do not say what lacks great use.
nuance: The bar rises here from useless to not greatly useful, and Parimelazhagar draws this out: words of small use are excluded too. His identification of the rare ends with release and higher destinies is his own; Manakkudavar says only 'rare matters'.

couplet: The men of vision pure, from wildering folly free,
Not e'en in thoughtless hour, speak words of vanity.
pope.gloss: Those wise men who are without faults and are freed from ignorance will not even forgetfully speak things that profit not.

reading: Those of stainless sight, freed from delusion, do not say meaningless things even by a lapse.
nuance: பொச்சாந்தும் moves the claim from choice to nature: for such people the restraint survives inattention.

couplet: If speak you will, speak words that fruit afford,
If speak you will, speak never fruitless word.
pope.gloss: Speak what is useful, and speak not useless words.

reading: Say what among words has use; do not say what among words has none.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that சொல்லில் is grammatically surplus and kept for the figure of repeated words. It may be a quiet wit that a chapter against waste in speech ends on a deliberate surplus, though that is my reading and no commentator's.

title: தீவினையச்சம்
theme: Fear of evil deeds is presented as a mark of excellence and as enlightened self-interest. Harm done to others does not stay with them: it pursues the doer as surely as a shadow, so whoever loves himself will refrain.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: why evil deeds should be feared (201-203), how those who harm others are themselves ruined (204-209), and the safety of the one who doesn't (210).
source_issues: 208: the verse text reads அஇஉறைந் தற்று, an evident corruption. Parimelazhagar's அடி உறைந்தற்று and Pope's 'heels' show that the word should be அடியுறைந் தற்று.
202, 209, 210: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.

couplet: With sinful act men cease to feel the dread of ill within,
The excellent will dread the wanton pride of cherished sin.
pope.gloss: Those who have experience of evil deeds will not fear, but the excellent will fear the pride of sin.

reading: Those given to evil deeds don't fear the intoxication called evil deed; the excellent do.
nuance: Fear is the sign of moral standing here, not a weakness. Parimelazhagar adds an insight about habit: long practice has removed the fear in one group, and never having done such things keeps it alive in the other.

couplet: Since evils new from evils ever grow,
Evil than fire works out more dreaded woe.
pope.gloss: Because evil produces evil, therefore should evil be feared more than fire.

reading: Since evil deeds yield evil, they are to be feared more than fire.
nuance: The verse's reason is only that evil begets evil, sounded in the play of தீயவை on தீ. Parimelazhagar supplies a further reason, that fire does not burn across time, place and bodies, which brings in rebirth that the verse doesn't state.

couplet: Even to those that hate make no return of ill;
So shalt thou wisdom's highest law, 'tis said, fulfil.
pope.gloss: To do no evil to enemies will be called the chief of all virtues.

reading: They say the chief of all understanding is to leave off doing harm even to those who hate you.
nuance: The word is அறிவு, not virtue as Pope's gloss has it. Forbearance appears here as the height of intelligence, and Parimelazhagar makes the logic prudential: refraining keeps suffering from coming back to oneself.

couplet: Though good thy soul forget, plot not thy neighbour's fall,
Thy plans shall 'virtue's Power' by ruin to thyself forestall.
pope.gloss: Even though forgetfulness meditate not the ruin of another. Virtue will meditate the ruin of him who thus meditates.

reading: Don't plot another's ruin even by a lapse; if you do, அறம் plots the ruin of the plotter.
nuance: The same verb, சூழ், serves both parties, so the plotting already sets the reply in motion and harm need never be carried out. Parimelazhagar draws the point: even thinking of it is forbidden.

couplet: Make not thy poverty a plea for ill;
Thy evil deeds will make thee poorer still.
pope.gloss: Commit not evil, saying, "I am poor": if you do, you will become poorer still.

reading: Don't do evil saying 'I have nothing'; if you do, you'll have nothing all over again.
nuance: The verse answers the strongest excuse for wrongdoing on its own terms: it doesn't defend the poor man's honour but says the plan won't work. Parimelazhagar also reports other glossators who take the second poverty as poverty of good qualities.

couplet: What ranks as evil spare to do, if thou would'st shun
Affliction sore through ill to thee by others done.
pope.gloss: Let him not do evil to others who desires not that sorrows should pursue him.

reading: One who doesn't want afflicting things to overpower him should not do evil things to others.
nuance: The balance of தீப்பால and நோய்ப்பால gives the rule its shape: what one portions out as evil returns as a portion of pain.

couplet: From every enmity incurred there is to 'scape, a way;
The wrath of evil deeds will dog men's steps, and slay.
pope.gloss: However great be the enmity men have incurred they may still live. The enmity of sin will incessantly pursue and kill.

reading: However great the enmity they've incurred, people survive it; the enmity of deeds doesn't die and follows them to kill.
nuance: The deed is made an enemy of a special kind, one that can't be outrun because it travels with the doer. Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss it as entering wherever one enters.

couplet: Man's shadow dogs his steps where'er he wends;
Destruction thus on sinful deeds attends.
pope.gloss: Destruction will dwell at the heels of those who commit evil even as their shadow that leaves them not.

reading: The ruin of those who do evil is like a person's shadow, which never perishes and stays at the foot.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a shadow that stretches far but comes back to rest at the foot, so a consequence can seem distant and still be right there. He expressly rejects another reading, in which the shadow stands for a deed latent until its time.

couplet: Beware, if to thyself thyself is dear,
Lest thou to aught that ranks as ill draw near!
pope.gloss: If a man love himself, let him not commit any sin however small.

reading: If a person loves himself, let him not go near the portion of evil deeds, however small.
nuance: The appeal rests on self-love, using காதலன், a word of real attachment. The verse doesn't ask a person to overcome self-regard: it asks him to think it through, and on Parimelazhagar's reading harm to others is harm to oneself.

couplet: The man, to devious way of sin that never turned aside,
From ruin rests secure, whatever ills betide.
pope.gloss: Know ye that he is freed from destruction who commits no evil, going to neither side of the right path.

reading: Know that one who doesn't stray aside and do evil is a person for whom ruin is rare.
nuance: அருங்கேடன் on its face says ruin is 'rare' or 'hard'. Parimelazhagar argues that அருமை here means absence, which turns a strong probability into a guarantee. Kalaignar also says no ruin at all.

title: ஒப்புரவறிதல்
theme: ஒப்புரவு is the obligation to make one's means serve the community, expecting nothing back as rain expects nothing. It is treated as the mark of being alive, and it holds even in poverty and at the cost of ruin.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of ஒப்புரவு (211-213), then 214 on not failing in it, how the wealth of such a person serves others (215-217), why poverty doesn't release one from it (218-219), and why loss through it is no loss (220).
source_issues: 214: the verse text reads ஒத்த தறவோன், while Parimelazhagar's gloss (ஒத்தது அறிவான்) and Pope's rendering point to the reading ஒத்த தறிவான். The readings here follow the commentators.
212: Parimelazhagar's text contains a stray character in எல்‘ம், evidently எல்லாம்.
220: Manakkudavar's text has the likely typo அஃறு for அஃது.

couplet: Duty demands no recompense; to clouds of heaven,
By men on earth, what answering gift is given?
pope.gloss: Benevolence seeks not a return. What does the world give back to the clouds ?

reading: Obligation seeks no return: what does the world do for the rain in exchange?
nuance: The word chosen is கடப்பாடு, what is owed, and not gift. Parimelazhagar points out that the name itself implies it can't be dropped. Giving with no return is therefore framed as debt, a nicely paradoxical idea.

couplet: The worthy say, when wealth rewards their toil-spent hours,
For uses of beneficence alone 'tis ours.
pope.gloss: All the wealth acquired with perseverance by the worthy is for the exercise of benevolence.

reading: All the wealth got through exertion exists for doing வேளாண்மை, with தக்கார் standing in some relation to it.
nuance: The grammar of தக்கார்க்கு decides whether this sets a limit on recipients or describes the owner, so I have left it open in the reading.

couplet: To 'due beneficence' no equal good we know,
Amid the happy gods, or in this world below.
pope.gloss: It is difficult to obtain another good equal to benevolence either in this world or in that of the gods.

reading: Whether in the world of புத்தேள் or here, it is hard to find any other thing as good as ஒப்புரவு.
nuance: Parimelazhagar offers a striking reason for the gods' world: all there are alike, with no giver and no receiver, so this good can't exist there. On that view the human condition of need is what makes the highest good possible.

couplet: Who knows what's human life's befitting grace,
He lives; the rest 'mongst dead men have their place.
pope.gloss: He truly lives who knows (and discharges) the proper duties (of benevolence). He who knows the m not will be reckoned among the dead.

reading: One who knows what is fitting truly lives; anyone else is counted among the dead.
nuance: Knowing here includes doing: Parimelazhagar glosses it as knowing and acting, because the dead neither know nor act.

couplet: The wealth of men who love the 'fitting way,' the truly wise,
Is as when water fills the lake that village needs supplies.
pope.gloss: The wealth of that man of eminent knowledge who desires to exercise the benevolence approved of by the world, is like the full waters of a city-tank.

reading: The wealth of a greatly wise person connected with the world's desiring is like water filling the village's drinking tank.
nuance: The image puts the wealth in a common place, and the owner disappears from the picture: people simply draw from it. This verse calls such a person பேரறிவாளன, wise, not merely generous.

couplet: A tree that fruits in th' hamlet's central mart,
Is wealth that falls to men of liberal heart.
pope.gloss: The wealth of a man (possessed of the virtue) of benevolence is like the ripening of a fruitful tree in the midst of a town.

reading: Wealth falling to one who has நயன் is like a fruit-giving tree ripening in the heart of the town.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says that நயன் here is ஒப்புரவு as the chief of worldly justice, Manakkudavar makes it being loved by others, and Kalaignar a tender heart. The tree's public position matters as much as its fruit, since no one has to go looking for it.

couplet: Unfailing tree that healing balm distils from every part,
Is ample wealth that falls to him of large and noble heart.
pope.gloss: If wealth be in the possession of a man who has the great excellence (of benevolence), it is like a tree which as a medicine is an infallible cure for disease.

reading: Wealth falling to one of great nobility is like a tree that is medicine and never fails.
nuance: This goes further than the fruit tree of 216. Parimelazhagar has every part of the tree serving as cure, with no regard for its own lack, which suggests giving that costs the giver something. He and Manakkudavar agree that தப்பா includes never being hidden from those who seek it.

couplet: E'en when resources fall, they weary not of 'kindness due,'-
They to whom Duty's self appears in vision true.
pope.gloss: The wise who know what is duty will not scant their benevolence even when they are without wealth.

reading: Even at a time without means, those whose sight knows what is due don't falter in ஒப்புரவு.
nuance: The verse cuts ஒப்புரவு free from wealth. If it were a by-product of surplus it would lapse with the surplus.

couplet: The kindly-hearted man is poor in this alone,
When power of doing deeds of goodness he finds none.
pope.gloss: The poverty of a benevolent man, is nothing but his inability to exercise the same.

reading: Poverty, for one with நயன், is just the condition of being unable to rest while what should be done goes undone.
nuance: Poverty is redefined from the inside. Parimelazhagar makes the contrast explicit: it isn't going without one's own enjoyments. The deprivation is of the power to give.

couplet: Though by 'beneficence,' the loss of all should come,
'Twere meet man sold himself, and bought it with the sum.
pope.gloss: If it be said that loss will result from benevolence, such loss is worth being procured even by the sale of one's self.

reading: If ruin is said to come through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth acquiring even by selling oneself.
nuance: The verse deals with an objection: 'if it is said'. For Parimelazhagar nothing is normally worth selling oneself for, so this is meant to startle, and the reason he gives is the fame such loss yields.

title: ஈகை
theme: True giving is giving to those who have nothing, and everything else is a kind of loan. The chapter ranks giving above reward, above ascetic endurance and even above life itself, and it argues from the giver's own joy and safety as well as from virtue.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the definition of ஈகை (221), the excellence of giving (222-227), and the fault of not giving (228-230).
source_issues: 222: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.

couplet: Call that a gift to needy men thou dost dispense,
All else is void of good, seeking for recompense.
pope.gloss: To give to the destitute is true charity. All other gifts have the nature of (what is done for) a measured return.

reading: Giving something to those who have nothing is what giving is; all the rest has the nature of a measured loan.
nuance: குறியெதிர்ப்பு is a technical word: taking a stated measure and returning that same measure, as Parimelazhagar glosses it. All gifts among equals are thus reclassified, however generous they feel.

couplet: Though men declare it heavenward path, yet to receive is ill;
Though upper heaven were not, to give is virtue still.
pope.gloss: To beg is evil, even though it were said that it is a good path (to heaven). To give is good, even though it were said that those who do so cannot obtain heaven.

reading: Even if it were called a good path, taking is bad; even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
nuance: The verse cuts the value of giving loose from its reward by a hypothetical. How strong that hypothetical is, is exactly what the commentators disagree about.

couplet: 'I've nought' is ne'er the high-born man's reply;
He gives to those who raise themselves that cry.
pope.gloss: (Even in a low state) not to adopt the mean expedient of saying "I have nothing," but to give, is the characteristic of the mad of noble birth.

reading: Not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, are found only in one of good family.
nuance: Parimelazhagar lists several rival interpretations, including giving before the asker has to speak, and giving so that he need not go on to ask anyone else.

couplet: The suppliants' cry for aid yields scant delight,
Until you see his face with grateful gladness bright.
pope.gloss: To see men begging from us in disagreeable, until we see their pleasant countenance.

reading: Being begged from is itself painful, until one sees the glad face of the one who begged.
nuance: A candid observation: being asked is uncomfortable even for the generous. Parimelazhagar attributes this to fear of not being able to give all that is sought.

couplet: 'Mid devotees they're great who hunger's pangs sustain,
Who hunger's pangs relieve a higher merit gain.
pope.gloss: The power of those who perform penance is the power of enduring hunger. It is inferior to the power of those who remove the hunger (of others).

reading: The strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that ranks behind the strength of those who remove hunger.
nuance: The verse says only ஆற்றுவார், those with strength. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both understand ascetics, which makes this a direct ranking of the giver over the renunciant. Parimelazhagar's reason is that the ascetic hungers and can't relieve others.

couplet: Let man relieve the wasting hunger men endure;
For treasure gained thus finds he treasure-house secure.
pope.gloss: The removal of the killing hunger of the poor is the place for one to lay up his wealth.

reading: Removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where a person who has come into wealth should store it.
nuance: அழிபசி is hunger that destroys: Parimelazhagar says all goods, Manakkudavar says a person's qualities. The financial image is made pointed by Parimelazhagar: the wealth comes back to help the giver. He supplies 'for virtue's sake' himself, so the verse is plainer about the bank than he is.

couplet: Whose soul delights with hungry men to share his meal,
The hand of hunger's sickness sore shall never feel.
pope.gloss: The fiery disease of hunger shall never touch him who habitually distributes his food to others.

reading: The evil disease called hunger is unlikely to touch one who is habituated to sharing his food.
nuance: Manakkudavar reads this as a reply to the miser's fear that giving will lead to hunger. Understood that way, the verse is a piece of argument rather than a promise. மரீஇ makes the claim about habit, not about any one gift.

couplet: Delight of glad'ning human hearts with gifts do they not know.
Men of unpitying eye, who hoard their wealth and lose it so?
pope.gloss: Do the hard-eyed who lay up and lose their possessions not know the happiness which springs from the pleasure of giving ?

reading: Do those hard-eyed people who hoard what they have and then lose it not know the joy of giving and gladdening?
nuance: The appeal is to pleasure, not to duty: the hoarder has simply missed out. 'Keep and lose' in one word, வைத்திழக்கும், makes the loss seem part of keeping. Parimelazhagar's own wording suggests the joy belongs to those with அருள், so this reaches forward to chapter 25.

couplet: They keep their garners full, for self alone the board they spread;-
'Tis greater pain, be sure, than begging daily bread!
pope.gloss: Solitary and unshared eating for the sake of filling up one's own riches is certainly much more unpleasant than begging.

reading: Eating alone to fill up one's own store is surely more bitter than begging.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's comparison: begging has only a moment's humiliation and no lasting poverty, while the solitary eater has both. The verse takes the worst thing most people can think of and names something worse.

couplet: 'Tis bitter pain to die, 'Tis worse to live.
For him who nothing finds to give!
pope.gloss: Nothing is more unpleasant than death: yet even that is pleasant where charity cannot be exercised.

reading: Nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach.
nuance: The chapter's last ranking sets giving above life. Parimelazhagar's reason is that it frees one from a bodily burden no use to anyone. This is hyperbole about value, not advice to die, and Kalaignar softens it to a comparison of pains.

title: புகழ்
theme: Renown, earned above all through giving, is the one gain that outlasts the body. The chapter treats a life without it as a disgrace and a burden on the earth, indeed as no life at all.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of fame (231-233), the elevation of those who have it (234-235), the lowness of those who lack it (236-239), and both together (240).
source_issues: 231, 232, 235: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.

234: Parimelazhagar's gloss has the misprint புதல்வரைப் for புலவரைப். Kalaignar's entry also ends with stray editorial text praising the interpretation (இவற்றுள் ஈற்றில் ...), which isn't commentary and wasn't used.

couplet: See that thy life the praise of generous gifts obtain;
Save this for living man exists no real gain.
pope.gloss: Give to the poor and live with praise. There is no greater profit to man than that.

reading: Give, and live so that renown arises: there is no other profit for a living being.
nuance: ஊதியம is a word for profit, so the verse puts its ethics in the language of a balance sheet. Parimelazhagar notes that learning and valour can also win fame, and that giving is named as the highest route to it.

couplet: The speech of all that speak agrees to crown
The men that give to those that ask, with fair renown.
pope.gloss: Whatsoever is spoken in the world will abide as praise upon that man who gives alms to the poor.

reading: All that speakers have to say amounts to praise resting on those who give something to those who ask.
nuance: Parimelazhagar extends speech to poets' song, and he dismisses a reading that lets others have praise too ('say what you will, fame stays with the giver'), because it misses fame's excellence. The verse's sweep ('all that speakers say') is a large claim, even as hyperbole.

couplet: Save praise alone that soars on high,
Nought lives on earth that shall not die.
pope.gloss: There is nothing that stands forth in the world imperishable, except fame, exalted in solitary greatness.

reading: Apart from towering, unmatched renown, there is nothing in the world that stands undying.
nuance: The verse doesn't say what makes fame unmatched. Parimelazhagar specifies gifts that are hardest to give, of life, limb and property, which raises the bar far above ordinary repute.

couplet: If men do virtuous deeds by world-wide ample glory crowned,
The heavens will cease to laud the sage for other gifts renowned.
pope.gloss: If one has acquired extensive fame within the limits of this earth, the world of the Gods will no longer praise those sages who have attained that world.

reading: If someone achieves far-reaching renown within the earth's bounds, the world of the gods doesn't honour the புலவர்.
nuance: The verse is elliptical: it doesn't say whom heaven honours in their place, and everything hinges on the identity of புலவர். I'm not confident any reading here is the verse's own. Parimelazhagar cites Purananuru 27 for the idea that the famous gain both worlds.

couplet: Loss that is gain, and death of life's true bliss fulfilled,
Are fruits which only wisdom rare can yield.
pope.gloss: Prosperity to the body of fame, resulting in poverty to the body of flesh and the stability to the former arising from the death of the latter, are achievable only by the wise.

reading: A ruin that is really growth and a death that is really existence are hard to come by except for the skilled.
nuance: வித்தகர் praises skill, not goodness: for Parimelazhagar, the art of turning what doesn't last into what does. The reading depends on his derivation of நத்தம் from நந்து, growth, and on taking போல் as a filler, so its foundation is a philological argument.

couplet: If man you walk the stage, appear adorned with glory's grace;
Save glorious you can shine, 'twere better hide your face.
pope.gloss: If you are born (in this world), be born with qualities conductive to fame. From those who are destitute of them it will be better not to be born.

reading: If you appear, appear with renown; for those without it, not appearing is better than appearing.
nuance: Taken as birth, a command about how to be born can't be obeyed. Each commentator has to resolve that oddity, and how they do it shapes their positions.

couplet: If you your days will spend devoid of goodly fame,
When men despise, why blame them? You've yourself to blame.
pope.gloss: Why do those who cannot live with praise, grieve those who despise them, instead of grieving themselves for their own inability.

reading: Those who cannot live with renown: why do they resent the people who scorn them, instead of resenting themselves?
nuance: The scorn is accepted as a fair verdict. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is that a good name was within reach, so the failure is one's own.

couplet: Fame is virtue's child, they say; if, then,
You childless live, you live the scorn of men.
pope.gloss: Not to beget fame will be esteemed a disgrace by the wise in this world.

reading: They say it is a disgrace for everyone in the world not to obtain the legacy called renown.
nuance: எச்சம் is what remains after one dies, and it also means offspring, which Pope's 'childless' seizes on. Manakkudavar and Parimelazhagar make a severe point: the lack of fame needs no other fault to justify disgrace.

couplet: The blameless fruits of fields' increase will dwindle down,
If earth the burthen bear of men without renown.
pope.gloss: The ground which supports a body without fame will diminish in its rich produce.

reading: Land that bears a body without renown will decline in its blameless rich yield.
nuance: யாக்கை, 'body', is pointed: for Parimelazhagar, what lacks renown is merely a body, a load the land must carry. Moral failure has an effect on the soil here, which Kalaignar weakens to how the land is regarded.

couplet: Who live without reproach, them living men we deem;
Who live without renown, live not, though living men they seem.
pope.gloss: Those live who live without disgrace. Those who live without fame live not.

reading: Those who live free of blame are the ones who live; those who live free of renown are the ones who don't.
nuance: The balanced form leaves no neutral ground, and Parimelazhagar states it outright: to lack blame is to have renown and to lack renown is to have blame. A quiet, harmless, obscure life has no place in this verse.

title: அருளுடைமை
theme: அருள், compassion extended to all living beings, is the highest wealth and the basis of other virtue. The chapter promises its possessor freedom from suffering and denies its lack any recovery, then closes by showing how it can be cultivated.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of அருள் (241-242), the absence of suffering in both worlds for those who have it (243-245), the faults of those without it (246-249), and how it is brought about (250).
source_issues: 242: the verse text has நல்லாற்றாள் where Parimelazhagar's gloss reads நல் ஆற்றான். No Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
241: Parimelazhagar's gloss has பவற்றுள்ளும, likely a misprint for பலவற்றுள்ளும.
249: Parimelazhagar's text has a stray character in அறங்கட்கெல்‘ம்.

couplet: Wealth 'mid wealth is wealth 'kindliness';
Wealth of goods the vilest too possess.
pope.gloss: The wealth of kindness is wealth of wealth, in as much as the wealth of property is possessed by the basest of men.

reading: The wealth of அருள் is the wealth among wealths, because the wealth of goods is found even among the base.
nuance: The argument is about distribution: what the worst can have can't be the best thing. It doesn't say goods are bad, and 247 will concede how much depends on them.

couplet: The law of 'grace' fulfil, by methods good due trial made,
Though many systems you explore, this is your only aid.
pope.gloss: (Stand) in the good path, consider, and be kind. Even considering according to the conflicting tenets of the different sects, kindness will be your best aid, (in the acquisition of heavenly bliss.)

reading: Examine by sound means and hold to அருள்; however many ways you investigate, that alone is the companion.
nuance: Compassion here is what inquiry concludes, not an alternative to it. Parimelazhagar reads பல்லாற்றால் as the competing religious systems, which disagree on means of knowledge and objects but converge here. The verse itself mentions no sects, so this ecumenical reading is his.

couplet: They in whose breast a 'gracious kindliness' resides,
See not the gruesome world, where darkness drear abides.
pope.gloss: They will never enter the world of darkness and wretchedness whose minds are the abode of kindness.

reading: Those whose hearts are joined with அருள் will not enter the painful world joined with darkness.
nuance: அருள் and இருள் rhyme across the verse, and the same word, சேர்ந்த, joins each to its noun.

couplet: Who for undying souls of men provides with gracious zeal,
In his own soul the dreaded guilt of sin shall never feel.
pope.gloss: (The wise) say that the evils, which his soul would dread, will never come upon the man who exercises kindness and protects the life (of other creatures)

reading: They say that one who sustains living beings and holds to அருள் has no deeds his own life need fear.
nuance: Care for other lives removes the fear for one's own. Parimelazhagar takes மன் as making souls eternal, a doctrine not required by the word, and gives a causal link: such a person won't kill, and hence won't go to hell.

couplet: The teeming earth's vast realm, round which the wild winds blow,
Is witness, men of ' grace' no woeful want shall know.
pope.gloss: This great rich earth over which the wind blows, is a witness that sorrow never comes upon the kind-hearted.

reading: Those who hold to அருள் have no distress, and the wide rich earth where the wind moves is the witness.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's witness is negative: no one has ever seen such a person suffer, so the whole world can testify. Kalaignar instead makes the wind an analogy for அருள் moving the mind. The claim of no distress is bold, and should be read with the reservation of 169.

couplet: Gain of true wealth oblivious they eschew,
Who 'grace' forsake, and graceless actions do.
pope.gloss: (The wise) say that those who neglect kindness and practise cruelties, neglected virtue (in their former birth), and forgot (the sorrows which they must suffer.)

reading: Those who abandon அருள் and carry on doing what should not be done, they say, have parted from பொருள் and forgotten.

couplet: As to impoverished men this present world is not;
The 'graceless' in you world have neither part nor lot.
pope.gloss: As this world is not for those who are without wealth, so that world is not for those who are without kindness.

reading: As this world is not for those without wealth, that world is not for those without அருள்.
nuance: The comparison gets its force from its blunt premise about money, which the verse states as obvious fact. A chapter that opened by belittling goods grants them complete authority over this world.

couplet: Who lose the flower of wealth, when seasons change, again may bloom;
Who lose 'benevolence', lose all; nothing can change their doom.
pope.gloss: Those who are without wealth may, at some future time, become prosperous; those who are destitute of kindness are utterly destitute; for them there is no change.

reading: Those without wealth may flower one day; those without அருள் are finished, and it is hard for them to become anything again.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees this as withdrawing the parallel just drawn in 247, since the two lacks aren't alike after all. His addition of 'through fate' to the poor man's state is not in the verse.

couplet: When souls unwise true wisdom's mystic vision see,
The 'graceless' man may work true works of charity.
pope.gloss: If you consider, the virtue of him who is without kindness is like the perception of the true being by him who is without wisdom.

reading: Virtue done by one without அருள், if examined, is like the muddled person seeing the true reality.
nuance: Parimelazhagar concludes that அருள் is the root of all other virtues. That goes beyond the comparison the verse draws, but it is a natural development.

couplet: When weaker men you front with threat'ning brow,
Think how you felt in presence of some stronger foe.
pope.gloss: When a man is about to rush upon those who are weaker than himself, let him remember how he has stood (trembling) before those who are stronger than himself.

reading: When you go against those weaker than yourself, think of yourself before those stronger.
nuance: The chapter's only instruction on how compassion arises doesn't appeal to a principle: it asks you to remember your own fear. Parimelazhagar calls this the means by which அருள் is born, and extends the weaker to animals too.

title: புலான்மறுத்தல்
theme: Eating flesh is incompatible with அருள், and the chapter argues this like a debate, answering those who say that intent is what matters and those who say that the guilt lies only with the killer. It ends by exalting the one who neither kills nor eats.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as refuting two opponents: those who claim flesh-eating doesn't harm அருள் if one means no harm (251-253), and those who claim the sin of killing stays with the killer (254-256). Then come flesh's repulsiveness (257) and the height of abstaining (258-260).
source_issues: 253: the verse text reads நன்னூக்காது, where Parimelazhagar's gloss has நன்று ஊக்காது. The readings follow the gloss.
254: the verse text has lost its first letter, ருளல்லது for அருளல்லது.
251, 260: Parimelazhagar's gloss is duplicated in the source.
253, 255: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
259: Kalaignar's entry ends with a stray verse number, 260.
258: Manakkudavar's entry begins with a fragment of the verse text.

couplet: How can the wont of 'kindly grace' to him be known,
Who other creatures' flesh consumes to feed his own?
pope.gloss: How can he be possessed of kindness, who to increase his own flesh, eats the flesh of other creatures.

reading: How can one who eats another's flesh to swell his own hold to அருள்?
nuance: ஊன் appears on both sides, so the eater is flesh too and the act is flesh feeding flesh. Parimelazhagar adds that fattening the body is itself useless, so the cruelty buys nothing.

couplet: No use of wealth have they who guard not their estate;
No use of grace have they with flesh who hunger sate.
pope.gloss: As those possess no property who do not take care of it, so those possess no kindness who feed on flesh.
