reading: Holding wealth isn't for those who don't guard it, and likewise holding அருள் isn't for those who eat flesh.
nuance: ஆட்சி, holding and using, is the operative word: compassion is a possession that lapses through neglect. For Parimelazhagar the verse answers those who say a flesh-eater who wishes no creature harm hasn't compromised அருள்.

couplet: Like heart of them that murderous weapons bear, his mind,
Who eats of savoury meat, no joy in good can find.
pope.gloss: Like the (murderous) mind of him who carries a weapon (in his hand), the mind of him who feasts with pleasure on the body of another (creature), has no regard for goodness.

reading: The mind of one who has relished another creature's body doesn't incline to good, like the heart of one holding a weapon.
nuance: The argument concerns attention rather than guilt: what the hand holds, or the tongue relishes, takes over the mind. சுவை matters here, since the verse speaks of savouring and not merely of eating.

couplet: 'What's grace, or lack of grace'? 'To kill' is this, that 'not to kill';
To eat dead flesh can never worthy end fulfil.
pope.gloss: If it be asked what is kindness and what its opposite, the answer would be preservation and destruction of life; and therefore it is not right to feed on the flesh (obtained by taking away life).

reading: If asked what is அருள் and what isn't, it comes down to not killing and killing; eating that flesh is not பொருள்.

couplet: If flesh you eat not, life's abodes unharmed remain;
Who eats, hell swallows him, and renders not again.
pope.gloss: Not to eat flesh contributes to the continuance of life; therefore if a man eat flesh, hell will not open its mouth (to let him escape out, after he has once fallen in).

reading: The standing of life lies in not eating flesh; if one eats, hell doesn't open its mouth.
nuance: The image is of a mouth that has swallowed and won't open to release. Parimelazhagar offers a population argument for உயிர்நிலை: creatures that are eaten dwindle while others multiply. Kalaignar takes அளறு as a mud pit, not the hell of the older commentators.

couplet: 'We eat the slain,' you say, by us no living creatures die;
Who'd kill and sell, I pray, if none came there the flesh to buy?
pope.gloss: If the world does not destroy life for the purpose of eating, then no one would sell flesh for the sake of money.

reading: If the world didn't kill for the sake of eating, nobody would bring flesh for the sake of a price.
nuance: This is a demand-and-supply argument. The buyer who says he killed nothing is told that his purchase causes the killing. Parimelazhagar formalizes the reply as inference by necessary implication.

couplet: With other beings' ulcerous wounds their hunger they appease;
If this they felt, desire to eat must surely cease.
pope.gloss: If men should come to know that flesh is nothing but the unclean ulcer of a body, let them abstain from eating it.

reading: If there were people who perceived flesh as another creature's wound, it would not be eaten.
nuance: பெறின் suggests such perceivers are rare. The commentators stress impurity, yet 'another's wound' can equally appeal to fellow-feeling, as the wound belongs to someone. That second emphasis is my own reading.

couplet: Whose souls the vision pure and passionless perceive,
Eat not the bodies men of life bereave.
pope.gloss: The wise, who have freed themselves from mental delusion, will not eat the flesh which has been severed from an animal.

reading: Those whose vision has parted from fault don't eat flesh that has parted from life.
nuance: The two lines mirror each other with தலைப்பிரிந்த: a person parted from defect faces flesh parted from life. Parimelazhagar says they see for themselves that it is a corpse, so no rule is needed.

couplet: Than thousand rich oblations, with libations rare,
Better the flesh of slaughtered beings not to share.
pope.gloss: Not to kill and eat (the flesh of) an animal, is better than the pouring forth of ghee etc., in a thousand sacrifices.

reading: Better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices is not taking one creature's life and eating.
nuance: A thousand rites weigh less than one abstention. The commentators treat this as a comparison of merit, but the verse can also be read as a challenge to ritual, and that sharper reading isn't one they give.

couplet: Who slays nought,- flesh rejects- his feet before
All living things with clasped hands adore.
pope.gloss: All creatures will join their hands together, and worship him who has never taken away life, nor eaten flesh.

reading: All living beings fold their hands and worship the one who doesn't kill and has refused flesh.
nuance: The beings that have been spared do the worshipping, an image rather than a report. Parimelazhagar insists that the two abstentions are only fruitful together, which closes the loophole of the previous verses.

title: தவம்
theme: தவம் is defined simply as bearing pain and harming no one, and is then credited with immense powers, over enemies, wishes, and even death. The chapter makes it the one truly self-regarding work and the reason so few prosper.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the definition of தவம் (261), its excellence (262-265), the height of those who practise it (266-269), and the lowness of those who don't (270).
source_issues: 262: the verse text reads ஆகும் அதனை, while Parimelazhagar's gloss shows அவம் அதனை. The word அவம், on which the sense 'futile' depends, has dropped from the text.
269: the verse text ends டவர்க்குல், an evident misprint for டவர்க்கு.

couplet: To bear due penitential pains, while no offence
He causes others, is the type of 'penitence'.
pope.gloss: The nature of religious discipline consists, in the endurance (by the ascetic) of the sufferings which it brings on himself, and in abstaining from giving pain to others.

reading: Bearing the pain that comes and causing no pain to living beings: such alone is the form of தவம்.
nuance: The definition mentions no gods, rites or forest, and half of it is ethical. Parimelazhagar takes the pain as self-imposed through such things as reduced food, while Manakkudavar says only pain that has come to one. Kalaignar turns it into a heart that can bear anything, which would make tapas available in any life.

couplet: To 'penitents' sincere avails their 'penitence';
Where that is not, 'tis but a vain pretence.
pope.gloss: Austerities can only be borne, and their benefits enjoyed, by those who have practised them (in a former birth); it will be useless for those who have not done so, to attempt to practise them (now).

reading: தவம் too comes to those who have தவம்; for those without it, taking it up is futile.
nuance: The form is circular, a discouraging one for a would-be beginner. The chapter's praise of effort in the following verses sits awkwardly with it.

couplet: Have other men forgotten 'penitence' who strive
To earn for penitents the things by which they live?
pope.gloss: It is to provide food etc, for the ascetics who have abandoned (the desire of earthly possessions) that other persons have forgotten (to practise) austerity ?

reading: Is it in wanting to provide for those who have renounced that the others have forgotten தவம்?
nuance: The chiding question implies that தவம் isn't reserved for renunciants. Both older commentators draw the conclusion that தவம் is greater than giving, but the verse only implies it.

couplet: Destruction to his foes, to friends increase of joy.
The 'penitent' can cause, if this his thoughts employ.
pope.gloss: If (the ascetic) desire the destruction of his enemies, or the aggrandizement of his friends, it will be effected by (the power of) his austerities.

reading: Crushing foes and raising those who rejoice with one come through தவம், if one so intends.
nuance: எண்ணின், 'if one thinks of it', is doing much here. Parimelazhagar takes it to imply that such people naturally don't think of it. An ascetic with enemies is a problem for him, and he solves it by moving the power to தவம் itself.

couplet: That what they wish may, as they wish, be won,
By men on earth are works of painful 'penance' done.
pope.gloss: Religious dislipline is practised in this world, because it secures the attainment of whatever one may wish to enjoy (in the world to come).

reading: Because whatever is wanted is obtained as it is wanted, தவம் is striven for here.
nuance: The motive offered is getting what you want, in a chapter that condemns desire in the very next verse. Parimelazhagar infers from ஈண்டு, 'here', that the results come in the next life and include release, but the verse doesn't say so.

couplet: Who works of 'penance' do, their end attain,
Others in passion's net enshared, toil but in vain.
pope.gloss: Those discharge their duty who perform austerities; all others accomplish their own destruction, through the entanglement of the desire (of riches and sensual pleasure).

reading: Those who do தவம் are doing their own work; the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile.
nuance: தங்கருமம் is telling: austerity is presented as true self-interest, and worldly activity as neglect of one's real business. Parimelazhagar adds 'having renounced' and identifies 'the rest' as those pursuing wealth and pleasure, which sweeps in most of life.

couplet: The hotter glows the fining fire, the gold the brighter shines;
The pain of penitence, like fire, the soul of man refines.
pope.gloss: Just as gold is purified as heated in the fire, will those shine, who have endured the burning of pain (in frequent austerities).

reading: For those able to endure, pain burning them makes them shine, as gold shines the more it is burned.
nuance: The doubled சுடச்சுட appears in both lines and makes the image of repeated firing audible. What the shining stands for is left open: for Parimelazhagar sin leaves and knowledge grows, for Manakkudavar deeds leave, and for Kalaignar it is fame.

couplet: Who gains himself in utter self-control,
Him worships every other living soul.
pope.gloss: All other creatures will worship him who has attained the control of his own soul.

reading: All other living beings worship the one who has completely gained his own self.
nuance: The disagreement is nearly a reversal: for one reading the person comes to own the self, and for the other he is rid of it.

couplet: E'en over death the victory he may gain,
If power by penance won his soul obtain.
pope.gloss: Those who have attained the power which religious discipline confers, will be able also to pass the limit of Yama, (the God of death).

reading: Even leaping past death becomes possible for those who have attained the power of austerity.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the 'even' can signal how nearly impossible it is. Manakkudavar illustrates with Markandeya, which is his example and isn't in the verse. Kalaignar takes it as conquering death through steadfastness.

couplet: The many all things lack! The cause is plain,
The 'penitents' are few. The many shun such pain.
pope.gloss: Because there are few who practise austerity and many who do not, there are many destitute and few rich in this world.

reading: The reason the have-nots are many: those who practise austerity are few and those who don't are many.
nuance: The verse says just 'those who lack', without saying what they lack. As an explanation of poverty it is arresting and severe, and the commentators each soften or redirect it.

title: கூடாவொழுக்கம்
theme: The false renunciant, whose outward form hides an unrenounced heart, is exposed through a run of precise images. The chapter insists that conduct, not appearance, is the test, and ends by declaring the outward marks of renunciation unnecessary.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the fault of such conduct (271-275), the fault of its practitioners and the need to recognize and avoid them (276-278), how to recognize them (279), and the excellence of those free of it (280).
source_issues: 277: the verse text has முக்கிற், where the commentators read மூக்கின் or மூக்கு.
278: Manakkudavar's entry has an empty (எ - று) marker, which doesn't affect the sense.

couplet: Who with deceitful mind in false way walks of covert sin,
The five-fold elements his frame compose, decide within.
pope.gloss: The five elements (of his body) will laugh within him at the feigned conduct of the deceitful minded man.

reading: The five elements laugh inwardly at the concealed conduct of one with a deceitful mind.
nuance: A hypocrite can't escape witnesses, because his own body is one of them. Parimelazhagar identifies the hidden conduct as sexual, and he carries this through 273 and 274, but the verse doesn't specify.

couplet: What gain, though virtue's semblance high as heaven his fame exalt,
If heart dies down through sense of self-detected fault?
pope.gloss: What avails an appearance (of sanctity) high as heaven, if his mind suffers (the indulgence) of conscious sin.

reading: What will an appearance as high as the sky do, if one's own heart sinks into a fault one knows to be a fault?
nuance: தான்அறி, 'that one knows', is the crux. Parimelazhagar's point is that a fault done unknowingly can be washed away, but one done knowingly can't, so the outward habit only frightens others.

couplet: As if a steer should graze wrapped round with tiger's skin,
Is show of virtuous might when weakness lurks within.
pope.gloss: The assumed appearance of power, by a man who has no power (to restrain his senses and perform austerity), is like a cow feeding on grass covered with a tiger's skin.

reading: A person without strength taking on the form of the strong is like a cow grazing wrapped in a tiger's skin.
nuance: Parimelazhagar presses the image hard. The guards don't chase the 'tiger' because tigers don't eat grass, and because they are afraid, and the cow leaves its own grass for another's crop. So the renouncer leaves his wife and pursues other men's. The strength lacking is mastery of one's own mind; the rest is his extrapolation.

couplet: 'Tis as a fowler, silly birds to snare, in thicket lurks.
When, clad in stern ascetic garb, one secret evil works.
pope.gloss: He who hides himself under the mask of an ascetic and commits sins, like a sportsman who conceals himself in the thicket to catch birds.

reading: Hiding in austerity and doing what isn't austerity is like a hunter hiding in a bush and snaring birds.
nuance: With 273 this gives two opposed animals: the cow is harmless inside a predator's skin, and the hunter is a predator behind harmless leaves. The hypocrite is both, weak before his desire and dangerous to others. That pairing is my own observation. Manakkudavar gives Arjuna as an example.

couplet: 'Our souls are free,' who say, yet practise evil secretly,
'What folly have we wrought!' by many shames o'er-whelmed, shall cry.
pope.gloss: The false conduct of those who say they have renounced all desire will one day bring them sorrows that will make them cry out, "Oh! what have we done, what have we done."

reading: The hidden conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' brings many evils, with cries of 'what, what!'
nuance: என்பார், 'those who say', quietly marks the claim as words only, and Parimelazhagar says that the attachment was only cut in speech.

couplet: In mind renouncing nought, in speech renouncing every tie,
Who guileful live,- no men are found than these of 'harder eye'.
pope.gloss: Amongst living men there are none so hard-hearted as those who without to saking (desire) in their heart, falsely take the appearance of those who have forsaken (it).

reading: None are more hard-eyed than those who, unrenounced in heart, live by deceiving as though they had renounced.
nuance: Why is deceit the height of cruelty? Parimelazhagar has a remarkable answer: the victims are donors, whose gifts to the unworthy earn them a low birth, so the fraud returns harm for help. He supports this from the Civakacintamani, not from the verse.

couplet: Outward, they shine as 'kunri' berry's scarlet bright;
Inward, like tip of 'kunri' bead, as black as night.
pope.gloss: (The world) contains persons whose outside appears (as fair) as the (red) berry of the Abrus, but whose inside is as black as the nose of that berry.

reading: The world holds those who, though looking outwardly like the red kunri seed, are inwardly black as its tip.
nuance: The kunri is a closely observed choice, since its red and black belong to a single small seed. உடைத்து, 'it holds', says only that such people exist. Manakkudavar takes this as a warning to the wise not to judge ascetics by form.

couplet: Many wash in hollowed waters, living lives of hidden shame;
Foul in heart, yet high upraised of men in virtuous fame.
pope.gloss: There are many men of masked conduct, who perform their ablutions, and (make a show) of greatness, while their mind is defiled (with guilt).

reading: Many people, with impurity in their minds, bathe as though distinguished and go about concealed.
nuance: பலர், 'many', comes right after the 'some' of 277 and is a social observation. Water cleans what isn't dirty and leaves what is. Parimelazhagar specifies the impurity as desire, anger and delusion.

couplet: Cruel is the arrow straight, the crooked lute is sweet,
Judge by their deeds the many forms of men you meet.
pope.gloss: As, in its use, the arrow is crooked, and the curved lute is straight, so by their deeds, (and not by their appearance) let (the uprightness or crookedness of) men be estimated.

reading: The arrow is cruel and the curved lute is straight, so know people by the nature of their deeds.
nuance: The verse makes shape deceive in both directions: the straight kills and the curved delights. It does more than warn that some who look good are bad, since it also suggests that some who look wrong are good.

couplet: What's the worth of shaven head or tresses long,
If you shun what all the world condemns as wrong?
pope.gloss: There is no need of a shaven crown, nor of tangled hair, if a man abstain from those deeds which the wise have condemned.

reading: Neither shaving nor long hair is needed, if one gives up what the world condemns.
nuance: The test of renunciation is set by what the ordinary world condemns, and not by a special ascetic code. Parimelazhagar narrows உலகம் to the high-minded, but Manakkudavar leaves it as people generally. The verse removes the outward marks, not renunciation itself.

title: கள்ளாமை
theme: Theft begins as a thought, and its wish alone is an offence. The chapter sets களவு against அளவு, stealth against measure, as two settled dispositions that can't live together, and promises ruin to the one and heaven to the other.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as addressed to renunciants: what theft is and that it must be avoided (281-282), the reasons (283-284), its incompatibility with renunciation (285-287), its contrast with virtue (288), how thieves come to ruin (289), and the fruits of both paths (290).
source_issues: 290: the verse text repeats கள்வார்க்குத் in the second line, where the sense and all three commentators require கள்ளார்க்குத். As printed, it would promise heaven to thieves. It also has உளகு for உலகு.
288: the verse text has அளவறாந்தார் for அளவறிந்தார்.
287: the verse text has கண்ட இல் for கண் இல் (Parimelazhagar: புரிந்தார்கண் இல்).
283: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse. Kalaignar's entry ends with a stray verse number, 284.

couplet: Who seeks heaven's joys, from impious levity secure,
Let him from every fraud preserve his spirit pure.
pope.gloss: Let him, who desires not to be despised, keep his mind from (the desire of) defrauding another of the smallest thing.

reading: One who is called a person wanting not to be scorned should guard his own heart against stealing anything at all.
nuance: The verse guards the heart, not the hand, and so the offence is relocated. Parimelazhagar uses எள்ளாமை for a long attack on Lokayata materialism, and this polemic is entirely his.

couplet: 'Tis sin if in the mind man but thought conceive;
'By fraud I will my neighbour of his wealth bereave.'
pope.gloss: Even the thought (of sin) is sin; think not then of crafiily stealing the property of another.

reading: Even thinking it in the mind is wrong, saying 'we will steal another's goods by stealth'.
nuance: Parimelazhagar limits this high standard to renunciants, whose minds he says are special, but the verse names no such group. The distinction matters, as a universal thought-crime is a stronger claim.

couplet: The gain that comes by fraud, although it seems to grow
With limitless increase, to ruin swift shall go.
pope.gloss: The property, which is acquired by fraud, will entirely perish, even while it seems to increase.

reading: Gain got by stealth will perish beyond all measure, even as it seems to grow.
nuance: ஆவது போல, 'as if growing', places the ruin inside the appearance of success. Parimelazhagar gives அளவிறந்து a sharp sense: as it goes, stolen wealth leaves sin and blame behind and takes earlier virtue along with it.

couplet: The lust inveterate of fraudful gain,
Yields as its fruit undying pain.
pope.gloss: The eager desire of defrauding others will, when it brings forth its fruit, produce undying sorrow.

reading: Love that has ripened in stealth yields, at harvest, a sorrow that doesn't die.
nuance: The verb and noun suggest a crop: கன்றிய, then விளைவு. Using காதல் for the urge to steal treats theft as an attachment, and Parimelazhagar makes the point that the craving breeds repetition, which is why the sorrow doesn't end.

couplet: 'Grace' is not in their thoughts, nor know they kind affection's power,
Who neighbour's goods desire, and watch for his unguarded hour.
pope.gloss: The study of kindness and the exercise of benevolence is not with those who watch for another's forgetfulness, though desire of his property.

reading: Having a loving nature with அருள் in view isn't found in those who, with goods in view, watch for others' lapses.
nuance: The rhyme of அருள்கருதி and பொருள்கருதி sets two objects of attention side by side as if a mind could hold only one. பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார் is a precise picture of the thief's patient watching.

couplet: They cannot walk restrained in wisdom's measured bound,
In whom inveterate lust of fraudful gain is found.
pope.gloss: They cannot walk steadfastly, according to rule, who eagerly desire to defraud others.

reading: Those whose love has ripened in stealth can't keep to the path of அளவு.
nuance: The rhyme அளவு and களவு runs through the next several verses, so the chapter has built its argument into one letter's difference.

couplet: Practice of fraud's dark cunning arts they shun,
Who long for power by 'measured wisdom' won.
pope.gloss: That black-knowledge which is called fraud, is not in those who desire that greatness which is called rectitude.

reading: The dark knowledge called stealth isn't found in those who have set their love on the strength called அளவு.
nuance: Stealth is granted to be a kind of intelligence, just a dark one, so cleverness alone is not a virtue in the Kural. Parimelazhagar says stealth and renunciation are opposed as dark and light.

couplet: As virtue dwells in heart that 'measured wisdom' gains;
Deceit in hearts of fraudful men established reigns.
pope.gloss: Deceit dwells in the mind of those who are conversant with fraud, even as virtue in the mind s of those who are conversant with rectitude.

reading: Deceit stands in the heart of those who know stealth, just as virtue stands in the heart of those who know அளவு.
nuance: The comparison gives vice the same stability as virtue. Manakkudavar draws the discouraging conclusion that once learned, stealth can't be given up.

couplet: Who have no lore save that which fraudful arts supply,
Acts of unmeasured vice committing straightway die.
pope.gloss: Those, who are acquainted with nothing but fraud, will perish in the very commission of transgression.

reading: Those who know nothing but stealth perish right there, having done what is beyond measure.

couplet: The fraudful forfeit life and being here below;
Who fraud eschew the bliss of heavenly beings know.
pope.gloss: Even their body will fail the fraudulent; but even the world of the gods will not fail those who are free from fraud.

reading: For those who steal, உயிர்நிலை falls away; for those who don't, the world of the gods doesn't fall away.
nuance: The shared verb தள்ளு balances the near against the far, in Parimelazhagar's phrase: even what is closest fails the one, and even what is remote doesn't fail the other.

title: வாய்மை
theme: Truthfulness is defined by what speech does rather than by whether it matches facts: speech without harm is truth, and a falsehood yielding faultless good counts as truth. The chapter then raises this virtue above austerity, giving, and every other good.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the definition of truth and falsehood (291-292), that falsehood can't be hidden (293), its fruit in this world (294), its fruit beyond (295-297), and its supremacy (298-300).
source_issues: 298: the verse text has புறள்தூய்மை for புறந்தூய்மை.

couplet: You ask, in lips of men what 'truth' may be;
'Tis speech from every taint of evil free.
pope.gloss: Truth is the speaking of such words as are free from the least degree of evil (to others).

reading: If you ask what truth is, it is speech containing no evil at all.
nuance: A surprising definition, because nothing here refers to facts. Parimelazhagar spells out the consequence: stating what happened isn't the definition, and even an accurate report is falsehood if it harms.

couplet: Falsehood may take the place of truthful word,
If blessing, free from fault, it can afford.
pope.gloss: Even falsehood has the nature of truth, if it confer a benefit that is free from fault.

reading: Even falsehood is in the place of truth, if it yields good that is free of fault.
nuance: புரைதீர்ந்த does the limiting work: this excuses no convenient lie. Parimelazhagar's example is a falsehood that saves a creature from ruin or death, and he builds 291 and 292 into a four-way scheme crossing fact with effect.

couplet: Speak not a word which false thy own heart knows
Self-kindled fire within the false one's spirit glows.
pope.gloss: Let not a man knowingly tell a lie; for after he has told the lie, his mind will burn him (with the memory of his guilt).

reading: Don't lie about what your own heart knows; once you lie, your own heart will burn you.
nuance: The harm returns by the same organ of knowing. Parimelazhagar has the heart as a witness that brings on the sin's result, and Manakkudavar has it as remorse on seeing what the lie did to others. Kalaignar's 'conscience' is a modern word for the same thing.

couplet: True to his inmost soul who lives,- enshrined
He lives in souls of all mankind.
pope.gloss: He who, in his conduct, preserves a mind free from deceit, will dwell in the minds of all men.

reading: If one conducts oneself without being false in one's heart, one lives in the hearts of all the world.
nuance: உள்ளம் appears on both sides of the verse: inner truth gives a place in others' inner lives. Parimelazhagar narrows 'the world' to the elevated, and says it is speech that has to match the heart. Manakkudavar and Kalaignar make it not even thinking a lie.

couplet: Greater is he who speaks the truth with full consenting mind.
Than men whose lives have penitence and charity combined.
pope.gloss: He, who speaks truth with all his heart, is superior to those who make gifts and practise austerities.

reading: If one speaks truth together with one's heart, one is above those who practise austerity along with giving.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is about levels of the person: acts of body are outward, but acts of mind and speech are inward. Note that truth is ranked here above the two virtues that chapters 23 and 27 have just exalted.

couplet: No praise like that of words from falsehood free;
This every virtue yields spontaneously.
pope.gloss: There is no praise like the praise of never uttering a falsehood: without causing any suffering, it will lead to every virtue.

reading: There is no renown like not lying, and it brings all virtue without எய்யாமை.

couplet: If all your life be utter truth, the truth alone,
'Tis well, though other virtuous acts be left undone.
pope.gloss: If a man has the power to abstain from falsehood, it will be well with him, even though he practise no other virtue.

reading: If one keeps up not lying, not lying, then not doing other virtues, not doing them, is good.
nuance: The commentators' opposed readings depend on where the doubled words are divided. Parimelazhagar knows and rejects a reading like Manakkudavar's.

couplet: Outward purity the water will bestow;
Inward purity from truth alone will flow.
pope.gloss: Purity of body is produced by water and purity of mind by truthfulness.

reading: Outer purity comes about through water; inner purity is seen through truth.
nuance: காணப்படும் is more ambiguous than it looks. Parimelazhagar explains that what is seen exists, so truth produces purity, whereas Manakkudavar says purity is known by truthful speech, which makes truth its evidence. Parimelazhagar also infers that renunciants need both purities.

couplet: Every lamp is not a lamp in wise men's sight;
That's the lamp with truth's pure radiance bright.
pope.gloss: All lamps of nature are not lamps; the lamp of truth is the lamp of the wise.

reading: Not all lamps are lamps; for the worthy, the unfailing lamp alone is the lamp.
nuance: பொய்யா, 'unfailing' and also 'unlying', makes truth a kind of light that shows things as they are.

couplet: Of all good things we've scanned with studious care,
There's nought that can with truthfulness compare.
pope.gloss: Amidst all that we have seen (described) as real (excellence), there is nothing so good as truthfulness.

reading: Among the things we have seen as true, there is nothing at all better than truthfulness.
nuance: The first person, யாம், is a rare moment when the poet speaks as himself. Parimelazhagar turns 'what we have seen' into the scriptures revealed by the Lord, but Manakkudavar keeps it simple as what we have found to be true, and nothing in the verse mentions texts.

title: வெகுளாமை
theme: Anger is the self-destroying fire: it kills smiles and joy, burns the raft that would save a person, and returns on the one who holds it. Restraint counts only where anger could have had its way, and the one who drops it equals those who have renounced everything.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: where non-anger applies (301), the evil of anger (302-304), the harm to the angry person (305-307), the good of non-anger (308), what the non-angry gain (309), and the fruits of both (310).
source_issues: 304, 309: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
304: Parimelazhagar's gloss has உவகையம் for உவகையும் and பகையம் for பகையும்.
303: Manakkudavar's entry begins with a fragment of the verse text.

couplet: Where thou hast power thy angry will to work, thy wrath restrain;
Where power is none, what matter if thou check or give it rein?
pope.gloss: He restrains his anger who restrains it when it can injure; when it cannot injure, what does it matter whether he restrain it, or not ?

reading: One who guards his anger where it can take effect truly guards it; where it can't, what does guarding or not guarding matter?
nuance: Virtue is located only where power is. Patience toward those who could crush you may be just caution, and the verse declines to count it.

couplet: Where power is none to wreak thy wrath, wrath importent is ill;
Where thou hast power thy will to work, 'tis greater, evil still.
pope.gloss: Anger is bad, even when it cannot injure; when it can injure; there is no greater evil.

reading: Anger is bad where it can't take effect; where it can, nothing else is worse.
nuance: This closes the gap left by 301, which could be misread as permission to rage where it doesn't matter. Parimelazhagar sets out why: at the strong it rebounds, and at the weak it brings both blame and sin.

couplet: If any rouse thy wrath, the trespass straight forget;
For wrath an endless train of evils will beget.
pope.gloss: Forget anger towards every one, as fountains of evil spring from it.

reading: Forget anger at anyone at all; evils are born from it.
nuance: The verb is மறத்தல், to forget, not to suppress: the instruction asks for anger to go out of mind and not to be held down. Pope's 'trespass' moves the forgetting from the anger to the offence, which the Tamil doesn't do.

couplet: Wrath robs the face of smiles, the heart of joy,
What other foe to man works such annoy?
pope.gloss: Is there a greater enemy than anger, which kills both laughter and joy ?

reading: Is there any other enemy than the anger that kills both the smile and the joy?
nuance: Parimelazhagar assigns the smile to the face and the joy to the heart, so anger destroys both outer and inner. He adds that renunciants have no outer enemies, which is why this inner one stands alone.

couplet: If thou would'st guard thyself, guard against wrath alway;
'Gainst wrath who guards not, him his wrath shall sla y.
pope.gloss: If a man would guard himself, let him guard against anger; if he do not guard it, anger will kill him.

reading: If you would guard yourself, guard against anger; if you don't, it is yourself that anger kills.
nuance: தன்னையே, 'yourself and no other', turns anger's target around. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in light of curses: the ascetic who spends his power cursing loses it, so 'kills' means extreme suffering. Manakkudavar takes it as a threat to life.

couplet: Wrath, the fire that slayeth whose draweth near,
Will burn the helpful 'raft' of kindred dear.
pope.gloss: The fire of anger will burn up even the pleasant raft of friendship.

reading: Anger, the fire that kills what it comes near, burns even the safe raft of one's own people.
nuance: The name சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி is a coinage for fire, 'killer of those it joins'. Parimelazhagar finds a contrast with ordinary fire, which burns only where it touches. It also matters that a raft is being burned by someone who needs it to survive.

couplet: The hand that smites the earth unfailing feels the sting;
So perish they who nurse their wrath as noble thing.
pope.gloss: Destruction will come upon him who ragards anger as a good thing, as surely as the hand of him who strikes the ground will not fail.

reading: The ruin of one who takes anger to be a thing of worth is like the hand of one who strikes the ground, which can't miss.
nuance: பொருள் also varies: Parimelazhagar makes it a quality that displays one's power, citing Vaisesika usage, and Manakkudavar seems to take it as wealth when he speaks of loss of goods. The image is a fine one because the ground is untouched by the blow.

couplet: Though men should work thee woe, like touch of tongues of fire.
'Tis well if thou canst save thy soul from burning ire.
pope.gloss: Though one commit things against you as painful (to bear) as if a bundle of fire had been thrust upon you, it will be well, to refrain, if possible, from anger.

reading: Even if harm is done to you like the touch of massed flames, not being angry, if you can manage it, is good.
nuance: புணரின், 'if it can be managed', is a rare concession in such a chapter. Parimelazhagar notes that such treatment would anger even sages. The commandment admits its own difficulty.

couplet: If man his soul preserve from wrathful fires,
He gains with that whate'er his soul desires.
pope.gloss: If a man never indulges anger in his heart, he will at once obtain whatever he has thought of.

reading: All one has thought of comes together at once, if one doesn't think of anger in the heart.
nuance: The root உள் runs through the whole verse: thought, heart, not thinking. It sets one kind of thinking against another. The promise is enormous, and Parimelazhagar assigns it to the ascetic, though the verse itself doesn't.

couplet: Men of surpassing wrath are like the men who've passed away;
Who wrath renounce, equals of all-renouncing sages they.
pope.gloss: Those, who give way to excessive anger, are no better than dead men; but those, who are freed from it, are equal to those who are freed (from death).

reading: Those who go to excess in anger are like the dead; those who renounce anger are equal to those who have renounced.
nuance: Wordplay carries the argument: இறந்தார் is both 'those who exceed' and 'those who have died'. துறந்தார் doubles in the same way, so a single renunciation is set equal to total renunciation.

title: இன்னாசெய்யாமை
theme: Doing no hurt holds even when hurt would bring great wealth and even toward those who hurt first. The chapter's ground is self-knowledge, since a person who knows pain in his own life has no reason to inflict it, and it adds that hurt returns to its doer by the same day's end.
structure_note: Going by Parimelazhagar's summary remarks, the chapter forbids hurt done for one's own gain (311), hurt done from enmity (312-314), and hurt done carelessly (315), then hurt generally (316-318), and closes on what it brings the doer (319-320). His glosses for 314-319 are misfiled in this source and have not been used for those verses.
source_issues: 313-319: Parimelazhagar's glosses are misaligned. The entry for 313 has its own gloss with 314's gloss run on after it; the entries for 314, 315, 316, 317 and 318 hold his glosses for 315, 316, 317, 318 and 319 respectively; and 319 is marked as not aligned. I didn't use his text for 314-319, and only the first part of the entry for 313.
318: the verse text has தன்னுயிர்ககு ஏன்னாமை for தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை.

couplet: Though ill to neighbour wrought should glorious pride of wealth secure,
No ill to do is fixed decree of men in spirit pure.
pope.gloss: It is the determination of the spotless not to cause sorrow to others, although they could (by so causing) obtain the wealth which confers greatness.

reading: Even if it would bring wealth that gives eminence, not hurting others is the settled stand of the stainless.
nuance: கோள் is a stance held, not a rule obeyed. The verse puts the temptation first and at its strongest, then refuses it in a word.

couplet: Though malice work its worst, planning no ill return, to endure,
And work no ill, is fixed decree of men in spirit pure.
pope.gloss: It is the determination of the spotless not to do evil, even in return, to those who have cherished enmity and done them evil.

reading: Even when someone in hatred has done them hurt, not hurting in return is the settled stand of the stainless.
nuance: Manakkudavar supplies a detail that alters the verse's pairing with 313: here the other person's anger was aroused by one's own fault, whereas 313 treats enmity with no cause. On his view, the two verses together cover both provoked and unprovoked enemies.

couplet: Though unprovoked thy soul malicious foes should sting,
Retaliation wrought inevitable woes will bring.
pope.gloss: In an ascetic inflict suffering even on those who hate him, when he has not done them any evil, it will afterwards give him irretrievable sorrow.

reading: Doing hurt, even to those who hated you though you did nothing, brings sorrow there is no escaping.
nuance: The verse chooses the case where retaliation looks most justified, an unprovoked enemy, and says it still rebounds. Parimelazhagar explains the sorrow by an ascetic's loss of austerity and takes the actor to be a renunciant, as Pope's gloss follows him in doing, but the verse doesn't name one.

couplet: To punish wrong, with kindly benefits the doers ply;
Thus shame their souls; but pass the ill unheeded by.
pope.gloss: The (proper) punishment to those who have done evil (to you), is to put them to shame by showing them kindness, in return and to forget both the evil and the good done on both sides.

reading: The way to punish those who have hurt you is to shame them by doing them good, and then let it go.
nuance: ஒறுத்தல், to punish, is kept: retribution isn't abolished but redefined, and shame remains its instrument, so this isn't quite unconditional love. விடல் adds that one should leave the matter there, without savouring the effect.

couplet: From wisdom's vaunted lore what doth the learner gain,
If as his own he guard not others' souls from pain?
pope.gloss: What benefit has he derived from his knowledge, who does not endeavour to keep off pain from another as much as from himself ?

reading: What comes of understanding, if one doesn't guard against another's pain as one's own?
nuance: பிறிதின், 'of another', is neuter and so can reach beyond humans. போற்று is active guarding, so understanding that doesn't produce care is judged to have no result at all.

couplet: What his own soul has felt as bitter pain,
From making others feel should man abstain.
pope.gloss: Let not a man consent to do those things to another which, he knows, will cause sorrow.

reading: What one has perceived to be painful, one must not come near doing to another.
nuance: A negative golden rule, but with உணர்ந்தவை, what has been felt or perceived, as the basis rather than a principle. Pope's couplet says 'his own soul has felt', and Kalaignar too says known through experience, while Manakkudavar only says known.

couplet: To work no wilful woe, in any wise, through all the days,
To any living soul, is virtue's highest praise.
pope.gloss: It is the chief of all virtues not knowingly to do any person evil, even in the lowest degree, and at any time.

reading: Not doing ill of any degree, at any time, to anyone, with the mind, is the highest thing.
nuance: Three universals pile up before the verse arrives at மனத்தானாம், which pulls in two directions. Manakkudavar and Kalaignar extend the ban to harm even in thought, while Pope's 'wilful' and 'knowingly' limit it to harm that is intended.

couplet: Whose soul has felt the bitter smart of wrong, how can
He wrongs inflict on ever-living soul of man?
pope.gloss: Why does a man inflict upon other creatures those sufferings, which he has found by experience are sufferings to himself ?

reading: Why does one who knows what is hurtful to his own life do hurtful things to other living beings?
nuance: This is posed as a real question and isn't answered. Manakkudavar's touch is that a person differs from unconscious objects in knowing his pain, which is exactly why this conduct is puzzling.

couplet: If, ere the noontide, you to others evil do,
Before the eventide will evil visit you.
pope.gloss: If a man inflict sorrow upon others in the morning, it will come upon him unsought in the very evening.

reading: If you do hurt to others in the forenoon, hurts to you will come in the afternoon, of themselves.
nuance: தாமே, 'of themselves', removes any agent: as Manakkudavar says, nobody else need do it. The speed is rhetorical, since the verse is not a report on timing.

couplet: O'er every evil-doer evil broodeth still;
He evil shuns who freedom seeks from ill.
pope.gloss: Sorrow will come upon those who cause pain to others; therfore those, who desire to be free from sorrow, give no pain to others.

reading: All pains rest on those who caused pain; those who want to be without pain cause none.
nuance: நோய் occurs four times. Taken strictly, 'all pains' has a hard consequence: anyone who suffers must have caused suffering. Manakkudavar accepts it by a time scheme in which present pain derives from past harm, and in that way this chapter leads into the claim of 330.

title: கொல்லாமை
theme: Not killing is the first of all goods, ranked explicitly above truthfulness and above all renunciation. It is absolute, holding even at the cost of one's own life and regardless of any gain, and the chapter ends with the fate of those who kill.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (321-323), that only the path containing it is good (324), the height of the one who keeps it (325), its benefit (326), the fault of killing (327-328), and the harm to killers (329-330).
source_issues: 330: Manakkudavar's text has தீய பனை வாழ்க்கை, likely a misprint for தீய வாழ்க்கை or similar.

couplet: What is the work of virtue? 'Not to kill';
For 'killing' leads to every work of ill.
pope.gloss: Never to destroy life is the sum of all virtuous conduct. The destruction of life leads to every evil.

reading: If you ask what virtuous action is, it is not killing; killing brings all the other kind of deed.
nuance: பிறவினை, 'other deeds', leaves the wrongness to be inferred. Parimelazhagar takes it as a claim about results: the suffering killing yields exceeds that of all other sins combined.

couplet: Let those that need partake your meal; guard every-thing that lives;
This the chief and sum of lore that hoarded wisdom gives.
pope.gloss: The chief of all (the virtues) which authors have summed up, is the partaking of food that has been shared with others, and the preservation of the mainfold life of other creatures.

reading: Sharing one's food and sustaining many lives is the chief of all that the authors have gathered.
nuance: Inside a chapter on not killing, the crown goes to a positive act of feeding, so non-harm here isn't only refraining. Parimelazhagar assigns the summary to renunciants, Manakkudavar says it is good for all faiths, and Kalaignar reads an egalitarian creed into it.

couplet: Alone, first of goods things, is 'not to slay';
The second is, no untrue word to say.
pope.gloss: Not to destroy life is an incomparably (great) good next to it in goodness ranks freedom from falsehood.

reading: Good beyond compare is not killing; following behind it, not lying is good.
nuance: A rare moment of the Kural ranking two of its own highest claims. Parimelazhagar recognizes this: since 297 and 300 raised doubt about which is greater, this verse settles it, and it can do so because truth depends on results and therefore shifts.

couplet: You ask, What is the good and perfect way?
'Tis path of him who studies nought to slay.
pope.gloss: Good path is that which considers how it may avoid killing any creature.

reading: If you ask what is called the good path, it is the way that keeps in view not killing anything at all.
nuance: The question form follows 291 and 321, as if the Kural is defining terms. யாதொன்றும் is wide, and Parimelazhagar says it takes in even one-sensed life. சூழும் makes it a matter of constant attention rather than a single vow.

couplet: Of those who 'being' dread, and all renounce, the chief are they,
Who dreading crime of slaughter, study nought to slay.
pope.gloss: Of all those who, fearing the permanence of earthly births, have abandoned desire, he is the chief who, fearing (the guilt of) murder, considers how he may avoid the destruction of life.

reading: Among all who renounced out of fear of their condition, the one who fears killing and keeps not killing in view is chief.
nuance: Two fears are set side by side with the repeated அஞ்சி, one about one's own state and the other about another's life. The second outranks the first.

couplet: Ev'n death that life devours, their happy days shall spare,
Who law, 'Thou shall not kill', uphold with reverent care.
pope.gloss: Yama, the destroyer of life, will not attack the life of him, who acts under the determination of never destroying life.

reading: Death, the devourer of life, does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing.
nuance: The symmetry is exact: the one who won't kill is not killed, and the killer of all refrains here.

couplet: Though thine own life for that spared life the price must pay,
Take not from aught that lives gift of sweet life away.
pope.gloss: Let no one do that which would destroy the life of another, although he should by so doing, lose his own life.

reading: Even if your own life should go, do not do the deed that takes away another's sweet life.
nuance: இன்னுயிர் gives the other's life the word for sweetness, while one's own is just உயிர். This is the Kural's hardest statement of the rule, and it allows no exception of necessity.

couplet: Though great the gain of good should seem, the wise
Will any gain by staughter won despise.
pope.gloss: The advantage which might flow from destroying life in sacrifice, is dishonourable to the wise (who renounced the world), even although it should be said to be productive of great good.

reading: However great the gain that would bring good, gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy.
nuance: The verse mentions no sacrifice. That whole issue comes from the older commentators and through them Pope's gloss.

couplet: Whose trade is 'killing', always vile they show,
To minds of them who what is vileness know.
pope.gloss: Men who destroy life are base men, in the estimation of those who know the nature of meanness.

reading: People whose work is killing are of base occupation in the eyes of those who discern what baseness is.
nuance: Baseness is assigned by work, not birth, as both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar stress, though the word புலை itself carries caste weight. Parimelazhagar's claim here that sacrifice isn't killing at all fits awkwardly with his note on 328.

tamil: உயிர் உடம்பின் நீக்கியார் என்ப செயிர் உடம்பின்

couplet: Who lead a loathed life in bodies sorely pained,
Are men, the wise declare, by guilt of slaughter stained.
pope.gloss: (The wise) will say that men of diseased bodies, who live in degradation and in poverty, are those who separated the life from the body of animals (in a former birth).

reading: Those in wretched bodies, leading an evil and failing life, they say, are people who separated life from body.
nuance: என்ப, 'they say', is the verse's own hedge. It doesn't mention a former birth, which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar supply. Its logic runs backward from a sufferer to his guilt, and that makes it one of the more troubling claims in this section.

title: நிலையாமை
theme: Nothing lasts: wealth disperses like a theatre crowd, each day is a blade, and life is a lodger in the body. The error is mistaking this for permanence, and the practical conclusion is urgency: do good now.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the error of taking the passing for lasting (331), the impermanence of wealth (332-333), and the impermanence of the body (334-340), which he traces step by step through days passing, death, sudden loss, uncertainty, the corpse, the round of births, and the body not being the soul's own.
source_issues: 333: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse. Parimelazhagar's gloss has the misprint இயல்பினையுடையப்து.
334: Manakkudavar's closing note is garbled (நிலை பா ைக றிற்று), and Parimelazhagar's gloss has several misprints.
338: Parimelazhagar spells the word குடும்பை where the verse has குடம்பை.
340: Parimelazhagar's closing remark has இவை ஏது பாட்டானும், evidently ஏழு (seven verses, 334-340).

couplet: Lowest and meanest lore, that bids men trust secure,
In things that pass away, as things that shall endure!
pope.gloss: That ignorance which considers those things to be stable which are not so, is dishonourable (to the wise).

reading: The paltry understanding that takes what doesn't last for what lasts is the lowest.
nuance: The fault is cognitive before it is moral: a mistake of knowledge, sarcastically dignified with ஆண்மை, mastery. Parimelazhagar limits 'lowest' to those seeking release, for whom this error feeds attachment, and the verse doesn't state that limit.

couplet: As crowds round dancers fill the hall, is wealth's increase;
Its loss, as throngs dispersing, when the dances cease.
pope.gloss: The acquisition of wealth is like the gathering together of an assembly for a theatre; its expenditure is like the breaking up of that assembly.

reading: The coming of great wealth is like a crowd gathering at a dance hall, and its going is like that crowd breaking up.
nuance: A crowd has its own reason for being there, and Parimelazhagar presses this: wealth comes because of good deeds, of its own accord, and leaves when that cause is spent. So the owner is no more than the hall. His addition that this includes heavenly wealth is his own.

couplet: Unenduring is all wealth; if you wealth enjoy,
Enduring works in working wealth straightway employ.
pope.gloss: Wealth is perishable; let those who obtain it immediately practise those (virtues) which are imperishable.

reading: Wealth has the nature of not staying; if you get it, do straight away what stays.
nuance: அற்கா and அற்குப play on one root, so what doesn't stay can be converted into what does. For Parimelazhagar 'what stays' means worship and giving without expecting fruit, leading to release, though the verse doesn't name them.

couplet: As 'day' it vaunts itself; well understood, 'tis knife',
That daily cuts away a portion from thy life.
pope.gloss: Time, which shows itself (to the ignorant) as if it were something (real) is in the estimation of the wise (only) a saw which cuts down life.

reading: It shows itself as a thing called a day, but it is a blade that saws through life, if one can find those who perceive it.
nuance: Parimelazhagar: the fool rejoices that time is passing, and doesn't realize it is his own time. He grammatically dismisses a rival division of the words at length. உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் admits how few will ever see it this way.

couplet: Before the tongue lie powerless, 'mid the gasp of gur gling breath,
Arouse thyself, and do good deeds beyond the power of death.
pope.gloss: Let virtuous deeds be done quickly, before the biccup comes making the tongue silent.

reading: Before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue, good deeds must be rushed to.
nuance: The image is the plain physical detail of the death rattle, with no metaphor. Parimelazhagar notes that it is the tongue being stopped, meaning that one can't even instruct others to act, and that no one knows when it will come.

couplet: Existing yesterday, today to nothing hurled!-
Such greatness owns this transitory world.
pope.gloss: This world possesses the greatness that one who yesterday was is not today.

reading: This world has the greatness that one who was here yesterday isn't here today.
nuance: பெருமை is bitter here. Parimelazhagar takes it as excess, an overflow of impermanence, while Manakkudavar simply repeats 'greatness'. Kalaignar makes it the world's arrogance, boasting of having killed. All three hear the irony, in different keys.

couplet: Who know not if their happy lives shall last the day,
In fancies infinite beguile the hours away!
pope.gloss: Innumerable are the thoughts which occupy the mind of (the unwise), who know not that they shall live another moment.

reading: Those who can't know they will live one moment more have thoughts in the many crores.
nuance: The disproportion, a moment against crores, is the joke. Parimelazhagar gives a delightful catalogue of what such people plan: acquiring, guarding, overcoming, and raising friends and ruining rivals.

couplet: Birds fly away, and leave the nest deserted bare;
Such is the short-lived friendship soul and body share.
pope.gloss: The love of the soul to the body is like (the love of) a bird to its egg which it flies away from and leaves empty.

reading: The friendship between body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its குடம்பை alone.
nuance: நட்பு, friendship, is heavily ironic: for Parimelazhagar there is none, only a union forced by deeds.

couplet: Death is sinking into slumbers deep;
Birth again is waking out of sleep.
pope.gloss: Death is like sleep; birth is like awaking from it.

reading: Death is like falling asleep, and birth is like waking after sleep.
nuance: The verse is very short and calm, with nothing about what happens in between. Its tone can be taken as reassuring or as a further turn of the screw. Parimelazhagar says birth is included to show that impermanence is itself what is permanent.

couplet: The soul in fragile shed as lodger courts repose:-
Is it because no home's conclusive rest it knows?
pope.gloss: It seems as if the soul, which takes a temporary shelter in a body, had not attained a home.

reading: Has the life that sits as a lodger in the body not found a home of its own?
nuance: துச்சில், a lodger's corner in another's house, is homely and sad, and the verse is a soft question rather than a declaration.

title: துறவு
theme: Renunciation is the removal of attachment to what is 'mine' and even to the 'I'. It begins with freedom from each thing's pain and reaches release, while those who keep any hold stay in the net. The chapter ends in the paradox that one must cling to get free of clinging.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: giving up the outer attachment 'mine' (341-344), giving up the inner attachment 'I', that is, the body (345), release for those who give up both (346), both outcomes (347-349), and the means (350).
source_issues: 341: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.

couplet: From whatever, aye, whatever, man gets free,
From what, aye, from that, no more of pain hath he!
pope.gloss: Whatever thing, a man has renounced, by that thing; he cannot suffer pain.

reading: From whatever, whatever one has left, from that, from that, one has no pain.
nuance: The doubled words make this piecemeal, and Parimelazhagar accepts that: giving up everything at once is best, but each thing left removes its own pain. So renunciation isn't all or nothing in this verse.

couplet: 'Renunciation' made- ev'n here true pleasures men acquire;
'Renounce' while time is yet, if to those pleasures you aspire.
pope.gloss: After a man has renounced (all things), there will still be many things in this world (which he may enjoy); if he should desire them, let him, while it is time abandon. (the world).

reading: If you want it, renounce while there is time; after renouncing, there are many things that come about here.
nuance: The verse is elliptical. Parimelazhagar concedes that he has supplied both 'joys' and 'time', so much of what appears to be said is commentary. Its surprise, on his reading, is that renunciation brings joys in this life and not only the end of pain. It also starts with வேண்டின், 'if you want'.

couplet: 'Perceptions of the five' must all expire;-
Relinquished in its order each desire
pope.gloss: Let the five senses be destroyed; and at the same time, let everything be abandoned that (the ascetic) has (formerly) desired.

reading: The domain of the five must be crushed, and all that one has wanted must be let go at once.
nuance: புலம் is the field of the senses, their enjoyment, and not the organs that Pope's gloss has destroyed. Parimelazhagar gives the reason for 'at once': sense enjoyment fed with objects only burns higher, like fire with fuel.

couplet: 'Privation absolute' is penance true;
'Possession' brings bewilderment anew.
pope.gloss: To be altogether destitute is the proper condition of those who perform austerities; if they possess anything, it will change (their resolution) and bring them back to their confused state.

reading: Having nothing at all is natural to austerity; having anything brings back confusion all over again.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reading is psychological: keep one thing and everything given up returns through it. Manakkudavar links the confusion to further birth.

couplet: To those who sev'rance seek from being's varied strife,
Flesh is burthen sore; what then other bonds of life?
pope.gloss: What means the addition of other things those who are attempting to cut off (future) births, when even their body is too much (for them).

reading: For those set on cutting off births, even the body is excess; why then any further ties?
nuance: The body is the one tool needed for the work and still counts as excess. Parimelazhagar divides it into gross and subtle bodies, a doctrine the verse doesn't state, and makes this the renunciation of the inner 'I'.

tamil: யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு அறுப்பான் வானோர்க்கு

couplet: Who kills conceit that utters 'I' and 'mine',
Shall enter realms above the powers divine.
pope.gloss: He who destroys the pride which says "I", "mine" will enter a world which is difficult even to the Gods to attain.

reading: One who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'.
nuance: செருக்கு is glossed as delusion by the older commentators, as Parimelazhagar also does at 201: for them, the problem is a false identification and not arrogant manners. The body isn't 'I' and goods aren't 'mine'.

couplet: Who cling to things that cling and eager clasp,
Griefs cling to them with unrelaxing grasp.
pope.gloss: Sorrows will never let go their hold of those who give not up their hold of desire.

reading: Griefs that hold and won't let go hold those who hold attachment and won't let go.
nuance: The two lines use one verb for the person and the griefs, so that the grip one keeps and the grip one suffers are shown to be the same act.

couplet: Who thoroughly 'renounce' on highest height are set;
The rest bewildered, lie entangled in the net.
pope.gloss: Those who have entirely renounced (all things and all desire) have obtained (absorption into God); all others wander in confusion, entangled in the net of (many) births.

reading: Those who have thoroughly renounced have got to the head; the rest, in confusion, are in the net.
nuance: தலைப்பட்டார் doesn't say what has been reached, and the past tense suggests it is already done. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar say release, Kalaignar says a high state, and Pope's gloss has 'absorption into God', which adds a theology the Tamil doesn't have.

couplet: When that which clings falls off, severed is being's tie;
All else will then be seen as instability.
pope.gloss: At the moment in which desire has been abandoned, (other) births will be cut off; when that has not been done, instability will be seen.

reading: The moment attachment ends it cuts off births; otherwise impermanence is what is seen.
nuance: கண்ணே, 'at the very moment', makes release immediate, as an effect stops with its cause. Parimelazhagar takes மற்று as 'if not', and Pope's couplet and gloss diverge on it, the couplet making impermanence what is seen after the release, the gloss what is seen without it.

couplet: Cling thou to that which He, to Whom nought clings, hath bid thee cling,
Cling to that bond, to get thee free from every clinging thing.
pope.gloss: Desire the desire of Him who is without desire; in order to renounce desire, desire that desire.

reading: Cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging; cling to that clinging, in order to let clinging go.
nuance: பற்று comes six times in seven words, and the chapter on letting go ends by commanding a holding on. A useful attachment is the ladder that lets one drop the others.

title: மெய்யுணர்தல்
theme: Seeing what is really so is what ends suffering and birth: mistaking the unreal for the real starts it, and stripping off appearances ends it. The chapter never says what மெய்ப்பொருள் is, and this silence is where its commentators divide most.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads a sequence: confusion as the root of birth (351), true sight as the way to release (352-354), its definition (355), three means which he names hearing, reflection and contemplation (356, 357, 358), and how remaining suffering ends (359-360).
source_issues: 357: the verse text reads உணரான், 'does not know', while Parimelazhagar's gloss, உள்ளது உணரின், and Pope and the others all read the conditional உணரின். As printed, the verse would make no sense with the commentary.
360: the verse text has the corruption இநவ்முன்றன் for இவைமூன்றன்.
351: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.

couplet: Of things devoid of truth as real things men deem;-
Cause of degraded birth the fond delusive dream!
pope.gloss: Inglorious births are produced by the confusion (of mind) which considers those things to be real which are not real.

reading: A joyless birth comes from the confusion that perceives what isn't real as real.
nuance: The verse doesn't say which things are unreal. Parimelazhagar fills this in as denying rebirth, the fruit of deeds, and God, adding the stump mistaken for a man and shell for silver. Kalaignar has no birth in view, only a life that goes poorly.

couplet: Darkness departs, and rapture springs to men who see,
The mystic vision pure, from all delusion free.
pope.gloss: A clear, undimmed vision of things will deliver its possessors from the darkness of future births, and confer the felicity (of heaven).

reading: For those of stainless sight, who have left confusion behind, it removes darkness and brings joy.
nuance: What is the darkness? Parimelazhagar says hell, Manakkudavar and Kalaignar say ignorance, and Pope's gloss says the darkness of future births. The verse leaves it as a word.

couplet: When doubts disperse, and mists of error roll
Away, nearer is heav'n than earth to sage's soul.
pope.gloss: Heaven is nearer than earth to those men of purified minds who are freed from from doubt.

reading: For those who have left doubt and become clear, the sky is nearer than the earth they stand on.
nuance: Doubt here is the obstacle in its own right. Parimelazhagar makes an unusually candid point: every school's texts refute the others, so which is true can only be settled through one's own experience. The image of the far as nearer than the near is very bold.

couplet: Five-fold perception gained, what benefits accrue
To them whose spirits lack perception of the true?
pope.gloss: Even those who have all the knowledge which can be attained by the five senses, will derive no benefit from it, if they are without a knowledge of the true nature of things.

reading: Even having gained the five-fold awareness, there is no benefit for those who lack true perception.

couplet: Whatever thing, of whatsoever kind it be,
'Tis wisdom's part in each the very thing to see.
pope.gloss: (True) knowledge is the perception concerning every thing of whatever kind, that that thing is the true thing.

reading: Whatever a thing is and of whatever nature, seeing the true thing in that thing is understanding.
nuance: One of the Kural's best-known definitions, and it is doctrinally open. Parimelazhagar removes a Chera king's rank, lineage, looks and names as conventions, down to the elements and beyond, while Kalaignar asks only that we not be fooled by appearances. It is both a metaphysical and a practical line.

couplet: Who learn, and here the knowledge of the true obtain,
Shall find the path that hither cometh not again.
pope.gloss: They, who in this birth have learned to know the True Being, enter the road which returns not into this world.

reading: Those who have learned here and seen the true thing will reach the path of not coming back here.
nuance: Here learning is an actual route to the truth, in contrast to 373. For Parimelazhagar this is hearing from an experienced teacher, the first of his three means.

couplet: The mind that knows with certitude what is, and ponders well,
Its thoughts on birth again to other life need not to dwell.
pope.gloss: Let it not be thought that there is another birth for him whose mind having thoroughly considered (all it has been taught) has known the True Being.

reading: If the mind ponders and knows with certainty what is, one needn't think again of birth.
nuance: உள்ளது, 'what is', is the plainest of the chapter's names for the goal. This reading assumes the commentators' உணரின் over the verse text's உணரான், as noted in source_issues.

couplet: When folly, cause of births, departs; and soul can view
The truth of things, man's dignity- 'tis wisdom true.
pope.gloss: True knowledge consists in the removal of ignorance; which is (the cause of) births, and the perception of the True Being who is (the bestower of) heaven.

reading: Understanding is seeing the perfect thing called the excellent, so that the folly called birth departs.
nuance: The verse calls birth itself a folly, an astonishing metaphor that all three commentators have to unpack, each differently. Pope's 'man's dignity' for சிறப்பு goes in a different direction from all of them.

couplet: The true 'support' who knows- rejects 'supports' he sought before-
Sorrow that clings all destroys, shall cling to him no more.
pope.gloss: He who so lives as to know Him who is the support of all things and abandon all desire, will be freed from the evils which would otherwise cleave to him and destroy (his efforts after absorption).

reading: If one knows the support and lives so that supports perish, the pains due to cling won't destroy that life and cling.
nuance: One word, சார்பு, does double service. Parimelazhagar adds that the fruit even of good deeds counts as 'pain' here, because it causes birth, which is a hard saying.

couplet: When lust and wrath and error's triple tyranny is o'er,
Their very names for aye extinct, then pain shall be no more.
pope.gloss: If the very names of these three things, desire, anger, and confusion of mind, be destroyed, then will also perish evils (which flow from them).

reading: When even the names of the three, desire, anger and confusion, perish, pain perishes.
nuance: நாமம், 'the name', is what must go, so they aren't merely suppressed. This triad resembles the three poisons in Buddhist teaching, a comparison that is mine and no commentator's. Parimelazhagar derives it by reducing a Sanskrit list of five faults.

title: அவாவறுத்தல்
theme: Craving is the seed of all birth and the sorrow of sorrows, and its removal, not any other act, is the direct cause of an unchanging state. The whole section on renunciation ends here, by locating release at the moment when wanting stops.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: desire as the seed of birth (361), the excellence of not wanting (362-363), how release comes about (364), its praise from both sides (365), desire's danger (366), the benefit of cutting it (367), desire as the cause of sorrow (368), joy in this life (369), and what release is (370). Manakkudavar notes at 370 that the section on renunciation ends here.
source_issues: 361, 363, 365: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
366: Parimelazhagar's gloss has the misprint அவர் for அவா (கெடுக்கவல்லது அவர்).

couplet: The wise declare, through all the days, to every living thing.
That ceaseless round of birth from seed of strong desire doth spring.
pope.gloss: (The wise) say that the seed, which produces unceasing births, at all times, to all creatures, is desire.

reading: They say craving is the seed that, for all beings at all times, produces unceasing birth.
nuance: என்ப, 'they say', is read by Parimelazhagar as marking agreement among all schools. He supplies a mechanism: at death, craving carries the life to its next state. Kalaignar keeps the seed but removes birth.

couplet: If desire you feel, freedom from changing birth require!
'I' will come, if you desire to 'scape, set free from all desire.
pope.gloss: If anything be desired, freedom from births should be desired; that (freedom from births) will be attained by desiring to be without desire.

reading: If you must want, want not to be born; that comes when you want not to want.
nuance: A paradox as neat as 350. The verb வேண்டு occurs in every clause, and the verse doesn't pretend desire can simply be stopped. It redirects desire until it undoes itself.

couplet: No glorious wealth is here like freedom from desire;
To bliss like this not even there can soul aspire.
pope.gloss: There is in this world no excellence equal to freedom from desire; and even in that world, there is nothing like it.

reading: There is no fine wealth here like not wanting, and nothing there equals it either.
nuance: It is pointed to name wanting nothing as wealth. Parimelazhagar explains why it is the top: human and divine wealth always have something above them, so only not wanting has no superior.

couplet: Desire's decease as purity men know;
That, too, from yearning search for truth will grow.
pope.gloss: Purity (of mind) consists in freedom from desire; and that (freedom from desire) is the fruit of the love of truth.

reading: Purity is the absence of craving, and that comes by wanting வாய்மை.
nuance: The word தூய்மை also differs: for Parimelazhagar it is release itself, as the soul's stains are gone, and for Manakkudavar it is the removal of defilement.

couplet: Men freed from bonds of strong desire are free;
None other share such perfect lib erty.
pope.gloss: They are said to be free (from future birth) who are freed from desire; all others (who, whatever else they may be free from, are not freed from desire) are not thus free.

reading: Those called 'freed' are those freed of craving; the rest are not so freed.
nuance: அற்றார் is left without an object, and that is the wit. Being cut free of other things is a partial matter, which Parimelazhagar makes explicit: others have only avoided some pains.

couplet: Desire each soul beguiles;
True virtue dreads its wiles.
pope.gloss: It is the chief duty of (an ascetic) to watch against desire with (jealous) fear; for it has power to deceive (and destroy) him.

reading: It is virtue alone to fear; what deceives a person is craving.
nuance: Craving is a confidence trick: Manakkudavar has it stand in front like a benefactor and then lead one down. Parimelazhagar has it slip in through a moment's inattention, even for someone close to release. So vigilance has no end point.

couplet: Who thoroughly rids his life of passion-prompted deed,
Deeds of unfailing worth shall do, which, as he plans, succeed.
pope.gloss: If a man thoroughly cut off all desire, the deeds, which confer immortality, will come to him, in the path in which he seeks them.

reading: If one cuts off craving thoroughly, the deeds that don't fail come in the way one wishes.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes a bold antinomian comment: once craving is fully cut, no other virtue need be done, and everything one does is virtue. The verse says only that the right deeds arrive.

couplet: Affliction is not known where no desires abide;
Where these are, endless rises sorrow's tide.
pope.gloss: There is no sorrow to those who are without desire; but where that is, (sorrow) will incessantly come, more and more.

reading: Those without craving have no sorrow; if it exists, sorrow keeps coming, unfailing, on and on.
nuance: The claim seems too simple, since those without craving still get sick. Parimelazhagar sees this and limits it: the suffering that came with the body is already earned, and the verse means suffering created now.

couplet: When dies away desire, that woe of woes
Ev'n here the soul unceasing rapture knows.
pope.gloss: Even while in this body, joy will never depart (from the mind, in which) desire, that sorrow of sorrows, has been destroyed.

reading: Joy will be unbroken ஈண்டும், if the sorrow of sorrows called craving perishes.
nuance: Craving is not just the cause of sorrow but is itself the worst sorrow. Parimelazhagar explains that it hurts both at its source and in its fruit.

couplet: Drive from thy soul desire insatiate;
Straight'way is gained the moveless blissful state.
pope.gloss: The removal of desire, whose nature it is never to be satisfied, will immediately confer a nature that can never be changed.

reading: If one gives up craving, whose nature is never to be filled, right then it gives a nature that never shifts.
nuance: The rhyme of ஆரா and பேரா sets an insatiable nature against an immovable one, and அந்நிலையே makes it immediate. Parimelazhagar calls this person liberated while living and quotes the Tiruvaymoli. The verse says only that the nature doesn't move.

title: ஊழ்
theme: Fate as the force behind wealth, understanding, and pleasure and pain. It reaches even the qualities a person might rely on against it, such as effort and intelligence.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: fate's power over wealth (371-376), over enjoyment and suffering (377-379), and in general (380).

couplet: Wealth-giving fate power of unflinching effort brings;
From fate that takes away idle remissness springs.
pope.gloss: Perseverance comes from a prosperous fate, and idleness from an adverse fate.

reading: A fate of gain produces tireless effort and a fate of loss produces sloth.
nuance: Effort is presented as fate's product, not its rival, so the verse removes the usual escape route from fate.

couplet: The fate that loss ordains makes wise men's wisdom foolishness;
The fate that gain bestows with ampler powers will wisdom bless.
pope.gloss: An adverse fate produces folly, and a prosperous fate produces enlarged knowledge.

reading: A fate of loss makes a person foolish, and a fate of gain, when it arrives, enlarges their understanding.
nuance: Intelligence is not a fixed possession here; circumstances of fortune change it.

couplet: In subtle learning manifold though versed man be,
'The wisdom, truly his, will gain supremacy.
pope.gloss: Although (a man) may study the most polished treatises, the knowledge which fate has decreed to him will still prevail.

reading: However many subtle books a person studies, their own understanding still prevails.
nuance: The verse doesn't say whose understanding wins or why. The commentators fill that gap differently, and தன் உண்மை அறிவு carries the dispute.

couplet: Two fold the fashion of the world: some live in fortune's light;
While other some have souls in wisdom's radiance bright.
pope.gloss: There are (through fate) two different natures in the world, hence the difference (observable in men) in (their acquisition of) wealth, and in their attainment of knowledge.

reading: The world has two distinct natures: being wealthy is one thing, and being wise is another.
nuance: Parimelazhagar draws a pointed conclusion: since the wise can be poor and others rich, wealth does not need wisdom as a cause.

couplet: All things that good appear will oft have ill success;
All evil things prove good for gain of happiness.
pope.gloss: In the acquisition of property, every thing favourable becomes unfavourable, and (on the other hand) everything unfavourable becomes favourable, (through the power of fate).

reading: In making wealth, all that is favourable can turn out badly and all that is unfavourable can turn out well.

couplet: Things not your own will yield no good, howe'er you guard with pain;
Your own, howe'er you scatter them abroad, will yours remain.
pope.gloss: Whatever is not conferred by fate cannot be preserved although it be guarded with most painful care; and that, which fate has made his, cannot be lost, although one should even take it and throw it away.

reading: What is not yours will not stay however carefully you guard it, and what is yours will not leave though you throw it away.

couplet: Save as the 'sharer' shares to each in due degree,
To those who millions store enjoyment scarce can be.
pope.gloss: Even those who gather together millions will only enjoy them, as it has been determined by the disposer (of all things).

reading: Even those who have amassed millions can enjoy them only as the one who apportions has apportioned.
nuance: வகுத்தான் gives fate a personal agent. This is one of the chapter's clearest points of disagreement about whether a cosmic agent is present.

couplet: The destitute with ascetics merit share,
If fate to visit with predestined ills would spare.
pope.gloss: The destitute will renounce desire (and become ascetics), if (fate) do not make them suffer the hindrances to which they are liable, and they pass away.
