reading: The destitute would renounce the world, if only what they are bound to suffer would pass without afflicting them.
nuance: The irony is dry: the poor already lack what renunciation gives up, yet fate withholds even that peace.

couplet: When good things come, men view them all as gain;
When evils come, why then should they complain?
pope.gloss: How is it that those, who are pleased with good fortune, trouble themselves when evil comes, (since both are equally the decree of fa te) ?

reading: Those who accept things as good when good comes: why do they grieve when it doesn't?
nuance: After nine verses on fate's power, this one asks for a response. Fate here is the premise of equanimity.

couplet: What powers so great as those of Destiny? Man's skill
Some other thing contrives; but fate's beforehand still.
pope.gloss: What is stronger than fate ? If we think of an expedient (to avert it), it will itself be with us before (the thought).

reading: What is stronger than fate? Even when one devises another way, it gets there first.

title: இறைமாட்சி
theme: What makes a king excellent: not power alone but a set of resources and qualities that must be held without lapse, and above all how he is to the people who approach him. His standing is conferred from below, by those who praise him, shelter under him, and set him apart.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar opens with the six limbs of a kingdom (381), then treats the king's excellence (382-385) and excellence together with its fruits (386-390).
source_issues: 382: Parimelazhagar's gloss reads தீமையும் where the word glossed is அஞ்சாமை. It is probably a corruption, perhaps of திண்மையும், so I did not rely on it.

couplet: An army, people, wealth, a minister, friends, fort: six things-
Who owns them all, a lion lives amid the kings.
pope.gloss: He who possesses these six things, an army, a people, wealth, ministers, friends and a fortress, is a lion among kings.

reading: One who has all six, an army, a people, resources, ministers, allies and a fort, stands among kings as the male leads its herd.
nuance: ஏறு names the male of a species, not specifically a lion. Pope's and Kalaignar's lion is an interpretive choice. Parimelazhagar presses ஆறும்: lacking even one limb, royal policy doesn't function.

couplet: Courage, a liberal hand, wisdom, and energy: these four
Are qualities a king adorn for evermore.
pope.gloss: Never to fail in these four things, fearlessness, liberality, wisdom, and energy, is the kingly character.

reading: Fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive, these four never failing, are the nature of a king.
nuance: The weight is on எஞ்சாமை. Parimelazhagar explains that when one quality surfaces in a person others recede, and a king can't afford that, so the verse asks for constancy as well as possession.

couplet: A sleepless promptitude, knowledge, decision strong:
These three for aye to rulers of the land belong.
pope.gloss: These three things, viz., vigilance, learning, and bravery, should never be wanting in the ruler of a country.

reading: Promptness, learning and resolve: these three do not leave those who rule the land.

couplet: Kingship, in virtue failing not, all vice restrains,
In courage failing not, it honour's grace maintains.
pope.gloss: He is a king who, with manly modesty, swerves not from virtue, and refrains from vice.

reading: A king does not stray from virtue, removes what is not virtue, and keeps an honour that does not stray from valour.
nuance: The verse pairs அறன் with மறன், so virtue and martial valour stand side by side as parts of one honour. Parimelazhagar illustrates this honour with rules of war, such as not striking the young, the old or one who flees.

couplet: A king is he who treasure gains, stores up, defends,
And duly for his kingdom's weal expends.
pope.gloss: He is a king who is able to acquire (wealth), to lay it up, to guard, and to distribute it.

reading: A king is one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it, and apportion what is guarded.
nuance: Four verbs form a cycle that ends in distribution, not in holding. The verse doesn't say to whom. Parimelazhagar spreads the giving over virtue, wealth and pleasure, while Manakkudavar's example is equipping the army.

couplet: Where king is easy of access, where no harsh word repels,
That land's high praises every subject swells.
pope.gloss: The whole world will exalt the country of the king who is easy of access, and who is free from harsh language.

reading: If a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech, his land is spoken of above others.
nuance: The grammar praises the land, not the king. Parimelazhagar notes that praising the land makes praising the king unnecessary, though he has to supply the world as the speaker.

couplet: With pleasant speech, who gives and guards with powerful liberal hand,
He sees the world obedient all to his command.
pope.gloss: The world will praise and submit itself to the mind of the king who is able to give with affability, and to protect all who come to him.

reading: For those who can give and protect with pleasant words, this world falls in with their word and their intent.
nuance: The second line is compressed, and my reading of தன் சொலால் தான் கண்டனைத்து is tentative. Pleasant speech is named as what makes the giving work, not as an extra.

couplet: Who guards the realm and justice strict maintains,
That king as god o'er subject people reigns.
pope.gloss: That king, will be esteemed a God among men, who performs his own duties, and protects (his subjects).

reading: The ruler who does justice and protects is set apart as இறை for the people.
nuance: வைக்கப்படும் is passive and conditional: the status is awarded for doing justice, not held by right of office.

couplet: The king of worth, who can words bitter to his ear endure,
Beneath the shadow of his power the world abides secure.
pope.gloss: The whole world will dwell under the umbrella of the king, who can bear words that embitter the ear.

reading: The world rests under the parasol of a king with the character to bear words that are bitter to the ear.
nuance: செவிகைப்ப moves a taste onto the ear, as Parimelazhagar points out. Tolerance of bitterness is presented as what brings the world under the parasol, which reverses the usual picture of power as not having to listen.

couplet: Gifts, grace, right sceptre, care of people's weal;
These four a light of dreaded kings reveal.
pope.gloss: He is the light of kings who has there four things, beneficence, benevolence, rectitude, and care for his people.

reading: One who has these four, giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people, is a light among kings.
nuance: Manakkudavar reads all four as relief for struggling farmers, including seed and plough and deferred or waived dues. That makes the verse far more concrete than its abstract nouns suggest.

title: கல்வி
theme: Learning as the thing that makes a person see, belong anywhere, and possess what can't be lost. It begins and is only complete in conduct: to learn is also to stand by what is learned.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: what to learn and why (391), the instruments of letters and numbers (392), the height of the learned against the unlearned (393-395), and the distinction of learning itself (396-400).

couplet: So learn that you may full and faultless learning gain,
Then in obedience meet to lessons learnt remain.
pope.gloss: Let a man learn thoroughly whatever he may learn, and let his conduct be worthy of his learning.

reading: Learn what is to be learned without flaw, and having learned, stand in keeping with it.
nuance: நிற்க gives conduct a posture: the chapter's first verse makes learning unfinished until one stands by it. Parimelazhagar narrows கற்பவை to works on the aims of life, on the grounds that life is too short for the rest, but the verse leaves the scope open.

couplet: The twain that lore of numbers and of letters give
Are eyes, the wise declare, to all on earth that live.
pope.gloss: Letters and numbers are the two eyes of man.

reading: What are called numbers and what are called letters, these two, are called the eyes of living beings.
nuance: The verse says வாழும் உயிர்க்கு and doesn't restrict it. Parimelazhagar limits it to beings of special understanding and treats the two as tools for seeing the aims of life; Kalaignar goes further and makes them the test of being alive at all.

couplet: Men who learning gain have eyes, men say;
Blockheads' faces pairs of sores display.
pope.gloss: The learned are said to have eyes, but the unlearned have (merely) two sores in their face.

reading: Those called people with eyes are the learned; the unlearned have two sores on their face.
nuance: The insult works because the sore is in the same place and looks similar. Parimelazhagar adds that a merely physical eye gives pain through disease. Kalaignar draws an inference absent from the verse, that a blind person who is learned counts as having eyes.

couplet: You meet with joy, with pleasant thought you part;
Such is the learned scholar's wonderous art!
pope.gloss: It is the part of the learned to give joy to those whom they meet, and on leaving, to make them think (Oh! when shall we meet them again.)

reading: To meet with delight and part leaving others thinking of you: such is the way of the learned.
nuance: The measure of learning here is purely social, with no mention of knowledge. Manakkudavar makes it a comparison with two people who meet in joy and part in longing, an image close to love. Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் opens the அத்தன்மைத்து to include right conduct and counsel.

couplet: With soul submiss they stand, as paupers front a rich man's face;
Yet learned men are first; th'unlearned stand in lowest place.
pope.gloss: The unlearned are inferior to the learned, before whom they stand begging, as the destitute before the wealthy.

reading: Those who learned while yearning like the poor before the rich are the foremost; those who did not learn are the lowest.

couplet: In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below;
The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow.
pope.gloss: Water will flow from a well in the sand in proportion to the depth to which it is dug, and knowledge will flow from a man in proportion to his learning.

reading: A well in sand gives water as far as it is dug; for people, understanding wells up as far as they have learned.
nuance: ஊறும் matters: understanding seeps up from below rather than being poured in, so study opens something rather than simply filling a store. Parimelazhagar openly reconciles this with 373, saying it holds where fate doesn't oppose it.

couplet: The learned make each land their own, in every city find a home;
Who, till they die; learn nought, along what weary ways they roam!
pope.gloss: How is it that any one can remain without learning, even to his death, when (to the learned man) every country is his own (country), and every town his own (town) ?

reading: Any land becomes one's own, any town one's own; why then does a person stay unlearned until death?
nuance: The verse states the belonging without naming who has it; the commentators supply the learned. Parimelazhagar's reason is reception: others' lands give the learned gifts and honour. A reader today may hear something more cosmopolitan than that.

couplet: The man who store of learning gains,
In one, through seven worlds, bliss attains.
pope.gloss: The learning, which a man has acquired in one birth, will yield him pleasure during seven births.

reading: The learning one acquires in a single span serves as protection through seven.

couplet: Their joy is joy of all the world, they see; thus more
The learners learn to love their cherished lore.
pope.gloss: The learned will long (for more learning), when they see that while it gives pleasure to themselves, the world also derives pleasure from it.

reading: Seeing that what delights them delights the world, the learned come to love it all the more.

couplet: Learning is excellence of wealth that none destroy;
To man nought else affords reality of joy.
pope.gloss: Learning is the true imperishable riches; all other things are not riches.

reading: Learning is the imperishable, excellent wealth for a person; other things are not wealth.
nuance: மாடு is a plain word for property and cattle, and the verse flatly denies that other possessions deserve it. Parimelazhagar defines the imperishability as more than safety from thieves and kings: learning doesn't decrease when given away.

title: கல்லாமை
theme: The emptiness of being unlearned: the unlearned person's speech, native wit, looks, wealth and rank all fail to count. The chapter is the harshest in the book on this point, and its contempt is largely about assemblies and public standing.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the unlearned have no right to speak in assembly (401-403), the fault of their native understanding (404-405), then their uselessness, looks, wealth and rank (406-409), and their failure to attain the human (410).
source_issues: 407: Parimelazhagar's gloss reads சுவையான் where the verse has மண்; the sense suggests சுதையான் (of plaster), so this is probably a corruption.
404: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் reads நிலைபெற்ற தூல் அறிவுடையார், probably a corruption of நூல்.

couplet: Like those at draughts would play without the chequered square,
Men void of ample lore would counsels of the learned share.
pope.gloss: To speak in an assembly (of the learned) without fullness of knowledge, is like playing at chess (on a board) without squares.

reading: Holding forth in an assembly without complete learning is like playing a board game with no marked board.
nuance: The image is exact: a game without a board isn't a bad game, because no move can mean anything. The fault is the absence of a shared frame, not lack of cleverness.

couplet: Like those who doat on hoyden's undeveloped charms are they,
Of learning void, who eagerly their power of words display.
pope.gloss: The desire of the unlearned to speak (in an assembly), is like a woman without breasts desiring (the enjoyment of ) woman-hood.

reading: For the unlearned to set their heart on speech is like desiring womanhood, or a woman, in one who lacks both breasts.
nuance: A crude comparison that rests on a narrow view of women's bodies. It is one of the verses where the book's period shows, and it shouldn't be softened. The commentators disagree on who is desiring.

couplet: The blockheads, too, may men of worth appear,
If they can keep from speaking where the learned hear!
pope.gloss: The unlearned also are very excellent men, if they know how to keep silence before the learned.

reading: Even the unlearned are very good, if only they can stay silent before the learned.
nuance: Dry praise. Parimelazhagar takes பெறின் seriously: it marks the condition as hard to meet, since those who don't know themselves can't manage it. The verse's sting is that knowing when to be silent would itself take the knowledge they lack.

couplet: From blockheads' lips, when words of wisdom glibly flow,
The wise receive them not, though good they seem to show.
pope.gloss: Although the natural knowledge of an unlearned man may be very good, the wise will not accept for true knowledge.

reading: However excellent an unlearned person's brightness may be, the wise do not accept it.
nuance: The verse grants the brightness and refuses it recognition, so this is a claim about what the wise will credit and not about what the person has.

couplet: As worthless shows the worth of man unlearned,
When council meets, by words he speaks discerned.
pope.gloss: The self-conceit of an unlearned man will fade away, as soon as he speaks in an assembly (of thelearned).

reading: An unlearned person's standing wilts once he meets and speaks.
nuance: The verse doesn't say with whom; the commentators supply a learned person. தகைமை is taken three ways: Parimelazhagar as his self-estimate, Manakkudavar as real greatness, and Kalaignar as a false pose. The first and third make the loss self-delusion ending, while the second makes it a real loss.

couplet: 'They are': so much is true of men untaught;
But, like a barren field, they yield us nought!
pope.gloss: The unlearned are like worthless barren land: all that can be said of them is, that they exist.

reading: The unlearned can only be said to exist; beyond that they are like barren saline land that yields nothing.
nuance: உளர் என்னும் மாத்திரையர் reduces a person to the bare fact of being said to exist. Kalaignar's walking corpses is stronger than the verse's image, which is about yield.

couplet: Who lack the power of subtle, large, and penetrating sense,
Like puppet, decked with ornaments of clay, their beauty's vain pretence.
pope.gloss: The beauty and goodness of one who is destitute of knowledge by the study of great and exquisite works, is like (the beauty and goodness) of a painted earthen doll.

reading: The fine looks of one without subtle, penetrating understanding are like those of a well-made clay doll.
nuance: Parimelazhagar concedes that a fine body is itself a rare fruit of birth, which makes the point less a scorn of beauty than a statement that it needs learning to be worth anything.

couplet: To men unlearned, from fortune's favour greater-evil springs
Than poverty to men of goodly wisdom brings.
pope.gloss: Wealth, gained by the unlearned, will give more sorrow than the poverty which may come upon the learned.

reading: Wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good.
nuance: The verse says நல்லார், the good, and opposes it to கல்லார், the unlearned. The pairing makes the learned and the good one group by sound and by implication. Parimelazhagar glosses நல்லார் as கற்றார் outright.

couplet: Lower are men unlearned, though noble be their race,
Than low-born men adorned with learning's grace.
pope.gloss: The unlearned, though born in a high caste, are not equal in dignity to the learned; though they may have been born in a low caste.

reading: Though born high, the unlearned do not have the worth of those who are learned though born low.
nuance: The verse overturns the ranking but keeps the words மேல் and கீழ், so birth rank remains as something to be overturned. The argument is not that the distinction is false, only that learning outweighs it.

couplet: Learning's irradiating grace who gain,
Others excel, as men the bestial train.
pope.gloss: As beasts by the side of men, so are other men by the side of those who are learned in celebrated works.

reading: As beasts stand to people, so do others stand to those who have studied the shining books.
nuance: The chapter ends by removing the unlearned from the human as such. Parimelazhagar's logic is that the surplus of awareness which marks humans over animals is found in the learned, so the two aren't of one birth.

title: கேள்வி
theme: Listening to the wise as a form of learning open even to those who haven't studied. The chapter treats the ear as an organ of nourishment and taste, rivalling the mouth, and it softens the verdict of the previous chapter.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the distinction of listening (411-412), those who have it (413), the good it does them (414-417), and the fault of its absence (418-420).
source_issues: 411: The Manakkudavar entry is marked [#] and is close to Parimelazhagar's wording, so I did not treat it as independent.

couplet: Wealth of wealth is wealth acquired be ear attent;
Wealth mid all wealth supremely excellent.
pope.gloss: Wealth (gained) by the ear is wealth of wealth; that wealth is the chief of all wealth.

reading: The wealth among wealths is the wealth of the ear; that wealth stands first among all wealth.
nuance: The sound does the work, with செல்வம் in every half-line. After 400 has already denied other wealth the name, this verse places the ear at the head of that revalued wealth.

couplet: When 'tis no longer time the listening ear to feed
With trifling dole of food supply the body's need.
pope.gloss: When there is no food for the ear, give a little also to the stomach.

reading: When there is no food for the ear, a little may be given to the stomach too.
nuance: The verse is witty, not ascetic. Parimelazhagar catches the two loaded words: சிறிது, and ஈயப்படும், which treats the stomach as a beggar to be given alms. It also says the food is given so that one can go on listening.

couplet: Who feed their ear with learned teachings rare,
Are like the happy gods oblations rich who share.
pope.gloss: Those who in this world enjoy instruction which is the food of the ear, are equal to the Gods, who enjoy the food of the sacrifices.

reading: Those who have listening as food for the ear, though on earth, are equal to those fulfilled by the food of oblation.

couplet: Though learning none hath he, yet let him hear alway:
In weakness this shall prove a staff and stay.
pope.gloss: Although a man be without learning, let him listen (to the teaching of the learned); that will be to him a staff in adversity.

reading: Even if you haven't studied, listen; it will be a staff to lean on in one's faltering.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that the உம்மை in ஆயினும் keeps study as the first duty. Listening is not offered as an equal path, only as what remains. He also makes the faltering inward: a mind shaken by poverty or ignorance.

couplet: Like staff in hand of him in slippery ground who strays
Are words from mouth of those who walk in righteous ways.
pope.gloss: The words of the good are like a staff in a slippery place.

reading: The words from the mouths of those of good conduct are like a staff on slippery ground.
nuance: The authority comes from the speaker's conduct, not learning. Parimelazhagar makes the exclusion explicit: the learned without conduct are not to be heard at all. So the chapter's listening is listening to a kind of person.

couplet: Let each man good things learn, for e'en as he
Shall learn, he gains increase of perfect dignity.
pope.gloss: Let a man listen, never so little, to good (instruction), even that will bring him great dignity.

reading: Listen to good things, however little; that much too will give full greatness.

couplet: Not e'en through inadvertence speak they foolish word,
With clear discerning mind who've learning's ample lessons heard.
pope.gloss: Not even when they have imperfectly understood (a matter), will those men speak foolishly, who have profoundly studied and diligently listened (to instruction).

reading: Those whose listening is gathered upon their own close investigation do not speak folly, even when they have misunderstood.
nuance: A subtle claim: being wrong and speaking foolishly are different things. Such a person can err and still not talk nonsense. இழைத்துணர்ந்து comes before கேள்வி, and Parimelazhagar reads this as one's own investigation first, confirmed by consulting those who know.

couplet: Where teaching hath not oped the learner's ear,
The man may listen, but he scarce can hear.
pope.gloss: The ear which has not been bored by instruction, although it hears, is deaf.

reading: Ears not pierced by listening are deaf even though they hear.
nuance: தோட்கப்படாத plays on pierced ears, ornament and all. Parimelazhagar's closing remark is apt: the old hole isn't a hole. Listening must make a new opening.

couplet: 'Tis hard for mouth to utter gentle, modest word,
When ears discourse of lore refined have never heard.
pope.gloss: It is a rare thing to find modesty, a reverend mouth- with those who have not received choice instruction.

reading: It is hard for those without fine listening to have a mouth that bows.
nuance: The bowing is done by the mouth, so this is humility as a way of speaking. The causal claim is striking: humility comes from having listened, because those who haven't heard much admire themselves, as Parimelazhagar explains.

couplet: His mouth can taste, but ear no taste of joy can give!
What matter if he die, or prosperous live?
pope.gloss: What does it matter whether those men live or die, who can judge of tastes by the mouth, and not by the ear ?

reading: What does it matter whether they die or live, these beings who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear?
nuance: The verse doesn't say to whom it doesn't matter; both older commentators supply the world, which makes it a social judgment of uselessness, not a cosmic one. மாக்கள் rather than மக்கள் also seems to me a deliberate demotion. It may also echo அவி of 413, oblation there and perishing here, though that is my suggestion.

title: அறிவுடைமை
theme: Understanding as protection and as practice: it steers the mind, tests what is heard, moves with the world, foresees what is coming and knows what to fear. After three chapters on acquiring knowledge, this one asks what it is to have it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the distinction of understanding (421), its definition (422-426), those who have it (427-428), and what they are spared and possess (429-430).
source_issues: 425: Manakkudavar is not aligned.

couplet: True wisdom wards off woes, A circling fortress high;
Its inner strength man's eager foes Unshaken will defy.
pope.gloss: Wisdom is a weapon to ward off destruction; it is an inner fortress which enemies cannot destroy.

reading: Understanding is the tool that guards against அற்றம், and an inner fortress enemies can't destroy.
nuance: The fort is one of the six limbs of a kingdom (381). This verse puts a fort inside the person, with உள் able to mean either inward or impenetrable from within, as Parimelazhagar notes.

couplet: Wisdom restrains, nor suffers mind to wander where it would;
From every evil calls it back, and guides in way of good.
pope.gloss: Not to permit the mind to go where it lists, to keep it from evil, and to employ it in good, this is wisdom.

reading: Understanding does not let one go wherever things have gone, but turns away from evil and steers toward good.
nuance: The verse doesn't name what wanders. Both commentators supply the mind, but they disagree on what is held back and how far.

couplet: Though things diverse from divers sages' lips we learn,
'Tis wisdom's part in each the true thing to discern.
pope.gloss: To discern the truth in every thing, by whomsoever spoken, is wisdom.

reading: Whatever is heard, from whoever's mouth, understanding is seeing the true substance of that very thing.
nuance: The repeated யார்யார் removes the speaker from the test. Parimelazhagar gives the sharp consequence: high matters may come from low mouths, harmful ones from friends. He takes மெய்ப்பொருள் as the thing's true use, not its truth in the abstract, which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar prefer.

couplet: Wisdom hath use of lucid speech, words that acceptance win,
And subtle sense of other men's discourse takes in.
pope.gloss: To speak so as that the meaning may easily enter the mind of the hearer, and to discern the subtlest thought which may lie hidden in the words of others, this is wisdom.

reading: Understanding is saying things so they go in easily, while seeing the subtle meaning in what comes from others.
nuance: The two directions are asymmetric: speech should make the hard simple, and listening should find the fine in the plain. Parimelazhagar goes further, saying to take the use from what others say even if it is flawed in expression.

couplet: Wisdom embraces frank the world, to no caprice exposed;
Unlike the lotus flower, now opened wide, now petals strictly closed.
pope.gloss: To secure the friendship of the great is true wisdom; it is (also) wisdom to keep (that friendship unchanged, and) not opening and closing (like the lotus flower).

reading: Embracing the world is brightness; not opening and closing is understanding.
nuance: Parimelazhagar narrows உலகம் to the worthy and contrasts a pond flower that closes with a tree flower that stays open.

couplet: As dwells the world, so with the world to dwell
In harmony- this is to wisely live and well.
pope.gloss: T o live as the world lives, is wisdom.

reading: As the world lives, so to live with the world is understanding.
nuance: This verse needs reading with 423, because the same chapter tells the reader to test everything and to go along.

couplet: The wise discern, the foolish fail to see,
And minds prepare for things about to be.
pope.gloss: The wise are those who know beforehand what will happen; those who do not know this are the unwise.

reading: Those with understanding know what will come to be; those without it cannot.
nuance: ஆவது could be what will happen or what is good for oneself; Parimelazhagar records both. His gloss makes foreknowledge an act of reasoning ahead, எண்ணி அறிதல், and not prophecy. Not knowing is defined as finding out once it arrives.

couplet: Folly meets fearful ills with fearless heart;
To fear where cause of fear exists is wisdom's part.
pope.gloss: Not to fear what ought to be feared, is folly; it is the work of the wise to fear what should be feared.

reading: Not fearing what is to be feared is folly; fearing what is to be feared is the work of the knowing.
nuance: Fear is treated as a skill, தொழில். Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both notice the conflict with the kingly fearlessness of 382 and resolve it. Parimelazhagar defines fear here as considering and refraining.

couplet: The wise with watchful soul who coming ills foresee;
From coming evil's dreaded shock are free.
pope.gloss: No terrifying calamity will happen to the wise, who (foresee) and guard against coming evils.

reading: Those whose understanding guards against what is coming have no affliction that comes to shake them.
nuance: அதிர வருவது is careful: the claim may be that no calamity shakes them, not that no calamity comes. Parimelazhagar's guarding means removing the cause.

couplet: The wise is rich, with ev'ry blessing blest;
The fool is poor, of everything possessed.
pope.gloss: Those who possess wisdom, possess every thing; those who have not wisdom, whatever they may possess, have nothing.

reading: Those with understanding have everything; those without it have nothing, whatever they have.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a practical reason, not a pious one: all wealth is made and kept by understanding, so the fool has no means of keeping what he has or rebuilding it.

title: குற்றங்கடிதல்
theme: A ruler's real enemy is his own faults: arrogance, anger, desire, avarice, misplaced pride and self-regard. Small ones must be treated as large and dealt with before they arrive, and only one who has cleared his own is fit to judge others.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: what the faults are (431-432), why they must be removed in general (433-436), then specific treatment: avarice (437-438), pride (439), and desire (440).
source_issues: 437: The Manakkudavar entry is marked [#] and labelled as Parimelazhagar's commentary, and is close to it in wording. I did not use it as an independent view.
440: Manakkudavar is not aligned.
439: Parimelazhagar's gloss reads நான்கு மதியாது, probably a corruption of நன்கு.
439: Manakkudavar's பொய்யனாக நினைத்து is obscure and may be corrupt, so I did not rely on it.

couplet: Who arrogance, and wrath, and littleness of low desire restrain,
To sure increase of lofty dignity attain.
pope.gloss: Truly great is the excellence of those (kings) who are free from pride, anger, and lust.

reading: The prosperity of those without arrogance, anger and smallness has a dignified quality.
nuance: The verse puts the virtue in the quality of the prosperity: the same wealth is dignified or not, depending on who holds it.

couplet: A niggard hand, o'erweening self-regard, and mirth
Unseemly, bring disgrace to men of kingly brith.
pope.gloss: Avarice, undignified pride, and low pleasures are faults in a king.

reading: Stinginess, honour that has passed beyond dignity, and joy that lacks dignity are faults in a ruler.
nuance: The surprising items are positive feelings gone wrong. Parimelazhagar makes the undignified joy excessive leniency, கழிகண்ணோட்டம், and the wrong honour includes refusing to bow to elders and carrying a thing through just because one intended it.

couplet: Though small as millet-seed the fault men deem;
As palm tree vast to those who fear disgrace 'twill seem.
pope.gloss: Those who fear guilt, if they commit a fault small as a millet seed, will consider it to be as large as a palmyra tree.

reading: Though a fault comes as small as a millet seed, those who are ashamed of blame take it to be as large as a palmyra.
nuance: The motive is shame at blame, பழிநாணுவார், so this is social conscience. Parimelazhagar makes the scale practical: treating it as large is how they ensure it doesn't come again.

couplet: Freedom from faults is wealth; watch heedfully
'Gainst these, for fault is fatal enmity.
pope.gloss: Guard against faults as a matter (of great consequence; for) faults are a deadly enemy.

reading: Guard against fault itself as your aim; fault alone is the enemy that brings ruin.
nuance: The double ஏ, குற்றமே twice, refuses any other candidate. Parimelazhagar draws a strong conclusion from a Sanskrit view: external enemies can only bring ruin through such faults. பொருளாக is 'as your aim' for him; Pope's 'wealth' is a different and weaker reading.

couplet: His joy who guards not 'gainst the coming evil day,
Like straw before the fire shall swift consume away.
pope.gloss: The prosperity of him who does not timely guard against faults, will perish like straw before fire.

reading: The life of one who doesn't guard before it comes will perish like straw set before a fire.

couplet: Faultless the king who first his own faults cures, and then
Permits himself to scan faults of other men.
pope.gloss: What fault will remain in the king who has put away his own evils, and looks after the evils of others.

reading: If he removes his own fault and can then see others' faults, what fault can attach to a ruler?
nuance: Parimelazhagar turns this into a condition of legitimacy: punishing others' faults is itself a fault until one has cleared one's own, after which it becomes justice. The verse's order, தன்... பிறர், supports him, though the claim about the right to judge is his.

couplet: Who leaves undone what should be done, with niggard mind,
His wealth shall perish, leaving not a wrack behind.
pope.gloss: The wealth of the avaricious man, who does not expend it for the purposes for which he ought to expend it will waste away and not continue.

reading: The wealth of one who clings to it, not doing what should be done with it, does not last but perishes.
nuance: Stinginess doesn't keep wealth, on this view; it loses it. Parimelazhagar's explanation is that wealth left unused for virtue and growth has nothing to sustain it.

couplet: The greed of soul that avarice men call,
When faults are summed, is worst of all.
pope.gloss: Griping avarice is not to be reckoned as one among other faults; (it stands alone - greater than all).

reading: The miserliness called the clinging heart is not a thing to be counted among any.
nuance: பற்றுள்ளம் uses a word close to the attachment renunciation speaks of, here applied to wealth in the Porul section.

couplet: Never indulge in self-complaisant mood,
Nor deed desire that yields no gain of good.
pope.gloss: Let no (one) praise himself, at any time; let him not desire to do useless things.

reading: Never admire yourself, and never set your heart on a deed that brings no good.
nuance: The two clauses could be separate, or the second a consequence of the first, as Manakkudavar and Kalaignar take it. Parimelazhagar connects them too: self-admiration blinds one to place, time and strength, the subjects of chapters 48 to 50.

couplet: If, to your foes unknown, you cherish what you love,
Counsels of men who wish you harm will harmless prove.
pope.gloss: If (a king) enjoys, privately the things which he desires, the designs of his enemies will be useless.

reading: If you can enjoy what you love without others knowing of the love, your enemies' schemes come to nothing.
nuance: A striking end. After a chapter on removing faults, the last verse manages one by concealing it. Parimelazhagar concedes that desire, anger and joy aren't to be wholly removed. The verse is a matter of security: a known desire is a door for the enemy.

title: பெரியாரைத் துணைக்கோடல்
theme: A ruler's power depends on those greater than himself whom he can win and keep, and above all on those who will correct him. The chapter counts this as the highest strength and calls its lack self-destruction.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: who the great are and how to win them (441-442), the distinction of having them (443-445), the fruits (446-447), and the fault of lacking them (448-450).

couplet: As friends the men who virtue know, and riper wisdom share,
Their worth weighed well, the king should choose with care.
pope.gloss: Let (a king) ponder well its value, and secure the friendship of men of virtue and of mature knowledge.

reading: Knowing their worth and the way to go about it, choose the friendship of those of understanding who have matured in knowledge of virtue.
nuance: மூத்த is not simply age: Parimelazhagar counts maturity in understanding, character and years. The verse doesn't say what office such people hold, though Manakkudavar takes them to be priests. For Parimelazhagar திறன் is the way of winning them, and for Manakkudavar it is their capacities.

couplet: Cherish the all-accomplished men as friends,
Whose skill the present ill removes, from coming ill defends.
pope.gloss: Let (a king) procure and kindly care for men who can overcome difficulties when they occur, and guard against them before they happen.

reading: Cherish and take as support those who have the quality of removing the affliction that has come and guarding before against what has not.

couplet: To cherish men of mighty soul, and make them all their own,
Of kingly treasures rare, as rarest gift is known.
pope.gloss: To cherish great men and make them his own, is the most difficult of all difficult things.

reading: To cherish the great and make them one's own is the rarest of all rare things.
nuance: அரிது can mean hard to do, as Manakkudavar has it, or rare to attain, as Parimelazhagar does. The second adds his observation that a king who can have every rare thing still prizes this one, because the others come through it.

couplet: To live with men of greatness that their own excels,
As cherished friends, is greatest power that with a monarch dwells.
pope.gloss: So to act as to make those men, his own, who are greater than himself is of all powers the highest.

reading: To conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own is the chief of all strengths.
nuance: A paradox of power: the supreme strength is standing under someone. Parimelazhagar's தாம் அவர் வழிநின்று makes the king the follower, and he ranks this above wealth, army and fortress on the ground that it reaches afflictions they can't.

couplet: The king, since counsellors are monarch's eyes,
Should counsellors select with counsel wise.
pope.gloss: As a king must use his ministers as eyes (in managing his kingdom), let him well examine their character and qualifications before he engages them.

reading: Since counsellors serve as his eyes, a ruler must take his counsellors after counsel.
nuance: The verse plays on சூழ், which means to deliberate, to plot and to surround, and the commentators split along those senses.

couplet: The king, who knows to live with worthy men allied,
Has nought to fear from any foeman's pride.
pope.gloss: There will be nothing left for enemies to do, against him who has the power of acting (so as to secure) the fellowship of worthy men.

reading: There is nothing enemies can do against one able to carry himself as one of the company of the worthy.
nuance: தான் ஒழுக வல்லான்: having good company isn't enough; he too must act accordingly. It is the ability that protects, not only the associates.

couplet: What power can work his fall, who faithful ministers
Employs, that thunder out reproaches when he errs.
pope.gloss: Who are great enough to destroy him who has servants that have power to rebuke him ?

reading: Who has the standing to ruin those who keep as their support people who will rebuke them?
nuance: ஆள்வாரை: such people must actually be employed and valued. Parimelazhagar adds that the rebuker needs to be free of the same faults and to love the king, so rebuke alone doesn't qualify.

couplet: The king with none to censure him, bereft of safeguards all,
Though none his ruin work, shall surely ruined fall.
pope.gloss: The king, who is without the guard of men who can rebuke him, will perish, even though there be no one to destroy him.

reading: A ruler without the guard of those who rebuke will perish even with no one to ruin him.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's image is an elephant with no mahout, going off the path and ruining itself. கெடுப்பார் இலானும் makes enemies unnecessary to the story, and 447 and 448 form a pair, protection and exposure.

couplet: Who owns no principal, can have no gain of usury;
Who lacks support of friends, knows no stability.
pope.gloss: There can be no gain to those who have no capital; and in like manner there can be no permanence to those who are without the support of adherents.

reading: Those without capital have no profit; those without the support of a pillar have no standing.
nuance: A merchant's image for a king's court. Allies are the principal rather than the return: everything else is earned on them. The verse doesn't limit itself to kings; the older commentators supply that.

couplet: Than hate of many foes incurred, works greater woe
Ten-fold, of worthy men the friendship to forego.
pope.gloss: It is tenfold more injurious to abandon the friendship of the good, than to incur the hatred of the many.

reading: To let go one's tie with the good is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many.
nuance: Pope and Kalaignar read கைவிடல் as abandoning a tie, whereas Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it as failing to take the great as support. His reason is practical: there are ways out of many enemies, but none out of having no good company.

title: சிற்றினஞ்சேராமை
theme: Understanding and goodness are not sealed within a person; they take on the nature of the company one keeps, as water takes on its soil. The chapter gradually grants the mind its goodness while insisting that company still strengthens or spoils it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as an argument: the small company doesn't suit the great (451), why, through the soil image (452), replies to those who locate everything in the mind (453-454), how understanding comes through company (455), and the merit of good company, to those who think it unneeded (456-459), ending with the positive and negative stated together (460).
source_issues: 459: Kalaignar's commentary reads much like his comment on 458 and doesn't address மறுமை. It appears to be about the right verse but may be thin rather than a deliberate position, so the contest here is weaker than it looks.

couplet: The great of soul will mean association fear;
The mean of soul regard mean men as kinsmen dear.
pope.gloss: (True) greatness fears the society of the base; it is only the low - minded who will regard them as friends.

reading: Greatness fears the small company; smallness at once takes it as kin.
nuance: The verse gives the fear to greatness, not to a person lacking resolve. Parimelazhagar explains it through self-knowledge: the wise know their judgment can bend, while the small see only likeness and suspect nothing.

couplet: The waters' virtues change with soil through which they flow;
As man's companionship so will his wisdom show.
pope.gloss: As water changes (its nature), from the nature of the soil (in which it flows), so will the character of men resemble that of their associates.

reading: As water changes by the nature of the land, so a person's understanding becomes the nature of their company.
nuance: Note the subject: it is அறிவு that changes, not behaviour or reputation. Parimelazhagar sharpens the image, with water pure in the sky and only turning on contact, and so with understanding held alone.

couplet: Perceptions manifold in men are of the mind alone;
The value of the man by his companionship is known.
pope.gloss: The power of knowing is from the mind; (but) his character is from that of his associates.

reading: A person's perception comes from the mind; the word 'such a one' comes from their company.
nuance: A clean division of labour: faculty is inner and reputation is social. Parimelazhagar assigns the mind only basic sense-awareness and gives all cultivated judgment to company, a step further than the verse says. Manakkudavar makes the word specifically blame.

couplet: Man's wisdom seems the offspring of his mind;
'Tis outcome of companionship we find.
pope.gloss: Wisdom appears to rest in the mind, but it really exists to a man in his companions.

reading: Understanding, while showing itself as though in the mind, lies for a person in their company.
nuance: The verse is one of the Kural's most radical on the self: where understanding appears to be is not where it is. Parimelazhagar's 'the mind is where it shows, the company is its root' makes it explicit. The verse doesn't explain why.

couplet: Both purity of mind, and purity of action clear,
Leaning no staff of pure companionship, to man draw near.
pope.gloss: Chaste company is the staff on which come, these two things, viz, purity of mind and purity of conduct.

reading: Purity of mind and purity of deeds, these two, come leaning on purity of company.
nuance: தூவா is a rare word, which Parimelazhagar glosses as a support and defends with a citation. The claim is causal: company is the thing the other two rest on, not a third kind of purity alongside them.

couplet: From true pure-minded men a virtuous race proceeds;
To men of pure companionship belong no evil deeds.
pope.gloss: To the pure-minded there will be a good posterity. By those whose associates are pure, no deeds will be done that are not good.

reading: Those pure of mind have a good எச்சம்; for those pure of company there is no deed that doesn't turn out well.

couplet: Goodness of mind to lives of men increaseth gain;
And good companionship doth all of praise obtain.
pope.gloss: Goodness of mind will give wealth, and good society will bring with it all praise, to men.

reading: Goodness of mind gains a person prosperity; goodness of company gives all praise as well.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason for the second clause is neat: those able to give praise are the good themselves, and they are the company.

couplet: To perfect men, though minds right good belong,
Yet good companionship is confirmation strong.
pope.gloss: Although they may have great (natural) goodness of mind, yet good society will tend to strengthen it.

reading: Though the worthy have goodness of mind in full, goodness of company is a protection to them.
nuance: The verse makes its concession to the mind here, then refuses to let it stand alone. Even சான்றோர் are not exempt.

couplet: Although to mental goodness joys of other life belong,
Y et good companionship is confirmation strong.
pope.gloss: Future bliss is (the result) of goodness of mind; and even this acquires strength from the society of the good.

reading: From goodness of mind comes the next world, and even that gains strength from goodness of company.
nuance: The verse names மறுமை in plain terms in the book on polity. Parimelazhagar notes that goodness of mind can slip from time to time, and good company holds it steady.

couplet: Than good companionship no surer help we know;
Than bad companionship nought causes direr woe.
pope.gloss: There is no greater help than the company of the good; there is no greater source of sorrow than the company of the wicked.

reading: There is no greater support than good company and nothing that brings more affliction than bad company.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says the chapter's title, avoiding small company, has been argued mainly from the reverse: by praising good company. Only this last verse states both sides together.

title: தெரிந்துசெயல்வகை
theme: Acting well begins before the act: weighing cost and return, taking counsel, and matching the means to the person and to one's own position. The chapter's vocabulary is that of a careful ledger, and its fear is less of failure than of being laughed at for failing.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: which deed to do and how (461-462), which to avoid and the cost of not avoiding it (463-465), do and don't stated together (466), then the means and to whom they suit (467-470).

couplet: Expenditure, return, and profit of the deed
In time to come; weigh these- than to the act proceed.
pope.gloss: Let a man reflect on what will be lost, what will be acquired and (from these) what will be his ultimate gain, and (then, let him) act.

reading: Weigh what will be lost, what will arise, and the gain that comes of it later, and then act.
nuance: The verse separates the immediate return from later gain. Parimelazhagar draws out the consequence: a deed that only breaks even now may still be worth doing if the later gain is there. So this is not a plain cost-benefit rule.

couplet: With chosen friends deliberate; next use the private thought;
Then act. By those who thus proceed all works with ease are wrought.
pope.gloss: There is nothing too difficult to (be attained by) those who, before they act, reflect well themselves, and thoroughly consider (the matter) with chosen friends.

reading: Nothing is out of reach for those who act after examining it with chosen company and considering it themselves.
nuance: Parimelazhagar takes the two verbs in order: first with the company, then alone. So consulting doesn't replace judgment. தெரிந்த also makes the counsellors themselves the first thing chosen.

couplet: To risk one's all and lose, aiming at added gain,
Is rash affair, from which the wise abstain.
pope.gloss: Wise men will not, in the hopes of profit, undertake works that will consume their principal.

reading: Those with understanding don't undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's example is political: marching to take another's land and losing one's own. He also reads செய்வினை as covering even work already begun, so sunk effort is no excuse.

couplet: A work of which the issue is not clear,
Begin not they reproachful scorn who fear.
pope.gloss: Those who fear reproach will not commence anything which has not been (thoroughly considered) and made clear to them.

reading: Those who fear the affliction called disgrace don't begin what isn't clear to them.
nuance: The stated motive is shame, not loss. Parimelazhagar explains தொடங்கார்: once begun, a thing can't be dropped midway, so scorn would be added to the failure.

couplet: With plans not well matured to rise against your foe,
Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow!
pope.gloss: One way to promote the prosperity of an enemy, is (for a king) to set out (to war) without having thoroughly weighed his ability (to cope with its chances).

reading: Rising up without thinking through every aspect is one way of bedding your enemy in good soil.
nuance: பாத்தி is a garden bed. The sting is that the hasty attacker does the enemy's cultivating for them: a failed attack strengthens its target.

couplet: 'Tis ruin if man do an unbefitting thing;
Fit things to leave undone will equal ruin bring.
pope.gloss: He will perish who does not what is not fit to do; and he also will perish who does not do what it is fit to do.

reading: One perishes by doing what is unfit to do, and perishes too by not doing what is fit.
nuance: Omission gets the same verdict as commission. தக்க is not obviously moral: Parimelazhagar's list of the unfit includes the too-laborious, the useless and the doubtful, which makes it prudential.

couplet: Think, and then dare the deed! Who cry,
'Deed dared, we'll think,' disgraced shall be.
pope.gloss: Consider, and then undertake a matter; after having undertaken it, to say "We will consider," is folly.

reading: Think and then resolve on a task; to say 'we'll think after resolving' is a lapse.
nuance: What is to be thought about isn't stated. For Parimelazhagar it is the means, the four strategies; for Manakkudavar it is the result. The first assumes the deed is already chosen.

couplet: On no right system if man toil and strive,
Though many men assist, no work can thrive.
pope.gloss: The work, which is not done by suitable methods, will fail though many stand to uphold it.

reading: Effort not made in the right way will collapse, even if many stand by to protect it.
nuance: The verse corrects the chapter 45 picture of allies as near-sufficient: support can't save effort that is on the wrong path. Parimelazhagar spells out which means suit which kind of person.

couplet: Though well the work be done, yet one mistake is made,
To habitudes of various men when no regard is paid.
pope.gloss: There are failures even in acting well, when it is done without knowing the various dispositions of men.

reading: Even in doing good there is error, when it is done without knowing each person's character.

couplet: Plan and perform no work that others may despise;
What misbeseems a king the world will not approve as wise.
pope.gloss: Let a man reflect, and do things which bring no reproach; the world will not approve, with him, of things which do not become of his position to adopt.

reading: Think and do what won't be scorned; the world doesn't accept what doesn't accord with oneself.

title: வலியறிதல்
theme: Knowing strength: the deed's, one's own, the opponent's and the allies', and treating wealth as a form of strength with a limit. The theme is limits, and most of the chapter warns against zeal, generosity and pride that outrun them.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the parts of strength and the reward for knowing them (471-472), the cost of not knowing one's own (473-474), the opponent's and allies' (475), the deed's (476), and wealth as a part of strength (477-480).
source_issues: 475: Kalaignar's comment says the cart gets so strong that the axle breaks, which appears garbled and doesn't fit the verse. I did not use it.

couplet: The force the strife demands, the force he owns, the force of foes,
The force of friends; these should he weigh ere to the war he goes.
pope.gloss: Let (one) weigh well the strength of the deed (he purposes to do), his own strength, the strength of his enemy, and the strength of the allies (of both), and then let him act.

reading: Weigh the strength of the deed, one's own strength, the opponent's strength and the strength of allies, and then act.
nuance: The first item is surprising: the deed itself has strength. Parimelazhagar adds a strict rule the verse doesn't state, that one should act only if one's own side is greater, and avoid even an equal contest, since victory there is doubtful.

couplet: Who know what can be wrought, with knowledge of the means, on this,
Their mind firm set, go forth, nought goes with them amiss.
pope.gloss: There is nothing which may not be accomplished by those who, before they attack (an enemy), make themselves acquainted with their own ability, and with whatever else is (needful) to be known, and apply themselves wholly to their object.

reading: For those who know what they can do and what must be known, and proceed resting in that, nothing fails.
nuance: The chapter's only verse of confidence, and it hangs on அதன்கண் தங்கி, where the commentators pull in nearly opposite directions.

couplet: Ill-deeming of their proper powers, have many monarchs striven,
And midmost of unequal conflict fallen asunder riven.
pope.gloss: There are many who, ignoran t of their (want of) power (to meet it), have haughtily set out to war, and broken down in the midst of it.

reading: Many, not knowing the strength they have, rose on enthusiasm and were broken midway.
nuance: A rare verse appealing to history, பலர். ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி uses the very quality demanded of kings in 382 as the cause of the fall. Not knowing runs both ways too, as உடைத்தம் வலி means the strength they do have.

couplet: Who not agrees with those around, no moderation knows,
In self-applause indulging, swift to ruin goes.
pope.gloss: He will quickly perish who, ignorant of his own resources flatters himself of his greatness, and does not live in peace with his neighbours.

reading: One who doesn't live in accord, doesn't know his measure and admires himself perishes quickly.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes ஆங்கு அமைந்து about neighbouring kings: one must be either a friend or an enemy who knows his strength. Others read it as a general composure, or as respect for people.

couplet: With peacock feathers light, you load the wain;
Yet, heaped too high, the axle snaps in twain.
pope.gloss: The axle tree of a bandy, loaded only with peacocks' feathers will break, if it be greatly overloaded.

reading: Even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle, if that load is piled too high.
nuance: The two உம் make both the cart strong and the load light. The verse speaks only of the cart, and the allegory is supplied by the commentators.

couplet: Who daring climbs, and would himself upraise
Beyond the branch's tip, with life the forfeit pays.
pope.gloss: There will be an end to the life of him who, having climbed out to the end of a branch, ventures to go further.

reading: Those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and strive further will end their life.
nuance: The climber has done well to get there, and that is the danger: this is a warning to the successful. The verse is purely image. Parimelazhagar applies it to a king who has gone as far as he can on a campaign, and Manakkudavar has him turn back.

couplet: With knowledge of the measure due, as virtue bids you give!
That is the way to guard your wealth, and seemly live.
pope.gloss: Let a man know the measure of his ability (to give), and let him give accordingly; such giving is the way to preserve his property.

reading: Give in the proper way, knowing the measure; that is the way of guarding wealth and bestowing it.
nuance: The verse fuses the two usually opposed, போற்றி and வழங்கு, into one way. Parimelazhagar's fixed ratio, two parts for spending, one for reserves and one for giving, comes from Tirikadugam, not the verse.

couplet: Incomings may be scant; but yet, no failure there,
If in expenditure you rightly learn to spare.
pope.gloss: Even though the income (of a king) be small, it will not cause his (ruin), if his outgoings be not larger than his income.

reading: Though the channel of income be narrow, there is no ruin, if the channel of outgo isn't wider.
nuance: ஆறு is a path or channel, which gives wealth a hydraulic image. Income's size doesn't determine ruin; only the ratio does. Parimelazhagar adds that even exact balance is safe.

couplet: Who prosperous lives and of enjoyment knows no bound,
His seeming wealth, departing, nowhere shall be found.
pope.gloss: The prosperity of him who lives without knowing the measure (of his property), will perish, even while it seems to continue.

reading: The life of one who doesn't live knowing the measure seems to exist, then is not, and perishes without a trace.
nuance: The verse has three stages: seeming, not being and not even seeming. Parimelazhagar points out that ruin isn't visible at the start, which is why the first stage is a seeming and the warning needed.

couplet: Beneficence that measures not its bound of means,
Will swiftly bring to nought the wealth on which it leans.
pope.gloss: The measure of his wealth will quickly perish, whose liberality weighs not the measure of his property.

reading: Helpfulness that doesn't weigh the limit of what one has quickly ends the limit of one's wealth.
nuance: Even the most praised social virtue gets a limit. Manakkudavar sees the objection coming: if spending must stay below income, how can one be helpful? This is presented as the answer.

title: காலமறிதல்
theme: Strength is not a fixed quantity but depends on when it is used. The chapter's real teaching is about waiting: holding back, even bowing and hiding one's anger, then striking without hesitation when the moment comes. Its stance is cold and tactical.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the distinction of time (481), its fruits (482-484), what to do when the time has not come (485-488), and what to do when it has (489), with the heron giving both (490).
source_issues: 485: Manakkudavar is not aligned.
487: Manakkudavar's மனமொப்பர் and ஒப்புப் பொறாமையால் are obscure and may be corrupt, so I did not use them.

couplet: A crow will conquer owl in broad daylight;
The king that foes would crush, needs fitting time to fight.
pope.gloss: A crow will overcome an owl in the day time; so the king who would conquer his enemy must have (a suitable) time.

reading: By day the crow beats the owl; kings who would win a contest need the right time.
nuance: The image makes strength relational, as the same two birds reverse by night, a symmetry Manakkudavar makes explicit. Parimelazhagar's definition of time is unexpectedly concrete: weather that lets an army travel without disease and with food and water.

couplet: The bond binds fortune fast is ordered effort made,
Strictly observant still of favouring season's aid.
pope.gloss: Acting at the right season, is a cord that will immoveably bind success (to a king).

reading: Acting in accord with the season is the rope that binds fortune so that it doesn't leave.
nuance: A rope only makes sense for something that tends to run. Parimelazhagar draws this from தீராமை: fortune's nature is to leave. Kalaignar takes திருவினை differently, as the success of a good deed, but the older commentators read wealth.

couplet: Can any work be hard in very fact,
If men use fitting means in timely act?
pope.gloss: Is there anything difficult for him to do, who acts, with (the right) instruments at the right time ?

reading: Are there things said to be hard, if one acts with the right means and knows the time?
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that கருவியான் is there to say that even with the means, time is still needed: the tools don't make timing unnecessary.

couplet: The pendant world's dominion may be won,
In fitting time and place by action done.
pope.gloss: Though (a man) should meditate (the conquest of) the world, he may accomplish it if he acts in the right time, and at the right place.

reading: Even the world will come to hand if one thinks of the time and acts by the place.
nuance: This verse joins time and place and forms a bridge into the next chapter. The promise is grand, and the chapter's next verse immediately makes the same ambition the reason for doing nothing yet.

couplet: Who think the pendant world itself to subjugate,
With mind unruffled for the fitting time must wait.
pope.gloss: They who thoughtfully consider and wait for the (right) time (for action), may successfully meditate (the conquest of) the world.

reading: Those who have their mind on the world wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time.
nuance: Greater ambition means more waiting, not less. Parimelazhagar adds that this applies even if one's strength is already superior, and identifies இருப்பு as a recognised policy, one of six, the opposite of marching out. கலங்காது could go with either the waiting or the aim.

couplet: The men of mighty power their hidden energies repress,
As fighting ram recoils to rush on foe with heavier stress.
pope.gloss: The self-restraint of the energetic (while waiting for a suitable opportunity), is like the drawing back of a fighting-ram in order to butt.

reading: The holding back of the person of energy is like a fighting ram drawing back in order to charge.
nuance: It reframes restraint as part of attack, so ஒடுக்கம் doesn't signal a lack of ஊக்கம். Kalaignar adds that this is silence in the face of cruelty and that it isn't from fear, which the verse doesn't say.

couplet: The glorious once of wrath enkindled make no outward show,
At once; they bide their time, while hidden fires within them glow.
pope.gloss: The wise will not immediately and hastily shew out their anger; they will watch their time, and restrain it within.

reading: The bright don't flare up outwardly at once; watching the time, they burn within.
nuance: The anger isn't removed, only stored. Parimelazhagar gives the unusual reason that it must continue within: if it died away, one could not later stop the offender. Anger here is a resource.

couplet: If foes' detested form they see, with patience let them bear;
When fateful hour at last they spy,- the head lies there.
pope.gloss: If one meets his enemy, let him show him all respect, until the time for his destruction is come; when that is come, his head will be easily b rought low.

reading: Seeing those who would harm you, bear them; when you see their final limit, the head goes down.
nuance: The verse doesn't say what is to be carried or whose head falls. Manakkudavar's தலையினாற் சுமக்க is the literal image behind Parimelazhagar's reading: carry them on the head, then tip them off.

couplet: When hardest gain of opportunity at last is won,
With promptitude let hardest deed be done.
pope.gloss: If a rare opportunity occurs, while it lasts, let a man do that which is rarely to be accomplished (but for such an opportunity).

reading: When what is hard to get has come, do at that very point what is hard to do.
nuance: The double அரிய pairs them: rare time, rare deed. Parimelazhagar makes the best observation on அந்நிலையே: the moment won't stay. All the patience of the preceding verses exists for this one instant.

couplet: As heron stands with folded wing, so wait in waiting hour;
As heron snaps its prey, when fortune smiles, put forth your power.
pope.gloss: At the time when one should use self-control, let him restrain himself like a heron; and, let him like it, strike, when there is a favourable opportunity.

reading: When it is the season to fold up, be like the heron; when the moment is right, be like its strike.
nuance: One image holds both modes, and the verse compares the person first to the bird and then only to the bird's stab. Parimelazhagar notes that the heron looks as though lifeless while it waits, which adds a touch of menace.

title: இடனறிதல்
theme: Power belongs to the ground it stands on. Through animals and vehicles, the chapter shows the strong undone off their own ground and the weak made strong on theirs, and it warns against attacking even people with nothing but their home.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the place for besieging (491-494), the place for acting (495-497), and places not to approach and the cost of doing so (498-500).
source_issues: 497: Manakkudavar is not aligned.
499: Manakkudavar is not aligned.

couplet: Begin no work of war, depise no foe,
Till place where you can wholly circumvent you know.
pope.gloss: Let not (a king) despise (an enemy), nor undertake any thing (against him), until he has obtained (a suitable) place for besieging him.

reading: Begin no deed and scorn nothing until you have seen the ground for it in full.

couplet: Though skill in war combine with courage tried on battle-field,
The added gain of fort doth great advantage yield.
pope.gloss: Even to those who are men of power and expedients, an attack in connection with a fortification will yield many advantages.

reading: Even for those of contentious strength, the gain that comes by joining a fortress gives many benefits.
nuance: Even the strong: உம் concedes the objection. Manakkudavar takes the fort as one's own place, and Parimelazhagar, who thinks of a king on campaign, as a siege position. Either way, it is a protection for those who think they don't need it.

couplet: E'en weak ones mightily prevail, if place of strong defence,
They find, protect themselves, and work their foes offence.
pope.gloss: Even the powerless will become powerful and conquer, if they select a proper field (of action), and guard themselves, while they make war on their enemies.

reading: Even those without strength become strong and win, if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves.
nuance: The ஆற்றி in ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி plays on the same root: place does not merely help the weak but turns them into the strong.

couplet: The foes who thought to triumph, find their thoughts were vain,
If hosts advance, seize vantage ground, and thence the fight maintain.
pope.gloss: If they who draw near (to fight) choose a suitable place to approach (their enemy), the latter, will have to relinquish the thought which they once entertained, of conquering them.

reading: Those who had planned will lose their plan, if those who approach know the place and hold to it.
nuance: The loss is of a thought: the enemy's victory has been defeated before fighting starts.

couplet: The crocodile prevails in its own flow of water wide,
If this it leaves, 'tis slain by anything beside.
pope.gloss: In deep water, a crocodile will conquer (all other animals); but if it leave the water, other animals will conquer it.

reading: A crocodile wins in deep water; if it leaves the water, others kill it.
nuance: The very same animal, and the reversal is total: பிற, anything at all. Parimelazhagar's maxim is that everyone is strong on their own ground, and the practical point is to fight where the enemy can't stand.

couplet: The lofty car, with mighty wheel, sails not o'er watery main,
The boat that skims the sea, runs not on earth's hard plain.
pope.gloss: Wide chariots, with mighty wheels, will not run on the ocean; neither will ships that the traverse ocean, move on the earth.

reading: Long chariots with strong wheels don't run on the sea; ships that run on the sea don't run on land.
nuance: The verse states an obvious fact without comment, and the plainness is the point. Parimelazhagar notes the qualities listed, strong wheels and great size, as just those that don't transfer. He and Manakkudavar read it as being about fitting equipment to the terrain.

couplet: Save their own fearless might they need no other aid,
If in right place they fight, all due provision made.
pope.gloss: You will need no other aid than fearlessness, if you thoroughly reflect (on what you are to do), and select (a suitable) place for your operations.

reading: No support is needed but fearlessness, if you think everything through and act by the place.
nuance: This verse suggests an answer to how 382's fearlessness can sit with 428's fear of what should be feared: fearlessness is what remains once the thinking is complete, எஞ்சாமை எண்ணி. Parimelazhagar glosses அஞ்சாமை as firmness.

couplet: If lord of army vast the safe retreat assail
Of him whose host is small, his mightiest efforts fail.
pope.gloss: The power of one who has a large army will perish, if he goes into ground where only a small army can act.

reading: If one with a large army enters where one with a small army can move, his zeal is destroyed.
nuance: The large army's size becomes the problem. Parimelazhagar explains that it can't act together and has no practice on that ground. What is destroyed is ஊக்கம், the fighting spirit, not only the force.

couplet: Though fort be none, and store of wealth they lack,
'Tis hard a people's homesteads to attack!
pope.gloss: It is a hazardous thing to attack men in their own country, although they may neither have power nor a good fortress.

reading: Even if they have no fortress or standing, it is hard to take on people on the land where they live.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees the reason in psychology: attacked at home, such people won't resolve to flee; they will resolve to die, and even a large army breaks on that. The verse says மாந்தர், people, not soldiers.

couplet: The jackal slays, in miry paths of foot-betraying fen,
The elephant of fearless eye and tusks transfixing armed men.
pope.gloss: A fox can kill a fearless, warrior-faced elephant, if it go into mud in which its legs sink down.

reading: The jackal kills, in mud where feet sink, the unflinching elephant with a warrior's face.
nuance: The chapter closes with its most extreme reversal, the jackal over the elephant. கண் அஞ்சா also splits the commentators, between a beast unafraid at a glance and one that won't obey its handlers.

title: தெரிந்துதெளிதல்
theme: How a ruler comes to trust someone: test first and trust only after that, and once trust is settled, don't doubt it. The chapter doesn't expect the flawless. It looks at what predominates, and deeds are its final test.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter by means of knowing: testing by inference (501), reliable testimony (502) and direct observation (503), how to weigh the mixed (504), the instrument (505), then who not to trust, the cost, and the limit of trust (506-510).
source_issues: 503: Manakkudavar is not aligned.
508: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss reads ஆராய்ந்து தெளிந்த where the verse's தேரான் requires 'without examining'. The negative appears to have dropped out, so I did not rely on that clause.

couplet: How treats he virtue, wealth and pleasure? How, when life's at stake,
Comports himself? This four-fold test of man will full assurance make.
pope.gloss: Let (a minister) be chosen, after he has been tried by means of these four things, viz,-his virtue, (love of) money, (love of) sexual pleasure, and tear of (losing) life.

reading: A person is to be trusted after their nature has been examined through four things: virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life.
nuance: My observation: the usual fourth term after virtue, wealth and pleasure is liberation, and here it is fear for life, the most worldly substitute possible. Parimelazhagar defends the wording against a variant, உயிரெச்சம், saying others changed it for not knowing the Sanskrit source.

couplet: Of noble race, of faultless worth, of generous pride
That shrinks from shame or stain; in him may king confide.
pope.gloss: (The king's) choice should (fall) on him, who is of good family, who is free from faults, and who has the modesty which fears the wounds (of sin).

reading: Trust lies in one born of good family, free of faults and with a shame that recoils from any blemish.

couplet: Though deeply learned, unflecked by fault, 'tis rare to see,
When closely scanned, a man from all unwisdom free.
pope.gloss: When even men, who have studied the most difficult works, and who are free from faults, are (carefully) examined, it is a rare thing to find them without ignorance.

reading: Even in those who have studied the hard books and are flawless, it is rare, when examined, to find no blankness.
nuance: வெளிறு is whiteness or emptiness, a striking word for ignorance: a pale spot in a person otherwise solid. Coming right after the demand for faultlessness, this verse admits no one fully passes, which prepares 504. Parimelazhagar takes it as occasional, due to an unsteady mind.

couplet: Weigh well the good of each, his failings closely scan,
As these or those prevail, so estimate the man.
pope.gloss: Let (a king) consider (a man's) good qualities, as well as his faults, and then judge (of his character) by that which prevails.

reading: Examine the qualities, examine the faults too, examine which of these predominates, and take that.
nuance: நாடி three times. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is what makes the verse humane: no one in the world is only good or only bad. Dominance can be either in weight or in number, so this isn't simple counting.

couplet: Of greatness and of meanness too,
The deeds of each are touchstone true.
pope.gloss: A man's deeds are the touchstone of his greatness and littleness.

reading: For greatness and for smallness alike, one's own deeds are the touchstone.
nuance: The ஏ in கருமமே excludes other tests, which sits awkwardly with 502's demand for birth. Parimelazhagar says explicitly that birth, quality and understanding produce the greatness and that deeds are only the final test of it. Manakkudavar turns it into practice: give a small task first, then promote.

couplet: Beware of trusting men who have no kith of kin;
No bonds restrain such men, no shame deters from sin.
pope.gloss: Let (a king) avoid choosing men who have no relations; such men have no attachment, and thereforehave no fear of crime.

reading: Beware of trusting those who are cut off: they have no attachments and aren't ashamed of blame.
nuance: The logic is that attachment makes a person accountable: without ties there is nothing that shame can work on.

couplet: By fond affection led who trusts in men of unwise soul,
Yields all his being up to folly's blind control.
pope.gloss: To choose ignorant men, through partiality, is the height of folly.

reading: To trust the ignorant with fondness as your support brings every kind of folly.
nuance: Manakkudavar shows this is an argument, naming Parasara as holding that a king may trust those who love him. The verse refutes that. Parimelazhagar notes the folly is the king's, not only the appointee's.

couplet: Who trusts an untried stranger, brings disgrace,
Remediless, on all his race.
pope.gloss: Sorrow that will not leave even his posterity will come upon him chooses a stranger whose character he has not known.

reading: One who trusts an outsider without examining him brings trouble that doesn't end, even down his line.

couplet: Trust no man whom you have not fully tried,
When tested, in his prudence proved confide.
pope.gloss: Let (a king) choose no one without previous consideration; after he has made his choice, let him unhesitatingly select for each such duties as are appropriate.

reading: Trust no one without examining them; having examined, trust what is to be trusted.
nuance: The commentators limit the second half differently. For Parimelazhagar, trust comes for tasks suited to each person's capacity, while Manakkudavar has trust in one matter extend to all matters.

couplet: Trust where you have not tried, doubt of a friend to feel,
Once trusted, wounds inflict that nought can heal.
pope.gloss: To make choice of one who has not been examined, and to entertain doubts respecting one who has been chosen, will produce irremediable sorrow.

reading: Trusting without examining, and doubting one who has been trusted: both bring endless trouble.
nuance: The second error is the unusual one. Parimelazhagar's reason is practical: the person senses it and thinks 'this won't last', so he slackens and becomes easy for enemies to detach. Doubt creates the very betrayal it fears.

title: தெரிந்துவினையாடல்
theme: Having tested someone, how to use them: match person, means, task and time, hand the work over fully, and don't resent the familiarity it brings, yet look at their conduct every day. Trust and scrutiny are both required, and the chapter doesn't entirely settle how.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: who is fit for employment (511-513), who is to be excluded (514), the nature of work (515), how to employ them (516-519), and what to do after they are employed (520).
source_issues: 513: Parimelazhagar's gloss prints தோற்றம் for the verse's தேற்றம், and its meaning, not wavering, fits தேற்றம். This appears to be a transcription slip.
515: The Manakkudavar entry is marked [#] and is nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's, so I did not treat it as independent.
517: The Parimelazhagar entry repeats its bracketed note twice.

couplet: Who good and evil scanning, ever makes the good his joy;
