Such man of virtuous mood should king employ.
pope.gloss: He should be employed (by a king), whose nature leads him to choose the good, after having weighed both the evil and the good in any undertaking.

reading: One whose nature, having looked at good and bad, has settled on the good is to be employed.
nuance: Note the sequence: this person also looks at the bad. The verse doesn't ask for innocence. Parimelazhagar finds in the past tense புரிந்த a probationary stage: a trial task given first, then a more important one.

couplet: Who swells the revenues, spreads plenty o'er the land,
Seeks out what hinders progress, his the workman's hand.
pope.gloss: Let him do (the king's) work who can enlarge the sources (of revenue), increase wealth and considerately prevent the accidents (which would destroy it).

reading: Let him do the work who enlarges the sources, increases the yield and looks into what befalls them.
nuance: A purely administrative definition of a good servant, with no moral term. உற்றவை includes, for Parimelazhagar, what comes from the king himself, whose interference counts among the hazards.

couplet: A loyal love with wisdom, clearness, mind from avarice free;
Who hath these four good gifts should ever trusted be.
pope.gloss: Let the choice (of a king) fall upon him who largely possesses these four things, love, knowledge, a clear mind and freedom from covetousness.

reading: Trust lies in one who firmly has these four: love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire.
nuance: Love comes first, even after the warnings of 507. Parimelazhagar directs it to the king and places the absence of desire at the moment when money comes into his hands, which is a very specific temptation.

couplet: Even when tests of every kind are multiplied,
Full many a man proves otherwise, by action tried!
pope.gloss: Even when (a king) has tried them in every possible way, there are many men who change, from the nature of the works (in which they may be employed).

reading: Even when trusted after every kind of test, many people turn different through the nature of the work.
nuance: The cause of change is the job itself, வினைவகையான். Office alters the person. Parimelazhagar's example is Kattiyankaran, the treacherous minister of Jivaka Chintamani, and he says it is rare for people to resist the pleasures of royal power.

couplet: No specious fav'rite should the king's commission bear,
But he that knows, and work performs with patient care.
pope.gloss: (A king's) work can only be accomplished by a man of wisdom and patient endurance; it is not of a nature to be given to one from mere personal attachment.

reading: Work itself isn't such as to be given to anyone except one who knows and endures and can do it, just because he is favoured.
nuance: The grammar makes வினை the subject. Work has its own nature and doesn't admit of favourites. Parimelazhagar takes சிறந்தான் as someone dear to the king, and Kalaignar as someone merely thought excellent.

couplet: Let king first ask, 'Who shall the deed perform?' and 'What the deed?'
Of hour befitting both assured, let every work proceed.
pope.gloss: Let (a king) act, after having considered the agent (whom he is to employ), the deed (he desires to do), and the time which is suitable to it.

reading: Examine the doer, examine the deed, and act understanding how they fit with the time.
nuance: The doer comes before the deed, which is not the expected order. Parimelazhagar's last step is a judgment on the conjunction: at this time, one of this quality doing a deed of this nature will succeed.

couplet: 'This man, this work shall thus work out,' let thoughtful king command;
Then leave the matter wholly in his servant's hand.
pope.gloss: After having considered, "this man can accomplish this, by these means", let (the king) leave with him the discharge of that duty.

reading: Having reasoned 'this one will finish this by this means', leave that to him.
nuance: The verse is all pointing, with இதனை, இதனால், இவன், then அதனை, அவன். The distal pronouns of the second line themselves enact the handing over: the thing moves away from the king. விடல் is a real letting go.

couplet: As each man's special aptitude is known,
Bid each man make that special work his own.
pope.gloss: Having considered what work a man is fit for, let (the king) employ him in that work.

reading: After seeing a person is fit for the work, make him fully entitled to it.
nuance: Recognition isn't enough: authority has to be conferred. Parimelazhagar makes it elevation so that he can carry the work out himself, and warns that without it the work fails. Kalaignar reads this as simply examining then appointing, which leaves it close to 517.

couplet: Fortune deserts the king who ill can bear,
Informal friendly ways of men his tolls who share.
pope.gloss: Prosperity will leave (the king) who doubts the friendship of the man who steadily labours in the discharge of his duties.

reading: Fortune leaves one who takes differently the closeness of a person devoted to the work.
nuance: A rare observation about what success at work produces: familiarity. Parimelazhagar's setting is sharp: rivals tell the king this man acts as if he were family, and the king takes it as disrespect. If he punishes it, no one will commit themselves again.

couplet: Let king search out his servants' deeds each day;
When these do right, the world goes rightly on its way.
pope.gloss: Let a king daily examine the conduct of his servants; if they do not act crookedly, the world will not act crookedly.

reading: Let the ruler look into it daily: if the one doing the work doesn't bend, the world won't bend.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees the difficulty with trust and adds that the inspection should be done privately, without harming the person's entitlement.

title: சுற்றந்தழால்
theme: Holding kin close as a political and material matter: kin stay when wealth goes, their love multiplies gain, and wealth's use lies in being surrounded by them. They have to be kept through giving, soft speech and absence of anger, and they can be won back once estranged.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the distinction of kin (521), kinship as cause, protection and fruit of wealth (522-524), the means of holding them (525-528), and receiving those who left and returned (529-530).

couplet: When wealth is fled, old kindness still to show,
Is kindly grace that only kinsmen know.
pope.gloss: Even when (a man's) property is all gone, relatives will act towards him with their accustomed (kindness).

reading: Even when all is gone, to keep honouring old ties is found only among kin.
nuance: பழைமை points back to shared history. Parimelazhagar takes it as help the fallen man gave when he had means, which turns kin loyalty into a kind of remembered debt. Kalaignar turns the description into a definition: those with this trait are kin.

couplet: The gift of kin's unfailing love bestows
Much gain of good, like flower that fadeless blows.
pope.gloss: If (a man's) relatives remain attached to him with unchanging love, it will be a source of ever-increasing wealth.

reading: If kin whose love doesn't lapse come together, they yield many gains that keep on branching.
nuance: Pope's flower and fadeless blossom come from reading அருப்பு as a bud. The commentators read it as branching, கிளைத்தல், which gives a neat play: கிளை also means kin. So kin make wealth put out kin of its own, though that last step is my reading.

couplet: His joy of life who mingles not with kinsmen gathered round,
Is lake where streams pour in, with no encircling bound.
pope.gloss: The wealth of one who does not mingle freely with his relatives, will be like the filling of water in a spacious tank that has no banks.

reading: The life of one who doesn't mingle freely is like a broad tank filling with water, with no bank.
nuance: The tank does fill: the failure isn't in earning. Without kin, the wealth has nothing to hold it and spreads away uselessly. அளவளாவு is intimacy, and Parimelazhagar explains it through mutual sharing of mind, so mere proximity isn't enough.

couplet: The profit gained by wealth's increase,
Is living compassed round by relatives in peace.
pope.gloss: To live surrounded by relatives, is the advantage to be derived from the acquisition of wealth.

reading: The fruit of having gained wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin.
nuance: It is striking how far this goes: a whole purpose for wealth in four words. Parimelazhagar's reason keeps it in Porul: it is what enables ruling free of enemies. Read without him, it is more tender than that.

couplet: Who knows the use of pleasant words, and liberal gifts can give,
Connections, heaps of them, surrounding him shall live.
pope.gloss: He will be surrounded by numerous relatives who manifests generosity and affability.

reading: One who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in layer upon layer.
nuance: Parimelazhagar identifies these with the Sanskrit policies of dāna and sāma. So the tender acts of the household are also two of the four instruments of statecraft, which he used in 467 against enemies.

couplet: Than one who gifts bestows and wrath restrains,
Through the wide world none larger following gains.
pope.gloss: No one, in all the world, will have so many relatives (about him), as he who makes large gift, and does not give way to anger.

reading: No one on earth has more of a following than one who gives greatly and doesn't cherish anger.
nuance: பேணான் doesn't mean he has no anger, only that he doesn't tend it. Parimelazhagar even takes it as not exceeding what a king needs. In 487 anger is nursed within against enemies. The verses may simply be about different audiences.

couplet: The crows conceal not, call their friends to come, then eat;
Increase of good such worthy ones shall meet.
pope.gloss: The crows do not conceal (their prey), but will call out for others (to share with them) while they eat it; wealth will be with those who show a similar disposition (towards their relatives).

reading: Crows don't hide, they call and eat; gain too belongs only to those of that nature.
nuance: A humble bird is the model for royal conduct. The verse's உம் says gain too comes this way, and Parimelazhagar concludes that sharing yields wealth as well as virtue and pleasure. Hiding, கரவா, is what is excluded, so a person's private hoard is the fault.

couplet: Where king regards not all alike, but each in his degree,
'Neath such discerning rule many dwell happily.
pope.gloss: Many relatives will live near a king, when they observe that he does not look on all alike, but that he looks on each man according to his merit.

reading: If a king looks at people not in common but by rank, many will live looking to that.
nuance: A real problem: equal treatment drives away those who see themselves as higher. Parimelazhagar openly gives that as the reason.

couplet: Who once were his, and then forsook him, as before
Will come around, when cause of disagreement is no more.
pope.gloss: Those who have been friends and have afterwards forsaken him, will return and join themselves (to him), when the cause of disagreement is not to be found in him.

reading: Those who were kin and left will return to kinship when the cause of discord is gone.

couplet: Who causeless went away, then to return, for any cause, ask leave;
The king should sift their motives well, consider, and receive!
pope.gloss: When one may have left him, and for some cause has returned to him, let the king fulfil the object (for which he has come back) and thoughtfully receive him again.

reading: One who left and came back for a reason, the king should accept with care after attending to it.
nuance: The contrast with 529 is subtle, as Parimelazhagar notes: there a reason for leaving is removed, and here there was none for leaving, only one for returning. He advises to grant what the person came for, but stay cautious: otherwise he may go to the enemy, but he has also shown no love.

title: பொச்சாவாமை
theme: Heedlessness, especially the forgetting that comes with joy and success, is more dangerous than rage. To keep in mind what one has resolved is the skill on which everything else depends, and it is an inward fort or an inward leak.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the fault of heedlessness (531-532), what it brings on those who have it (533-535), the distinction of heedfulness (536-537), what to do with it (538), and how to attain it (539-540).
source_issues: 535: The Manakkudavar entry is marked [#] and is nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's, so I did not treat it as independent.

couplet: 'Tis greater ill, it rapture of o'erweening gladness to the soul
Bring self-forgetfulness than if transcendent wrath control.
pope.gloss: More evil than excessive anger, is forgetfulness which springs from the intoxication of great joy.

reading: The slackness that comes of the elation of great joy is worse than excessive anger.
nuance: A surprising ranking, because joy isn't usually the danger. சோர்வு is a letting go, and it comes when things go well. Parimelazhagar's reason is exact: anger sometimes at least kills an enemy, while this kills only oneself.

couplet: Perpetual, poverty is death to wisdom of the wise;
When man forgets himself his glory dies!
pope.gloss: Forgetfulness will destroy fame, even as constant poverty destroys knowledge.

reading: Heedlessness kills fame as unremitting poverty kills understanding.
nuance: The comparison is the striking claim. நிச்ச நிரப்பு is not poverty but chronic poverty, and Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar make it daily begging to fill the stomach. Understanding is treated as something that material conditions can destroy.

couplet: 'To self-oblivious men no praise'; this rule
Decisive wisdom sums of every school.
pope.gloss: Thoughtlessness will never acquire fame; and this tenet is upheld by all treatises in the world.

reading: The heedless have no fame: that is the settled view of writers of every kind in the world.
nuance: The Kural rarely appeals to an all-schools consensus. Parimelazhagar explains why it can: every aim of life fails when one is heedless, so the claim isn't limited to polity.

couplet: 'To cowards is no fort's defence'; e'en so
The self-oblivious men no blessing know.
pope.gloss: Just as the coward has no defence (by whatever fortifications ha may be surrounded), so the thoughtless has no good (whatever advantages he may possess).

reading: The fearful have no fortress; likewise the heedless have no good.
nuance: A fort is useless to one whose fear is inside it: the verse places the failure in the mind, not in the walls. So the heedless may have resources, and they do them no good.

couplet: To him who nought foresees, recks not of anything,
The after woe shall sure repentance bring.
pope.gloss: The thoughtless man, who provides not against the calamities that may happen, will afterwards repent for his fault.

reading: One who slipped by not guarding beforehand will later, when struck, grieve over his own error.
nuance: Regret is presented as the penalty. தன்பிழை matters: there is no one else to blame. Parimelazhagar adds that the things that could have been guarded against are enemies' moves, made by watching for such lapses.

couplet: Towards all unswerving, ever watchfulness of soul retain,
Where this is found there is no greater gain.
pope.gloss: There is nothing comparable with the possession of unfailing thoughtfulness at all times; and towards all persons.

reading: If not slipping, with anyone, at any time, is had without fail, nothing equals it.
nuance: Three universals. Parimelazhagar assigns each: toward all people, in good times and bad, in every matter. The condition வாயின் concedes how seldom this is met. Manakkudavar takes it as not making errors in giving justice, a narrower sense.

couplet: Though things are arduous deemed, there's nought may not be won,
When work with mind's unslumbering energy and thought is done.
pope.gloss: There is nothing too difficult to be accomplished, if a man set about it carefully, with unflinching endeavour.

reading: Nothing fails to be done on the ground of being hard, if done with the tool of unforgetting care.
nuance: Attention is called a கருவி, a tool. Parimelazhagar notes that it is an inner instrument, the mind, set beside the external means of 483.

couplet: Let things that merit praise thy watchful soul employ;
Who these despise attain through sevenfold births no joy.
pope.gloss: Let (a man) observe and do these things which have been praised (by the wise); if he neglects and fails to perform them, for him there will be no (happiness) throughout the seven births.

reading: What has been praised must be carefully done; those who slight it and don't do it have nothing through seven births.

couplet: Think on the men whom scornful mind hath brought to nought,
When exultation overwhelms thy wildered thought.
pope.gloss: Let (a king) think of those who have been ruined by neglect, when his mind is elated with joy.

reading: When swollen with one's own joy, think of those who were ruined by negligence.
nuance: A practical remedy: history is used deliberately against one's own mood, at the moment it is hardest to think of it. Parimelazhagar notes that negligence and ruin arise together.

couplet: 'Tis easy what thou hast in mind to gain,
If what thou hast in mind thy mind retain.
pope.gloss: It is easy for (one) to obtain whatever he may think of, if he can again think of it.

reading: To gain what one has thought of is easy, if one can keep thinking of what one has thought of.
nuance: The verse is built on repetition of உள்ளியது, which enacts its own lesson. Parimelazhagar catches the particle மன்: it hints what remains unsaid, that this is just what people can't do. So 'easy' is an ironic word. It is easy only in the way the conditional describes.

title: செங்கோன்மை
theme: Justice as the root of a king's power: the people live by his sceptre as the world lives by rain, and it wins him battles, brings rain and protects him in turn. The chapter ends by defending punishment, even death, as part of just rule.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the definition of just rule (541), its distinction (542-543), the fruits for one who keeps it (544-547), the ruin of one who doesn't (548), and punishment as no fault (549-550).
source_issues: 548: Manakkudavar is not aligned.
548: Kalaignar's ஆடம்பரமாகவும் doesn't correspond to எண்பதத்தான் as the other sources read it, so I didn't use it.

couplet: Search out, to no one favour show; with heart that justice loves
Consult, then act; this is the rule that right approves.
pope.gloss: To examine into (the crimes which may be committed), to show no favour (to any one), to desire to act with impartiality towards all, and to inflict (such punishments) as may be wisely resolved on, constitute rectitude.

reading: To investigate, show no favour to anyone, hold to what is fitting for a ruler and act after consideration: that is justice.
nuance: The definition is mainly procedural, four steps with no mention of outcome. கண்ணோடாது is a strong word for a book with a whole chapter praising கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar extends யார்மாட்டும் to those dearer than life, and Manakkudavar to one's own kin.

couplet: All earth looks up to heav'n whence raindrops fall;
All subjects look to king that ruleth all.
pope.gloss: When there is rain, the living creation thrives; and so when the king rules justly, his subjects thrive.

reading: All the world lives looking to the sky; the people live looking to the ruler's sceptre.
nuance: நோக்கி has the sense of dependence as well as looking up. Parimelazhagar narrows the point: the sky gives food and the sceptre gives security, and without security the food is no use to the people. So the sceptre is the more basic of the two for them.

couplet: Learning and virtue of the sages spring,
From all-controlling sceptre of the king.
pope.gloss: The sceptre of the king is the firm support of the Vedas of the Brahmin, and of all virtues therein described.

reading: The ruler's sceptre stands as the origin of the books of the அந்தணர் and of virtue.
nuance: ஆதி is a bold word. It makes politics the source of learning and morals, the opposite of what might be expected. Parimelazhagar notices this, because the Vedas are eternal for him, and explains ஆதி as meaning they don't function without the sceptre.

couplet: Whose heart embraces subjects all, lord over mighty land
Who rules, the world his feet embracing stands.
pope.gloss: The world will constantly embrace the feet of the great king who rules over his subjects with love.

reading: The world stands embracing the feet of the great ruler who embraces his people and wields the sceptre.
nuance: The same word தழீஇ appears twice, and the reciprocity is the point: the king embraces his people and the world embraces his feet. The embrace from above must come first.

couplet: Where king, who righteous laws regards, the sceptre wields,
There fall the showers, there rich abundance crowns the fields.
pope.gloss: Rain and plentiful crops will ever dwell together in the country of the king who sways his sceptre with justice.

reading: Rain and harvest gather together in the land of the ruler who wields the sceptre according to its nature.

couplet: Not lance gives kings the victory,
But sceptre swayed with equity.
pope.gloss: It is not the javelin that gives victory, but the king's sceptre, if it do no injustice.

reading: It is not the spear that gives victory but the ruler's sceptre, if it doesn't bend.
nuance: வேல் and கோல் rhyme and look alike as long shafts. The comparison also lets the sceptre be read as itself a weapon. The verse makes the claim without saying how justice wins battles. Parimelazhagar only says a spear strikes true when the sceptre is straight, and quotes a Sangam poem in support.

couplet: The king all the whole realm of earth protects;
And justice guards the king who right respects.
pope.gloss: The king defends the whole world; and justice, when administered without defect, defends the king.

reading: The ruler guards all the world; justice guards him, if he doesn't falter in it.
nuance: முட்டாச் செயின் means even when it costs. Parimelazhagar's examples are the most extreme ones in Tamil memory: the king who gave judgment on his own son and the king who cut off his own hand, both from the Silappatikaram. That shows what 'not faltering' is taken to require.

couplet: Hard o f access, nought searching out, with partial hand
The king who rules, shall sink and perish from the land.
pope.gloss: The king who gives not facile audience (to those who approach him), and who does not examine and pass judgment (on their complaints), will perish in disgrace.

reading: A ruler who isn't easily approached and who doesn't examine and do justice falls low and perishes by himself.
nuance: தானே கெடும் is close to 448: the ruin needs no enemy. Parimelazhagar's 'low state' is sin and blame, and he supports it by quoting that virtue is death to those who have done wrong.

couplet: Abroad to guard, at home to punish, brings
No just reproach; 'tis work assigned to kings.
pope.gloss: In guarding his subjects (against injury from others), and in preserving them himself; to punish crime is not a fault in a king, but a duty.

reading: Guarding the people, caring for them and removing wrongdoing are no stain on a king: they are his work.
nuance: வடு அன்று answers a charge that must have been in the air. Parimelazhagar makes it explicit: punishing one's subjects could seem against virtue, and he replies that purifying them of wrong is the king's caste duty.

couplet: By punishment of death the cruel to restrain,
Is as when farmer frees from weeds the tender grain.
pope.gloss: For a king to punish criminals with death, is like pulling up the weeds in the green corn.

reading: A king's dealing with the cruel by death is equal to weeding out the young crop.
nuance: The weeding image makes killing seem an act of care for the crop. It says nothing about who decides which are the weeds, and the next chapter opens on a king who may be one.

title: கொடுங்கோன்மை
theme: Oppressive rule as a crime and a self-destruction: the king who extorts is a murderer and a highwayman, and his people's tears wear away his wealth. Its effects reach everything, turning wealth into a burden, and in the older reading failing the rain, the cows and the sacred books.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the fault of oppression (551-552), what the oppressor suffers (553-556), what those under him suffer (557-558), and what befalls his land (559-560).

couplet: Than one who plies the murderer's trade, more cruel is the king
Who all injustice works, his subjects harassing.
pope.gloss: The king who gives himself up to oppression and acts unjustly (towards his subjects) is more cruel than the man who leads the life of a murderer.

reading: A king who takes up harassing people and goes on doing wrong is crueller than those who have taken up murder.
nuance: Both are given the same verb மேற்கொண்டு, taken up as a trade. Parimelazhagar's reason concerns duration: the killer's harm is for a moment, the oppressor's all the time. He adds the reason is wanting wealth.

couplet: As 'Give' the robber cries with lance uplift,
So kings with sceptred hand implore a gift.
pope.gloss: The request (for money) of him who holds the sceptre is like the word of a highway robber who stands with a weapon in hand and says "give up your wealth".

reading: The asking of one who stands with a sceptre is like one standing with a spear saying 'hand it over'.
nuance: The cutting word is இரவு: the king is begging, or calls it that. A request backed by the power to punish isn't a request. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar agree that this is about demands beyond the fixed dues. Manakkudavar adds it is like robbery even when worded as a request.

couplet: Who makes no daily search for wrongs, nor justly rules, that king
Doth day by day his realm to ruin bring.
pope.gloss: The country of the king who does not daily examine into the wrongs done and distribute justice, will daily fall to ruin.

reading: A ruler who doesn't examine daily and do justice loses his land day by day.
nuance: The repeated நாடொறும், and the play of நாடி and நாடு, make the decline as gradual as the neglect. Parimelazhagar notes two ways to read it: that the king loses the land's fruits or that the land itself decays.

couplet: Whose rod from right deflects, who counsel doth refuse,
At once his wealth and people utterly shall lose.
pope.gloss: The king, who, without reflecting (on its evil consequences), perverts justice, will lose at once both his wealth and his subjects.

reading: A ruler who bends the sceptre and acts without reflection loses resources and people together.
nuance: சூழாது is the failure here, not malice. Pope's 'who counsel doth refuse' is more specific than the Tamil. Parimelazhagar makes the people the source of future wealth, so a bad king loses past and future income at a stroke.

couplet: His people's tears of sorrow past endurance, are not they
Sharp instruments to wear the monarch's wealth away?
pope.gloss: Will not the tears, shed by a people who cannot endure the oppression which they suffer (from their king), become a saw to waste away his wealth ?

reading: Are not the tears shed by those who can't bear their affliction the weapon that wears away wealth?
nuance: தேய்க்கும் is slow wearing: tears work like an abrasive. Parimelazhagar sees a saw and a tree in it, and says the real agent is the sin of causing affliction, shifted onto the tears. So he supplies a moral mechanism the verse leaves unstated. Kalaignar has the tears destroy the regime, though the verse says wealth.

couplet: To rulers' rule stability is sceptre right;
When this is not, quenched is the rulers' light.
pope.gloss: Righteous government gives permanence to (the fame of) kings; without that their fame will have no endurance.

reading: For rulers, enduring is by just rule; without it, the lustre of rulers doesn't endure.
nuance: The verse plays on மன்னர், மன்னுதல், மன்னா, ruler and enduring in one root, as if a ruler is by definition one who lasts. Parimelazhagar takes ஒளி as fame and adds the implication that the ruler himself doesn't endure.

couplet: As lack of rain to thirsty lands beneath,
Is lack of grace in kings to all that breathe.
pope.gloss: As is the world without rain, so live a people whose king is without kindness.

reading: As the lack of rain is to the earth, so the king's lack of tender regard is to those who live.
nuance: The negative of 542, as Parimelazhagar points out. But note the shift: 542 needs the sceptre, and 557 fears the lack of அளி, kindness. The failure of a king here is one of feeling as well as of law.

couplet: To poverty it adds a sharper sting,
To live beneath the sway of unjust king.
pope.gloss: Property gives more sorrow than poverty, to those who live under the sceptre of a king without justice.

reading: Under the sceptre of a ruler who doesn't do justice, having is more painful than having nothing.
nuance: Pope's couplet, adding a sting to poverty, misses this, though his gloss has it. Parimelazhagar spells out the reason with grim realism: only those who have something get shackled and tortured for it.

couplet: Where king from right deflecting, makes unrighteous gain,
The seasons change, the clouds pour down no rain.
pope.gloss: If the king acts contrary to justice, rain will become unseasonable, and the heavens will withhold their showers.

reading: If the ruler bends justice in what he does, the sky, bending the rain, won't pour.
nuance: கோடி is used of both king and cloud, so the same bending passes between them, and the grammar itself does the work of linking them.

couplet: Where guardian guardeth not, udder of kine grows dry,
And Brahmans' sacred lore will all forgotten lie.
pope.gloss: If the guardian (of the country) neglects to guard it, the produce of the cows will fail, and the men of six duties viz., the Brahmins will forget the vedas.

reading: If the guardian doesn't guard, the yield of cows declines and those of the six occupations forget their books.

title: வெருவந்தசெய்யாமை
theme: Punishment belongs to rule, but dread does not. Disproportion, inaccessibility, a harsh face and harsh words turn subjects' fear into the slow or sudden ruin of the one who causes it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: what not causing dread means (561-562), the acts subjects fear and what they cost the king (563-567), what his own ministers fear (568), what the king himself comes to fear (569), and the overall fault (570).
source_issues: 563: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss reads செங்கோலன் where the verse has வெங்கோலன்; his own explanation then discusses வெங்கோலன், so this looks like a text error.

couplet: Who punishes, investigation made in due degree,
So as to stay advance of crime, a king is he.
pope.gloss: He is a king who having equitably examined (any injustice which has been brought to his notice), suitably punishes it, so that it may not be again committed.

reading: A king is one who weighs a case fairly and then punishes in proportion, so that the wrong does not go further.
nuance: The chapter opens by defining the king through punishment, not against it. As I read it, dread is set apart from penalty by inquiry and proportion; the two matching words தக்காங்கு and ஒத்தாங்கு carry the whole standard.

couplet: For length of days with still increasing joys on Heav'n who call,
Should raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall.
pope.gloss: Let the king, who desires that his prosperity may long remain, commence his preliminary enquires wi th strictness, and then punish with mildness.

reading: Those who want their prosperity to last long should raise the rod sharply and bring it down lightly.
nuance: The rod image gives two audiences to one act: the raising is seen by would-be wrongdoers and the light landing by everyone else. If Manakkudavar is right, this verse softens the exact proportion that 561 has just asked for.

couplet: Where subjects dread of cruel wrongs endure,
Ruin to unjust king is swift and sure.
pope.gloss: The cruel-sceptred king, who acts so as to put his subjects in fear, will certainly and quickly come to ruin.

reading: A cruel-sceptred ruler who goes on doing what terrifies people will certainly and quickly perish.
nuance: The verse supplies no mechanism: it asserts certainty (ஒருவந்தம்) and speed (ஒல்லை) and leaves the how to the verses that follow.

couplet: 'Ah! cruel is our king', where subjects sadly say,
His age shall dwindle, swift his joy of life decay.
pope.gloss: The king who is spoken of as cruel will quickly perish; his life becoming shortened.

reading: A king about whom the painful words 'our lord is harsh' are spoken will quickly perish, his tenure cut short.
nuance: The harmful speech here is arguably the subjects', not the king's. A phrase people say of him can do what no enemy has done.

couplet: Whom subjects scarce may see, of harsh forbidding countenance;
His ample wealth shall waste, blasted by demon's glance.
pope.gloss: The great wealth of him who is difficult of access and possesses a sternness of countenance, is like that which has been obtained by a devil.

reading: The great wealth of one who is hard to get an audience with and grim of face has something of the ghost about it.
nuance: Inaccessibility and a grim face count as violence here, though no one has been touched.

couplet: The tyrant, harsh in speach and hard of eye,
His ample joy, swift fading, soon shall die.
pope.gloss: The abundant wealth of the king whose words are harsh and whose looks are void of kindness, will instantly perish instead of abiding long, with him.

reading: If a ruler is harsh of speech and without kindly regard, even vast wealth is lost on the spot instead of lasting.
nuance: நெடுஞ்செல்வம் and ஆங்கே are set against each other: length of holdings gives no length of time. This verse's instant loss sits oddly beside the slow filing of 567, so the chapter seems to offer no single speed of ruin.

couplet: Harsh words and punishments severe beyond the right,
Are file that wears away the monarch's conquering might.
pope.gloss: Severe words and excessive punishments will be a file to waste away a king's power for destroying

reading: Harsh words and punishment past all bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength.
nuance: A file works by small repeated strokes, and here the king holds it against his own iron. Parimelazhagar assigns the harm: harsh words lose the army, and excessive punishment loses the country.

couplet: Who leaves the work to those around, and thinks of it no more;
If he in wrathful mood reprove, his prosperous days are o'er!
pope.gloss: The prosperity of that king will waste away, who without reflecting (on his affairs himself), commits them to his ministers, and (when a failure occurs) gives way to anger, and rages against them.

reading: The fortune of a king shrinks if he does not think matters through with his circle and then lashes out in anger.

couplet: Who builds no fort whence he may foe defy,
In time of war shall fear and swiftly die.
pope.gloss: The king who has not provided himself with a place of defence, will in times of war be seized with fear and quickly perish.

reading: A king who has not made his defences will, when war comes, be seized by fear and quickly perish.
nuance: வெரு returns here pointed the other way: in a chapter on causing dread, the king himself ends up dreading. Manakkudavar draws this out by saying that a king must also not do what brings fear on himself.

couplet: Tyrants with fools their counsels share:
Earth can no heavier burthen bear!
pope.gloss: The earth bears up no greater burden than ignorant men whom a cruel sceptre attaches to itself (as the ministers of its evil deeds).

reading: The harsh sceptre binds the unlearned to itself, and the earth carries no burden heavier than this.
nuance: Cruelty is presented as having a staffing logic: it gathers those who lack the learning to resist it. Parimelazhagar puts the weight on the alliance and Manakkudavar on the king who forms it, which comes to much the same.

title: கண்ணோட் டம்
theme: Kindly regard is what eyes are for and what keeps the world's dealings going; eyes without it are wounds or dead wood. Yet the chapter also sets a limit on it, that it must not undo one's duty, and then praises enduring poison for its sake.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (571-572), the fault of the eye that does not extend it (573-575), the low standing of those who withhold it (576-577), how to extend it (578), and its proper scope, namely wrongs done to oneself (579-580).
source_issues: 573: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned in the source.
576: Manakkudavar's text reads மாப்பாவை where his closing line has மரப்பாவை, which looks like a text error.

couplet: Since true benignity, that grace exceeding great, resides
In kingly souls, world in happy state abides.
pope.gloss: The world exists through that greatest ornament (of princes), a gracious demeanour.

reading: Because that surpassingly great beauty called kindly regard exists, this world exists.
nuance: A word of ornament (காரிகை) is given the weight of a cosmic condition. The chapter's elevated claim starts by calling kindness a beauty, not a duty.

couplet: The world goes on its wonted way, since grace benign is there;
All other men are burthen for the earth to bear.
pope.gloss: The prosperity of the world springs from the kindliness, the existence of those who have no (kindliness) is a burden to the earth.

reading: The world's ordinary workings rest on kindly regard, and the mere existence of those without it is a weight on the earth.
nuance: Parimelazhagar lists what உலகியல் consists of: mutual helpfulness, protection, and forgiving lapses. On that reading the grace of the eye is social infrastructure, not private sentiment.

couplet: Where not accordant with the song, what use of sounding chords?
What gain of eye that no benignant light affords?
pope.gloss: Of what avail is a song if it be inconsistent with harmony ? what is the use of eyes which possess no kindliness.

reading: Of what use is melody that does not fit the song? Of what use is an eye with no kindly regard?
nuance: The analogy treats kindness as attunement: the eye is related to regard as melody is related to singing, so it needs the other to fulfil itself. Parimelazhagar's long list of musical terms is a resource for the music tradition more than for the verse's argument.

couplet: The seeming eye of face gives no expressive light,
When not with duly meted kindness bright.
pope.gloss: Beyond appearing to be in the face, what good do they do, those eyes in which is no well-regulated kindness ?

reading: What do eyes that lack measured kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be there in the face?
nuance: அளவினால் is easy to skip: even while condemning the lack, the verse measures the virtue, and Parimelazhagar takes this as excluding excess of it. This prepares for 578.

couplet: Benignity is eyes' adorning grace;
Without it eyes are wounds disfiguring face.
pope.gloss: Kind looks are the ornaments of the eyes; without these they will be considered (by the wise) to be merely two sores.

reading: Kindly regard is the eye's only jewel, and without it the eye is known for a wound.
nuance: The wound is what the observer perceives (உணரப் படும்), so the verse judges the eye by how it meets others.

couplet: Whose eyes 'neath brow infixed diffuse no ray
Of grace; like tree in earth infixed are they.
pope.gloss: They resemble the trees of the earth, who although they have eyes, never look kindly (on others).

reading: Those who have eyes yet do not turn them kindly on others are like trees fixed in the soil.

couplet: Eyeless are they whose eyes with no benignant lustre shine;
Who've eyes can never lack the light of grace benign.
pope.gloss: Men without kind looks are men without eyes; those who (really) have eyes are also not devoid of kind looks.

reading: Those without kindly regard have no eyes, and those who truly have eyes do not lack it.
nuance: The verse redefines possession of eyes by function. The second half turns the first around, closing off the idea of a sighted person who merely chooses not to look kindly.

couplet: Who can benignant smile, yet leave no work undone;
By them as very own may all the earth be won.
pope.gloss: The world is theirs (kings) who are able to show kindness, without injury to their affairs, (administration of justice).

reading: The world belongs to those able to extend kindly regard without damaging the task at hand.
nuance: வல்லார் marks this as a skill and a difficult one. After seven verses of unqualified praise, the condition here gives the whole chapter its hard edge.

couplet: To smile on those that vex, with kindly face,
Enduring long, is most excelling grace.
pope.gloss: Patiently to bear with, and show kindness to those who grieve us, is the most excellent of all dispositions.

reading: The highest disposition is to extend kindly regard and bear with even those whose way is to hurt you.

couplet: They drink with smiling grace, though poison interfused they see,
Who seek the praise of all-esteemed courtesy.
pope.gloss: Those who desire (to cultivate that degree of) urbanity which all shall love, even after swallowing the poison served to them by their friends, will be friendly with them.

reading: Those who want a refinement worth loving will see poison poured, drink it, and stay at ease.
nuance: The verse names no pourer: the 'friends' in Pope and the associates in Parimelazhagar are supplied. Parimelazhagar's support comes from Natrinai 355, which offers a thread beyond the Kural, and it is where the identification of நாகரிகம with kindly regard rests.

title: ஒற்றாடல்
theme: Intelligence-gathering is treated as the sight of the state and as a discipline of evidence: a spy must watch everyone and hold firm, and the king must not trust any one spy.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (581), the duty it serves (582), the fault of neglecting it (583), the spy's characteristics (584-587), and how to employ spies, verify their reports, and reward them (588-590).
source_issues: 585: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned in the source.

couplet: These two: the code renowned and spies,
In these let king confide as eyes.
pope.gloss: Let a king consider as his eyes these two things, a spy and a book (of laws) universally esteemed.

reading: Let a ruler hold spies and the well-regarded treatise, these two, firmly as his eyes.
nuance: Immediately after a chapter that defines the eye by kindness, the eye is redefined by information. Parimelazhagar's pairing makes the spy the eye of flesh, which sees what is happening, and the treatise the eye of wisdom, which says what to do about it.

couplet: Each day, of every subject every deed,
'Tis duty of the king to learn with speed.
pope.gloss: It is the duty of a king to know quickly (by a spy) what all happens, daily, amongst all men.

reading: To know quickly, at all times, everything happening to everyone is the king's work.
nuance: Knowing is called the work itself. Parimelazhagar explains that this is a figure, since both favour and punishment depend on timely knowledge.

couplet: By spies who spies, not weighing things they bring,
Nothing can victory give to that unwary king.
pope.gloss: There is no way for a king to obtain conquests, who knows not the advantage of discoveries made by a spy.

reading: A ruler who does not gather through spies and discern what it all means has no victory lying ready to take.
nuance: The verse has two conditions: spying and discerning (பொருள் தெரியா). Gathering reports without weighing them fails as well.

couplet: His officers, his friends, his enemies,
All these who watch are trusty spies.
pope.gloss: He is a spy who watches all men, to wit, those who are in the king's employment, his relatives, and his enemies.

reading: A spy is one who examines everyone: those doing the king's work, his kin, and those who wish him ill.
nuance: The list begins with the king's own servants and relatives; enemies come last. Surveillance turns inward first, and Kalaignar draws out of this a professional ethic: the spy must not sort people by favour.

couplet: Of unsuspected mien and all-unfearing eyes,
Who let no secret out, are trusty spies.
pope.gloss: A spy is one who is able to assume an appearance which may create no suspicion (in the minds of others), who fears no man's face, and who never reveals (his purpose).

reading: A spy is one who can take an appearance that raises no suspicion, not flinch before eyes that probe him, and never let anything spill.
nuance: உகாஅமை is the image of not spilling. Parimelazhagar's gloss shows his own social world: the unsuspected forms are those of Brahmins, merchants and the like.

couplet: As monk or devotee, through every hindrance making way,
A spy, whate'er men do, must watchful mind display.
pope.gloss: He is a spy who, assuming the appearance of an ascetic, goes into (whatever place he wishes), examines into (all, that is needful), and never discovers himself, whatever may be done to him.

reading: A spy goes in the guise of renunciants, pushes through to examine what must be examined, and gives nothing away whatever is done to him.
nuance: என்செயினும் quietly admits torture. Parimelazhagar sees this: having mentioned the four methods already, he says force is raised again because it is the hardest to bear.

couplet: A spy must search each hidden matter out,
And full report must render, free from doubt.
pope.gloss: A spy is one who is able to discover what is hidden and who retains no doubt concerning what he has known.

reading: A spy is one able to hear what has been concealed and to be free of doubt about what he has learned.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is practical: a king can't act on a report delivered with doubt. The next verse then refuses to accept the spy's certainty, so in this chapter confidence is required of the source but not trusted by the user.

couplet: Spying by spies, the things they tell
To test by other spies is well.
pope.gloss: Let not a king receive the information which a spy has discovered and made known to him, until he has examined it by another spy.

reading: Even what a spy has found and brought back should be confirmed through another spy.
nuance: The commentators explain why from a suspicion of corruption: Parimelazhagar thinks of collusion with those being watched, and Manakkudavar of a spy taking money from rival kings.

couplet: One spy must not another see: contrive it so;
And things by three confirmed as truth you know.
pope.gloss: Let a king employ spies so that one may have no knowledge of the other; and when the information of three agrees together, let him receive it.

reading: Run spies so that one does not know of another, and accept what three say in agreement.
nuance: This is a statement about independent evidence: agreement counts only among witnesses who could not have conferred. Parimelazhagar adds that agreement need only be in substance (பயனால்), and that if the accounts differ, the inquiry continues.

couplet: Reward not trusty spy in others' sight,
Or all the mystery will come to light.
pope.gloss: Let not a king publicly confer on a spy any marks of his favour; if he does, he will divulge his own secret.

reading: Do not honour a spy where others can see it; if the king does, he has himself let out the secret.
nuance: The exposure comes from the patron, not the spy, and from gratitude, not carelessness: the honour itself is the leak. The verse does not forbid the reward, only its being seen.

title: ஊக்கமுடைமை
theme: Energy of mind is the only possession that truly belongs to a person. Wealth leaves and returns, but this inner drive sets how high one rises, and without it strength and even humanity count for little.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: energy outranks the wealth it causes (591-594), the rise of those who have it (595-597), and the low standing of those who lack it (598-600).
source_issues: 591: Manakkudavar's text reads ஒற்றரையுடைமை, which makes no sense here and may be a garbled word.
593: The verse's first word is missing its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), as the commentaries show. Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.
594: The verse's first word is missing its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), as the commentaries show.
598: Parimelazhagar's text reads பெற்றார் where the sense and the verse's எய்தார் need a negative such as பெறார்.
599: The verse's second line has a corrupted character at the start (஦வ்ருஉம்); the commentary gives வெரூஉம். Parimelazhagar's lemma reads பரியத for பரியது.

couplet: 'Tis energy gives men o'er that they own a true control;
They nothing own who own not energy of soul.
pope.gloss: Energy makes out the man of property; as for those who are destitute of it, do they (really) possess what they possess ?

reading: What makes someone 'one who has' is energy of mind; without it, do people really have even what they have?
nuance: Ownership is put in question, not merely wealth's worth. Parimelazhagar supplies a practical reason: without the power to guard it, they will lose it too.

couplet: The wealth of mind man owns a real worth imparts,
Material wealth man owns endures not, utterly departs.
pope.gloss: The possession of (energy of) mind is true property; the possession of wealth passes away and abides not.

reading: Possession of the inner drive is real possession; possession of goods does not stay and slips away.
nuance: The verse's word is உள்ளம், not ஊக்கம். Parimelazhagar makes the identification by metonymy, and Pope's '(energy of)' imports it, so the verse itself may be claiming somewhat more broadly that the mind is the true holding.

couplet: 'Lost is our wealth,' they utter not this cry distressed,
The men of firm concentred energy of soul possessed.
pope.gloss: They who are possessed of enduring energy will not trouble themselves, saying, "we have lost our property."

reading: Those who hold steady energy as their cash in hand do not fret, 'We have lost our gains'.
nuance: கைத்து is money in the hand, and the image is the verse's point: energy is liquid in a way that lost property is not. Their calm is a calculation of assets, not detachment, and this differs from the equanimity grounded in fate at 379.

couplet: The man of en ergy of soul inflexible,
Good fortune seeks him out and comes a friend to dwell.
pope.gloss: Wealth will find its own way to the man of unfailing energy.

reading: Prosperity itself asks the way and goes to the one whose energy does not waver.
nuance: Wealth is personified as a traveller who asks directions, so the seeker has become the sought. Parimelazhagar glosses அசைவின்மை as not flagging in hardship.

couplet: With rising flood the rising lotus flower its stem unwinds;
The dignity of men is measured by their minds.
pope.gloss: The stalks of water-flowers are proportionate to the depth of water; so is men's greatness proportionate to their minds.

reading: The length of a water-flower's stem matches the depth of the water, and a person's height matches their inner drive.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the point of the image: the stem keeps lengthening as long as the water rises, so there is no fixed ceiling. The analogy has a gap, though: water is outside the plant, whereas the mind is within. 'Lotus' is Pope's and Kalaignar's addition; the verse says only மலர்.

couplet: Whate'er you ponder, let your aim be loftly still,
Fate cannot hinder always, thwart you as it will.
pope.gloss: In all that a king thinks of, let him think of his greatness; and if it should be thrust from him (by fate), it will have the nature of not being thrust from him.

reading: Whatever you think about, think of rising; even if it is thrust aside, it has the quality of not having been thrust aside.
nuance: The verse names nothing that thrusts the aim aside. 'Fate' comes from Pope and from Parimelazhagar's பால்வகை, so this is less clearly a verse about fate than it appears in English.

couplet: The men of lofty mind quail not in ruin's fateful hour,
The elephant retains his dignity mind arrows' deadly shower.
pope.gloss: The strong minded will not faint, even when all is lost; the elephant stands firm, even when wounded by a shower of arrows.

reading: The strong in mind do not give way when things fall apart, as a bull elephant holds its ground under a sheaf of arrows.
nuance: Parimelazhagar reads a crossover: 'not giving way' belongs to the elephant and 'upholding one's greatness' to the strong, so that each half lends the other its verb.

couplet: The soulless man can never gain
Th' ennobling sense of power with men.
pope.gloss: Those who have no (greatness of) mind, will not acquire the joy of saying in the world, "we have excercised liaberality".

reading: Those without inner drive never reach, in this world, the proud joy of saying 'we have been generous'.
nuance: செருக்கு is a fault in 431, yet here it is a joy worth wanting. Generosity is presented as something one may feel proud about, and this is not a usual picture of selfless giving.

couplet: Huge bulk of elephant with pointed tusk all armed,
When tiger threatens shrinks away alarmed!
pope.gloss: Although the elephant has a large body, and a sharp tusk, yet it fears the attack of the tiger.

reading: Though its body is huge and its tusks are sharp, an elephant fears when a tiger attacks.
nuance: The verse says nothing about energy or kings. Parimelazhagar names it an allegory (பிறிது மொழிதல்), and the chapter's setting is all that justifies the moral.

couplet: Firmness of soul in man is real excellance;
Others are trees, their human form a mere pretence.
pope.gloss: Energy is mental wealth; those men who are destitute of it are only trees in the form of men.

reading: A person's real firmness is the abundance of the inner drive; those without it are trees, and being human is the only difference.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sharpens the insult: trees bear fruit and serve in temples, houses, chariots and ships, so the only thing left separating such people from trees is that they are not as useful. He also reads உரம் as understanding, as in 24, which joins will and intelligence.

title: மடியின்மை
theme: Sloth is not a private weakness but the ruin of a lineage: it puts out the family's light, hands a person to enemies, and can be reversed only by the one who harbours it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter around the evil of sloth (601-604), the qualities that accompany it and their costs (605-608), and the rewards of being free of it (609-610).
source_issues: 607: Parimelazhagar's lemma reads மடிந்து புரிந்து where the verse has மடிபுரிந்து.
608: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned in the source.

couplet: Of household dignity the lustre beaming bright,
Flickers and dies when sluggish foulness dims its light.
pope.gloss: By the darkness, of idleness, the indestructible lamp of family (rank) will be extinguished.

reading: The unfailing lamp called lineage goes dark and dies when the grime called sloth creeps over it.
nuance: A lamp said to be unfailing fails. Parimelazhagar explains மாசு through tamas (தாமத குணம்); that is his Samkhya vocabulary, which the verse does not use.

couplet: Let indolence, the death of effort, die,
If you'd uphold your household's dignity.
pope.gloss: Let those, who desire that their family may be illustrious, put away all idleness from their conduct.

reading: Those who want their family to be a family should conduct themselves with sloth treated as sloth.
nuance: The repetition is the verse's device: மடியை மடியா and குடியைக் குடியாக. To be a family is an achievement here, not a birth fact.

couplet: Who fosters indolence within his breast, the silly elf!
The house from which he springs shall perish ere himself.
pope.gloss: The (lustre of the) family of the ignorant man, who acts under the influence of destructive laziness will perish, even before he is dead.

reading: The family of a fool who carries deadly sloth inside him dies before he does.
nuance: The cruelty is in the order: he survives to see it. Parimelazhagar's reason is that the family depends on him for support.

couplet: His family decays, and faults unheeded thrive,
Who, sunk in sloth, for noble objects doth not strive.
pope.gloss: Family (greatness) will be destroyed, and faults will increase, in those men who give way to laziness, and put forth no dignified exertions.

reading: For those sunk in sloth without any excellent effort, the family declines and faults multiply.
nuance: The contrast is not sloth against mere activity but against மாண்ட உஞற்று, refined exertion. The verse thus sets a higher bar than being busy; 607 repeats the phrase.

couplet: Delay, oblivion, sloth, and sleep: these four
Are pleasure-boat to bear the doomed to ruin's shore.
pope.gloss: Procrastination, forgetfulness, idleness, and sleep, these four things, form the vessel which is desired by those destined to destruction.

reading: Delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep, these four, are the pleasure-craft of those bound for ruin.
nuance: The image lies in காமக் கலன்: a boat you board because you want to, and which then drops you mid-sea. Parimelazhagar records but does not accept a reading of கலன் as a desired ornament. Manakkudavar reads the four as one sequence: delaying a task, forgetting it, slacking, and sleeping instead.

couplet: Though lords of earth unearned possessions gain,
The slothful ones no yield of good obtain.
pope.gloss: It is a rare thing for the idle, even when possessed of the riches of kings who ruled over the whole earth, to derive any great benefit from it.

reading: Even when what world-rulers possess comes to them, the slothful rarely reach any great fruit.

couplet: Who hug their sloth, nor noble works attempt,
Shall bear reproofs and words of just contempt.
pope.gloss: Those who through idleness, and do not engage themselves in dignified exertion, will subject themselves to rebukes and reproaches.

reading: Those who cling to sloth and make no excellent effort end up hearing words of rebuke and scorn.
nuance: கேட்பர் may hold the sting: they can only listen. Parimelazhagar builds a small story from இடி: friends scold first, see no result, and only then turn to contempt, and if friends do this, others need not be mentioned.

couplet: If sloth a dwelling find mid noble family,
Bondsmen to them that hate them shall they be.
pope.gloss: If idleness take up its abode in a king of high birth, it will make him a slave of his enemies.

reading: If sloth settles in one of a family-building nature, it delivers him into slavery to his enemies.
nuance: மடிமை, குடிமை and அடிமை rhyme in sequence, and the sound performs the fall from sloth through standing to bondage.

couplet: Who changes slothful habits saves
Himself from all that household rule depraves.
pope.gloss: When a man puts away idleness, the reproach which has come upon himself and his family will disappear.

reading: When a person ends the rule of sloth over him, the faults that have come into his family and his manhood are gone.
nuance: Sloth is a ruler here (மடியாண்மை), and one's own effort deposes it. This is the chapter's one verse of repair. Parimelazhagar makes the promise wide, since even faults from other causes vanish; Manakkudavar limits the faults to neglecting what the family needs.

couplet: The king whose life from sluggishness is ri d,
Shall rule o'er all by foot of mighty god bestrid.
pope.gloss: The king who never gives way to idleness will obtain entire possession of (the whole earth) passed over by him who measured (the worlds) with His foot.

reading: A ruler free from sloth obtains, all at once, the whole expanse crossed by the one who measured with his foot.

title: ஆள்வினையுடைமை
theme: Sustained labour builds the doer, funds the virtue of giving and supports one's kin. Faced with fate, the chapter shifts the question: failure of fortune carries no blame, labour always earns its wage, and persistence can outlast what opposes it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of effort (611-613), the fault of lacking it (614), the good of having it (615), effort and its absence as causes of wealth and poverty (616-617), and effort despite fate (618-620).
source_issues: 611: Parimelazhagar's commentary is truncated at the start: the gloss of the first line is missing.
617: The verse reads தாளுளான் where Parimelazhagar's gloss has தாள் உளாள், matching the feminine subject. It may be a text variant or an error.
620: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is almost entirely missing; only the explanation survives.

couplet: Say not, 'Tis hard', in weak, desponding hour,
For strenuous effort gives prevailing power.
pope.gloss: Yield not to the feebleness which says, "this is too difficult to be done"; labour will give the greatness (of mind) which is necessary (to do it).

reading: One must not slacken by saying 'this is hard', because effort brings the greatness needed.
nuance: Difficulty is measured against a self that labour itself enlarges, so the calculation 'this is too much for me' is wrong in its premise. Parimelazhagar makes this explicit.

couplet: In action be thou, 'ware of act's defeat;
The world leaves those who work leave incomplete!
pope.gloss: Take care not to give up exertion in the midst of a work; the world will abandon those who abandon their unfinished work.

reading: Guard against letting a task die in the middle of the doing, for the world's bond with a person turns on how they have dealt with the work's unmet need.
nuance: A short verse gives opposite readings of தீர்ந்தார்: those who left the work or those who finished it. Parimelazhagar glosses குறை from Purananuru 188, which is a thread beyond the Kural.

couplet: In strenuous effort doth reside
The power of helping others: noble pride!
pope.gloss: The lustre of munificence will dwell only with the dignity of laboriousness or efforts.

reading: The proud distinction called helping others stands on the quality called labour.
nuance: Manakkudavar draws the implication plainly: even doing virtue comes from this. A moral excellence has an economic foundation, and தாளாண்மை and வேளாண்மை rhyme to tie them.

couplet: Beneficent intent in men by whom no strenuous work is wrought,
Like battle-axe in sexless being's hand availeth nought.
pope.gloss: The liberality of him, who does not labour, will fail, like the manliness of a hermaphrodite, who has a sword in its hand.

reading: The generosity of one who won't labour comes to nothing, like a sword in the hand of a பேடி.
nuance: The image depends on a period contempt for a third-gender person, which commentators extend by saying the figure wishes to fight but is too afraid. Manakkudavar alone drops the word and says 'one who fears at the sight of arms'.

couplet: Whose heart delighteth not in pleasure, but in action finds delight,
He wipes away his kinsmen's grief and stands the pillar of their might.
pope.gloss: He who desires not pleasure, but desires labour, will be a pillar to sustain his relations, wiping away their sorrows.

reading: One who desires the work and not pleasure is a pillar who wipes away his kin's troubles and bears them up.
nuance: Parimelazhagar finds a principle of causes here: wanting the cause rather than the effect gets all effects, and wanting the effect without the cause gets nothing. The pillar stands under others' weight, so personal renunciation of pleasure is here for one's household, not for liberation.

couplet: Effort brings fortune's sure increase,
Its absence brings to nothingness.
pope.gloss: Labour will produce wealth; idleness will bring poverty.

reading: Effort builds prosperity, and the absence of effort ushers in the absence of everything.
nuance: முயற்றின்மை இன்மை: absence brings absence. The verse's symmetry leaves no room for a third cause, and that is what 371 and 377 dispute.

couplet: In sluggishness is seen misfortune's lurid form, the wise declare;
Where man unslothful toils, she of the lotus flower is there!
pope.gloss: They say that the black Mudevi (the goddess of adversity) dwells with laziness, and the Latchmi (the goddess of prosperity) dwells with the labour of the industrious.

reading: They say the dark goddess of misfortune lives in sloth, and she of the lotus lives in the labour of the unslothful.
nuance: என்ப, 'they say', keeps a little distance from the claim: the verse reports it. தாள் can mean both foot and exertion, and so Lakshmi may be at the feet of the one who works.

couplet: 'Tis no reproach unpropitious fate should ban;
But not to do man's work is foul disgrace to man!
pope.gloss: Adverse fate is no disgrace to any one; to be without exertion and without knowing what should be known, is disgrace.

reading: Lacking good fortune is no one's disgrace; failing to work, after learning what must be known, is the disgrace.
nuance: The verse does not say effort defeats fate. It moves the question from causes to blame, and that is a different and more defensible claim than 620's. அறிவறிந்து adds a condition: blind labour isn't what is being asked for.

couplet: Though fate-divine should make your labour vain;
Effort its labour's sure reward will gain.
pope.gloss: Although it be said that, through fate, it cannot be attained, yet labour, with bodily exertion, will yield its reward.

reading: Though divine order may deny the end sought, effort still pays the wage of the body's strain.
nuance: கூலி is a modest word: a labourer's wage, not the prize. The verse concedes the goal may be lost, and secures only a floor.

couplet: Who strive with undismayed, unfaltering mind,
At length shall leave opposing fate behind.
pope.gloss: They who labour on, without fear and without fainting will see even fate (put) behind their back.

reading: Those who toil on without flagging or delay will see even fate's back.
nuance: உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் is a battle image: to see an enemy's back as it retreats. Pope's rendering, with fate put 'behind their back', turns the image around.

title: இடுக்கணழியாமை
theme: Trouble need not break a person: it can be laughed at, thought away, outlasted, or expected as the body's lot, until suffering itself seems to suffer. The chapter is a series of stances, not one remedy, and it closes the book's treatment of the king.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar sorts the chapter by source of trouble: fate (621-625), loss of wealth (626), and bodily strain (627-630). Manakkudavar maps it differently, taking 621-623 as general, 626 as loss of wealth, 627 as the hardship of austerity and 629 as the pain of desire; he ends the section on kingship at 630.
source_issues: 621: Parimelazhagar's commentary is truncated at the start: the gloss before பிறிதில்லையாகலான் is missing.

couplet: Smile, with patient, hopeful heart, in troublous hour;
Meet and so vanquish grief; nothing hath equal power.
pope.gloss: If troubles come, laugh; there is nothing like that, to press upon and drive away sorrow.

reading: When trouble comes, laugh; nothing else presses back on it as well.
nuance: The laugh is treated as a tactic, not a sign of being unaffected. Parimelazhagar says it borrows the joy of a finished task in the middle of the task, and that the lift it gives supplies the strength to push through.

couplet: Though sorrow, like a flood, comes rolling on,
When wise men's mind regards it,- it is gone.
pope.gloss: A flood of troubles will be overcome by the (courageous) thought which the minds of the wise will entertain, even in sorrow.

reading: Even a flood of suffering is gone when a person of understanding merely thinks it through in the mind.
nuance: The verse doesn't say which thought. That gap is the whole dispute, and Pope's '(courageous)' fills it with one more answer.

couplet: Who griefs confront with meek, ungrieving heart,
From them griefs, put to grief, depart.
pope.gloss: They give sorrow to sorrow, who in sorrow do not suffer sorrow.

reading: Those who do not suffer at suffering make suffering suffer.
nuance: The verse enacts its turn in four occurrences of one word. This reversal of subject and object recurs in 624 and 625, so the chapter's signature is grammatical. Parimelazhagar gives the mechanism: persisting finishes the task, and finishing ends all the troubles.

couplet: Like bullock struggle on through each obstructed way;
From such an one will troubles, troubled, roll away.
pope.gloss: Troubles will vanish (i.e., will be troubled) before the man who (struggles against difficulties) as a buffalo (drawing a cart) through deep mire.

reading: Trouble that meets one who pulls through every obstruction like a draught ox itself has trouble.
nuance: Nothing about this image is heroic: Parimelazhagar cites Civakacintamani's picture of the ox on its side, nose to the ground. It sits beside the elephant of 597 and shows a humbler kind of strength.

couplet: When griefs press on, but fail to crush the patient heart,
Then griefs defeated, put to grief, depart.
pope.gloss: The troubles of that man will be troubled (and disappear) who, however thickly they may come upon him , does not abandon (his purpose).

reading: Though they come stacked one on another, the troubles of one who is not undone are themselves in trouble.

couplet: Who boasted not of wealth, nor gave it all their heart,
Will not bemoan the loss, when prosperous days depart.
pope.gloss: Will those men ever cry out in sorrow, "we are destitute" who, (in their prosperity), give not way to (undue desire) to keep their wealth.

reading: Would those who never knew how to clutch at wealth, saying 'we have got it', grieve, saying 'we have lost it'?
nuance: Grief at losing is settled earlier, at the moment of having. The verse praises a lack of skill (தேற்றாதவர்), which is a wry way to describe a virtue.

couplet: 'Man's frame is sorrow's target', the noble mind reflects,
Nor meets with troubled mind the sorrows it expects.
pope.gloss: The great will not regard trouble as trouble, knowing that the body is the butt of trouble.

reading: Knowing that the body is a target for suffering, they do not take trouble as a thing to be shaken by.

couplet: He seeks not joy, to sorrow man is born, he knows;
Such man will walk unharmed by touch of human woes.
pope.gloss: That man never experiences sorrow, who does not seek for pleasure, and who considers distress to be natural (to man).

reading: One who does not chase pleasure and calls suffering natural does not come to pain.
nuance: Pain is prevented by an expectation, not a defence. Parimelazhagar sees two conditions: wanting pleasure brings pain, and so does trying to ward off suffering as if it were not natural.

couplet: Mid joys he yields not heart to joys' control.
Mid sorrows, sorrow cannot touch his soul.
pope.gloss: He does not suffer sorrow, in sorrow who does not look for pleasure in pleasure.

reading: One who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not feel the pain within pain.
nuance: The experience is not denied: the phrasing இன்பத்துள், துன்பத்துள் places a person within each. Parimelazhagar says they undergo them, yet do not desire or grieve, so that the deeds bear no fruit. That karmic consequence is his addition.

couplet: Who pain as pleasure takes, he shall acquire
The bliss to which his foes in vain aspire.
pope.gloss: The elevation, which even his enemies will esteem, will be gained by him, who regards pain as pleasure.

reading: If a person takes what hurts as pleasure, there comes to him a distinction even his enemies admire.
nuance: The reward is a rival's respect, which is the one kind that can't be flattery. Parimelazhagar's reason is philosophical: pain is no part of the self but a passing mental stance (கணிகம், momentary), which the verse does not claim.

title: அமைச்சு
theme: The minister is defined by what he can do: judge means and time, split and join alliances, unite innate acuity with learning and with the ways of the world. The chapter also assigns him a duty to speak even to a king who won't listen, and warns that a false minister is worse than a multitude of enemies.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the minister's qualities (631-635), his distinction (636), his conduct (637-638), and the faults of ministers to be discarded (639-640). He ties the five limbs in 631 to Sanskrit treatises' limbs of counsel.
source_issues: 639: The verse reads பக்கததுள் (likely பக்கத்துள்), and Parimelazhagar's lemma has ஓரேழுபதுகோடி. He also notes variant readings. Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.

couplet: A minister is he who grasps, with wisdom large,
Means, time, work's mode, and functions rare he must discharge.
pope.gloss: The minister is one who can make an excellent choice of means, time, manner of execution, and the difficult undertaking (itself).

reading: A minister is one excellent in means, timing, method and the difficult task itself.
nuance: Manakkudavar makes this concrete in a military way: the hard task is seizing another's realm, the means elephants and horses, and the time a season with water and shade. The verse itself says nothing so specific.

couplet: A minister must greatness own of guardian power, determined mind,
Learn'd wisdom, manly effort with the former five combined.
pope.gloss: The minister is one who in addition to the aforesaid five things excels in the possession of firmness, protection of subjects, clearness by learning, and perseverance.

reading: A minister is one excellent in five things together, including resolve, protecting the people, learned knowing and labour.
nuance: வன்கண் is hard-heartedness when it condemns impostors in 276, but here it is a qualification for office. The word's moral value depends on where it is pointed.

couplet: A minister is he whose power can foes divide,
Attach more firmly friends, of severed ones can heal the breaches wide.
pope.gloss: The minister is one who can effect discord (among foes), maintain the good-will of his friends and restore to friendship those who have seceded (from him).

reading: A minister is one able to divide others, keep his own side close, and bring back those who have broken away.
nuance: The verse states three skills of division and joining, with no moral comment. Kalaignar's '(for the nation's good)' and his 'those who reformed' are moral framing added by him. Parimelazhagar links two of them to Sanskrit terms.

couplet: A minister has power to see the methods help afford,
To ponder long, then utter calm conclusive word.
pope.gloss: The minister is one who is able to comprehend (the whole nature of an undertaking), execute it in the best manner possible, and offer assuring advice (in time of necessity).

reading: A minister is one able to discern, to act after weighing, and to speak in a way that settles the matter.
nuance: ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல் doesn't name its audience. For Parimelazhagar the settling speech is aimed at the parties being divided or joined, and for Manakkudavar it settles doubtful matters, so eloquence here is persuasion on one view and judgement on the other.

couplet: The man who virtue knows, has use of wise and pleasant words.
With plans for every season apt, in counsel aid affords.
pope.gloss: He is the best helper (of the king) who understanding the duties, of the latter, is by his special learning, able to tender the fullest advice, and at all times conversant with the best method (of

reading: One who knows what is right, whose speech is rich and settled, and who always knows the ways of doing things is the companion for deliberation.
nuance: Virtue comes first in the list, in a chapter otherwise about competence. But Parimelazhagar narrows it to 'virtues done by the king', which makes it knowledge of duties more than the minister's own goodness.

couplet: When native subtilty combines with sound scholastic lore,
'Tis subtilty surpassing all, which nothing stands before.
pope.gloss: What (contrivances) are there so acute as to resist those who possess natural acuteness in addition to learning ?.

reading: What over-subtle scheme can stand before those who have keen native intelligence together with treatises?
nuance: Parimelazhagar names மதிநுட்பம் first since it must be given by the divine, leaving effort to the learning alone. His contrast of natural and artificial knowledge is a useful frame for the next verse. He also defends the text அதிநுட்பம் against அதினுட்பம், 'finer than that', the sense Manakkudavar's gloss gives; the verse's point survives either way.

couplet: Though knowing all that books can teach, 'tis truest tact
To follow common sense of men in act.
pope.gloss: Though you are acquainted with the (theoretical) methods (of performing an act), understand the ways of the world and act accordingly.

reading: Even after knowing the method of doing a thing, act with knowledge of how the world goes.
nuance: செயற்கை and இயற்கை are opposed: the made and the given. In this verse a treatise's knowledge is the artifice and the world is the nature, which is a surprising way to rank them.

couplet: 'Tis duty of the man in place aloud to say
The very truth, though unwise king may cast his words away.
pope.gloss: Although the king be utterly ignorant, it is the duty of the minister to give (him) sound advice.

reading: Though the king destroys wise counsel and himself knows nothing, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is good for him.
nuance: The word for the minister here is உழையிருந்தான், 'the one close by'. Duty arises from nearness, and Parimelazhagar adds that the world will lay the king's fall at the silent minister's door.

couplet: A minister who by king's side plots evil things
Worse woes than countless foemen brings.
pope.gloss: Far better are seventy crores of enemies (for a king) than a minister at his side who intends (his) ruin.

reading: Better seventy crore enemies than a minister at one's side who plots harm.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is that open enemies can be guarded against, but the one inside cannot. 'Seventy crore' is his example of a huge number, not a figure with meaning.

couplet: For gain of end desired just counsel nought avails
To minister, when tact in execution fails.
pope.gloss: Those ministers who are destitute of (executive) ability will fail to carry out their projects, although they may have contrived aright.

reading: Though they plan things properly, those without practical capacity do only what comes to no conclusion.
nuance: A good plan is not enough. Parimelazhagar splits capacity into knowing remedies for obstacles and being firm in oneself, so this anticipates the chapter on firmness in action.

title: சொல்வன்மை
theme: Speech is an excellence in its own right and a source of gain and ruin. Its mastery means fitting the hearer, being unanswerable, being brief when one can and expansive when one must; learning that can't be spoken has no fragrance.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: why speech is indispensable (641-642), what speech is (643), how to speak (644-646), the distinction of those able to speak so (647-648), and the low standing of those who can't (649-650). He reads the whole as addressed to ministers.
source_issues: 641: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned in the source.
648: Parimelazhagar's lemma reads செல்லுதல் where the verse has சொல்லுதல்.
