650: The verse begins இண்ருழ்த்தும், a typographical error for இணரூழ்த்தும் (commentaries give இணர் ஊழ்த்தும்).

couplet: A tongue that rightly speaks the right is greatest gain,
It stands alone midst goodly things that men obtain.
pope.gloss: The possession of that goodness which is called the goodness of speech is (even to others) better than any other goodness.

reading: Having the goodness called goodness of tongue is a good that isn't contained in any other good.
nuance: The verse is about the excellence of speech as such; it does not mention ministers. Parimelazhagar draws them in from the chapter's position and also argues that if others need it, ministers need it more.

couplet: Since gain and loss in life on speech depend,
From careless slip in speech thyself defend.
pope.gloss: Since (both) wealth and evil result from (their) speech, ministers should most carefully guard themselves against faultiness therein.

reading: Since gain and ruin both come from it, guard against any lapse in speech.
nuance: சோர்வு is a slip, not malice. Parimelazhagar widens the stakes: a minister's lapse falls on all living beings at once.

couplet: 'Tis speech that spell-bound holds the listening ear,
While those who have not heard desire to hear.
pope.gloss: The (minister's) speech is that which seeks (to express) elements as bind his friends (to himself) and is so delivered as to make even his enemies desire (his friendship).

reading: Speech is what is said so that it binds those who hear it and makes even those who have not heard want it.
nuance: The second half is the striking one: speech is judged partly by its effect on those not present. Parimelazhagar lists good speech's qualities here as freedom from error, brevity, clarity, sweetness and valuable result.

couplet: Speak words adapted well to various hearers' state;
No higher virtue lives, no gain more surely great.
pope.gloss: Understand the qualities (of your hearers) and (then) make your speech; for superior to it, there is neither virtue nor wealth.

reading: Speak with knowledge of what the moment and hearer require, for no virtue or gain goes beyond that.
nuance: A surprising claim: fit speech ranks at the top of both virtue and gain. Parimelazhagar explains that the cause stands for the effect.

couplet: Speak out your speech, when once 'tis past dispute
That none can utter speech that shall your speech refute.
pope.gloss: Deliver your speech, after assuring yourself that no counter speech can defeat your own.

reading: Speak your word once you know there is no other word that can defeat it.
nuance: சொல் occurs five times, so the verse is a sort of closed argument. Parimelazhagar says winning means excelling in the qualities of speech, which is a broader standard than mere refutation.

couplet: Charming each hearer's ear, of others' words to seize the sense,
Is method wise of men of spotless excellence.
pope.gloss: It is the opinion of those who are free from defects in diplomacy that the minister should speak so as to make his hearers desire (to hear more) and grasp the meaning of what he hears himself.

reading: It is the way of those without blemish in excellence to speak so that others want more and to take the fruit from what others say.
nuance: Mastery of speech includes a discipline of hearing. Parimelazhagar adds generosity: a master doesn't scorn others' faulty words, and takes what is useful in them.

couplet: Mighty in word, of unforgetful mind, of fearless speech,
'Tis hard for hostile power such man to overreach.
pope.gloss: It is impossible for any one to conquer him by intrique who possesses power of speech, and is neither faulty nor timid.

reading: It's hard for anyone to beat in a contest a person who can speak, doesn't slip, and isn't afraid.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss of 'speaking so that it is accepted' is uncomfortable: making people decide 'yes' even where the thing isn't actually in their interest. Eloquence, in that reading, isn't truthful by nature, and the chapter doesn't address this.

couplet: Swiftly the listening world will gather round,
When men of mighty speech the weighty theme propound.
pope.gloss: If there be those who can speak on various subjects in their proper order and in a pleasing manner, the world would readily accept them.

reading: The world quickly responds if it gets those who can speak in order and sweetly.
nuance: பெறின், 'if it gets', implies rarity. Parimelazhagar cites a Sanskrit saying that a true speaker is one in a hundred thousand.

couplet: Who have not skill ten faultless words to utter plain,
Their tongues will itch with thousand words man's ears to pain.
pope.gloss: They will desire to utter many words, who do not know how to speak a few faultless ones.

reading: Those who don't know how to say a few faultless words surely long to say many.
nuance: Loquacity is explained as a substitute for an ability, not an excess of it. Parimelazhagar takes மன்ற as a firm answer to those who actually admire nonstop speech as eloquence.

couplet: Like scentless flower in blooming garland bound
Are men who can't their lore acquired to other's ears expound.
pope.gloss: Those who are unable to set forth their acquirements (before others) are like flowers blossoming in a cluster and yet without fragrance.

reading: Those who can't unfold what they've learned so that others understand are like flowers blooming in clusters without scent.
nuance: Coming right after 649's praise of few words, this verse praises expansion. Manakkudavar notices this: brevity alone isn't enough, and one must also expand where needed. In the image, learning is already in bloom; what is missing is the part that travels to others.

title: வினைத்தூய்மை
theme: The worth of an action lies in its cleanness: no gain, necessity or even a mother's hunger justifies what the worthy condemn, because tainted gain departs as it came and leaves ruin behind.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of clean action (651), the instruction not to do what brings sin and blame (652-656), and the reasons (657-660).
source_issues: 651: The verse reads த்ருஉம், a typographical error for தரூஉம் (as in Parimelazhagar's lemma).
653: The verse reads ஒஓதல் for ஓஒதல், and Parimelazhagar glosses ஓதல் as a shortened form of ஓவுதல்.

couplet: The good external help confers is worldly gain;
By action good men every needed gift obtain.
pope.gloss: The efficacy of support will yield (only) wealth; (but) the efficacy of action will yield all that is desired.

reading: Good companions bring prosperity, while good action brings everything one could want.
nuance: The verse does not say what 'everything' includes. Parimelazhagar expands it to virtue, wealth and pleasure here and desired stations hereafter, and he frames the contrast as between the visible good of allies and the inferred good of deeds.

couplet: From action evermore thyself restrain
Of glory and of good that yields no gain.
pope.gloss: Ministers should at all times avoid acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit (for the future).

reading: One must at all times avoid action that yields neither renown nor good.
nuance: என்றும் is pointed. Parimelazhagar says it holds in rising, shrinking and stable circumstances; Manakkudavar says it holds even when one has no means of doing anything else. The rule doesn't relax under pressure.

couplet: Who tell themselves that nobler things shall yet be won
All deeds that dim the light of glory must they shun.
pope.gloss: Those who say, "we will become (better)" should avoid the performance of acts that would destroy (their fame).

reading: Those who say 'we shall rise' must refrain from the deed that dims their light.
nuance: Ambition itself is the ground of the restraint. Parimelazhagar's summary is that gain that dims one's light isn't gain.

couplet: Though troubles press, no shameful deed they do,
Whose eyes the ever-during vision view.
pope.gloss: Those who have infallible judgement though threatened with peril will not do acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers).

reading: Even when caught in trouble, those of unshaken clarity won't do what is degrading.
nuance: Pope's 'ever-during vision' suggests mysticism; the Tamil நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி is steadiness of judgement. Parimelazhagar's reasoning is a calculation: trouble passes but disgrace doesn't, and what must come will come anyway.

couplet: Do nought that soul repent ing must deplore,
If thou hast sinned, 'tis well if thou dost sin no more.
pope.gloss: Let a minister never do acts of which he would have to grieve saying, "what is this I have done"; (but) should he do (them), it were good that he grieved not.

reading: Do nothing that makes you cry out 'What have I done!'; but if you do, it's good not to do the like.
nuance: The second line turns on what அன்ன points to. Pope gives both answers: his couplet says sin no more, and his gloss says do not grieve.

couplet: Though her that bore thee hung'ring thou behold, no deed
Do thou, that men of perfect soul have crime decreed.
pope.gloss: Though a minister may see his mother starve; let him do not act which the wise would (treat with contempt).

reading: Even if you must watch the mother who bore you go hungry, don't do what the worthy condemn.
nuance: The verse picks the hardest case it can imagine and refuses the exception. Its reach is the dispute.

couplet: Than store of wealth guilt-laden souls obtain,
The sorest poverty of perfect soul is richer gain.
pope.gloss: Far more excellent is the extreme poverty of the wise than wealth obtained by heaping up of sinful deeds.

reading: The utter poverty of the worthy is above wealth gained under a load of blame.
nuance: Manakkudavar sees this as a reply to an objection: living by these rules will leave you poor. The verse concedes it. Poverty is not denied or softened by கழி, 'extreme'.

couplet: To those who hate reproof and do forbidden thing.
What prospers now, in after days shall anguish bring.
pope.gloss: The actions of those, who have not desisted from doing deeds forbidden (by the great), will, even if they succeed, cause them sorrow.

reading: Even when they succeed, the forbidden things people do without shunning them bring anguish.
nuance: முடிந்தாலும் answers the practical objection that the end might come off. Parimelazhagar goes further and doubts it: such acts won't usually succeed, and even if somehow they do, pain follows.

couplet: What's gained through tears with tears shall go;
From loss good deeds entail harvests of blessings grow.
pope.gloss: All that has been obtained with tears (to the victim) will depart with tears (to himself); but what has been by fair means; though with loss at first, will afterwards yield fruit.

reading: All that is taken with tears leaves with tears; what comes from good ways, even if lost, pays later.
nuance: The verse names no one in அழ. The commentators divide the tears, so the victim weeps on taking and the taker on losing, and this moral symmetry is part of the sound of the line. பின் covers the next birth for Parimelazhagar, which the verse does not specify.

couplet: In pot of clay unburnt he water pours and would retain,
Who seeks by wrong the realm in wealth and safety to maintain.
pope.gloss: (For a minister) to protect (his king) with wealth obtained by foul means is like preserving a vessel of wet clay by filling it with water.

reading: Making wealth by deceit and feeling secure in it is like pouring water into an unfired clay pot.
nuance: Both pot and water are lost: the wrongly got wealth also destroys the one it was meant to protect.

title: வினைத்திட்பம்
theme: Firmness in action is firmness of mind, and nothing else substitutes for it. Speaking is easy and doing is hard, but one who stays firm gets what he has thought of, however small he looks and whatever pain lies on the way.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: what firmness is (661), its branches (662-663), its difficulty (664), its distinction (665), its fruit (666), how to recognise those who have it (667), how they act (668-669), and the low standing of those without it (670).
source_issues: 665: Parimelazhagar's lemma for the second line is run together with its gloss, so the words ஊறெய்தி உள்ளப் படும் are not set out separately.
666: The verse reads எய்து where the metre and Parimelazhagar's lemma require எய்துப. Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.

couplet: What men call 'power in action' know for 'power of mind'
Externe to man all other aids you find.
pope.gloss: Firmness in action is (simply) one's firmness of mind; all other (abilities) are not of this nature.

reading: What is called firmness in action is one's firmness of mind; all else is something other.
nuance: Parimelazhagar points to the word choice: மற்றைய admits these others are related, and பிற denies that they count here. Manakkudavar takes 'the others' to be means and methods.

couplet: 'Each hindrance shun', 'unyielding onward press, If obstacle be there,'
These two define your way, so those that search out truth declare.
pope.gloss: Not to perform a ruinous act, and not to be discouraged by the ruinous termination of an act, are the two maxims which, the wise say, from the principles of those who have investigated the subject.

reading: Avoiding harm beforehand and not giving way once it has come are, those who have studied it say, the path of these two.
nuance: Parimelazhagar traces the maxim to the ministers of gods and demons, Jupiter and Venus, and so explains why clean action slips in here. The verse itself mentions only 'those who have studied'.

couplet: Man's fitting work is known but by success achieved;
In midst the plan revealed brings ruin ne'er to be retrieved.
pope.gloss: So to perform an act as to publish it (only) at its termination is (true) manliness; for to announce it beforehand, will cause irremediable sorrow.

reading: True manliness is doing it so that it comes round only at the end; if it comes round midway, it brings unending trouble.
nuance: The verb கொட்க carries the verse, and firmness comes out as secrecy on one reading and as persistence on the other. The two make different claims about what ஆண்மை is.

couplet: Easy to every man the speech that shows the way;
Hard thing to shape one's life by words they say!
pope.gloss: To say (how an act is to be performed) is (indeed) easy for any one; but far difficult it is to do according to what has been said.

reading: Speaking is easy for anyone; doing as one has spoken is hard.
nuance: Pope's 'shape one's life' turns it into a general moral. Both early commentators restrict it to the plan: saying 'this is how we will do this'. After a full chapter on eloquence, this comes as a quiet correction.

couplet: The power in act of men renowned and great,
With king acceptance finds and fame through all the state.
pope.gloss: The firmness in action of those who have become great by the excellence (of their counsel) will, by attaining its fulfilment in the person of the king, be esteemed (by all).

reading: The firmness in action of those great in excellence, once it takes effect on the king, comes to be held in everyone's regard.
nuance: On Parimelazhagar's reading the fruits lodge in the king, wealth and fame being his; the minister's firmness earns only regard. Kalaignar seems to have the firmness attract the ruler instead, so what ஊறெய்தி describes is unclear.

couplet: Whate'er men think, ev'n as they think, may men obtain,
If those who think can steadfastness of will retain.
pope.gloss: If those who have planned (an undertaking) possess firmness (in executing it) they will obtain what they have desired even as they have desired it.

reading: What people have thought of, they obtain as they thought of it, if those who thought it turn out firm.
nuance: The first line sounds unconditional, and it is often quoted that way. The condition is in the second line: thinking must be backed by firmness. Parimelazhagar adds that such people don't think otherwise.

couplet: Despise not men of modest bearing; Look not at form, but what men are:
For some there live, high functions sharing, Like linch-pin of the mighty car!
pope.gloss: Let none be despised for (their) size; (for) the world has those who resemble the linch-pin of the big rolling car.

reading: Do not scorn anyone for how they look: the great rolling chariot has its linchpin.
nuance: The image answers the appearance: the pin bears great loads because it is placed exactly at the point of strain. Parimelazhagar applies this to small-bodied ministers while Manakkudavar applies it to everyone (யாவரையும்).

couplet: What clearly eye discerns as right, with steadfast will,
And mind unslumbering, that should man fulfil.
pope.gloss: An act that has been firmly resolved on must be as firmly carried out without delay.

reading: With the deed one has looked at clearly and decided, act unwaveringly and without delay.
nuance: Sequence matters: கலங்காது before துளங்காது. Clarity comes first, then speed, and Parimelazhagar notes that a confused mind makes what should be dropped seem worth doing. தூக்கம் here is delay, not sleep as in Pope's 'unslumbering'.

couplet: Though toil and trouble face thee, firm resolve hold fast,
And do the deeds that pleasure yield at last.
pope.gloss: Though it should cause increasing sorrow (at the outset), do with firmness the act that yield bliss (in the end).

reading: Even though pain closes in, do resolutely the deed that yields joy.
nuance: Parimelazhagar uses technical language to weigh momentary pain of effort (கணிகம்) against the lasting pleasure of the result (பரிணாம இன்பம்). The verse only says 'joy-yielding'.

couplet: The world desires not men of every power possessed,
Who power in act desire not,- crown of all the rest.
pope.gloss: The great will not esteem those who esteem not firmness of action, whatever other abilities the latter may possess.

reading: Whatever other firmness they have attained, the world doesn't want those who don't want firmness of action.
nuance: வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது mirrors the rejection. Parimelazhagar reads உலகு as 'the high', and Pope's gloss has 'the great', but the verse's own word is the world.

title: வினைசெயல்வகை
theme: Deliberation ends in decision and decision must not stall; beyond that, the chapter gives a practical method of action and alliance, measured to whether one is stronger, an equal, or weaker than the other side.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: general method (671-672), the three positions and the strong one's way (673-674), the equal's way (675-677), and the weak one's way (678-680).
source_issues: 672: Parimelazhagar's gloss repeats a phrase, தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை தூங்கற்க, and contains a garbled sequence. Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.
673: The verse's first word reads ஙல்லும்வா, a typographical error for ஒல்லும்வா (as in Parimelazhagar's lemma).
680: Parimelazhagar's lemma has கொள்வார் where the verse has கொள்வர், and he later writes கொள்வர்.

couplet: Resolve is counsel's end. If resolutions halt
In weak delays, still unfulfilled, ‘tis grievous fault.
pope.gloss: Consultation ends in forming a resolution (to act); (but) delay in the execution of that resolve is an evil,”

reading: Deliberation ends in arriving at resolve, and it's a fault if that resolve lingers in delay.
nuance: The verse gives thought a limit from both sides: it must run until resolve, as Parimelazhagar notes, and it has no right to run after. Manakkudavar supplies the risk: enemies learn of the delay and take precautions.

couplet: Slumber when sleepy work's in hand: beware
Thou slumber not when action calls for sleepless care;
pope.gloss: Sleep over such (actions) as may be slept over; (but) never over such as may not be slept over.

reading: Sleep over what should be done slowly; do not sleep over what should be done without sleeping.
nuance: தூங்கு means both to sleep and to delay. The verse repeats it so that the word itself has to be sorted, and it does not tell you how to tell the two kinds of task apart; Parimelazhagar says they are known through strength and timing.

couplet: When way is clear, prompt let your action be;
When not, watch till some open path you see.
pope.gloss: Whenever it is possible to overcome your enemy the act {of fighting) is certainly good; if not, endeavour to employ some more ‘successful method,

reading: Wherever it's possible, the deed is good; where it isn't, act by looking for a way that will go.

couplet: With work or foe, when you neglect some little thing,
If you reflect, like smouldering fire, ‘twill ruin bring.
pope.gloss: When duly considered, the incomplete execution of an undertaking and hostility will grow and destroy one like the {unextinguished} remnant of a fire,

reading: If you think about it, what is left over from a task or an enmity scorches like what is left over from a fire.
nuance: நினையுங்கால் suggests that this only becomes clear on reflection: a remainder seems small at the moment. Parimelazhagar assigns this to the stronger party, for whom leaving things unfinished seems safe.

couplet: Treasure and instrument and time and deed and place of act:
These five, till every doubt remove, think o'ver with care exact.
pope.gloss: Do an act alter a due consideration of the {following} five, viz., Money, means, time, execution and place.

reading: Act after thinking through until the darkness clears these five: resources, means, time, the deed and the place.
nuance: The list recalls that of 631, but both early commentators double each item: one's own and the enemy's. The verse doesn't say this, and Kalaignar's checklist has only one side. If they're right, this is a list about comparison.

couplet: Accomplishment, the hindrances, large profits won
By effort: these compare, then let the work be done!
pope.gloss: An act is to be performed after considering the exertion required, the obstacles to be encountered, and the great to be gained {on its completion).

reading: Act after looking at how it would be finished, what will hinder it, and the great yield when complete.
nuance: Parimelazhagar states it as a cost-benefit test: act if the yield outweighs the effort and obstacles. Manakkudavar reads முடிவு as the manner of ending, and Parimelazhagar as effort by metonymy.

couplet: Who would succeed must thus begin: first let hin ask
The thoughts of them who throughly know the task.
pope.gloss: The method of performance for one who has begun an act is to ascertain the mind of him who knows the secret thereof,

reading: The proper way for someone doing a task is to learn the mind of the one who knows it from inside.
nuance: After the preceding checklists, this verse says they aren't enough, and that someone who has done it should be consulted. Parimelazhagar's உள் அறிவான் is the person who has done this before.

couplet: By one thing done you reach a second work's accomplishment;
So furious elephant to snare its fellow brute is sent.
pope.gloss: To make one undertaking the means of accomplishing another (similar to it) is like making one rutting elephant the means of capturing arother.

reading: Using one task to accomplish another is like binding a rutting elephant with another elephant.
nuance: The image takes for granted the practice of capturing elephants with an elephant, and பிணித்தல் is itself a skill of the deed. The elephants of 597 and 599 are about character; this one is about technique.

couplet: Than kindly acts to friends more urgent thing to do,
Is making foes to cling as friends attached to you.
pope.gloss: One should rather hasten to secure the alliance of the foes (of one's foes} rather than perform good offices to one’s friends,

reading: Bringing the unallied over to one's side is more urgent than doing good to one's friends.
nuance: Friends can wait because they are friends. This chilly ranking of urgency is about strategy, not love, and Parimelazhagar's reason is timing: it must be done before enemies see one's weakness.

couplet: The men of lesser realm, fearing the people's inward dread,
Accepting granted terms, to mightier ruler bow the head.
pope.gloss: Ministers of smali states, afraid of their people being frightened will yield to and acknowledge thelr superior foes, it the latter offer them a chance of reconciliation

reading: Those whose domain is small, afraid of the trembling within, will bow to the great and accept what they can get if it is offered.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees the verse's tone: since bowing isn't what the honourable would choose, கொள்வர் reports what is done, without praising it. His reason is that if one's own side panics, all is lost.

title: தூது
theme: An envoy must combine love, knowledge, learning and presence with exact speech, courage and incorruptibility, and must carry his sovereign's interest to a foreign court even at the cost of his life.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: qualities common to both kinds of envoy (681-682), the envoy who composes his own message (683-687), and the one who repeats the message as given (688-690). He relates this to a Sanskrit grading of envoys as highest, middle and lowest.
source_issues: 686: Kalaignar's text starts with a stray fragment of the verse and a number (தக்க தறிவதாந் தூது. 686) before the commentary.
687: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned. Parimelazhagar's text reads உரைப்பான் தரை for தலை.

couplet: Benevolence high birth, the courtesy kings love:-
These qualities the envoy of a king approve.
pope.gloss: The qualification of an ambassador are affection (for his relations) a fitting birth, and the possession of attributes pleasing to royalty.

reading: Love, birth in an honourable family, and qualities kings desire make up the nature of one who carries a message.
nuance: Whatever அன்பு means here, the envoy's list begins from the affections, not the skills. Parimelazhagar's 'qualities kings desire' also serve abroad: foreign kings too come under his sway.

couplet: Love, knowledge, power of chosen words, three things,
Should he possess who speaks the words of kings.
pope.gloss: Love (to his sovereign), knowledge (of his affairs), and a discriminating power of speech (before other sovereigns) are the three sine qua non qualifications of an ambassador.

reading: Love, knowledge and carefully considered eloquence are the three things an envoy can't do without.
nuance: ஆராய்ந்த qualifies eloquence, and Parimelazhagar takes it as choosing words that will win assent. Parimelazhagar reads this verse's love as being for the king, so he has given the two adjacent verses two different objects of love.

couplet: Mighty in lore amongst the learned must he be,
Midst jav'lin-bearing kings who speaks the words of victory.
pope.gloss: To be powerful in politics among those who are learned (in ethics) is the character of him who speaks to lance-bearing kings on matters of triumph (to his own sovereign).

reading: It is the mark of one who speaks of victory among spear-bearers to be strong in the treatises among those who know them.
nuance: The two audiences are set side by side: those with treatises and those with spears. Parimelazhagar sharpens the first: the ministers there merely understand the texts, while the envoy must be able to set them out.

couplet: Sense, goodly grace, and knowledge exquisite.
Who hath these three for envoy's task is fit.
pope.gloss: He may go on a mission (to foreign rulers) who has combined in him all these three. viz., (natural) sense, an attractive bearing and well-tried learning.

reading: Let one who has these three together go on this work: understanding, presence and well-tested learning.
nuance: உரு, bodily presence, counts as a requirement. Parimelazhagar says all three earn respect, on which the work depends, and that such a combination in one person is rare.

couplet: In terms concise, avoiding wrathful speech, who utters pleasant word,
An envoy he who gains advantage for his lord.
pope.gloss: He is an ambassador who (in the presence of foreign rulers) speaks briefly, avoids harshness, talks so as to make them smile, and thus brings good (to his own sovereign).

reading: The envoy is one who speaks in brief, removes what would offend, speaks so as to bring a smile, and thereby gets good done.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives each tactic a psychology: when told a compressed reason, hearers who would refuse many matters come round; when told in a pleasing way, they accept hard things without noticing they are hard. Courtesy is presented as technique.

couplet: An envoy meet is he, well-learned, of fearless eye
Who speaks right home, prepared for each emergency.
pope.gloss: He is an ambassador who having studied (politics) talks impressively, is not afraid of angry looks, and knows (to employ) the art suited to the time.

reading: The envoy is one who is learned, does not fear hostile eyes, speaks so that it goes home, and knows what fits the time.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that காலத்தால் தக்கது allows for ends reached by means other than what the treatises taught. Manakkudavar makes the learning very specific: how to turn aside the enemy king's anger.

couplet: He is the best who knows what's due, the time considered well,
The place selects, then ponders long ere he his errand tell.
pope.gloss: He is chief (among ambassadors) who understands the proper decorum (before foreign princes), seeks the (proper) occasion, knows the (most suitable) place, and delivers his message after (due) consideration.

reading: The highest is the one who knows the protocol, considers the moment, knows the place, and speaks after thinking it through.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's எண்ணி is rehearsal in chains: what I say, what they answer, what I say next. His இடம் is a place where one's allies are present, so a place is political, not physical.

couplet: Integrity, resources, soul determined, truthfulness.
Who rightly speaks his message must these marks possess.
pope.gloss: The qualifications of him who faithfully delivers his (sovereign's) message are purity, the support (of foreign ministers), and boldness, with truthfulness in addition to the (aforesaid) three.

reading: Purity, support, resolve and truthfulness in these three mark the one who delivers the message faithfully.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's purity is immunity to bribes of money and women, so that the message isn't altered. Truth here is a qualification for being believed. These are professional virtues as he explains them, not an inner holiness.

couplet: His faltering lips must utter no unworthy thing,
Who stands, with steady eye, to speak the mandates of his king.
pope.gloss: He alone is fit to communicate (his sovereign's) reply, who possesses the firmness not to utter even inadvertently what may reflect discredit (on the latter).

reading: One who conveys the king's reply to kings is a hard man whose mouth will not let slip a word that shames.
nuance: வன்கண் is again a virtue, as in 632, and Parimelazhagar shows why: the temptation comes from fear for oneself. The slip would be a phrase softening his king's standing in order to save his skin.

couplet: Death to the faithful one his embassy may bring;
To envoy gains assured advantage for his king.
pope.gloss: He is the ambassador who fearlessly seeks his sovereign's good though it should cost him his life (to deliver his message).

reading: The envoy is one who, even if it brings his end, doesn't hold back and secures what is good for his lord.
nuance: இறுதி is the limit, and the chapter stops there. The ideal is unconditional, and the verse gives no reason why the envoy should owe so much; it's taken for granted.

title: மன்னரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுதல்
theme: Serving a king is like warming oneself at a fire: useful, dangerous, and demanding constant awareness of distance. The chapter gives rules for courtiers who can't presume on favour, age, kinship or old intimacy, and is candid about the danger behind the courtesy.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: general rules (691-693), specific conduct (694-697), and the warning that one shouldn't do what displeases on the assumption that he will bear with it (698-700).
source_issues: 692: Pope's couplet and gloss are run together with a stray '< br>' tag, leaving the gloss field empty after the separator.
699: Parimelazhagar's explanation has a word missing its opening letter (ன்னையராகவே, likely தன்னையராகவே).

couplet: Who warm them at the fire draw not too near, nor keep too much aloof;
Thus let them act who dwell beneath of warlike kings the palace-roof.
pope.gloss: Ministers who serve under fickle-minded monarchs should, like those who warm themselves at the fire, be neither (too) far, nor (too) near.

reading: Those who attach themselves to quarrelsome kings should be like people warming at a fire: not going off, not going close.
nuance: The image avoids praising or blaming the king: fire doesn't have intentions. Parimelazhagar spells out both halves: at a distance one gets nothing, and up close one is burned. இகல் doesn't say which kings, and may imply all of them.

couplet: To those who prize not state that kings are wont to prize,
The king himself abundant wealth supplies. < br> For ministers not to cover the things desired by their kings will through the kings themselves yield them everlasting wealth.

reading: Not desiring what kings desire brings, through those kings, lasting prosperity.
nuance: A kind of worldly detachment that works as strategy. Parimelazhagar gives the mechanism: kings fear those who would rival them in pleasures, finery and rank, and they reward one who doesn't. So the restraint is prudence and may not be virtue at all.

couplet: Who would walk warily, let him of greater faults beware;
To clear suspicions once aroused is an achievement rare.
pope.gloss: Ministers who would save themselves should avoid (the commission of) serious errors for if the king's suspicion is once roused, no one can remove it.

reading: If you would guard yourself, guard against the gravest things; once suspicion has arisen, nobody can clear it.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's list of grave faults is betrayal, intimacy with royal women and seizing treasure. His comparison is memorable: like a debt that comes to mind at each sight of the debtor, a cleared suspicion recurs each time the king sees you.

couplet: All whispered words and interchange of smiles repress,
In presence of the men who kingly power possess.
pope.gloss: While in the presence of the sovereign, ministers should neither whisper to nor smile at others.

reading: In the presence of the great and established, suppress whispers and shared smiles.
nuance: These small signs are dangerous because a ruler reads them: Parimelazhagar says he will assume they concern his own faults. The next chapter's interest in reading signs here falls on those who are read. The verse says 'great ones', and only commentators limit this to kings.

couplet: Seek not, ask not, the secret of the king to hear;
But if he lets the matter forth, give ear!
pope.gloss: (When the king is engaged) in secret counsel (with others), ministers should neither over-hear anything whatever nor pry into it with inquisitive questions, but (wait to) listen when it is divulged (by the king himself).

reading: Don't listen in to anything or press for anything; hear a secret when it has been let go.
nuance: Manakkudavar says that even the desire to hear is a fault. The whole risk is that curiosity about power looks like a threat to it.

couplet: Knowing the signs, waiting for fitting time, with courteous care,
Things not displeasing, needful things, declare.
pope.gloss: Knowing the (king's disposition and seeking the right time, (the minister) should in a pleasing manner suggest things such as are desirable and not disagreeable.

reading: Knowing the mood and considering the time, say what is needed and not disliked, so that it is wanted.
nuance: Each word is doing work: வெறுப்பில, 'not disliked', is a test of the hearer, while வேண்டுப, 'needed', is a test of the matter. Parimelazhagar explains that a thing a king doesn't accept won't get done, so the point is practical, and that during lust or anger advice is useless.

couplet: Speak pleasant things, but never utter idle word;
Not though by monarch's ears with pleasure heard.
pope.gloss: Ministers should (always) give agreeable advice but on no occasion recommend useless actions, though requested (to do so).

reading: Say what is wanted, and never say what is useless even if you are asked.

couplet: Say not, 'He's young, my kinsman,' despising thus your king;
But reverence the glory kingly state doth bring.
pope.gloss: Ministers should behave in accordance with the (Divine) light in the person of kings and not despise them saying, "He is our junior (in age) and connected with our family!".

reading: Without belittling him as 'he's younger' or 'he's kin of such a degree', one should conduct oneself in keeping with the light he stands in.
nuance: நின்ற ஒளி: the light is one he stands in, and this can be read as belonging to the office, whoever holds it. Pope's '(Divine)' comes from Parimelazhagar.

couplet: 'We've gained his grace, boots nought what graceless acts we do',
So deem not sages who the changeless vision view.
pope.gloss: Those whose judgement is firm will not do what is disagreeable (to the sovereign) saying (within themselves) "We are esteemed by the king".

reading: Those of unshaken clarity won't, thinking 'we are in favour', do what is unacceptable.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's diagnosis is one of changed self-image: those who fall think of themselves as new people after being favoured. Clarity, then, is seeing that one is the same person as before.

couplet: Who think 'We're ancient friends' and do unseemly things;
To these familiarity sure ruin brings.
pope.gloss: The (foolish) claim with which a minister does unbecoming acts because of his (long) familiarity (with the king) will ensure his ruin.

reading: The intimacy that, thinking 'we go back a long way', does what is improper brings ruin.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's explanation is the chapter's coldest note: when the king can no longer bear it, he takes the life without any kindly regard for the old bond. The chapter on kindly regard asks for exactly what the courtier here can't count on.

title: குறிப்பறிதல்
theme: Reading what is unspoken from face and eye is the highest social faculty. The chapter places this skill near the divine, treats the eyes that can't do it as useless, and holds that the face betrays what the heart holds.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the distinction of those who read signs (701-703), the low standing of those who can't (704-705), the face as the instrument of reading (706-708), and the gaze as its finest instrument (709-710). Chapter 110 has the same title, in the setting of love.
source_issues: 707: Parimelazhagar's text reads கருதியும் where the parallel with மலர்ந்தும் and Manakkudavar's 706 suggest கருகியும்.
708: Parimelazhagar's explanation reads இறல்பு, likely a typographical error for இயல்பு.

couplet: Who knows the sign, and reads unuttered thought, the gem is he,
Of earth round traversed by the changeless sea.
pope.gloss: The minister who by looking (at the king) understands his mind without being told (of it), will be a perpetual ornament to the world which is surrounded by a never-drying sea.

reading: One who sees and knows what is meant before it is said is an ornament to the earth, whose waters never fail.
nuance: The verse doesn't say whose mind is being read. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as the king's, Kalaignar as anyone's. After the previous chapter, a minister's skill seems likely, though it is not stated.

couplet: Undoubting, who the minds of men can scan,
As deity regard that gifted man.
pope.gloss: He is to be esteemed a god who is able to ascertain without a doubt what is within (one's mind).

reading: Regard as equal to a god one who knows, without doubt, what is within.
nuance: ஐயப்படாஅது is the claim's high bar: accurate conjecture isn't enough. Parimelazhagar locates the divinity narrowly in this one capacity, while the person stays human in body. Kalaignar's phrase 'if it is said that this power is god's' hedges the verse.

couplet: Who by the sign the signs interprets plain,
Give any member up his aid to gain.
pope.gloss: The king should ever give whatever (is asked) of his belongings and secure him who, by the indications (of his own mind) is able to read those of another.

reading: Give whatever part of what you have, and gain those who read a sign by a sign.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reading contains a small theory of other minds: since inner workings are alike in all people, knowing one's own gives access to another's. The verse's குறிப்பிற் குறிப்பு is short enough to allow this but does not state it.

couplet: Who reads what's shown by signs, though words unspoken be,
In form may seem as other men, in function nobler far is he.
pope.gloss: Those who understand one's thoughts without being informed (thereof) and those who do not, may (indeed) resemble one another bodily; still are they different (mentally).

reading: Those who take what is meant without its being said and all the others are alike in limbs, yet they are different.
nuance: Parimelazhagar completes the thought: lacking the highest knowing, the others are to be classed as beasts. The verse just says வேறு, 'different', and the understatement may be stronger than the gloss.

couplet: By sign who knows not sings to comprehend, what gain,
'Mid all his members, from his eyes does he obtain?
pope.gloss: Of what use are the eyes amongst one's members, if they cannot by their own indications dive those of another ?.

reading: If they can't read a sign by a sign, of what use, among one's limbs, are eyes?
nuance: Eyes are asked to do what is not seeing in the ordinary sense. Parimelazhagar says awareness itself is being attributed to the eye here because of how much it helps. Manakkudavar says such people are like the blind.

couplet: As forms around in crystal mirrored clear we find,
The face will show what's throbbing in the mind.
pope.gloss: As the mirror reflects what is near so does the face show what is uppermost in the mind.

reading: As crystal shows what is near it, the face shows what is strongest in the heart.
nuance: பளிங்கு is crystal, and it takes on a neighbouring colour. Pope and Kalaignar's 'mirror' changes the figure: a mirror shows what stands opposite, and crystal changes colour within itself. கடுத்தது is what is most intense, so the face shows peaks and not everything.

couplet: Than speaking countenance hath aught more prescient skill?
Rejoice or burn with rage, 'tis the first herald still!
pope.gloss: Is there anything so full of knowledge as the face ? (No.) it precedes the mind, whether (the latter is) pleased or vexed.

reading: Is there anything as knowing as the face? Whether one is pleased or angry, it gets there first.
nuance: Parimelazhagar treats this as a rejoinder to those who say a face, made of elements, can't know anything, and reads the verse's question as a mock refutation. The point isn't that it knows, but that it arrives before the words do.

couplet: To see the face is quite enough, in presence brought,
When men can look within and know the lurking thought.
pope.gloss: If the king gets those who by looking into his mind can understand (and remove) what has occurred (to him) it is enough that he stand looking at their face.

reading: If you have those who look within and understand what has happened, it's enough to stand and look them in the face.

couplet: The eye speaks out the hate or friendly soul of man;
To those who know the eye's swift varying moods to scan.
pope.gloss: If a king gets ministers who can read the movements of the eye, the eyes (of foreign kings) will (themselves) reveal (to him) their hatred or friendship.

reading: The eye itself will tell of enmity and friendship, if you have those who understand the eye's kinds.
nuance: The eye is said to speak (உரைக்கும்), and speech itself isn't needed. Parimelazhagar applies this to foreign kings as read by ministers, so this is diplomatic intelligence at its most subtle.

couplet: The men of keen discerning soul no other test apply
(When you their secret ask) than man's revealing eye.
pope.gloss: The measuring-rod of those (ministers) who say "we are acute" will on inquiry be found to be their (own) eyes and nothing else.

reading: When you look into it, the measuring rod of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye.
nuance: என்பார் may carry a slight smile: 'those who say we are fine-minded'. Parimelazhagar explains why the eye: gesture, form, action and speech can all be hidden once one knows they're being read, but a gaze is mixed with the mind. He also records a variant reading, அலைக்குங்கோல்.

title: அவையறிதல்
theme: Speech can't be judged apart from its hearers. One must read the assembly and adjust: shine among the bright, stay silent or whitewashed among the dull, step carefully among the great, and never spill nectar where it can't be received.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: speak only after knowing the assembly (711-712), the fault of not doing so (713), a summary of how to behave (714), conduct before superiors (715-716), before equals (717-718), and before inferiors (719-720).
source_issues: 711: The verse reads அவையறிநது, a typographical error for அவையறிந்து.
712: Parimelazhagar's text has an encoding error (தௌ¢ந்து for தெளிந்து).
714: Parimelazhagar's text has an encoding error (ஔÿபுள்ளிÿளியாரவைக்) and reads கதையின் where the verse needs சுதையின், and it ends with a stray ') ---'.
719: The verse's second line reads நன்குசலச், a typographical error for நன்கு செலச் (as in Parimelazhagar's lemma).
720: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned. Parimelazhagar's text places the label விளக்கம் in the middle of the explanation.

couplet: Men pure in heart, who know of words the varied force,
Should to their audience known adapt their well-arranged discourse.
pope.gloss: Let the pure who know the arrangement of words speak with deliberation after ascertaining (the nature of) the court (then assembled).

reading: Those whose purity lies in knowing the body of words should speak after knowing the assembly and examining the matter.
nuance: Pope's 'pure in heart' gives the wrong impression. For Parimelazhagar, தூய்மை here is selection: discarding what doesn't suit and keeping what does. It's a purity of diction, not of character, though the verse doesn't rule out more.

couplet: Good men to whom the arts of eloquence are known,
Should seek occasion meet, and say what well they've made their own.
pope.gloss: Let the good who know the uses of words speak with a clear knowledge after ascertaining the time (suited to the court).

reading: Those with the goodness of knowing how words work should discern the opening, understand clearly, and then speak.

couplet: Unversed in councils, who essays to speak.
Knows not the way of suasive words,- and all is weak.
pope.gloss: Those who undertake to speak without knowing the (nature of the) court are ignorant of the quality of words as well as devoid of the power (of learning).

reading: Those who undertake to speak without knowing the assembly don't know the kinds of speech, and have no ability at all.
nuance: A strong claim about what speech is. Parimelazhagar's reason is that kinds of speech follow from kinds of hearers' understanding, so if you don't know the hearer, you don't know the words.

couplet: Before the bright ones shine as doth the light!
Before the dull ones be as purest stucco white!
pope.gloss: Ministers should be lights in the assembly of the enlightned, but assume the pure whiteness of mortar (ignorance) in that of fools.

reading: Before the bright be bright; before the empty, take on the colour of pure white plaster.
nuance: The verse plays on வெளி, the blank and white. Parimelazhagar connects it to வெளிறு, wood without heart, and says one should appear even whiter than they are so they will respect you. It's unusually candid advice to feign emptiness; the commentators don't soften it.

couplet: Midst all good things the best is modest grace,
That speaks not first before the elders' face.
pope.gloss: The modesty by which one does not rush forward and speak in (an assembly of) superiors is the best among all (one's) good qualities.

reading: The best of all things called good is the restraint of not speaking first among elders.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the exact limit: only speaking first is forbidden, so speaking with them or after them remains allowed. Manakkudavar extends முதுவர் beyond age to austerity, family and learning, and this matters because the verse gives only the one word.

couplet: As in the way one tottering falls, is slip before
The men whose minds are filled with varied lore.
pope.gloss: (For a minister) to blunder in the presence of those who have acquired a vast store of learning and know (the value thereof) is like a good man stumbling (and falling away) from the path (of virtue).

reading: A slip before those who have taken in and understood wide learning is like faltering from one's footing on the path.

couplet: The learning of the learned sage shines bright
To those whose faultless skill can value it aright.
pope.gloss: The learning of those who have read and understood (much) will shine in the assembly of those who faultlessly examine (the nature of) words.

reading: The learning of those who have studied and understood shines where people can examine words faultlessly.
nuance: Learning needs a qualified audience to appear at all. Manakkudavar puts this as a limit: only the learned can tell how good learning is.

couplet: To speak where understanding hearers you obtain,
Is sprinkling water on the fields of growing grain!
pope.gloss: Lecturing to those who have the ability to understand (for themselves) is like watering a bed of plants that are growing (of themselves).

reading: Speaking before those with understanding is like pouring water on a bed where the crop is already growing.
nuance: The image could suggest redundancy, since the crop grows anyway. Parimelazhagar takes the opposite point: what would grow by itself grows all the more, and what grows is the speaker's own learning.

couplet: In councils of the good, who speak good things with penetrating power,
In councils of the mean, let them say nought, e'en in oblivious hour.
pope.gloss: Those who are able to speak good things impressively in an assembly of the good should not even forgetfully speak them in that of the low

reading: Those able to speak well and effectively in a good assembly should not, even by forgetting, speak in a mean one.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is double: the good assembly scorns you for not knowing your audience, and the mean one for not grasping the matter. பொச்சாந்தும், 'even by forgetting', treats it as a slip one must be on guard against.

couplet: Ambrosia in the sewer spilt, is word
Spoken in presence of the alien herd.
pope.gloss: To utter (a good word) in the assembly of those who are of inferior rank is like dropping nectar on the ground.

reading: Holding forth before those who aren't of one's own group is like nectar spilled in a dirty yard.
nuance: The verse's division is தங்கணத்தார் அல்லார், those not of one's group, which is a matter of fit and not explicitly of worth. Pope's 'alien herd' and 'inferior rank' sharpen it. Parimelazhagar sees the waste as twofold: those who would know it as deathless food never get it, and the yard gains nothing.

title: அவையஞ்சாமை
theme: Fearlessness before an assembly is rarer than courage in battle, and it's the test of learning: knowledge that can't be spoken there is a sword in a frightened hand, and its holder counts for less than the unlearned and little more than the dead.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the distinction of those without fear of the assembly (721-723), one benefit (724), its cause, the study of logic (725), and the low standing of those who fear it (726-730).
source_issues: 721: Manakkudavar's text starts with a stray line fragment of the verse, and his closing 'அமைச்சியல் முற்றிற்று' appears at this verse.
724: Parimelazhagar's text places the label விளக்கம் after a clause of its own explanation.
725: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.
727: Parimelazhagar's text has an encoding error (ஔÿபுள்ளிÿவாள், for ஒள்வாள்) and his lemma reads பகையத்து. Manakkudavar's text reads பசையிண்கண் for பகையின்கண்.

couplet: Men, pure in heart, who know of words the varied force,
The mighty council's moods discern, nor fail in their discourse.
pope.gloss: The pure who know the classification of words having first ascertained the nature (of the court) will not (through fear) falter in their speech before the powerful body.

reading: Those whose purity lies in knowing the body of words, having known the kinds, don't let their speech slip before the capable.
nuance: The second line is identical to 711's. There the same people adjust to their hearers, and here they keep from faltering. Parimelazhagar brings in fear from the chapter's title; the verse only says வாய்சோரார்.

couplet: Who what they've learned, in penetrating words heve learned to say,
Before the learn'd among the learn'd most learn'd are they.
pope.gloss: Those who can agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned will be regarded as the most learned among the learned.

reading: Those who make what they've learned go home before the learned are called learned among the learned.
nuance: The verse is about reputation (எனப்படுவர்). Parimelazhagar's reasoning is that the world only knows the learned through such occasions, so public recognition depends on this one skill, not on how much is known.

couplet: Many encountering death in face of foe will hold their ground;
Who speak undaunted in the council hall are rarely found.
pope.gloss: Many indeed may (fearlessly) die in the presence of (their) foes; (but) few are those who are fearless in the assembly (of the learned).

reading: Those who die amid enemies are easy to find; those who don't fear within an assembly are hard to find.
nuance: பகையகத்து and அவையகத்து are parallel: the assembly is a battlefield with a higher casualty of nerve. This is one of the Kural's boldest reversals of martial values. Parimelazhagar reads எளியர் simply as 'many' and அரியர் as 'few', so the claim concerns numbers and isn't a ranking of worth.

couplet: What you have learned, in penetrating words speak out before
The learn'd; but learn what men more learn'd can teach you more.
pope.gloss: (Ministers) should agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned and acquire more (knowledge) from their superiors (in learning).

reading: Make what you have learned go home before the learned, and take the more from those who know more.
nuance: Fearlessness has an epistemic pay-off. Parimelazhagar's reason: no one can learn everything, so speaking in a mixed assembly prompts others to speak. Manakkudavar goes so far as to define fearlessness of the assembly as this exchange.

couplet: By rule, to dialectic art your mind apply,
That in the council fearless you may make an apt reply.
pope.gloss: In order to reply fearlessly before a foreign court, (ministers) should learn logic according to the rules (of grammar).

reading: Learn by the proper path and with its measure, so as to give replies in the assembly without fear.
nuance: Fear is treated as a gap in training, not of temperament. The verse's ஆற்றின் அளவு is brief; Parimelazhagar expands it into grammar followed by logic, listing Nyaya terms for disputation. Pope follows him. That learned apparatus isn't in the verse itself.

couplet: To those who lack the hero's eye what can the sword avail?
Or science what, to those before the council keen who quail?
pope.gloss: What have they to do with a sword who are not valiant, or they with learning who are afraid of an intelligent assembly ?

reading: What is a sword to those who are not hard-eyed? What are treatises to those who fear a subtle assembly?
nuance: வன்கண் is once again positive, as in 632 and 689. Parimelazhagar's conclusion is that such people have no claim on the treatises, and this goes further than saying they fail to use them.

couplet: As shining sword before the foe which 'sexless being' bears,
Is science learned by him the council's face who fears.
pope.gloss: The learning of him who is diffident before an assembly is like the shining sword of an hermaphrodite in the presence of his foes.

reading: The treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி in the midst of enemies.
nuance: The image relies on a period contempt, and Manakkudavar again drops the word, saying only 'one who fears'. Parimelazhagar works the comparison out carefully: field and sword are both good, so the failure lies wholly in the holder, as with the assembly and the book.

couplet: Though many things they've learned, yet useless are they all,
To man who cannot well and strongly speak in council hall.
pope.gloss: Those who cannot agreeably speak good things before a good assembly are indeed unprofitable persons inspite of all their various acquirements.

reading: Though they learn many things, they are of no use if they can't speak well and tellingly in a good assembly.
nuance: Parimelazhagar reads பயமிலர் as of no use to the world, and records another view, that they have no fruit from their learning. Who is deprived is therefore not settled, the world or the scholar. The verse's own 'good assembly' is the same condition as 719.

couplet: Who, though they've learned, before the council of the good men quake,
Than men unlearn'd a lower place must take.
pope.gloss: They who, though they have learned and understood, are yet afraid of the assembly of the good, are said to be inferior (even) to the illiterate.

reading: They say that those who have studied and understood, and yet fear an assembly of the good, are lower than the unlearned.
nuance: என்ப, 'they say', reports this as public opinion. Parimelazhagar makes it pointed: such people benefit neither themselves nor others and have obtained only the pain of study.

couplet: Who what they've learned, in penetrating words know not to say,
The council fearing, though they live, as dead are they.
pope.gloss: Those who through fear of the assembly are unable to set forth their learning in an interesting manner, though alive, are yet like the dead.

reading: Those who, fearing the arena, can't make what they've learned go home are like the absent, even though they exist.
nuance: The chapter ends with a social death: to Parimelazhagar they are like the dead since the world doesn't count them. களன் can be a battlefield as well, so the word may close the chapter on the same comparison as 723, though Parimelazhagar glosses it as those seated there.

title: நாடு
theme: What makes a land deserve the name: people and yield that do not fail, resilience under burden and damage, and freedom from hunger, disease and faction. All of it is void if land and ruler are not in accord.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the marks of a land (731-736), its limbs (737), its beauty (738), and its defects (739-740). The final verse undoes the whole list, a move repeated at the close of the fort and army chapters (750, 770).
source_issues: 734: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is a copy of 733's (பொறை ஒருங்கு ...). His விளக்கம் does address 734, so only that part was used.

couplet: Where spreads fertility unfailing, where resides a band,
Of virtuous men, and those of ample wealth, call that a 'land'
pope.gloss: A kingdom is that in which (those who carry on) a complete cultivation, virtuous persons, and merchants with inexhaustible wealth, dwell together.

reading: A land is where unfailing yield, worthy people and wealthy people whose wealth does not sink all come together.
nuance: The definition opens with who and what gathers in a place, not with territory or borders. A land here is a convergence.

couplet: That is a 'land' which men desire for wealth's abundant share,
Yielding rich increase, where calamities are rare.
pope.gloss: A kingdom is that which is desire for its immense wealth, and which grows greatly in prosperity, being free from destructive causes.

reading: A land is desirable for its great wealth and yields abundantly because ruin rarely touches it.
nuance: The verse names no king. Parimelazhagar lists six calamities and credits their absence to the king's virtue and his might, which is his addition.

couplet: When burthens press, it bears; Yet, With unfailing hand
To king due tribute pays: that is the 'land'
pope.gloss: A kingdom is that which can bear any burden that may be pressed on it (from adjoining kingdoms) and (yet) pay the full tribute to its sovereign.

reading: A land bears burdens that fall on it all at once and still gives its ruler his full due.
nuance: நேர்வது suggests consent as well as payment. Parimelazhagar's gloss உடம்பட்டு makes the land a willing payer, not a squeezed one.

couplet: That is a 'land' whose peaceful anna ls know,
Nor famine fierce, nor wasting plague, nor ravage of the foe.
pope.gloss: A kingdom is that which continues to be free from excessive starvation, irremediable epidemics, and destructive foes.

reading: A land is one that goes on without severe hunger, unceasing disease or destructive enemies coming to it.
nuance: சேரா answers சேர்வது in 731. The chapter defines a land by what gathers in it and then by what does not. Each ill also carries an intensifier, so the verse excludes the crushing forms and not all hardship.

couplet: From factions free, and desolating civil strife, and band
Of lurking murderers that king afflict, that is the 'land'.
pope.gloss: A kingdom is that which is without various (irregular) associations, destructive internal enemies, and murderous savages who (sometimes) harass the sovereign.

reading: A land is free of many factions, of ruinous enemies within, and of murderous marauders who harass the king.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says the factions are united by caste or by god, a striking gloss on பல்குழு, and his 'enemies within' include robbers, slanderers and even wild animals. Chapter 89 uses உட்பகை much more intimately.

couplet: Chief of all lands is that, where nought disturbs its peace;
Or, if invaders come, still yields its rich increase.
pope.gloss: The learned say that the best kingdom is that which knows no evil (from its foes), and, if injured (at all), suffers no diminution in its fruitfulness.

reading: The foremost of lands is one that does not know ruin, and whose richness does not fall even if ruin comes.
nuance: The verse does not rest on safety alone. It adds a second test for after the first has failed, so the highest praise goes to resilience. The commentators disagree about the ruin: Parimelazhagar means enemies, Manakkudavar pests and storms.

couplet: Waters from rains and springs, a mountain near, and waters thence;
These make a land, with fortress' sure defence.
pope.gloss: The constituents of a kingdom are the two waters (from above and below), well situated hills and an undestructible fort.

reading: The limbs of a land are the two waters, a well-placed hill, the water that comes from it, and a strong fort.
nuance: Three of the four limbs involve water or its source, and the fort comes last. Parimelazhagar's hill stores rain and releases it in summer, a piece of water reasoning.

couplet: A country's jewels are these five: unfailing health,
Fertility, and joy, a sure defence, and wealth.
pope.gloss: Freedom from epidemics, wealth, produce, happiness and protection (to subjects); these five, the learned, say, are the ornaments of a kingdom.

reading: Freedom from disease, wealth, yield, happiness and protection: these five, they say, are a land's ornaments.
nuance: Health stands ahead of wealth. Calling these ornaments rather than foundations is odd, and Parimelazhagar's explanation is that such beauty makes people of other lands desire it.

couplet: That is a land that yields increase unsought,
That is no land whose gifts with toil are bought.
pope.gloss: The learned say that those are kingdom whose wealth is not laboured for, and those not, whose wealth is only obtained through labour.

reading: They call those lands whose riches need no seeking; lands that give riches only when sought are no lands.
nuance: The verse puns on நாடு as land and as seek. The verdict is on the land, not on the person who toils, but it still sits awkwardly with a text that honours labour. Parimelazhagar treats seeking as hardship, and the verse does not say no work at all is done.

couplet: Though blest with all these varied gifts' increase,
A land gains nought that is not with its king at peace.
pope.gloss: Although in possession of all the above mentioned excellences, these are indeed of no use to a country, in the absence of harmony between the sovereign and the sujects.

reading: Even with all these attained, a land is without use if it has no accord with its king.
nuance: After nine verses of conditions, the tenth makes them insufficient.

title: அரண்
theme: The fort: what makes it hard to take and easy to hold, from terrain and walls to food, arms and fighters. Its last verse says all of this depends on the people inside knowing how to act.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its importance (741), its marks (742-748), and its dependence on defenders, as he groups it (749-750).
source_issues: 742: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.
749: Kalaignar's text ends with a stray '750.'
747: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption (தௌ¢ந்தோரை).

couplet: A fort is wealth to those who act against their foes;
Is wealth to them who, fearing, guard themselves from woes.
pope.gloss: A fort is an object of importance to those who march (against their foes) as well as to those who through fear (of pursuers) would seek it for shelter.

reading: A fort matters to those strong enough to march out, and it matters as much to those who, afraid, look to their own safety.
nuance: The verse sets no shame on அஞ்சி. Fear is a normal condition of statecraft here. Parimelazhagar names the strong first because even they perish without a fort.

couplet: A fort is that which owns fount of waters crystal clear,
An open space, a hill, and shade of beauteous forest near.
pope.gloss: A fort is that which has everlasting water, plains, mountains and cool shady forests.

reading: A fort has jewel-clear water, open ground, a hill, and a forest of dense shade.

couplet: Height, breadth, strength, difficult access:
Science declares a fort must these possess.
pope.gloss: The learned say that a fortress is an enclosure having these four (qualities) viz., height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility.

reading: The treatises say a fort is a wall with height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility in full.
nuance: The verse appeals openly to a technical literature (நூல்), which Valluvar is summarizing. Parimelazhagar fills in அருமை with a long catalogue of war machines from the Silappatikaram, which the verse doesn't list.

couplet: A fort must need but slight defence, yet ample be,
Defying all the foeman's energy.
pope.gloss: A fort is that which has an extensive space within, but only small places to be guarded, and such as can destroy the courage of besieging foes.

reading: A fort has little to guard and much room within, and it breaks the spirit of the enemy who comes against it.
nuance: The final test is psychological. For Parimelazhagar the enemy who comes meaning to take it at once loses heart merely on seeing it, so a good fort wins some of its battle before it begins.

couplet: Impregnable, containing ample stores of food,
A fort for those within, must be a warlike station good.
pope.gloss: A fort is that which cannot be captured, which abounds in suitable provisions, and affords a position of easy defence to its inmates.

reading: A fort is hard to seize, holds stored food, and is easy for those inside to hold their ground in.

couplet: A fort, with all munitions amply stored,
In time of need should good reserves afford.
pope.gloss: A fort is that which has all (needful) things, and excellent heroes that can help it against destruction (by foes).

reading: A fort has every needed thing and good men who help at the critical place.
nuance: நல்லாள் is not merely a strong man. Parimelazhagar reads the 'good' as love of the king, honour, valour and vigilance, so the defenders' character is already part of the fort's definition.

couplet: A fort should be impregnable to foes who gird it round,
Or aim there darts from far, or mine beneath the ground.
pope.gloss: A fort is that which cannot be captured by blockading, assaulting, or undermining it.

reading: A fort is hard to take by encircling it, by storming it without encircling, or by working on those inside.
nuance: Pope's 'mine beneath the ground' turns அறைப்படுத்தல் into tunnelling, while Parimelazhagar makes it subversion, turning trusted insiders so they open the gates. On his reading the third danger is treachery. He says stores answer the first threat and good men the other two, so walls answer none of them.

couplet: Howe'er the circling foe may strive access to win,
A fort should give the victory to those who guard within.
pope.gloss: That is a fort whose inmates are able to overcome without losing their ground, even abler men who have besieged it.

reading: A fort lets those who hold it stand fast and defeat even those strong enough to besiege it.
nuance: Parimelazhagar stresses that a small force does not merely endure a large one but wins, which raises the claim from survival to victory. He also says others explain this verse differently, and his text doesn't give their view.

couplet: At outset of the strife a fort should foes dismay;
And greatness gain by deeds in every glorious day.
pope.gloss: A fort is that which derives excellence from the stratagems made (by its inmates) to defeat their enemies in the battlefield.

reading: A fort gains its distinction from the actions by which its people bring down enemies as soon as battle begins.
nuance: The chapter's language shifts here from what the fort has to what is done in it, preparing for 750.

couplet: Howe'er majestic castled walls may rise,
To craven souls no fortress strength supplies.
pope.gloss: Although a fort may possess all (the above-said) excellence, it is, as it were without these, if its inmates possess not the excellence of action.

reading: Whatever excellences it has, a fort is nothing in the hands of those without excellence in action.
nuance: Pope's 'craven souls' narrows this to cowardice. வினைமாட்சி is broader, and Parimelazhagar includes sitting idle, acting without measure and doing what is unsuitable. A brave incompetent would fail this verse as well.

title: பொருள்செயல்வகை
theme: The making of wealth: it is the great social force that raises the despised, drives out enemies and brings virtue and pleasure within reach, but only wealth rightly gained deserves pursuit.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its importance (751-753), the way to gain it (754-756), and what it yields (757-760).
source_issues: 752: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் repeats his whole word-gloss before the actual comment.
755: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.

couplet: Nothing exists save wealth, that can
Change man of nought to worthy man.
pope.gloss: Besides wealth there is nothing that can change people of no importance into those of (some) importance.

reading: Apart from wealth, nothing makes persons of no account into persons of account.
nuance: பொருள் appears four times, playing on 'wealth' and 'something that counts'. Whether this is approval or a dry observation is left open. Parimelazhagar names the unlearned and low-born and concludes that wealth alone should be amassed, while Kalaignar calls those raised unworthy of regard, which has an edge.

couplet: Those who have nought all will despise;
All raise the wealthy to the skies.
pope.gloss: All despise the poor; (but) all praise the rich.

reading: Everyone scorns those who have nothing and everyone honours the rich.
nuance: The verse states a social fact without saying it is just. Parimelazhagar sharpens it, adding that the poor are scorned though they have every good and the rich honoured though they have every evil, words which aren't in the verse.

couplet: Wealth, the lamp unfailing, speeds to every land,
Dispersing darkness at its lord's command.
pope.gloss: The imperishable light of wealth goes into regions desired (by its owner) and destroys the darkness (of enmity therein).

reading: The unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind and cuts away the darkness.
nuance: Unlike a lamp, this one travels to where it is intended.

couplet: Their wealth, who blameless means can use aright,
Is source of virtue and of choice delight.
pope.gloss: The wealth acquired with a knowledge of the proper means and without foul practices will yield virtue and happiness.

reading: Wealth that comes with knowledge of the right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure.
nuance: The commentators differ on the audience. Parimelazhagar makes 'without wrong' a matter of a king not being tyrannical, while Manakkudavar means no harm to anyone else, and the verse itself names no king.

couplet: Wealth gained by loss of love and grace,
Let man cast off from his embrace.
pope.gloss: (Kings) should rather avoid than seek the accumulation of wealth which does not flow in with mercy and love.

reading: Accumulation of wealth that does not come with grace and love should not be embraced, but let go.
nuance: புல்லார் புரள விடல் is more than refusing. It is the gesture of letting something roll away. Coming right after 754 and before 756, it is the chapter's clearest limit.

couplet: Wealth that falls to him as heir, wealth from the kingdom's dues,
The spoils of slaughtered foes; these are the royal revenues.
pope.gloss: Unclaimed wealth, wealth acquired by taxes, and wealth (got) by conquest of foes are (all) the wealth of the king.

reading: Wealth that falls in on its own, wealth from customs, and wealth from crushing his enemies are the king's wealth.
nuance: Parimelazhagar takes this as the income beyond the one-sixth of 755. Without that bridge, an income by force would sit oddly next to wealth that comes with grace.

couplet: 'Tis love that kindliness as offspring bears:
And wealth as bounteous nurse the infant rears.
pope.gloss: The child mercy which is borne by love grows under the care of the rich nurse of wealth.

reading: The child called grace, born of love, is raised by the wealthy foster-mother called wealth.
nuance: This gives a genealogy of compassion. Parimelazhagar distinguishes love, which runs along ties, from grace, which goes to any sufferer. The mother gives birth but cannot rear alone, so wealth is necessary without being the source.

couplet: As one to view the strife of elephants who takes his stand,
On hill he's climbed, is he who works with money in his hand.
pope.gloss: An undertaking of one who has wealth in one's hands is like viewing an elephant-fight from a hill-top.

reading: Undertaking a task with money in hand is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop.
nuance: The picture's point is the safety of distance. Parimelazhagar says the funded person commissions the able and finishes the work without fear or strain, which is a view of capital as insulation from risk.

couplet: Make money! Foeman's insolence o'ergrown
To lop away no keener steel is known.
pope.gloss: Accumulate wealth; it will destroy the arrogance of (your) foes; there is no weapon sharper than it.

reading: Make wealth; there is no steel sharper than it for cutting down the pride of enemies.
nuance: The target is செருக்கு and not the enemy's body. Parimelazhagar seizes on this: other blades can't cut an intangible. The verse is one of the chapter's few bald imperatives.

couplet: Who plenteous store of glorious wealth have gained,
By them the other two are easily obtained.
pope.gloss: To those who have honestly acquired an abundance of riches, the other two, (virtue and pleasure) are things easy (of acquisition).

reading: For those who have made bright wealth in full measure, the other two are easily had, together.
nuance: ஒண் does a lot of work: the claim is for bright wealth and not for any wealth. Parimelazhagar reads ஒண் as wealth gained by the right path, while Manakkudavar simply glosses it as bright. Everything else in the claim hinges on that adjective.

title: படைமாட்சி
theme: What makes an army: inherited courage, unity before death, honour, and discipline rather than numbers. It fails when the king neglects it or when it lacks leaders.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the army's rank among a king's assets, the old force's rank within the army, and the hero's rank within that (761-763); its marks (764-767); and its failures through lack of display, royal neglect and leaders (768-770).
source_issues: 768: Manakkudavar not aligned.
769: Manakkudavar's text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's word-gloss, so it may not be independent; not used as a separate voice.

couplet: A conquering host, complete in all its limbs, that fears no wound,
Mid treasures of the king is chiefest found.
pope.gloss: The army which is complete in (its) parts and conquers without fear of wounds is the chief wealth of the king.

reading: A conquering army complete in its parts and unafraid of wounds is the chief of all a king's wealth.
nuance: வெறுக்கை calls the army wealth, directly after the chapter on wealth. Parimelazhagar's reason is that it guards the other limbs of the state and the king himself. The commentators count the parts differently: he has four, Manakkudavar five.

couplet: In adverse hour, to face undaunted might of conquering foe,
Is bravery that only veteran host can show.
pope.gloss: Ancient army can alone have the valour which makes it stand by its king at the time of defeat, fearless of wounds and unmindful of its reduced strength.

reading: The hardness that fears no wound when the king is faltering and the force itself is reduced is rare except in an ancient army.
nuance: The verse locates courage in continuity. Only தொல் is the verse's own; Parimelazhagar makes it a technical term, ranking the ancestral force first among six kinds, above hired, allied and enemy-derived troops.

couplet: Though, like the sea, the angry mice send forth their battle cry;
What then? The dragon breathes upon them, and they die!
pope.gloss: What if (a host of) hostile rats roar like the sea ? They will perish at the mere breath of the cobra.

reading: What if a host of hostile rats roar like the sea? They perish when the cobra merely breathes.
nuance: The verse doesn't mention armies at all. Parimelazhagar reads it as an allegory recommending one hero over many who are not. The cobra doesn't even strike: its breath is enough.

couplet: That is a host, by no defeats, by no desertions shamed,
For old hereditary courage famed.
pope.gloss: That indeed is an army which has stood firm of old without suffering destruction or deserting (to the enemy).

reading: An army is one that does not collapse, cannot be turned by subversion, and has courage that has come down to it.
