nuance: அறைபோகாது repeats the danger of 747: the same threat of being turned from inside. Parimelazhagar's supporting verse is a woman's boast of the men of her house who fell in battle, so the inheritance includes grief.

couplet: That is a 'host' that joins its ranks, and mightily withstands,
Though death with sudden wrath should fall upon its bands.
pope.gloss: That indeed is an army which is capable of offering a united resistance, even if Yama advances against it with fury.

reading: An army is one that, even when Death comes raging at it, has the power to stand together and face it.
nuance: The operative word is கூடி. The courage asked for is collective. Parimelazhagar says the many are of one heart because they love the king, and that ஆற்றல் here is strength of mind.

couplet: Valour with honour, sure advance in glory's path, with confidence;
To warlike host these four are sure defence.
pope.gloss: Valour, honour, following in the excellent-footsteps (of its predecessors) and trust-worthiness; these four alone constitute the safeguard of an army.

reading: Valour, honour, walking the proven path and தேற்றம் are the four things that protect an army.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's 'path' includes not striking those who have turned their backs, so honour limits valour. He concludes that such men need no other fort.

couplet: A valiant army bears the onslaught, onward goes,
Well taught with marshalled ranks to meet their coming foes.
pope.gloss: That is an army which knowing the art of warding off an impending struggle, can bear against the dust-van (of a hostile force).

reading: An army is one that knows how to meet the battle coming at it and advances bearing the தார்.
nuance: This is the chapter's one verse about skill. Parimelazhagar sends readers to Sanskrit treatises on battle formation and declines to describe them.

couplet: Though not in war offensive or defensive skilled;
An army gains applause when well equipped and drilled.
pope.gloss: Though destitute of courage to fight and strength (to endure), an army may yet gain renown by the splendour of its appearance.

reading: Even without striking power or endurance, an army gains stature through its martial bearing.
nuance: A surprising concession that appearance has real force. Parimelazhagar's பாடு is the fear an army causes at first sight, so display works on the enemy's mind as 744's fort does.

couplet: Where weakness, clinging fear and poverty
Are not, the host will gain the victory.
pope.gloss: An army can triumph (over its foes) if it is free from diminution; irremediable aversion and poverty.

reading: An army wins if it is free of shrinking, of a resentment that will not leave, and of poverty.
nuance: The verse states an army's conditions, but Parimelazhagar assigns the blame upward. Desertion and poverty come from a king who doesn't pay, and resentment from outrages such as seizing their women. A verse on the army becomes a verse on the king's conduct.

couplet: Though men abound, all ready for the war,
No army is where no fit leaders are.
pope.gloss: Though an army may contain a large number of permanent soldiers, it cannot last if it has no generals.

reading: Even with plenty of steadfast men, there is no army where there are no leaders.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's explanation is striking. If leaders go, the men say there is no one to witness and leave too. On this view courage needs an audience.

title: படைச்செருக்கு
theme: The warrior's pride, spoken largely from within: boast, disdain for easy prey, mercy as courage's edge, and death sought as honour. Its ethic is one of glory and is not softened by the rest of the Kural.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar ties several verses to the conventions of heroic poetry (Purapporul Venba Malai), and groups 777-780 as not cherishing life. Manakkudavar's commentary marks the end of a section at 780.
source_issues: 771: Parimelazhagar's text is cut off mid-citation at the end ([பு.வெ.மா.வஞ்சி. 1 ---).
776: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் is cut off mid-sentence (அது பெறாத ---).
773, 778: Manakkudavar not aligned.
774: Manakkudavar's text ends with a stray '5'.

couplet: Ye foes! stand not before my lord! for many a one
Who did my lord withstand, now stands in stone!
pope.gloss: O my foes, stand not before my leader; (for) many are those who did so but afterwards stood (in the shape of) statues.

reading: Enemies, do not stand before my lord; many who stood before him now stand in stone.
nuance: The verse puns on நில்: to stand in battle and to stand as a hero-stone. The stone is both a threat and an honour, a fact that makes the boast double-edged. It is a voice in the Kural that isn't Valluvar's own, and Parimelazhagar notes the warrior places his valour on his king.

couplet: Who aims at elephant, though dart should fail, has greater praise.
Than he who woodland hare with winged arrow slays.
pope.gloss: It is more pleasant to hold the dart that has missed an elephant than that which has hit hare in the forest.

reading: Carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than carrying an arrow that hit a forest hare.
nuance: The verse measures an act by its target, not its result. Parimelazhagar supplies a dramatic setting, a warrior ashamed that the opposing force fled, but the verse itself gives only the comparison.

couplet: Fierceness in hour of strife heroic greatness shows;
Its edge is kindness to our suffering foes.
pope.gloss: The learned say that fierceness (incontest with a foe) is indeed great valour; but to become a benefactor in case of accident (to a foe) is the extreme (limit) of that valour.

reading: They call fierceness great manhood; but when something befalls the foe, generous help is its cutting edge.
nuance: The image is exact: the kindness isn't an exception to valour but its sharpest point. Parimelazhagar's example is Rama telling the defeated Ravana to go and come back tomorrow, an epic illustration that the verse doesn't state.

couplet: At elephant he hurls the dart in hand; for weapon pressed,
He laughs and plucks the javelin from his wounded breast.
pope.gloss: The hero who after casting the lance in his hand on an elephant, comes (in search of another) will pluck the one (that sticks) in his body and laugh (exultingly).

reading: Having sent his spear away with an elephant, he comes on seeking another, and laughs as he pulls one from his own body.
nuance: The laugh is the verse's whole shock. For Parimelazhagar he is happy because he has found what he was seeking, and rage had kept him from noticing the wound. A wound registers as supply.

couplet: To hero fearless must it not defeat appear,
If he but wink his eye when foemen hurls his spear.
pope.gloss: Is it not a defeat to the valiant to wink and destroy their ferocious look when a lance in cast at them (by their foe) ?

reading: When the eye that glares at the enemy gives way and blinks at a flung spear, is that not flight, to the fierce?
nuance: Valour is carried to the reflex. Parimelazhagar's line is that even withdrawing the angry gaze counts as retreat.

couplet: The heroes, counting up their days, set down as vain
Each day when they no glorious wound sustain.
pope.gloss: The hero will reckon among wasted days all those on which he had not received severe wounds.

reading: Going over his days, he sets among the wasted all those on which he took no noble wound.
nuance: விழுப்புண் is a wound of a certain kind. Parimelazhagar restricts it to face and chest, so that it marks one who did not turn. A ledger of days is a sober image for a very unsober ethic.

couplet: Who seek for world-wide fame, regardless of their life,
The glorious clasp adorns, sign of heroic strife.
pope.gloss: The fastening of ankle-ring by those who disire a world-wide renown and not (the safety of) their lives is like adorning (themselves).

reading: For those who want fame that circles the world and do not want life, the tying on of the war-anklet is an adornment.
nuance: The verse names only fame. Parimelazhagar adds heaven (துறக்கம்), saying fame remains encircling the earth while the hero goes on, so the afterlife is his reading. காரிகை turns a mark of danger into jewellery.

couplet: Fearless they rush where'er 'the tide of battle rolls';
The king's reproof damps not the ardour of their eager souls.
pope.gloss: The heroes who are not afraid of losing their life in a contest will not cool their ardour, even if the king prohibits (their fighting).

reading: Warriors who do not fear for their lives when battle comes will not lessen in their distinction even if their lord is angry.
nuance: This verse makes a real space between warrior and king, which the army chapter's language of loyalty doesn't.

couplet: Who says they err, and visits them scorn,
Who die and faithful guard the vow they've sworn?
pope.gloss: Who would reproach with failure those who seal their oath with their death ?

reading: Who could reproach those who die so that what they vowed is not broken, for having failed?
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes a bold move: dying in the attempt counts as fulfilling the vow. The verse's rhetorical question closes off blame for one who failed, without calling the failure a success.

couplet: If monarch's eyes o'erflow with tears for hero slain,
Who wou ld not beg such boon of glorious death to gain?
pope.gloss: If (heroes) can so die as to fill with tears the eyes of their rulers, such a death deserves to be obtained even by begging.

reading: If one can die so that the eyes of those who sustained one fill with tears, that death is worth begging for.
nuance: The measure of the death is another's tears, and the one who weeps is the patron. Parimelazhagar sets it against dying sick at home among weeping kin, which only spends old deeds, whereas this earns heaven. The verse itself mentions neither of those.

title: நட்பு
theme: Friendship as a rare achievement and the strongest guard. It grows with use, lives in the heart rather than on the face, corrects as well as comforts, and moves to help as instinctively as a hand to a slipping garment.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its importance (781), the reasons for it (782-783), its use (784), its chief cause (785), and its marks (786-790).
source_issues: 785: Parimelazhagar's entry opens with his complete comment on 784 before reaching 785. Only the later part was used.
787: Manakkudavar not aligned.

couplet: What so hard for men to gain as friendship true?
What so sure defence 'gainst all that foe can do?
pope.gloss: What things are there so difficult to acquire as friendship ? What guards are there so difficult to break through by the efforts (of one's foes) ?

reading: What is as hard to make as friendship, and what guard is as hard for hostile deeds to get past?
nuance: The two questions are linked: the difficulty of getting it is the reason for its value as protection. Parimelazhagar opens by classifying friendship as natural or made and says this chapter treats the made kind, kin being treated elsewhere.

couplet: Friendship with men fulfilled of good Waxes like the crescent moon;
Friendship with men of foolish mood, Like the full orb, waneth soon.
pope.gloss: The friendship of the wise waxes like the new moon; (but) that of fools wanes like the full moon.

reading: Friendship with the good grows like the crescent moon filling, and that of fools shrinks like the moon after it is full.
nuance: The moon's phases make growth depend on the starting point: the good begin small and fools begin large. Parimelazhagar's reason is knowledge. Each pair at first doesn't know the other and later does, and it is that knowing which makes one friendship grow and the other shrink.

couplet: Learned scroll the more you ponder, Sweeter grows the mental food;
So the heart by use grows fonder, Bound in friendship with the good.
pope.gloss: Like learning, the friendship of the noble, the more it is cultivated, the more delightful does it become.

reading: The more it is practised, the bond with people of character is like the more a book is studied, its nayam.

couplet: Nor for laughter only friendship all the pleasant day,
But for strokes of sharp reproving, when from right you stray.
pope.gloss: Friendship is to be practised not for the purpose of laughing but for that of being beforehand in giving one another sharp rebukes in case of transgression.

reading: Friendship is not for laughing together, but for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps.
nuance: மேற்சென்று has timing in it. The rebuke goes out before the wrong is done, says Parimelazhagar, and it is harsh because sweet words will not turn the person back. This is not a claim that friends should never laugh, only that laughter isn't the purpose.

couplet: Not association constant, not affection's token bind;
'Tis the unison of feeling friends unites of kindred mind.
pope.gloss: Living together and holding frequent intercourse are not necessary (for friendship); (mutual) understanding can alone create a claim for it.

reading: Neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed; a shared feeling alone gives the claim of friendship.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's example is Kopperuncholan and Pisirandaiyar, who never met and whose bond was so close that one died with the other. The verse itself offers no example and says nothing of dying together.

couplet: Not the face's smile of welcome shows the friend sincere,
But the heart's rejoicing gladness when the friend is near.
pope.gloss: The love that dwells (merely in the smiles of the face is not friendship; (but) that which dwells deep in the smiles of the heart is true friendship.

reading: Friendship that makes the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart within smile is friendship.
nuance: The verse sounds as if the face doesn't matter. Parimelazhagar says that an implied 'also' is present, so both should bloom together. That softens a sharper opposition in the Tamil.

couplet: Friendship from ruin saves, in way of virtue keeps;
In troublous time, it weeps with him who weeps.
pope.gloss: (True) friendship turns aside from evil (ways) makes (him) walk in the (good) way, and, in case of loss if shares his sorrow (with him).

reading: Friendship turns one away from what destroys, sets one on the path, and in ruin shares the suffering.
nuance: The order is a plan of action: prevent, then guide, then, if all that fails, suffer alongside. Parimelazhagar adds that ruin in the third stage comes from a divine cause and so can't be averted. The verse names no such cause.

couplet: As hand of him whose vesture slips away,
Friendship at once the coming grief will stay.
pope.gloss: (True) friendship hastens to the rescue of the afflicted (as readily) as the hand of one whose garment is loosened (before an assembly).

reading: Like the hand of a man whose garment slips, friendship clears away distress there and then.
nuance: The simile is about speed and also about no deliberation. Parimelazhagar notes that the hand gets there before the mind does. The garment also implies that the friend's trouble is a shame to be covered, and that the friend is as close as one's own limb.

couplet: And where is friendship's royal seat? In stable mind,
Where friend in every time of need support may find.
pope.gloss: Friendship may be said to be on its throne when it possesses the power of supporting one at all times and under all circumstances, (in the practice or virtue and wealth).

reading: Where does friendship sit enthroned? In standing firm without wavering, supporting however one can.
nuance: ஒல்லும்வாய் sets a realistic limit: as far as one is able. The throne is unwavering support, not unlimited power. Parimelazhagar specifies support in virtue and wealth, which Pope follows in parentheses, while the verse itself gives no object.

couplet: Mean is the friendship that men blazon forth,
'He's thus to me' and 'such to him my worth'.
pope.gloss: Though friends may praise one another saying, "He is so intimate with us, and we so much (with him)"; (still) such friendship will appear mean.

reading: 'They are this to us and we are that to them': even when so adorned, friendship looks shabby.
nuance: A subtle point. For Parimelazhagar friendship has no 'I' and 'they', so that listing what each is to the other brings in a difference that did not exist. The praise itself is what damages it.

title: நட்பாராய்தல்
theme: Testing friends before committing, because a friendship once formed should not be left. It asks what to test for, finds that ruin is the most reliable test, and accepts that bad friendships must sometimes be paid to end.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the harm of not testing (791-792), how to test and whom to choose (793-796), whom not to befriend (797-799), and a summary of both (800).
source_issues: 797: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் is garbled, with a stray § and a repeated passage.

couplet: To make an untried man your friend is ruin sure;
For friendship formed unbroken must endure.
pope.gloss: As those who are of a friendly nature will not forsake (a friend) after once loving (him), there is no evil so great as contracting a friendship without due inquiry.

reading: Nothing brings ruin like befriending without inquiry, since for those devoted to friendship there is no leaving once it is formed.
nuance: The logic turns on faithfulness: the reason for caution is precisely the commitment to stay. Parimelazhagar adds that with no distinction between friends, the friend's sins and blame become one's own.

couplet: Alliance with the man you have not proved and proved again,
In length of days will give you mortal pain.
pope.gloss: The friendship contracted by him who has not made repeated inquiry will in the end grieve (him) to death.

reading: The friendship of one who does not inquire again and again ends by bringing grief that kills him.
nuance: The doubled ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து asks for repeated testing and not a single check. For Parimelazhagar no enemy is needed, for one brings it on oneself, and the bad friend's enemies become one's own.

couplet: Temper, descent, defects, associations free
From blame: know these, then let the man be friend to thee.
pope.gloss: Make friendship (with one) after ascertaining (his) character, birth, defects and the whole of one's relations.

reading: Know his qualities, his family, his faults and his inan, and only then form a friendship.
nuance: Faults are on the list to be known, not to be absent. Parimelazhagar's point is that no one is faultless, so the question is whether the faults can be borne.

couplet: Who, born of noble race, from guilt would shrink with shame,
Pay any price so yo u as friend that man may claim.
pope.gloss: The friendship of one who belongs to a (good) family and is afraid of (being charged with) guilt, is worth even purchasing.

reading: One of good family who feels shame at blame on himself: that friendship should be had even by giving.
nuance: பழிநாணுவான் is a person who is governed by shame. The commercial phrase is startling for something the previous chapter praises so highly. Kalaignar softens it to 'by any means', while Parimelazhagar says plainly: buy it for a price.

couplet: Make them your chosen friend whose words repentance move,
With power prescription's path to show, while evil they reprove.
pope.gloss: You should examine and secure the friendship of those who can speak so as to make you weep over a crime (before its commission) or rebuke you severely (after you have done it) and are able to teach you (the ways of) the world.

reading: Inquire and take the friendship of those able to speak until one weeps, to rebuke, and to teach what is proper.

couplet: Ruin itself one blessing lends:
'Tis staff that measures out one's friends.
pope.gloss: Even in ruin there is some good; (for) it is a rod by which one may measure fully (the affection of one's) relations.

reading: Even in ruin there is one benefit: it is a rod that measures one's people to full length.
nuance: The benefit is knowledge rather than comfort. Parimelazhagar says the true extent of each friend's bond stays hidden in wealthy times, and that ruin measures it for choosing better afterward.

couplet: 'Tis gain to any man, the sages say,
Friendship of fools to put away.
pope.gloss: It is indead a gain for one to renounce the friendship of fools.

reading: Gain for a person means giving up and leaving the friendship of fools.
nuance: The verse calls a loss a gain. Parimelazhagar says one must also move away, because like sandal and vengai burning together, nearness alone brings harm.

couplet: Think not the thoughts that dwarf the soul; nor take
For friends the men who friends in time of grief forsake.
pope.gloss: Do not think of things that discourage your mind, nor contract friendship with those who would forsake you in adversity.

reading: Do not think on what shrinks the spirit, and do not take the friendship of those who cut away in distress.
nuance: The verse pairs a rule about thought and a rule about company, and Parimelazhagar treats the first as an illustration of the second. Fair-weather friends are thus a thing that shrinks the mind.

couplet: Of friends deserting us on ruin's brink,
'Tis torture e'en in life's last hour to think.
pope.gloss: The very thought of the friendship of those who have deserted one at the approach of adversity will burn one's mind at the time of death.

reading: Friendship with those who forsake one in ruin burns the heart, even to think of, at the moment of death.
nuance: Betrayal is measured against death and is what burns. Parimelazhagar goes further: the mere thought of it is worse than Death, and even for an unconnected person who thinks of it. He also records another reading in which the thought is of the harm one brought on oneself.

couplet: Cling to the friendship of the spotless one's; whate'er you pay.
Renounce alliance with the men of evil way.
pope.gloss: Continue to enjoy the friendship of the pure; (but) renounce even with a gift, the friendship of those who do not agree (with the world).

reading: Keep close to the friendship of the stainless; give something if you must, but leave the friendship of those who are oppilar.
nuance: The cost of a bad friendship is paid at the end as well. It balances 794: one may pay to get a friend and pay to be rid of one.

title: பழைமை
theme: Old friendship as the freedom to take liberties with each other. It teaches welcoming what a friend presumes to do, reading hurt charitably, and staying even through harm the friend causes.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: what it is (801), the value of its liberty (802-803), welcoming what is done unasked (804), reading harm charitably (805), not leaving through harm (806-807), bearing faults (808), and what it earns (809-810).
source_issues: 809: Manakkudavar's entry opens with a fragment of the verse and ends with a stray '9'.

couplet: Familiarity is friendship's silent pact,
That puts restraint on no familiar act.
pope.gloss: Imtimate friendship is that which cannot in the least be injured by (things done through the) right (of longstanding intimacy).

reading: What is called old friendship? It is friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties that intimacy gives.
nuance: The definition is not about time, and Parimelazhagar says so outright. His list of permitted liberties is concrete: acting without asking, even acting to one's harm, taking what one needs, showing neither deference nor fear.

couplet: Familiar freedom friendship's very frame supplies;
To be its savour sweet is duty of the wise.
pope.gloss: The constituents of friendship are (things done through) the right of intimacy; to be pleased with such a right is the duty of the wise.

reading: Intimate liberty is a limb of friendship, and being as salt to it is the duty of the worthy.
nuance: உப்பு: the worthy person doesn't merely tolerate liberties but gives them savour. Manakkudavar gives a homely comparison: a bitter gourd stays bitter however much seasoning goes in, so without consent no sweetness comes.

couplet: When to familiar acts men kind response refuse,
What fruit from ancient friendship's use?
pope.gloss: Of what avail is long-standing friendship, if friends do not admit as their own actions done through the right of intimacy ?

reading: What use is long-practised friendship if one does not accept a friend's liberty as if one had done it oneself?
nuance: செய்தாங்கு is the core: treat the act as your own. Parimelazhagar adds that this holds even for what one wouldn't agree to, which is where the test really lies.

couplet: When friends unbidden do familiar acts with loving heart,
Friends take the kindly deed in friendly part.
pope.gloss: If friends, through the right of friendship, do (anything) without being asked, the wise will be pleased with them on account of its desirability.

reading: When friends act unasked out of intimacy, those who are wise welcome it for how desirable it is.

couplet: Not folly merely, but familiar carelessness,
Esteem it, when your friends cause you distress.
pope.gloss: If friends should perform what is painful, understand that it is owing not only to ignorance, but also to the strong claims of intimacy.

reading: If friends do something that hurts, understand it as either folly or great intimacy.
nuance: The verse is a rule of interpretation: two readings are allowed, and lack of love isn't one of them. Parimelazhagar brings in fate, saying the folly comes from a fate of loss. The verse does not. Pope's 'not only... but also' blurs the either-or that the commentators find.

couplet: Who stand within the bounds quit not, though loss impends,
Association with the old familiar friends.
pope.gloss: Those who stand within the limits (of true friendship) will not even in adversity give up the intimacy of long-standing friends.

reading: Those who hold to the bounds will not give up the bond of those who stand in old friendship, even when ruin comes.
nuance: For Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar the ruin comes from that friend, which makes this harder than loyalty in hard times. The verse's தொலைவிடத்தும் doesn't itself say who caused the ruin.

couplet: True friends, well versed in loving ways,
Cease not to love, when friend their love betrays.
pope.gloss: Those who have (long) stood in the path of affection will not give it up even if their friends cause (them) their ruin.

reading: Even when destructive things are done to them, those whose bond has come by the way of love do not cut off love.
nuance: The verse does not say the friendship goes unaltered in every way, only that அன்பு does not end. It locates the constancy in love and not in the deeds.

couplet: In strength of friendship rare of friend's disgrace who will not hear,
The day his friend offends will day of grace to him appear.
pope.gloss: To those who understand that by which they should not listen to (tales about) the faults of their friends, that is a (profitable) day on which the latter may commit a fault.

reading: For those who have the strength of intimacy not to listen to reports of a friend's lapse, the day the friend lapses has its own meaning.
nuance: The verse has a sting: the lapse is what reveals the strength. Parimelazhagar says the bond only shows when it is tested, so other days don't count.

couplet: Friendship of old and faithful friends,
Who ne'er for sake, the world commends.
pope.gloss: They will be loved by the world, who have not forsaken the friendship of those with whom they have kept up an unbroken long-standing intimacy.

reading: The world loves those who do not give up the friendship of friends whose bond has come down unbroken.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a motive: everyone reasons that such a person would be like this to them too, and comes to seek friendship. Loyalty to one is an advertisement to all. Manakkudavar's வழிவந்த points rather to friendship inherited through family.

couplet: Ill-wishers even wish them well, who guard.
For ancient friends, their wonted kind regard.
pope.gloss: Even enemies will love those who have never changed in their affection to their long-standingfriends.

reading: Those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them.
nuance: The commentators take விழையார் as enemies. The verse's own word is softer, 'those who don't desire', and the tight wordplay விழையார் விழையப் works without naming any foe.

title: தீ நட்பு
theme: A catalogue of false friendship: the self-serving, the unreliable, fools, jesters and the two-faced. Its rhetoric of comparison ranks all of them below loneliness and even below enemies.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: harm of such friendship in general (811), then by type: those who look to their own gain (812-813), those who fail in need (814-815), fools, jesters and those who won't do what they can (816-818), and deceivers (819-820).
source_issues: 812: The Tamil of the verse reads அறின்ஙருஉம் in kg/core/kural.jsonl. Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அறின் ஒரூஉம், so this looks like a corrupted character.
812: Manakkudavar not aligned.
816: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.

couplet: Though evil men should all-absorbing friendship show,
Their love had better die away than grow.
pope.gloss: The decrease of friendship with those who look as if they would eat you up (through excess of love) while they are really destitute of goodness is far better than its increase.

reading: Though they seem to drink you up, the friendship of those without character is better shrinking than growing.
nuance: பருகுவார் is the language of passion. Parimelazhagar cites a matching line of poetry and Manakkudavar adds 'with the eyes'. The verse warns that intensity is not evidence. The advice is modest too, since it only says that shrinking is better.

couplet: What though you gain or lose friendship of men of alien heart,
Who when you thrive are friends, and when you fail depart?
pope.gloss: Of what avail is it to get or lose the friendship of those who love when there is gain and leave when there is none ?

reading: What does it matter whether one gains or loses the friendship of misfits who are friends when there is profit and leave when there is none?
nuance: The rhetorical shrug is the point. Parimelazhagar concludes that one should simply be neutral toward them (நொதுமல்). They are neither to be sought nor fought, which sets them apart from the verses that say to run.

couplet: These are alike: the friends who ponder friendship's gain
Those who accept whate'er you give, and all the plundering train.
pope.gloss: Friendship who calculate the profits (of their friendship), prostitutes who are bent on obtaining their gains, and thieves are (all) of the same character.

reading: Friends who weigh what they stand to gain, those who take what they get, and thieves are all alike.
nuance: The middle term in the verse says only 'those who take what they get'. It is the commentators who identify them as prostitutes. In the verse's shape, the calculation of friends is the real target and the other two are comparisons.

couplet: A steed untrained will leave you in the tug of war;
Than friends like that to dwell alone is better far.
pope.gloss: Solitude is more to be desired than the society of those who resemble the untrained horses which throw down (their riders) in the fields of battle.

reading: Better solitude than having as one's own those like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle.
nuance: The horse has been carrying its rider well until the moment that counts. Parimelazhagar also notes the verse doesn't praise solitude, which is only less bad. Valluvar isn't recommending it.

couplet: 'Tis better not to gain than gain the friendship profitless
Of men of little minds, who succour fails when dangers press.
pope.gloss: It is far better to avoid that to contract the evil friendship of the base who cannot protect (their friends) even when appointed to do so.

reading: It is better not to get than to get the poor friendship of the small, who are no protection even after one has made them friends.
nuance: ஏமம் brings in the guard of 781 again: a friend who doesn't protect has failed the definition.

couplet: Better ten million times incur the wise man's hate,
Than form with foolish men a friendship intimate.
pope.gloss: The hatred of the wise is ten-million times more profitable than the excessive intimacy of the fool.

reading: Being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool.
nuance: ஏதின்மை is literally not-belonging. Pope and the commentators read it as enmity. Parimelazhagar's argument is that the enmity of the wise does no harm while the fool's friendship does every harm.

couplet: From foes ten million fold a greater good you gain,
Than friendship yields that's formed with laughers vain.
pope.gloss: What comes from enemies is a hundred million times more profitable than what comes from the friendship of those who cause only laughter.

reading: Ten crore times better than friendship of the kind that is all laughter is what comes from enemies.
nuance: The multiplier goes up ten times from 816. Parimelazhagar says even the pains that enemies cause exceed the pleasures of these friends, identifies them as hangers-on who amuse for profit, and dismisses other commentators' readings as ungrammatical.

couplet: Those men who make a grievous toil of what they do
On your behalf, their friendship silently eschew.
pope.gloss: Gradually abandon without revealing (beforehand) the friendship of those who pretend inability to carry out what they (really) could do.

reading: With those who make hard work of what they could easily do, let the friendship slip without a word.
nuance: A practical subtlety. Parimelazhagar says speaking would only lead them to patch things up and go on, so the silence is tactical. It is the opposite of a formal break.

couplet: E'en in a dream the intercourse is bitterness
With men whose deeds are other than their words profess.
pope.gloss: The friendship of those whose actions do not agree with their words will distress (one) even in (one's) dreams.

reading: Even in a dream, the bond with those whose deeds are one thing and words another is bitter.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss is exact: enemies in deed and friends in word. The dream adds that the harm follows into sleep, a place where in other verses love is what lives.

couplet: In anywise maintain not intercourse with those,
Who in the house are friends, in hall are slandering foes.
pope.gloss: Avoid even the least approach to a contraction of friendship with those who would love you in private but ridicule you in public.

reading: Take care not to come near at all to the bond of those who are friendly at home and defame you in the assembly.
nuance: The contrast is between private and public, and it's the public that matters: a friend is tested by what is said in the மன்று. எனைத்தும் leaves no room for degree, unlike the 'better to shrink' of 811.

title: கூடாநட்பு
theme: Friendship with one who is inwardly hostile: smiles, soft words, folded hands and even tears can hide a weapon. In the end the chapter tells the reader to answer such a person with the same outward show.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the defect of such friendship (821-822), why it is cruel (823-824), not to trust their words (825-827), not to trust their acts (828), and how to deal with them (829-830).
source_issues: 822: Parimelazhagar's text starts with a verse fragment and a stray HTML piece (br>).
825, 827, 828, 830: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption (தௌ¢, வௌ¢).
829: Manakkudavar's text is marked [#] and is nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's word-gloss, so it may not be independent; not used as a separate voice.

couplet: Anvil where thou shalt smitten be, when men occasion find,
Is friendship's form without consenting mind.
pope.gloss: The friendship of those who behave like friends without inward affection is a weapon that may be thrown when a favourable opportunity presents itself.

reading: The friendship of those who come close without inner consent is an anvil for striking, once they find the right place.
nuance: A பட்டடை seems to hold a thing up and in fact is what makes the blow cut, so Pope's gloss 'weapon' loses the image. The false friend need not be the blade. The support he gives is what enables it.

couplet: Friendship of those who seem our kin, but are not really kind.
Will change from hour to hour like woman's mind.
pope.gloss: The friendship of those who seem to be friends while they are not, will change like the love of women.

reading: The friendship of those who seem one's own but aren't will change the way women's minds change.
nuance: The verse itself makes a general comparison about women, and the commentators' responses show how uneasy it is.

couplet: To heartfelt goodness men ignoble hardly may attain,
Although abundant stores of goodly lore they gain.
pope.gloss: Though (one's) enemies may have mastered many good books, it will be impossible for them to become truly loving at heart.

reading: Though they have studied many good things, it is hard for the unworthy to become good at heart.
nuance: The verse separates learning from moral change. This limit matters to a text that elsewhere praises study so highly.

couplet: 'Tis fitting you should dread dissemblers' guile,
Whose hearts are bitter while their faces smile.
pope.gloss: One should fear the deceitful who smile sweetly with their face but never love with their heart.

reading: Fear the deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while within they are bitter.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives the reason for fear: the face is the instrument for reading intentions, and here the malice doesn't show on it.

couplet: When minds are not in unison, 'its never; just,
In any words men speak to put your trust.
pope.gloss: In nothing whatever is it proper to rely on the words of those who do not love with their heart.

reading: Those not in accord with you in mind are not to be trusted on the strength of their words in anything.
nuance: The verse states no authority, but Parimelazhagar supplies one: 'the treatises on policy' say so. He reads the line as counsel on whom to trust in practical affairs (கருமங்கள்).

couplet: Though many goodly words they speak in friendly tone,
The words of foes will speedily be known.
pope.gloss: Though (one's) foes may utter good things as though they were friends, once will at once understand (their evil, import).

reading: Though they say good things as friends do, the words of the unreconciled are quickly seen through.
nuance: This verse is more optimistic than its neighbours about detection. Parimelazhagar reads the concession to mean they rarely say good things at all.

couplet: To pliant speech from hostile lips give thou no ear;
'Tis pliant bow that show the deadly peril near!
pope.gloss: Since the bending of the bow bespeaks evil, one should not accept (as good) the humiliating speeches of one's foes.

reading: Do not take humility in an enemy's speech as humility, for the bending of a bow means harm.
nuance: Parimelazhagar marks it as 'word-bowing' and not real bowing, since the man himself doesn't bow. The bend is what stores the force, so the humility may be the very preparation.

couplet: In hands that worship weapon ten hidden lies;
Such are the tears that fall from foeman's eyes.
pope.gloss: A weapon may be hid in the very hands with which (one's) foes adore (him) (and) the tears they shed are of the same nature.

reading: A weapon hides even inside hands folded in worship, and an enemy's shed tears are the same.
nuance: The chapter moves from words to the body, and it picks the gestures hardest to doubt, reverence and grief. Parimelazhagar's line is that those able to read intent see the weapon even in the moment of reassurance.

couplet: 'Tis just, when men make much of you, and then despise,
To make them smile, and slap in friendship's guise.
pope.gloss: It is the duty of kings to affect great love but make it die (inwardly); as regard those foes who shew them great friendship but despise them (in their heart).

reading: Those who overdo friendship and despise you inwardly should be made to smile, and embraced in friendship so that it dies.
nuance: The verse itself gives no audience, but Parimelazhagar supplies 'royal policy' and says plainly that having one thing inside and another outside is wrong in general but proper toward enemies. He treats it as a licensed exception. சாப்புல்லல் is a hard phrase: this reading follows the commentators, and Pope's couplet ('slap') goes elsewhere.

couplet: When time shall come that foes as friends appear,
Then thou, to hide a hostile heart, a smiling face may'st wear.
pope.gloss: When one's foes begin to affect friendship, one should love them with one's looks, and, cherishing no love in the heart, give up (even the former).

reading: When the time comes that an enemy turns friend, befriend with the face, let go in the heart, and then let it go altogether.
nuance: Parimelazhagar narrows the permission to a moment when open rejection isn't possible, and stresses a final exit. So the mask is a temporary means, not a settled way of life.

title: பேதைமை
theme: Folly as choosing loss over gain. It is not ignorance as such: its worst form belongs to the learned who do not restrain themselves, and it spoils whatever the fool touches, whether work, wealth, friendship or an assembly.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its definition (831-832), the fool's conduct in general (833-834), his fate after death (835), how he gets and uses wealth (836-838), his friendship (839), and his place in an assembly (840).
source_issues: 837: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss opens with a misprint, பதை for பேதை.

couplet: What one thing merits folly's special name.
Letting gain go, loss for one's own to claim!
pope.gloss: Folly is one (of the chief defects); it is that which (makes one) incur loss and forego gain.

reading: What is the one thing called folly? It is taking hold of harm and letting gain go.
nuance: This is a definition by behaviour rather than by lack of knowledge. Parimelazhagar lists poverty, blame and sin as the harm and wealth, fame and virtue as the gain, so he reads the choice as ruining both worlds.

couplet: 'Mid follies chiefest folly is to fix your love
On deeds which to your station unbefitting prove.
pope.gloss: The greatest folly is that which leads one to take delight in doing what is forbidden.

reading: Of all follies the worst is to set one's love on what is not for one's hand.

couplet: Ashamed of nothing, searching nothing out, of loveless heart,
Nought cherishing, 'tis thus the fool will play his part.
pope.gloss: Shamelessness indifference (to what must be sought after), harshness, and aversion for everything (that ought to be desired) are the qualities of the fool.

reading: No shame, no searching, no tenderness, no care for anything: this is what a fool does.
nuance: The fool is described by four absences, in a chain of words ending in -மை. தொழில் suggests something habitual: Parimelazhagar says these are his constant nature. நார் is a fibre, a bond, and also fellow-feeling.

couplet: The sacred law he reads and learns, to other men expounds,-
Himself obeys not; where can greater fool be found?
pope.gloss: There are no greater fools than he who, though he has read and understood (a great deal) and even taught it to others, does not walk according to his own teaching.

reading: There is no greater fool than one who studies, understands and teaches others but does not restrain himself.
nuance: All three stages of learning are granted, and restraint alone is missing. Parimelazhagar makes it medical: this folly isn't cured by its own remedy, and no other remedy exists.

couplet: The fool will merit hell in one brief life on earth,
In which he entering sinks through sevenfold round of birth.
pope.gloss: A fool can procure in a single birth a hell into which he may enter and suffer through all the seven births.

reading: A fool can, in one life's doing, make the mire he will enter and sink into for seven.

couplet: When fool some task attempts with uninstructed pains,
It fails; nor that alone, himself he binds with chains.
pope.gloss: If the fool, who knows not how to act undertakes a work, he will (certainly) fail. (But) is it all ? He will even adorn himself with fetters.

reading: If a fool who doesn't know how takes up a task, it comes to nothing, and more than that, he wears fetters.
nuance: பூணும் is what one does with jewellery, so the fetters are worn like ornaments. Manakkudavar takes பொய்படும் to mean he himself gets called false, whereas Parimelazhagar means the work collapses inside.

couplet: When fools are blessed with fortune's bounteous store,
Their foes feed full, their friends are prey to hunger sore.
pope.gloss: If a fool happens to get an immense fortune, his neighbours will enjoy it while his relations starve.

reading: When a fool gets great wealth, strangers feast and his own people go hungry.
nuance: The verse says உற்றக்கடை, 'when it has come to him'. Parimelazhagar takes this as wealth got by fate, on the argument that a fool couldn't have made it himself. The next verse's பெறின் gets the same treatment. Both are his additions.

couplet: When folly's hand grasps wealth's increase, 'twill be
As when a mad man raves in drunken glee.
pope.gloss: A fool happening to possess something is like the intoxication of one who is (already) giddy.

reading: When a fool gets something into his hand, it is like a man already deranged getting drunk.
nuance: The image is of something added to an existing state. Wealth doesn't produce the folly but compounds it, and ஒன்று, 'some one thing', suggests it doesn't take much.

couplet: Friendship of fools i s very pleasant thing,
Parting with them will leave behind no sting.
pope.gloss: The friendship between fools is exceedingly delightful (to each other): for at parting there will be nothing to cause them pain.

reading: The friendship of fools is very sweet, for there is nothing painful about parting from them.
nuance: பிரிவு is a word that carries great weight in the Book of Love, so the 'sweetness' measured by painless parting reads like the opposite of what love is.

couplet: Like him who seeks his couch with unwashed feet,
Is fool whose foot intrudes where wise men meet.
pope.gloss: The appearance of a fool in an assembly of the learned is like placing (one's) unwashed feet on a bed.

reading: A fool's entering an assembly of the worthy is like placing an unwashed foot on a bed.
nuance: The harm passes to the place: the bed and the assembly are both defiled, not the foot or the fool. Parimelazhagar notes that 'unwashed' is a polite cover for what the foot has trodden, which Kalaignar spells out.

title: புல்லறிவாண்மை
theme: Petty knowledge that thinks itself wise. It is the poverty that counts most, it does worse harm than any enemy, and it can't be taught, because the person who has it is already sure that he knows.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its defect (841), its inability to do good to oneself and its doing of harm (842-843), self-admiration (844-846), and refusal of good counsel (847-850).

couplet: Want of knowledge, 'mid all wants the sorest want we deem;
Want of other things the world will not as want esteem.
pope.gloss: The want of wisdom is the greatest of all wants; but that of wealth the world will not regard as such.

reading: Lack of understanding is the poverty of poverties; other lack the world does not count as lack.
nuance: வையாது உலகு attributes the valuation to the world. Parimelazhagar's reason is that the wise keep this world's and the next world's fruit even in poverty, whereas the petty-minded don't even with wealth.

couplet: The gift of foolish man, with willing heart bestowed, is nought,
But blessing by receiver's penance bought.
pope.gloss: (The cause of) a fool cheerfully giving (something) is nothing else but the receiver's merit (in a former birth).

reading: When a person without understanding gives with a glad heart, the cause is nothing other than the receiver's merit.
nuance: A strange and rather cold claim: a good act by such a person earns him nothing. Parimelazhagar raises and rebuts the objection that fools also do good. Kalaignar has simply good luck (பெற்றபேறு), which removes தவம் from the picture.

couplet: With keener anguish foolish men their own hearts wring,
Than aught that even malice of their foes can bring.
pope.gloss: The suffering that fools inflict upon themselves is hardly possible even to foes.

reading: The suffering those without understanding do to themselves is hard even for their enemies to do.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a clever reason: an enemy has to watch for a moment and knows only so much, whereas self-injury never pauses and reaches poverty, blame and sin all at once.

couplet: What is stupidity? The arrogance that cries,
'Behold, we claim the glory of the wise.'
pope.gloss: What is called want of wisdom is the vanity which says, "We are wise".

reading: What is called வெண்மை? It is the pride that says 'we have brightness.'
nuance: வெண்மை, whiteness, is rawness or unripeness. ஒண்மை is brightness. The two words sound alike and describe opposite things, and the fool can't tell whether he is lit or blank. Parimelazhagar calls it a delusion because such people persist knowing the world mocks them.

couplet: If men what they have never learned assume to know,
Upon their real learning's power a doubt 'twill throw.
pope.gloss: Fools pretending to know what has not been read (by them) will rouse suspicion even as to what they have thoroughly mastered.

reading: Taking on what one hasn't learned brings doubt even on what one has mastered without flaw.
nuance: The verse is about how credibility works. The pretence costs real knowledge too. This is not a moral claim but a practical one about reputation, and it grants that the pretender may have actual skill.

couplet: Fools are they who their nakedness conceal,
And yet their faults unveiled reveal.
pope.gloss: Even to cover one's nakedness would be folly, if (one's) faults were not covered (by forsaking them).

reading: Is covering one's nakedness not itself petty, when one's faults aren't covered?

couplet: From out his soul who lets the mystic teachings die,
Entails upon himself abiding misery.
pope.gloss: The fool who neglects precious counsel does, of his own accord, a great injury to himself.

reading: One without understanding who lets slip the precious மறை does great harm to himself by himself.

couplet: Advised, he heeds not; of himself knows nothing wise;
This man's whole life is all one plague until he dies.
pope.gloss: The fool will not perform (his duties) even when advised nor ascertain them himself; such a soul is a burden (to the earth) till it departs (from the body).

reading: Not doing it when told, not seeing it himself, that life is a disease until it departs.
nuance: The verse doesn't say for whom. Parimelazhagar says for the earth that bears him, Manakkudavar for the people of the world, and Kalaignar for himself. These are three very different diseases. The verse's two failures also cover both routes to knowledge, one's own and another's.

couplet: That man is blind to eyes that will not see who knowledge shows;-
The blind man still in his blind fashion knows.
pope.gloss: One who would teach a fool will (simply) betray his folly; and the fool would (still) think himself "wise in his own conceit".

reading: One who shows things to a person who doesn't see becomes himself unseeing, and the unseeing one goes on having seen what he saw.
nuance: The compact wordplay on காண் is the content: the teacher fails and the pupil remains satisfied. Parimelazhagar says the teacher is blamed by the pupil and ends up the ignorant one, and concludes that good sense can't be instilled here by any means.

couplet: Who what the world affirms as false proclaim,
O'er all the earth receive a demon's name.
pope.gloss: He who denies the existence of what the world believes in will be regarded as a demon on earth.

reading: One who says 'it isn't' to what the world says is will be set down on this earth as a demon.
nuance: The verse names neither what's denied nor who 'the world' is, and everything turns on those blanks.

title: இகல்
theme: Hostility, as a disease of the disposition to quarrel. Giving it up is shown as gain and strength more than as saintliness, and pursuing it as a way to one's own ruin.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its defect (851), the good of not quarrelling (852-855), the harm of quarrelling (856-857), and both together (858-860).
source_issues: 858, 860: Manakkudavar not aligned.
856: Manakkudavar's text is cut off at the end (உண்டாமென்).

couplet: Hostility disunion's plague will bring,
That evil quality, to every living thing.
pope.gloss: The disease which fosters the evil of disunion among all creatures is termed hatred by the wise.

reading: They call hostility the disease that spreads, among all living beings, the ill nature of division.
nuance: Hostility here is not an event but a disease that spreads a disposition. Parimelazhagar sees in எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் a judgement: quarrelling humans are being put with the animals.

couplet: Though men disunion plan, and do thee much despite
'Tis best no enmity to plan, nor evil deeds requite.
pope.gloss: Though disagreeable things may be done from (a feeling of) disunion, it is far better that nothing painful be done from (that of) hatred.

reading: Even if someone does what you can't bear, intending division, it is best not to do harm in return, intending hostility.
nuance: The reason Parimelazhagar gives is strategic rather than saintly. Retaliate and enmity grows and you sink, abstain and it dies down and you rise. This is non-retaliation argued in the Book of Wealth's terms.

couplet: If enmity, that grievous plague, you shun,
Endless undying praises shall be won.
pope.gloss: To rid one-self of the distressing dtsease of hatred will bestow (on one) a never-decreasing imperishable fame.

reading: If the painful disease called hostility is removed, it gives a light that doesn't diminish and has no flaw.
nuance: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar differ on விளக்கம்: fame for one, radiance for the other. His route to fame is a long chain. Everyone becomes a friend, then every wealth comes, then giving, then renown. The verse takes no such steps.

couplet: Joy of joys abundant grows,
When malice dies that woe of woes.
pope.gloss: If hatred which is the greatest misery is destroyed, it will yield the greatest delight.

reading: If the suffering of sufferings called hostility is destroyed, it brings the joy of joys.

couplet: If men from enmity can keep their spirits free,
Who over them shall gain the victory?
pope.gloss: Who indeed would think of conquering those who naturally shrink back from hatred ?

reading: Who would set out to defeat those who are able to lean away from hostility?
nuance: வல்லாரை marks it as an ability, not a weakness. Manakkudavar faces the objection directly: wouldn't giving way be a defeat? The verse answers that no one can defeat them. Parimelazhagar adds it is particularly hard for kings.

couplet: The life of those who cherished enmity hold dear,
To grievous fault and utter death is near.
pope.gloss: Failure and ruin are not far from him who says it is sweet to excel in hatred.

reading: The life of one who says it is sweet to excel in hostility is close to failure and to ruin.
nuance: The problem is the relish: என்பவன் indicts the person who enjoys conflict and not one drawn into it. Kalaignar gives 'easy' (எளிது) for the verse's 'sweet' (இனிது), which changes the charge from pleasure to overconfidence.

couplet: The very truth that greatness gives their eyes can never see,
Who only know to work men woe, fulfilled of enmity.
pope.gloss: Those whose judgement brings misery through its connection with hatred cannot understand the triumphant nature of truth.

reading: Those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the true thing that holds victory.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's point: hostility itself clouds the mind, so that the very quarrel blinds one to how to win. A combative person is therefore bad at conflict.

couplet: 'Tis gain to turn the soul from enmity;
Ruin reigns where this hath mastery.
pope.gloss: Shrinking back from hatred will yield wealth; indulging in its increase will hasten ruin.

reading: Leaning away from hostility is gain; if one drives on to excel at it, ruin drives on to come.
nuance: Ruin mirrors what one does: ஊக்கின் ஊக்கும். Parimelazhagar locates the turning point in one's own mind, at the moment when hostility arises and isn't taken up.

couplet: Men think not hostile thought in fortune's favouring hour,
They cherish enmity when in misfortune's power.
pope.gloss: At the approach of wealth one will not think of hatred (but) to secure one's ruin, one will look to its increase.

reading: When gain is coming one doesn't look at hostility, and to bring on ruin one looks to excel at it.
nuance: This complicates 858. Hostility may not be the cause of ruin but the sign of it. Parimelazhagar says these are forerunners of gain and loss, and Manakkudavar links them to one's merit, which reduces how much the choice in 858 is really free.

couplet: From enmity do all afflictive evils flow;
But friendliness doth wealth of kindly good bestow.
pope.gloss: All calamities are caused by hatred; but by the delight (of friendship) is caused the great wealth of good virtues.

reading: From hostility come all ills, and from friendly gladness comes the pride of good and fitting ways.
nuance: செருக்கு is usually a fault in the Kural (844) and here it is praise. Parimelazhagar reads it as great wealth, and நன்னயம் as good policy. So the virtue is presented as a prosperous kind of wisdom.

title: பகைமாட்சி
theme: The enemy worth having, seen coldly: pick the weak, and notice who makes himself easy to beat through anger, ignorance, stinginess and isolation. Read another way, its list of vices is a portrait of how not to become someone's easy enemy.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the general rule (861), the specific marks of a beatable foe (862-867), and the fruit of such enmity (868-870). The chapter never says it is addressed to the reader's own faults, but its catalogue works that way.
source_issues: 862, 863: Manakkudavar not aligned.
869: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.

couplet: With stronger than thyself, turn from the strife away;
With weaker shun not, rather court the fray.
pope.gloss: Avoid offering resistance to the strong; (but) never fail to cherish enmity towards the weak.

reading: Avoid opposing the strong, and without holding back, favour enmity against the weak.
nuance: Whatever this is, it is not a moral teaching, which is why the commentators' disagreement matters so much.

couplet: No kinsman's love, no strength of friends has he;
How can he bear his foeman's enmity?
pope.gloss: How can he who is unloving, destitute of powerful aids, and himself without strength overcome the might of his foe ?

reading: With no love, no worthy allies and no strength of his own, how can he wear down an enemy's might?
nuance: அன்பு appears in a list of military assets. For Parimelazhagar it is love of one's kin, so without it there's no kin, and for an attacker such a person only adds strength.

couplet: A craven thing! knows nought, accords with none, gives nought away;
To wrath of any foe he falls an easy prey.
pope.gloss: In the estimation of foes miserably weak is he, who is timid, ignorant, unsociable and niggardly.

reading: He fears, doesn't know, doesn't fit in with others, doesn't give: he is utterly easy for an enemy.
nuance: The list includes not giving, which is an ethical failing elsewhere and here is a military one. Kalaignar's 'compassion' softens the word. Parimelazhagar says அஞ்சும் means fearing what needn't be feared, the mirror of 428.

couplet: His wrath still blazes, every secret told; each day
This man's in every place to every foe an easy prey.
pope.gloss: He who neither refrains from anger nor keeps his secrets will at all times and in all places be easily conquered by all.

reading: Not free from rage and without நிறை: at any time, in any place, he is easy for anyone.
nuance: The commentators differ on நிறை. Parimelazhagar means keeping secrets and Kalaignar means self-control. Parimelazhagar's logic is neat: the enemy no longer needs to watch for the right time, place or strength because the angry man's leaked plans give it all away.

couplet: No way of right he scans, no precepts bind, no crimes affright,
No grace of good he owns; such man's his foes' delight.
pope.gloss: (A) pleasing (object) to his foes is he who reads not moral works, does nothing that is enjoined by them cares not for reproach and is not possessed of good qualities.

reading: He doesn't look to the வழி, doesn't do what is suitable, doesn't look to blame, has no character: he is a pleasure to his enemies.

couplet: Blind in his rage, his lustful passions rage and swell;
If such a man mislikes you, like it well.
pope.gloss: Highly to be desired is the hatred of him whose anger is blind, and whose lust increases beyond measure.

reading: One of blinding anger and ever-growing lust: his not caring for you is something to care for.
nuance: பேணாமை பேணப்படும் is the wordplay and the whole point. Such a person's hostility is an asset, since he will destroy himself. Parimelazhagar says all become his enemies through the anger, and in the lust he loses sight of his affairs. Kalaignar turns காமம் into greed.

couplet: Unseemly are his deeds, yet proffering aid, the man draws nigh:
His hate- 'tis cheap at any price- be sure to buy!
pope.gloss: It is indeed necessary to obtain even by purchase the hatred of him who having begun (a work) does what is not conductive (to its accomplishment).

reading: One who stays close and does what is unbecoming: it is truly necessary to get his enmity, even by giving something.
nuance: Even the enmity has a price worth paying. The verse's hardest word is அடுத்திருந்து, and the commentators each supply a different object.

couplet: No gracious gifts he owns, faults many cloud his fame;
His foes rejoice, for none with kindred claim.
pope.gloss: He will become friendless who is without (any good) qualities. and whose faults are many; (such a character) is a help to (his) foes.

reading: With no qualities and many faults he has no one around him, and this is a protection to his enemies.
nuance: ஏமாப்பு, the word for protection, has been turned around. A man's faults become his enemies' shield. Parimelazhagar lists what deserts him: kin, friends, wealth, army.

couplet: The joy of victory is never far removed from those
Who've luck to meet with ignorant and timid foes.
pope.gloss: There will be no end of lofty delights to the victorious, if their foes are (both) ignorant and timid.

reading: Joy doesn't go far from those fighting, if they get enemies who are unknowing and afraid.
nuance: பெறின் sounds like luck. Parimelazhagar says that's because foes with neither knowledge nor resolve are rare.

couplet: The task of angry war with men unlearned in virtue's lore
Who will not meet, glory shall meet him never more.
pope.gloss: The light (of fame) will never be gained by him who gains not the trifling reputation of having fought an unlearned (foe).

reading: Fame will never come to one who cannot manage the small thing of being angry at the unlearned.
nuance: The syntax is hard and the commentaries don't converge. The reading given follows Parimelazhagar, who says others have not kept to the chapter's subject.

title: பகைத்திறந்தெரிதல்
theme: How to handle enmity as a strategic matter. Don't seek it, avoid certain enemies above all, turn some into friends and others into neutrals, hide your weakness, and cut the rest down while they are still young.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the fault of taking on enmity (871-873), who is to be made friend (874-875), and neutral (876), how to conduct oneself (877), what to do in oneself to remove it (878), when to remove it (879), and the cost of not doing so (880).
source_issues: 875: Manakkudavar not aligned.

couplet: For Hate, that ill-conditioned thing not e'en in jest.
Let any evil lon ging rule your breast.
pope.gloss: The evil of hatred is not of a nature to be desired by one even in sport.

reading: The thing called enmity, which has no good in it, shouldn't be wanted by anyone, even in jest.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a psychological reason for நகையேயும்: desired in play, the resentment grows and it becomes real. The verse sits at odds with the chapter that comes just before it.

couplet: Although you hate incur of those whose ploughs are bows,
Make not the men whose ploughs are words your foes!
pope.gloss: Though you may incur the hatred of warriors whose ploughs are bows, incur not that of ministers whose ploughs are words.

reading: Though you take on the enmity of ploughmen whose plough is the bow, do not take on that of ploughmen whose plough is the word.
nuance: A famous line, often read now as about writers and poets, but the older commentators don't read it that way. Parimelazhagar means those with counsel and policy, whose harm reaches one's descendants, and Manakkudavar means ministers. Kalaignar's 'learned' is the broadest. Both groups are 'ploughmen', borrowing the honour chapter 104 gives to that work.

couplet: Than men of mind diseased, a wretch more utterly forlorn,
Is he who stands alone, object of many foeman's scorn.
pope.gloss: He who being alone, incurs the hatred of many is more infatuated than even mad men.

reading: One who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many is more wretched than those who are ஏமுற்றவர்.

couplet: The world secure on his dexterity depends,
Whose worthy rule can change his foes to friends.
pope.gloss: The world abides in the greatness of that good-natured man who behaves so as to turn hatred into friendship.

reading: The world rests in the greatness of a person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship.
nuance: நட்பாக் கொண்டு is ambiguous: making them friends, or treating them as friends? The whole verse turns on it.

couplet: Without ally, who fights with twofold enemy o'ermatched,
Must render one of these a friend attached.
pope.gloss: He who is alone and helpless while his foes are two should secure one of them as an agreeable help (to himself).

reading: If you have no ally and two enemies, being alone, take one of them as a pleasing ally.
nuance: The word is இன்துணை, a sweet ally, which is warm for what it describes. Parimelazhagar adds 'for that time', and picks the one suited to defeating the other. The temporariness is his addition, though it's probably correct as politics.

couplet: Whether you trust or not, in time of sore distress,
Questions of diff'rence or agreement cease to press.
pope.gloss: Though (one's foe is) aware or not of one's misfortune one should act so as neither to join nor separate (from him).

reading: Whether or not you have trusted him, when ruin comes neither join with him nor break from him; let him be.
nuance: A rule for neutrality. Parimelazhagar explains the two halves separately: don't join, because he could harm from inside; don't break, because he could help your ruin along. In adversity an enemy is best left unprovoked.

couplet: To those who know them not, complain not of your woes;
Nor to your foeman's eyes infirmities disclose.
pope.gloss: Relate not your suffering even to friends who are ignorant of it, nor refer to your weakness in the presence of your foes.

reading: Don't complain to those who don't know of your pain, and don't show softness in front of enemies.
nuance: The pairing is the surprise. Parimelazhagar takes those who don't know to be friends who haven't noticed on their own, which is itself a judgement on them. Pain should be read and not announced, which ties this to the chapters on signs.

couplet: Know thou the way, then do thy part, thyself defend;
Thus shall the pride of those that hate thee have an end.
pope.gloss: The joy of one's foes will be destroyed if one guards oneself by knowing the way (of acting) and securing assistance.

reading: Knowing the way, building oneself up and guarding oneself will end the swagger on the enemy's side.
nuance: All three verbs are about oneself and none about the enemy, yet the enemy is what changes. Parimelazhagar's enemy is celebrating an expected win. Manakkudavar calls this 'the way to kill enemies', which shows how much he thinks self-strengthening does.

couplet: Destroy the thorn, while tender point can work thee no offence;
Matured by time, 'twill pierce the hand that plucks it thence.
pope.gloss: A thorny tree should be felled while young, (for) when it is grown it will destroy the hand of the feller.

reading: Cut a thorn tree while it is young; grown hard, it will destroy the hand that cuts it.
nuance: The verse itself doesn't mention enemies, and Parimelazhagar labels it allegory. Its logic of acting before a threat matures has no room in it for what a sapling might have become, or for whether it is really a thorn.

couplet: But breathe upon them, and they surely die,
Who fail to tame the pride of angry enemy.
pope.gloss: Those who do not destroy the pride of those who hate (them) will certainly not exist even to breathe.

reading: Those who don't break the pride of those hostile to them are, surely, not alive even to breathe.
nuance: Parimelazhagar adds that this is about one who could do it and neglects it out of contempt.

title: உட்பகை
theme: The enemy within the circle: kin and companions whose hostility is hidden. It is worse than an open foe because it is unseen, it wears a family down slowly, and even a sesame-sized amount of it holds ruin.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as about a king's court: why to avoid such enmity (881-882), guarding oneself (883), harm to the king (884-886), harm to his house (887-888), not to dismiss it (889), and the end (890). Several verses only name a family or a person, so that royal frame is his.
source_issues: 884, 885: Manakkudavar not aligned.
890: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் ends with a bracketed remark on கண்ணோடாதவர் that fits this verse poorly and has an unmatched '['.

couplet: Water and shade, if they unwholesome prove, will bring you pain.
And qualities of friends who treacherous act, will be your bane.
pope.gloss: Shade and water are not pleasant, (if) they cause disease; so are the qualities of (one's) relations not agreeable, (if) they cause pain.

reading: Even shade and water are bad if they do harm, and the நீர் of one's own people too is bad, if it does harm.
nuance: நீர் does double work, as water and as nature: தமர்நீர் is the nature of kin, sitting right next to actual water. Parimelazhagar's kin are specifically the relatives who could become inner enemies, and his illnesses from bad water are quite concrete. Manakkudavar reads நிழல்நீர் as one thing, the water in the shade.

couplet: Dread not the foes that as drawn swords appear;
Friendship of foes, who seem like kinsmen, fear!
pope.gloss: Fear not foes (who say they would cut) like a sword; (but) fear the friendship of foes (who seemingly act) like relations.

reading: Don't fear enemies who are like swords, but fear the bond with enemies who are like kin.
nuance: The verse says to fear the தொடர்பு and not the person. Parimelazhagar explains that the danger already lies in the existing bond, the one that has been made, and that open foes can be guarded against because they are known.

couplet: Of hidden hate beware, and guard thy life;
In troublous time 'twill deeper wound than potter's knife.
pope.gloss: Fear internal enmity and guard yourself; (if not) it will destroy (you) in an evil hour, as surely as the tool which cuts the potter's clay.

reading: Fear the enemy within and guard yourself; when you falter, it will cut surely, like the potter's cutter.
nuance: A மட்பகை is what the potter uses to take a pot off the wheel. Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's point is that the cut is clean and unnoticed. உலைவிடத்து adds patience, as this enemy doesn't need to attack until you are already down.

couplet: If secret enmities arise that minds pervert,
Then even kin unkind will work thee grievous hurt.
pope.gloss: The secret enmity of a person whose mind in unreformed will lead to many evils causing disaffection among (one's) relations.

reading: If an inner enmity of unreformed mind appears, it brings many ills of a circle that has gone bad.
nuance: The damage is secondary: it spoils the other relationships. Parimelazhagar's analysis is that the enemy works from within to turn others, the king's trust then fails too, and the whole thing compounds. Kalaignar places the mind that won't reform in the person himself, not in another.

couplet: Amid one's relatives if hidden hath arise,
'Twill hurt inflict in deadly wise.
pope.gloss: If there appears internal hatred in a (king's) family; it will lead to many a fatal crime.

reading: If an inner enmity appears that has the form of kinship, it brings many ills that have the form of death.
nuance: The verse's two lines balance on முறையான், so the closer the tie, the closer to death.

couplet: If discord finds a place midst those who dwelt at one before,
'Tis ever hard to keep destruction from the door.
pope.gloss: If hatred arises among (one's) own people, it will be hardly possible (for one) to escape death.

reading: If not-being-one arises among those who are one, it is ever hard to reach not-dying.
nuance: The wordplay runs through three lines: ஒன்றாமை, ஒன்றியார், ஒன்றல். Oneness is what is broken and also what is needed. Parimelazhagar's எஞ்ஞான்றும் means even when one is at the peak of power.

couplet: As casket with its cover, though in one they live alway,
No union to th e house where hate concealed hath sway.
pope.gloss: Never indeed will a family subject to internal hatred unite (really) though it may present an apparent union like that of a casket and its lid.

reading: Though joined like a casket and its lid, a family that has inner enmity is not joined.
nuance: The image shows a perfect fit with a seam all the same. The lid and the box remain two objects.

couplet: As gold with which the file contends is worn away,
So strength of house declines where hate concealed hath sway.
pope.gloss: A family subject to internal hatred will wear out and lose its strength like iron that has been filed away.

reading: As பொன் that is rubbed by a file wears away, a family with inner enmity wears down its strength by rubbing against itself.

couplet: Though slight as shred of 'seasame' seed it be,
Destruction lurks in hidden enmity.
pope.gloss: Although internal hatred be as small as the fragment of the sesamum (seed), still does destruction dwell in it.

reading: Though only as small as a split sesame seed, inner enmity has ruin within it.
nuance: உள்ளதாம் lets the word play with உட்பகை: the ruin is inside what is inside. Parimelazhagar notes the smallness is relative to a king's greatness, and that the large ruin stays contained until its hour comes.

couplet: Domestic life with those who don't agree,
Is dwelling in a shed with snake for company.
pope.gloss: Living with those who do not agree (with one) is like dwelling with a cobra (in the same) hut.

reading: Living with those not in accord with you is like living with a snake inside a hut.
nuance: Pope's 'domestic life' narrows what the verse leaves open. It says only 'those not in accord', which could be anyone one lives with. Parimelazhagar's point is about smallness and familiarity: in a confined space with long proximity, the bite is a certainty.

title: பெரியாரைப் பிழையாமை
theme: Not offending the great: to slight those with real power is to call down one's own ruin, and no wealth, fort or ally protects against them. Who the great are is the key question, and the verses themselves mostly leave it open.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the great into two: kings who can destroy (893-895) and ascetics whose anger can do anything (896-900). Manakkudavar also has ascetics in view, but the verses don't name them. Kalaignar reads them throughout as worthy or capable people, with no curses.
source_issues: 896: Parimelazhagar's comment cites '(குறள் -6)' for the point about wrath lasting a moment, but that wording matches 29. This looks like a citation error.
899: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is scrambled (இடை வேந்த முரிந்து) and the quote used has a likely misprint (இடைய for இடையே).

couplet: The chiefest care of those who guard themselves from ill,
Is not to slight the powers of those who work their mighty will.
pope.gloss: Not to disregard the power of those who can carry out (their wishes) is more important than all the watchfulness of those who guard (themselves against evil).

reading: Not slighting the power of those able to act is the highest of all safeguards for those who guard themselves.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes a large claim from this: fort, army, wealth and friends can all be undone by such people, so this safeguard outranks them. It closes a stretch of chapters that were all about those other safeguards.

couplet: If men will lead their lives reckless of great men's will,
Such life, through great men's powers, will bring perpetual ill.
pope.gloss: To behave without respect for the great (rulers) will make them do (us) irremediable evils.

reading: Going on without regard for the great will, through the great, bring ills that do not leave.
nuance: The grammar makes the conduct itself the agent, and the great are only the instrument. Parimelazhagar says this was meant to show people do it to themselves. He has the king as the one at fault, whereas Manakkudavar has a person failing to honour sages.

couplet: Who ruin covet let them shut their ears, and do despite
To those who, where they list to ruin have the might.
pope.gloss: If a person desires ruin, let him not listen to the righteous dictates of law, but commit crimes against those who are able to slay (other sovereigns).

reading: If you want to be ruined, don't listen, and commit a fault against those able to destroy.
nuance: A piece of grim irony, phrased as an instruction. The commentators differ on what isn't listened to: Parimelazhagar means the treatises on policy, and Manakkudavar means the great themselves. His Purananuru citation makes such kings swifter than Death, who at least waits for the time.

couplet: When powerless man 'gainst men of power will evil deeds essay,
Tis beck'ning with the hand for Death to seize them for its prey.
pope.gloss: The weak doing evil to the strong is like beckoning Yama to come (and destroy them).

reading: For those who can't do harm to those who can is like beckoning Death with the hand.
nuance: The word is விளி, to call, so the gesture does it. Parimelazhagar adds that Death would have come anyway, so the action only brings it sooner, and that the hand gesture itself carries a scornful tone.

couplet: Who dare the fiery wrath of monarchs dread,
Where'er they flee, are numbered with the dead.
pope.gloss: Those who have incurred the wrath of a cruel and mighty potentate will not prosper wherever they may go.

reading: Wherever they go, they won't exist anywhere, those who've drawn the anger of a king of fierce might.
nuance: Parimelazhagar is shrewdly political: other kings won't shelter the fugitive and may kill him to win favour or his goods. The verse's point is not the king's reach but what everyone around him will do because of it.
