couplet: Though in the conflagration caught, he may escape from thence:
He 'scapes not who in life to great ones gives offence.
pope.gloss: Though burnt by a fire (from a forest), one may perhaps live; (but) never will he live who has shown disrespect to the great (devotees).

reading: Even if burned by fire, there can be survival; those who go on offending the great will not survive.

couplet: Though every royal gift, and stores of wealth your life should crown,
What are they, if the worthy men of mighty virtue frown?
pope.gloss: If a king incurs the wrath of the righteous great, what will become of his government with its splendid auxiliaries and (all) its untold wealth ?

reading: What are a fully appointed life and lofty wealth, if worthy ones of great stature are angered?
nuance: Parimelazhagar says தகை means greatness that can curse and bless. Note his remark that செறின் implies they usually don't get angry, which holds for the verses after this. The verse's question doesn't state a mechanism, while he describes royal wealth burning up in a moment.

couplet: If they, whose virtues like a mountain rise, are light esteemed;
They die from earth who, with their households, ever-during seemed.
pope.gloss: If (the) hill-like (devotees) resolve on destruction, those who seemed to be everlasting will be destroyed root and branch from the earth.

reading: If hill-like people are held low or themselves turn to bringing low, those who seemed to stand forever will vanish from earth with their line.
nuance: நின்றன்னார், those who 'seem to stand', and குன்றன்னார், those who 'are like hills': the verse compares two kinds of standing. குன்ற is also a verbal pun on the hill.

couplet: When blazes forth the wrath of men of lofty fame,
Kings even fall from high estate and perish in the flame.
pope.gloss: If those of exalted vows burst in a rage, even (Indra) the king will suffer a sudden loss and be entirely ruined.

reading: If those of exalted resolve flare up, even the வேந்தன் breaks midway and loses his kingship.
nuance: ஏந்திய கொள்கை and வேந்தன் carry all the weight in this verse, and the disagreement could hardly be wider, from gods and vows to politics.

couplet: Though all-surpassing wealth of aid the boast,
If men in glorious virtue great are wrath, they're lost.
pope.gloss: Though in possession of numerous auxiliaries, they will perish who are-exposed to the wrath of the noble whose penance is boundless.

reading: Even those with overwhelming support will not survive if those of supreme distinction are angered.
nuance: சார்பு gets a precise list from Parimelazhagar: fort, army, wealth, friends, which are the chapters just passed through. His example is the burning of the three cities. The verse's own சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் doesn't specify asceticism or any cause.

title: பெண்வழிச்சேறல்
theme: A man who lets his wife's will or his desire for her govern him loses virtue, wealth, standing and even pleasure. The chapter treats household subordination as a failure of his own agency and of his duties to others, and it speaks throughout from the husband's side.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter by fault: desiring the wife (901-902), fearing her (903-906), obeying her (907-909), and a negative summary of all three (910). Kalaignar repeatedly rewrites the chapter so that its target is a bad or arrogant wife, or a man besotted with beauty, not wives as such.
source_issues: 903: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
901-902: Pope's gloss says 'lust after' and 'feminine nature', which are stronger than மனைவிழைவார் and பெண்விழைவான்; these come from Parimelazhagar's framing.

couplet: Who give their soul to love of wife acquire not nobler gain;
Who give their soul to strenuous deeds such meaner joys disdain.
pope.gloss: Those who lust after their wives will not attain the excellence of virtue; and it is just this that is not desired by those who are bent on acquiring wealth.

reading: Men who fix their desire on the wife do not reach the fine fruit of life, and this same desire is what men intent on action refuse to want.
nuance: The verse says only மனை, 'home', and மாண்பயன், 'fine fruit', without naming either. Parimelazhagar supplies virtue as the fruit and wealth-making as the action, so the claim that the household's own goal is lost is partly his construction.

couplet: Who gives himself to love of wife, careless of noble name
His wealth will clothe him with o'erwhelming shame.
pope.gloss: The wealth of him who, regardless (of his manliness), devotes himself to his wife's feminine nature will cause great shame (to ali men) and to himself;

reading: The prosperity of one who desires his woman without caring for something else brings him shame, and a great shame in the world besides.
nuance: பேணாது has no object in the verse, so what is being neglected is exactly what the commentators must decide.

couplet: Who to his wife submits, his strange, unmanly mood
Will daily bring him shame among the good.
pope.gloss: The frailty that stoops to a wife will always make (her husband) feel ashamed among the good.

reading: The unnatural condition of stooping before one's wife brings a man shame among good people at all times.
nuance: The shame is social and comparative. It arises among நல்லார், not in the house.

couplet: No glory crowns e'en manly actions wrought
By him who dreads his wife, nor gives the other world a thought.
pope.gloss: The undertaking of one, who fears his wife and is therefore destitute of (bliss), will never be applauded.

reading: A man who fears his wife and has no share in the other life gets no distinction from his capacity for action.

couplet: Who quakes before his wife will ever tremble too,
Good deeds to men of good deserts to do.
pope.gloss: He that fears his wife will always be afraid of doing good deeds (even) to the good.

reading: One who fears his wife will always be afraid to do good to good people.
nuance: The harm named is the loss of generosity to outsiders, so fear in the house is treated as a public failure of giving.

couplet: Though, like the demi-gods, in bliss they dwell secure from harm,
Those have no dignity who fear the housewife's slender arm.
pope.gloss: They that fear the bamboo-like shoulders of their wives will be destitute of manliness though they may flourish like the Gods.

reading: Even if they live like the gods, those who fear the bamboo-like shoulders of their wives have no worth.
nuance: The bamboo epithet is usually praise, but here it makes the fear ridiculous: Parimelazhagar takes it to show how slight the object of terror is, and contrasts it with warriors' shoulders. Kalaignar again limits the verse, to a wife lacking wisdom and character.

couplet: The dignity of modest womanhood excels
His manliness, obedient to a woman's law who dwells.
pope.gloss: Even shame faced womanhood is more to be esteemed than the shameless manhood that performs the behests of a wife.

reading: A woman who has shame holds more greatness than the manhood of one who goes about doing a woman's bidding.
nuance: The verse uses gender as a rank and then overturns it: நாண் outranks manhood. Its force still depends on the assumption that being below a woman is a disgrace, so it cuts both ways.

couplet: Who to the will of her with beauteous brow their lives conform,
Aid not their friends in need, nor acts of charity perform.
pope.gloss: Those who yield to the wishes of their wives will neither relieve the wants of (their) friends nor perform virtuous deeds.

reading: Those who act as the woman of the fine brow wishes neither meet their friends' needs nor do good.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is practical: she can neither issue the needed orders on her own nor hand over the wealth, so the household's decision-making stalls.

couplet: No virtuous deed, no seemly wealth, no pleasure, rests
With them who live obedient to their wives' behests.
pope.gloss: From those who obey the commands of their wives are to be expected neither deeds of virtue, nor those of wealth nor (even) those of pleasure.

reading: Deeds of virtue, ample wealth and the other pursuits are absent in those who do a woman's bidding.
nuance: பிறவினை is left open. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as pleasure, which gives the verse its sting: the man who surrenders for the sake of pleasure ends up losing pleasure too.

couplet: Where pleasures of the mind, that dwell in realms of thought, abound,
Folly, that springs from overweening woman's love, is never found.
pope.gloss: The foolishness that results from devotion to a wife will never be found in those who possess a reflecting mind and a prosperity (flowing) therefrom.

reading: Those whose minds hold deliberation and who have strength of heart will never have the foolishness that comes of attachment to a woman.
nuance: The positive turns the chapter into a claim about mind, not women: the fault is called பேதைமை and is the man's own. Commentators split on இடன், which Parimelazhagar takes as wealth in kings and Manakkudavar as breadth of mind, while Kalaignar hears firmness of heart.

title: வரைவின்மகளிர்
theme: Women who sell intimacy are portrayed as a danger to men because their words and embrace are divided from their hearts. The chapter's argument is that the falseness is detectable, and that who touches them reveals the quality of the man. It gives no view from the women's side.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: their words and acts are false (911-913), the high-minded will not touch them (914-916), and those who do are the low (917-920). He notes that 920 pairs them with drink and dice to introduce the next two chapters.
source_issues: 913: Pope's couplet makes the client the one embracing the corpse, while Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar make the woman the embracer; Pope's gloss mentions 'hired men', drawn from Parimelazhagar.

couplet: Those that choice armlets wear who seek not thee with love,
But seek thy wealth, their pleasant words will ruin prove.
pope.gloss: The sweet words of elegant braceleted (prostitutes) who desire (a man) not from affection but from avarice, will cause sorrow.

reading: The sweet words of bangled women who desire a man for his wealth and not from love will bring him harm.
nuance: The harm is located in the sweet speech, not the sex. The chapter opens as a chapter on deceptive language.

couplet: Who weigh the gain, and utter virtuous words with vicious heart,
Weighing such women's worth, from their society depart.
pope.gloss: One must ascertain the character of the ill-natured women who after ascertaining the wealth (of a man) speak (as if they were) good natured-ones, and avoid intercourse (with them).

reading: Weigh the conduct of faithless women who weigh the profit and then speak of their own virtue, and keep away from them.
nuance: தூக்கி is repeated: she weighs the gain, so he must weigh her in return. Parimelazhagar calls this behaviour their சாதி தருமம், which is a commentator's social classification and not in the verse.

couplet: As one in darkened room, some stranger corpse inarms,
Is he who seeks delight in mercenary women's charms!
pope.gloss: The false embraces of wealth-loving women are like (hired men) embracing a strange corpse in a dark room.

reading: The false embrace of women of wealth is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room.
nuance: A quick reader takes the client to be holding a corpse, as Pope's couplet does. Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar make the woman the embracer: she is the hired bearer, and the unwanted client is the corpse she handles for pay. On that reading the disgust is hers, which complicates the chapter's usual stance.

couplet: Their worthless charms, whose only weal is wealth of gain,
From touch of these the wise, who seek the wealth of grace, abstain.
pope.gloss: The wise who seek the wealth of grace will not desire the base favours of those who regard wealth (and not pleasure) as (their) riches.

reading: Those whose understanding weighs the wealth of grace will not plunge into the base charms of women whose wealth is only wealth.

couplet: From contact with their worthless charms, whose charms to all are free,
The men with sense of good and lofty wisdom blest will flee;
pope.gloss: Those whose knowledge is made excellent by their (natural) sense will not covet the trffling delights of those whose favours are common (to all).

reading: Those whose knowledge has been refined by the goodness of their intellect will not plunge into the base charms of those whose goodness belongs to everyone.
nuance: பொதுநலம், 'common goodness', is a pointed phrase, since நலம் elsewhere means personal excellence. Parimelazhagar explains மதிநலம் as clarity earned in former births; the verse names no births.

couplet: From touch of those who worthless cha rms, with wanton arts, display,
The men who would their own true good maintain will turn away.
pope.gloss: Those who would spread (the fame of) their own goodness will not desire the shoulders of those,who rejoice in their accomplishments and bestow their despicable favours (on all who pay).

reading: Those who would spread their own goodness will not touch the shoulders of women who, proud of their charm, spread a base goodness.
nuance: The same verb பாரிப்பார் is used for both parties: each is spreading a நலம், and the verse sets reputation against availability as two kinds of publicity.

couplet: Who cherish alien thoughts while folding in their feigned embrace,
These none approach save those devoid of virtue's grace.
pope.gloss: Those who are destitute of a perfectly (reformed) mind will covet the shoulders of those who embrace (them) while their hearts covet other things.

reading: Those with no firmness of heart touch the shoulders of women who join with them while tending other things in their hearts.
nuance: A divided heart on one side is paired with an unguarded heart on the other. The verse's பிற is unspecified; the commentators fill it with wealth.

couplet: As demoness who lures to ruin woman's treacherous love
To men devoid of wisdom's searching power will prove.
pope.gloss: The wise say that to such as are destitute of discerning sense the embraces of faithless women are (as ruinous as those of) the celestail female.

reading: For those lacking discerning understanding, the embrace of deceiving women is said to be an அணங்கு.

couplet: The wanton's tender arm, with gleaming jewels decked,
Is hell, where sink degraded souls of men abject.
pope.gloss: The delicate shoulders of prostitutes with excellent jewels are a hell into which are plunged the ignorant base.

reading: The soft shoulders of women of fine jewels who draw no line are the mire in which base men with no worth sink.
nuance: வரைவு, 'limit', gives the chapter its title. Parimelazhagar says it means no line between high and low clients, and insists பூரியர் here means low in understanding, not in caste. அளறு means hell and mire at once, and softness of shoulder fits sinking.

couplet: Women of double minds, strong drink, and dice; to these giv'n o'er,
Are those on whom the light of Fortune shines no more.
pope.gloss: Treacherous women, liquor, and gambling are the associates of such as have forsaken by Fortune.

reading: Double-minded women, liquor and dice are the company of those whom Fortune has cast off.

title: கள்ளுண்ணாமை
theme: Drink destroys standing, shame and understanding, can't be hidden, and can't be argued away. The only exit the chapter offers is the drinker's own recognition during a sober moment.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's notes: loss of standing (921-924), loss of understanding (925-926), drink cannot be concealed (927-928), a drunkard cannot be reasoned with (929), and the way it could end (930).
source_issues: 925: Parimelazhagar's commentary is cut off mid-quotation.
926: Pope's gloss makes the verse's two halves a simile ('likewise'), following Parimelazhagar's reading; the Tamil has no such marker.
930: Parimelazhagar's lemma begins கண் உண்ணாப் where the verse has கள்ளுண்ணாப், which appears to be a transcription error.

couplet: Who love the palm's intoxicating juice, each day,
No rev'rence they command, their glory fades away.
pope.gloss: Those who always thirst after drink will neither inspire fear (in others) nor retain the light (of their fame).

reading: Those who go on loving liquor are never held in awe, and they lose their lustre.
nuance: Parimelazhagar reads this as a king's loss of enemies' fear, while Manakkudavar has ordinary esteem from others, so the same verse can be statecraft or general ethics.

couplet: Drink not inebriating draught. Let him count well the cost.
Who drinks, by drinking, all good men's esteem is lost.
pope.gloss: Let no liquor be drunk; if it is desired, let it be drunk by those who care not for esteem of the great.

reading: Do not drink; if anyone does, let it be those who don't wish to be counted by the worthy.
nuance: The permission is a trap. It sounds like a concession but actually states the price.

couplet: The drunkard's joy is sorrow to his mother's eyes;
What must it be in presence of the truly wise?
pope.gloss: Intoxication is painful even in the presence of (one's) mother; what will it not then be in that of the wise ?

reading: Drunken joy is painful even in the sight of the woman who bore you; what then in the sight of the worthy?
nuance: The argument runs from the most forgiving audience to the least, so the mother works as a limit case. களி, the word for drunken joy, is otherwise a word of delight.

couplet: Shame, goodly maid, will turn her back for aye on them
Who sin the drunkard's grievous sin, that all condemn.
pope.gloss: The fair maid of modesty will turn her back on those who are guilty of the great and abominable crime of drunkenness.

reading: Shame, the good woman, turns her back on those with the great and repugnant fault called liquor.
nuance: புறங்கொடுக்கும் may carry a battlefield sense of turning one's back in flight; that is my suggestion, not a commentator's. Parimelazhagar explains the feminine personification as following a Sanskrit convention.

couplet: With gift of goods who self-oblivion buys,
Is ignorant of all that man should prize.
pope.gloss: To give money and purchase unconsciousness is the result of one's ignorance of (one's own actions).

reading: To give up wealth and take self-oblivion in return must come from கையறியாமை.
nuance: The irony is commercial: one pays good money to buy ignorance.

couplet: Sleepers are as the dead, no otherwise they seem;
Who drink intoxicating draughts, they poison quaff, we deem.
pope.gloss: They that sleep resemble the deed; (likewise) they that drink are no other than poison-eaters.

reading: Those asleep are no different from the dead, and those who drink are always eating poison.

couplet: Who turn aside to drink, and droop their heavy eye,
Shall be their townsmen's jest, when they the fault espy.
pope.gloss: Those who always intoxicate themselves by a private (indulgence in) drink; will have their secrets detected and laughed at by their fellow-townsmen.

reading: Those who always seek out liquor and sink with drooping eyes are seen through and laughed at by their own town.
nuance: ஒற்றி occurs twice: he resorts to drink in hiding, and the town spies out what is within. Parimelazhagar says it is secret drinking and Manakkudavar seeking out where liquor is.

couplet: No more in secret drink, and then deny thy hidden fraud;
What in thy mind lies hid shall soon be known abroad.
pope.gloss: Let (the drunkard) give up saying "I have never drunk"; (for) the moment (he drinks) he will simply betray his former attempt to conceal.

reading: Give up saying you have never been drunk, because what is hidden in the heart grows on that very spot.

couplet: Like him who, lamp in hand, would seek one sunk beneath the wave.
Is he who strives to sober drunken man with reasonings grave.
pope.gloss: Reasoning with a drunkard is like going under water with a torch in search of a drowned man.

reading: To offer reasons to the drunk is like reaching with fire for one who has plunged beneath the water.

couplet: When one, in sober interval, a drunken man espies,
Does he not think, 'Such is my folly in my revelries'?
pope.gloss: When (a drunkard) who is sober sees one who is not, it looks as if he remembered not the evil effects of his (own) drink.

reading: When sober, and seeing another man drunk, doesn't he reflect on the lapse of his own drinking?
nuance: After 929's closed door the chapter leaves one open: self-recognition. Parimelazhagar names the logic as inference: what he sees in the other he could infer about himself. The question form suggests the chance is seldom taken.

title: சூது
theme: Gambling is ruin even when it pays, because a win is the bait that holds the player. It takes wealth first, then truthfulness, compassion and the basics of living, and the attachment grows with each loss.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: it brings poverty (931-935), it does many small harms and ruins both worlds (936-939), and it is hard to quit, which shows the greatness of those who do (940).
source_issues: 939, 940: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
932: Parimelazhagar's lemma reads ஒன்று உய்தி where the verse has ஒன்றெய்தி, apparently a transcription error.
933: Manakkudavar's text ends with a stray digit 4.
936: Pope's gloss has 'pangs of hell in the next world' from Parimelazhagar; the verse says only அல்லல் உழப்பர்.
938: the Parimelazhagar text records a variant reading, பொருள் கொடுத்து.

couplet: Seek not the gamester's play; though you should win,
Your gain is as the baited hook the fish takes in.
pope.gloss: Though able to win, let not one desire gambling; (for) even what is won is like a fish swallowing the iron in fish-hook.

reading: Don't want gambling even if you can win, for what you win is like the metal of the hook swallowed by a fish.
nuance: The verse attacks gambling at its strongest case, a win. Parimelazhagar adds that the winnings are a shackle keeping the gambler from leaving. பொன் here means the hook's metal, not gold, though the sound of 'gold' sharpens the image.

couplet: Is there for gamblers, too, that gaining one a hundred lose, some way
That they may good obtain, and see a prosperous day?
pope.gloss: Is there indeed a means of livelihood that can bestow happiness on gamblers who gain one and lose a hundred ?

reading: Is there any way of living well for gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred?
nuance: ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் is sequence as well as ratio. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar hear the hope that follows the first gain, so the loss is driven by the win.

couplet: If prince unceasing speak of nought but play,
Treasure and revenue will pass from him away.
pope.gloss: If the king is incessantly addicted to the rolling dice in the hope of gain, his wealth and the resources thereof will take their departure and fall into other's hands.

reading: If one keeps calling the falling of the dice, the gains of wealth will leave and pass elsewhere.
nuance: The chiming of உருளாயம் and பொருளாயம் sets one income against another: the income of the dice swallows the income of wealth. Parimelazhagar makes the subject a king and the destination his enemies, which the verse doesn't state.

couplet: Gaming brings many woes, and ruins fair renown;
Nothing to want brings men so surely down.
pope.gloss: There is nothing else that brings (us) poverty like gambling which causes many a misery and destroys (one's) reputation.

reading: There is nothing that gives poverty like gambling, which does many small harms and destroys distinction.
nuance: சிறுமை elsewhere is smallness of character. The commentators read it here as miseries, but both senses are available, since gambling diminishes a person as well as afflicting him.

couplet: The dice, and gaming-hall, and gamester's art, they eager sought,
Thirsting for gain- the men in other days who came to nought.
pope.gloss: Penniless are those who by reason of their attachment would never forsake gambling, the gambling-place and the handling (of dice).

reading: Those who, in pride, clung to the dice, the gaming hall and the skilled hand have come to nothing.
nuance: The past tense makes this an appeal to history. Parimelazhagar names the example: the Pandavas losing their kingdom and going to the forest. The verse names no one, so this epic reference is his.

couplet: Gambling's Misfortune's other name: o'er whom she casts her veil,
They suffer grievous want, and sorrows sore bewail.
pope.gloss: Those who are swallowed by the goddess called "gambling" will never have their hunger satisfied, but suffer the pangs of hell in the next world.

reading: Those covered by the goddess of misfortune named gambling will not fill themselves and will suffer distress.

couplet: Ancestral wealth and noble fame to ruin haste,
If men in gambler's halls their precious moments waste.
pope.gloss: To waste time at the place of gambling will destroy inherited wealth and goodness of character.

reading: If காலை enters the gaming hall, it will ruin long-held wealth and character.
nuance: Whichever reading is taken, time is the stake, not money: ruin comes from what the hours would have been spent on.

couplet: Gambling wastes wealth, to falsehood bends the soul: it drives away
All grace, and leaves the man to utter misery a prey.
pope.gloss: Gambling destroys property, teaches falsehood, puts an end to benevolence, and brings in misery (here and hereafter).

reading: Gambling destroys wealth, makes one take up lying, destroys compassion and drives one through misery.
nuance: The list is a causal ladder, and the moral rungs come after the financial one. Parimelazhagar assigns the means: loss robs, the winner's position breeds lies, and the rancour of the game kills compassion. In his reading, then, wins and losses alike do damage.

couplet: Clothes, wealth, food, praise, and learning, all depart
From him on gambler's gain who sets his heart.
pope.gloss: The habit of gambling prevents the attainment of these five: clothing, wealth, food, fame and learning.

reading: Clothing, wealth, food, lustre and learning, these five don't come near one who takes to gaming.
nuance: அடையாவாம் says that they won't arrive, while Pope's 'depart' adds that they were held already. The list runs from bare needs to learning, and puts survival and culture under one head.

couplet: Howe'er he lose, the gambler's heart is ever in the play;
E'en so the soul, despite its griefs, would live on earth alway.
pope.gloss: As the gambler loves (his vice) the more he loses by it, so does the soul love (the body) the more it suffers through it.

reading: As a gambler loves the game more with every loss, so the living being's love grows with every suffering it goes through.
nuance: An unexpected turn to the human condition: the chapter's closing verse uses gambling to diagnose attachment to life itself. Parimelazhagar insists the real target is the gambler, with the soul there to drive the point home, but the verse's grammar makes the soul the thing explained.

title: மருந்து
theme: Medicine as a matter of measure. Illness comes from imbalance, the best remedy is eating with judgment so that no remedy is needed, and when illness does come, healing depends on careful diagnosis and on a whole system of people.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: what causes disease (941), food and its measure, time and fruits (942-945), lapses (946-947), the physician's cure (948-949), and the four parts of treatment (950). Most of a chapter titled 'medicine' argues for not needing it. Manakkudavar's text closes a section (துன்பவியல்) at 947, so his arrangement may differ from the received one.
source_issues: 943, 946: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
947: Manakkudavar's text ends with a section colophon, துன்பவியல் முற்றிற்று.
941: Pope's gloss adds food and work from Parimelazhagar, and turns the three into flatulence, biliousness and phlegm, which the verse doesn't name beyond வளி.

couplet: The learned books count three, with wind as first; of these,
As any one prevail, or fail; 'twill cause disease.
pope.gloss: If (food and work are either) excessive or deficient, the three things enumerated by (medical) writers, flatulence, biliousness, and phlegm, will cause (one) disease.

reading: The three counted by the learned, starting with wind, cause disease whether they exceed or fall short.
nuance: Deficiency is as dangerous as excess. The verse defers to the நூலோர் and doesn't claim the theory as its own.

couplet: No need of medicine to heal your body's pain,
If, what you ate before digested well, you eat again.
pope.gloss: No medicine is necessary for him who eats after assuring (himself) that what he has (already) eaten has been digested.

reading: No medicine is called for by the body if one eats only after attending to the digestion of what was eaten.
nuance: போற்றி, 'with care', turns digestion into something to watch. Parimelazhagar lists bodily signs of it, such as lightness and clean belching. His remark on உணின் concedes that this is hard to do.

couplet: Who has a body gained may long the gift retain,
If, food digested well, in measure due he eat again.
pope.gloss: If (one's food has been) digested let one eat with moderation; (for) that is the way to prolong the life of an embodied soul.

reading: When digestion is complete, eat knowing the measure: that is how one who has gained a body can carry it far.
nuance: உடம்பு பெற்றான், 'one who has received a body', treats the body as a gift. Parimelazhagar pushes further: a human body is the only vehicle for this world, the next and liberation, so length of life serves those ends. The verse itself states no such purpose.

couplet: Knowing the food digested well, when hunger prompteth thee,
With constant care, the viands choose that well agree.
pope.gloss: (First) assure yourself that your food has been digested and never fail to eat, when very hungry, whatever is not disagreeable (to you).

reading: Knowing the food is digested, hold to what is not incompatible and eat it after real hunger.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sets out three kinds of incompatibility: with one's constitution, with the season and hour, and between foods. His example is honey and ghee in equal amounts turning to poison, which Manakkudavar shares.

couplet: With self-denial take the well-selected meal;
So shall thy frame no sudden sickness feel.
pope.gloss: There will be no disaster to one's life if on e eats with moderation, food that is not disagreeable.

reading: If one eats with மறுத்து food that has no incompatibility, life takes no injury.
nuance: I'm unsure of Manakkudavar's sense. His gloss, with its example of ginger after jackfruit, doesn't obviously fit the verse, and I record it without claiming to understand it fully.

couplet: On modest temperance as pleasures pure,
So pain attends the greedy epicure.
pope.gloss: As pleasure dwells with him who eats moderately, so disease (dwells) with the glutton who eats voraciously.

reading: As joy stays with the one who eats knowing how to stop short, disease stays with the one who eats enormously.
nuance: இரையான், 'feeder', is a word for animals' feed. Parimelazhagar notes that this likens the glutton to a beast. The contrast is inbam and noy, not health and disease: moderation yields pleasure, so restraint isn't presented as a sacrifice.

couplet: Who largely feeds, nor measure of the fire within maintains,
That thoughtless man shall feel unmeasured pains.
pope.gloss: He will be afflicted with numberless diseases, who eats immoderately, ignorant (of the rules of health).

reading: If one eats hugely, not discerning the measure of the fire within, disease will arise beyond all measure.
nuance: அளவு occurs on both sides: disregard the measure of the fire, and disease loses its measure. Manakkudavar and Kalaignar read தீ simply as hunger, while Parimelazhagar reads it as the belly's fire.

couplet: Disease, its cause, what may abate the ill:
Let leech examine these, then use his skill.
pope.gloss: Let the physician enquire into the (nature of the) disease, its cause and its method of cure and treat it faithfully according to (medical rule).

reading: Investigate the disease, then its root, then the means that subdue it, and act so as to get it right.
nuance: நாடி recurs three times and sets the order: identify, trace, select, then act. Kalaignar adds that this applies to the diseases of society, which is his extension. Parimelazhagar lists surgery and cautery among the means.

couplet: The habitudes of patient and disease, the crises of the ill
These must the learned leech think over well, then use his skill.
pope.gloss: The learned (physician) should ascertain the condition of his patient; the nature of his disease, and the season (of the year) and (then) proceed (with his treatment).

reading: The learned one should act having considered the measure of the patient, the measure of the illness and the time.
nuance: Learning alone isn't enough: the verse makes the patient's measure come first, so that treatment is individual. Parimelazhagar explicitly wants both the book's way and the physician's own discernment.

couplet: For patient, leech, and remedies, and him who waits by patient's side,
The art of medicine must fourfold code of laws provide.
pope.gloss: Medical science consists of four parts, viz., patient, physician, medicine and compounder; and each of these (again) contains four sub-divisions.

reading: The patient, the healer, the medicine and the one who attends: medicine has these four parts.
nuance: The verse calls the whole arrangement மருந்து, so the patient is himself part of the medicine, not its recipient.

title: குடிமை
theme: High birth as a set of obligations and marks: integrity, shame, truthfulness, generous speech and giving, held to even in poverty. The chapter speaks as if birth produced these qualities, while its own tests make conduct the evidence of birth, and the commentators pull hard in opposite directions on that point.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the nature of the well-born (951-953), they don't change even in poverty (954-956), the disgrace that follows change (957-958), and what lineage requires (959-960).
source_issues: 951: Parimelazhagar's lemma reads இப்பிறந்தார் where the verse has இற்பிறந்தார், apparently a transcription error.
955: Parimelazhagar's text repeats விளக்கம் with a stray parenthesis, suggesting a formatting fault.
958: Pope's couplet supplies 'some goodly name', which is not what commentators take நலம் to be.

couplet: Save in the scions of a noble house, you never find
Instinctive sense of right and virtuous shame combined.
pope.gloss: Consistency (of thought, word and deed) and fear (of sin) are conjointly natural only to the high-born.

reading: Only in those born to a good house do integrity and shame exist together, naturally.
nuance: இயல்பாக and ஒருங்கு both limit the claim: it is about these qualities coming naturally and together, which leaves open whether others can acquire them.

couplet: In these three things the men of noble birth fail not:
In virtuous deed and truthful word, and chastened thought.
pope.gloss: The high-born will never deviate from these three; good manners, truthfulness and modesty.

reading: Those of good birth don't slip in these three: conduct, truthfulness and shame.
nuance: Parimelazhagar maps the three onto body, speech and mind, and adds that this comes without learning. Manakkudavar takes நாண் physically, as covering one's nakedness, while Kalaignar has honour instead and again makes these the test of who counts as high-born.

couplet: The smile, the gift, the pleasant word, unfailing courtesy
These are the signs, they say, of true nobility.
pope.gloss: A cheerful countenance, liberality, pleasant words, and an unreviling disposition, these four are said to be the proper qualities of the truly high-born.

reading: A smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning: these four, they say, belong to a truly good lineage.
nuance: None of the four is about ancestry, and all are ways of treating someone else. Parimelazhagar specifies the setting: when the destitute come, for everyone scorns those who have nothing. That turns etiquette into a test.

couplet: Millions on millions piled would never win
The men of noble race to soul-degrading sin.
pope.gloss: Though blessed with immense wealth, the noble will never do anything unbecoming.

reading: Even if they gain crores upon crores, the well-born do nothing that diminishes them.
nuance: பெறினும் can mean holding wealth or being offered it. Parimelazhagar and Pope lean toward the first, and Kalaignar toward a bribe, which makes this a claim about being unbuyable.

couplet: Though stores for charity should fail within, the ancient race
Will never lose its old ancestral grace.
pope.gloss: Though their means fall off, those born in ancient families, will not lose their character (for liberality).

reading: Even when what they can give has shrunk, an old family doesn't part from its nature.
nuance: The verse measures their poverty by what they can give, not by what they have. Parimelazhagar explains பழங்குடி with the Chera, Chola and Pandya, excellent since creation, which ties this to royal houses.

couplet: Whose minds are set to live as fits their sire's unspotted fame,
Stooping to low deceit, commit no deeds that gender shame.
pope.gloss: Those who seek to preserve the irreproachable honour of their families will not viciously do what is detrimental thereto.

reading: Those who say 'we will live holding to our spotless lineage' will not do unworthy things through deceit.
nuance: என்பார் makes lineage a resolve: it applies to those who declare they will live by it. That moves lineage from something one has to something one takes on. Parimelazhagar adds 'even in poverty'.

couplet: The faults of men of noble race are seen by every eye,
As spots on her bright orb that walks sublime the evening sky.
pope.gloss: The defects of the noble will be observed as clearly as the dark spots in the moon.

reading: A fault in the well-born stands out high, like the spot on the moon in the sky.
nuance: A cost of height: the fault is not larger, but more visible. Each part maps: lineage to sky, virtues to moon, fault to spot. Manakkudavar draws the practical moral.

couplet: If lack of love appear in those who bear some goodly name,
'Twill make men doubt the ancestry they claim.
pope.gloss: If one of a good family betrays want of affection, his descent from it will be called in question.

reading: If want of affection shows in one of a good house, people will have doubts about his lineage.
nuance: The chapter's claim protects itself here: when a well-born man is cruel, the doubt falls on his birth and not on the rule that birth gives virtue. Reading conduct as evidence of birth also makes the doubt a slur on his parentage, which is not stated.

couplet: Of soil the plants that spring thereout will show the worth:
The words they speak declare the men of noble birth.
pope.gloss: As the sprout indicates the nature of the soil, (so) the speech of the noble indicates (that of one's birth).

reading: A sprout shows what lies in the ground; the words from the mouth show the lineage of the one born in it.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the disguise: it looks as if the verse is teaching how to identify lineage, but it is really a command to speak sweetly. Note கால், a sprout: the evidence appears at the earliest moment. Kalaignar's version has the mature crop.

couplet: Who seek for good the grace of virtuous shame must know;
Who seek for noble name to all must reverence show.
pope.gloss: He who desires a good name must desire modesty; and he who desires (the continuance of) a family greatness must be submissive to all.

reading: If you want goodness, want shame; if you want lineage, want humility toward all.
nuance: வேண்டின் treats lineage as something one can want and go after. This is the verse most at odds with 951, since a thing given by birth need not be wanted.

title: மானம்
theme: Honour ranks above profit, fame and survival itself: one abandons even indispensable acts that would lower one, and one who has lost standing is as worthless as fallen hair. The chapter ends by praising those who would rather die than live degraded.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar, reading it as the sequel to the chapter on lineage: not doing what lowers one (961-963), the fault of doing it (964-966), and the excellence of dying for honour (967-970).
source_issues: 963: Parimelazhagar's text is truncated and begins partway through his gloss, with no treatment of பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்.
962: Manakkudavar's text ends with a stray digit 3.
967: Pope's gloss adds 'in his usual state' for அந்நிலையே and 'died'; the Tamil has கெட்டான்.
968: Pope's couplet says 'as nectar sweet', while his gloss says 'remedy against death'; the Tamil has மருந்து, and only the commentators add death.

couplet: Though linked to splendours man no otherwise may gain,
Reject each act that may thine honour's clearness stain.
pope.gloss: Actions that would degrade (one's) family should not be done; though they may be so important that not doing them would end in death.

reading: Even if they are so excellent as to be indispensable, give up things that would diminish you.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes this a deliberate polemic: he says it rejects a Sanskrit rule that one may do degrading things to survive. The verse names no rival.

couplet: Who seek with glory to combine honour's untarnished fame,
Do no inglorious deeds, though men accord them glory's name.
pope.gloss: Those who desire (to maintain their) honour, will surely do nothing dishonourable, even for the sake of fame.

reading: Those who want renown and great manliness together won't do unworthy things even for renown.
nuance: சீர் is used against itself: renown bought with unworthy acts is not renown. பேராண்மை is explained by Parimelazhagar as a firmness that doesn't falter anywhere, and he takes it here as honour, not prowess.

couplet: Bow down thy soul, with increase blest, in happy hour;
Lift up thy heart, when stript of all by fortune's power.
pope.gloss: In great prosperity humility is becoming; dignity, in great adversity.

reading: In abundance you must bow, and in slight and shrunken circumstances you must stand tall.
nuance: The posture runs against the circumstances: humility when the world would permit pride, and height when the world would press one down. Humility and honour, often seen as rivals, are the same discipline at different times.

couplet: Like hairs from off the head that fall to earth,
When fall'n from high estate are men of noble birth.
pope.gloss: They who have fallen from their (high) position are like the hair which has fallen from the head.

reading: People who have fallen from their position are like hair that has fallen from the head.
nuance: The verse says மாந்தர், people generally, and Parimelazhagar narrows it to the well-born. Nothing about the hair changes when it falls, only its place, so worth is presented as depending on where it stands.

couplet: If meanness, slight as 'abrus' grain, by men be wrought,
Though like a hill their high estate, they sink to nought.
pope.gloss: Even those who are exalted like a hill will be thought low, if they commit deeds that are debasing.

reading: Even those like a hill will sink, if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed.
nuance: குன்று works four ways: hill, sinking, lowering, and the tiny red seed குன்றி. The sound itself demonstrates how little separates the great from the small.

couplet: It yields no praise, nor to the land of Gods throws wide the gate:
Why follow men who scorn, and at their bidding wait?
pope.gloss: Of what good is it (for the high-born) to go and stand in vain before those who revile him ? it only brings him loss of honour and exclusion from heaven.

reading: It brings no praise and doesn't carry one to the gods' land: why then go and stand behind those who scorn you?
nuance: The argument is from utility, not pride: it weighs both possible rewards and finds neither.

couplet: Better 'twere said, 'He's perished!' than to gain
The means to live, following in foeman's train.
pope.gloss: It is better for a man to be said of him that he died in his usual state than that he eked out his life by following those who disgraced him.

reading: Rather than live by following those who don't accept you, it is better to be called ruined in that very condition.
nuance: கெட்டான் means ruined and can mean dead. Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar take death, while Manakkudavar stays with the word. Parimelazhagar says this replies to someone who would still go for wealth and survival. The verse's சொல் is about what is said of a person, so reputation is the stake.

couplet: When high estate has lost its pride of honour meet,
Is life, that nurses this poor flesh, as nectar sweet?
pope.gloss: For the high-born to keep their body in life when their honour is gone will certainly not prove a remedy against death.

reading: When greatness comes to be stripped of its dignity, is a life nursing the flesh a medicine?
nuance: The commentators complete the question: medicine against dying. Since death will come anyway, living on buys nothing. ஊன் reduces the body to meat, which Parimelazhagar notes is what a person is after honour goes.

couplet: Like the wild ox that, of its tuft bereft, will pine away,
Are those who, of their honour shorn, will quit the light of day.
pope.gloss: Those who give up (their) life when (their) honour is at stake are like the yark which kills itself at the loss of (even one of) its hairs.

reading: Those who are like the yak that won't live once its hair is gone give up their lives when honour's moment comes.
nuance: The image is presented as nature, which Parimelazhagar says shows that this is inborn in them. Kalaignar distances himself with என்பார்கள், 'people say'. The verse doesn't say whether the death is by one's own hand; Kalaignar's next gloss, on 970, does.

couplet: Who, when dishonour comes, refuse to live, their honoured memory
Will live in worship and applause of all the world for aye!
pope.gloss: The world will (always) praise and adore the fame of the honourable who would rather die than suffer indignity.

reading: The world worships and praises the radiance of the honourable who won't live when disgrace comes.
nuance: The reward is entirely posthumous and in others' mouths, and ஒளி is the fame that outlasts the person. Parimelazhagar adds heaven by citing Purananuru, which reverses 966's point only in appearance, since there heaven was what degrading service failed to earn.

title: பெருமை
theme: Greatness is not given by birth, rank or wealth. It consists of high aim, self-guarding, doing the rare thing, freedom from conceit and covering others' weakness, and smallness is the same set of features reversed.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the excellence of greatness (971), it isn't produced by birth or wealth alone (972-973), how it arises (974), what those who have it do (975), what those without it do (976-977), and both together (978-980).
source_issues: 971: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
974: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's gloss, so it may not be independent.
972: Pope renders எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் as 'all men', narrowing the verse in line with Parimelazhagar's மக்களுயிர்.
973: Pope's couplet uses 'lofty line' and 'lowly birth', while the commentators take the position as wealth or seat.
977: Manakkudavar's text appears corrupt at நிதியை இறப்பாரிடத்தே பொருந்தின்.

couplet: The light of life is mental energy; disgrace is his
Who says, 'I 'ill lead a happy life devoid of this.'
pope.gloss: One's light is the abundance of one's courage; one's darkness is the desire to live destitute of such (a state of mind.)

reading: One's radiance is the wealth of aspiration, and one's disgrace is saying 'we will live without it'.
nuance: ஒளி and இளி close the previous chapter's last verse (970) and open this one, so the two chapters are stitched together by these words. வெறுக்கை means wealth, so aspiration is presented as a holding. Disgrace lies in the stated resolve to live without it, not in any failure.

couplet: All men that live are one in circumstances of birth;
Diversities of works give each his special worth.
pope.gloss: All human beings agree as regards their birth but differ as regards their characteristics, because of the different qualities of their actions.

reading: Birth is alike for all living beings, and distinction is unequal because of the difference in the work they do.
nuance: The verse says எல்லா உயிர்க்கும், wider than humanity. செய்தொழில் could be occupation or conduct, and the whole verse's social force depends on that word.

couplet: The men of lofty line, whose souls are mean, are never great
The men of lowly birth, when high of soul, are not of low estate.
pope.gloss: Though (raised) above, the base cannot become great; though (brought) low, the great cannot become base.

reading: Those who aren't high are not high even when placed high, and those who aren't low are not low even when placed low.
nuance: A single word, மேல் or கீழ், names both position and worth, and the verse pries them apart. Pope's couplet takes the position as birth, but Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as the seat that wealth gives, a high couch against bare ground.

couplet: Like single-hearted women, greatness too,
Exists while to itself is true.
pope.gloss: Even greatness, like a woman's chastity, belongs only to him who guards himself.

reading: Greatness too, like single-minded women, exists only if one holds on to oneself.
nuance: The model of masculine greatness is a woman. Conduct expected of wives becomes the standard for great men, a striking move given chapter 91. Parimelazhagar explains self-holding as restraint of mind, speech and body.

couplet: The man endowed with greatness true,
Rare deeds in perfect wise will do.
pope.gloss: (Though reduced) the great will be able to perform, in the proper way, deeds difficult (for others to do).

reading: Those with greatness will accomplish in the right way what is hard to do.
nuance: ஆற்றின் adds a limit: the rare deed must be done in the right way. Parimelazhagar adds 'even when poor', which the verse doesn't say. Kalaignar reverses the direction, so that those who do such things are the ones who become great.

couplet: 'As votaries of the truly great we will ourselves enroll,'
Is thought that enters not the mind of men of little soul.
pope.gloss: It is never in the nature of the base to seek the society of the great and partake of their nature.

reading: The aim of cherishing and taking on the great does not exist in the minds of the small.

couplet: Whene'er distinction lights on some unworthy head,
Then deeds of haughty insolence are bred.
pope.gloss: Even nobility of birth, wealth and learning, if in (the possession of) the base, will (only) produce everincreasing pride.

reading: Even distinction, should it fall to the unworthy, turns entirely into acts of excess.
nuance: Distinction is morally neutral and amplifies whoever has it. Manakkudavar takes சிறப்பு as wealth, while Parimelazhagar takes it as the surplus of birth, wealth and learning.

couplet: Greatness humbly bends, but littleness always
Spreads out its plumes, and loads itself with praise.
pope.gloss: The great will always humble himself; but the mean will exalt himself in self-admiration.

reading: Greatness always bows, and smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself.
nuance: பணியும் and அணியும் rhyme, so what looks like opposite motions sound alike. Parimelazhagar reports another reading in which this is a wonder at the way of the world: the high go low and the low go high.

couplet: Greatness is absence of conceit; meanness, we deem,
Riding on car of vanity supreme.
pope.gloss: Freedom from conceit is (the nature of true) greatness; (while) obstinacy therein is (that of) meanness.

reading: Greatness is the absence of pride, and smallness is riding on pride and being done with it.
nuance: பெருமிதம், 'pride', shares its root with பெருமை, so the verse defines greatness by the absence of what sounds like its own excess. Manakkudavar marks this as where the chapter turns from negative points to defining greatness.

couplet: Greatness will hide a neighbour's shame;
Meanness his faults to all the world proclaim.
pope.gloss: The great hide the faults of others; the base only divulge them.

reading: Greatness hides another's weakness, and smallness only tells their faults.
nuance: அற்றம் is literally a vulnerable exposure, so this hides a nakedness as much as a fault. Silence, not achievement, finishes the portrait of greatness that opened with high aim.

title: சான்றாண்மை
theme: Fullness of character: the worthy hold all good qualities as their own, rest on five pillars, don't tell others' faults, and do good to those who harm them. This fullness doesn't depend on poverty or wealth, and the chapter finally places the earth's stability upon it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the qualities suited to fullness in general (981-982), and specific ones (983-987), the excellence of those filled with them (988-990).
source_issues: 988: the Parimelazhagar text runs on into the gloss for 989; only the part before சான்றாண்மைக்கு ஆழி was used.
986, 990: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's gloss, so it may not be independent. 981 and 989 are also very close to it.
987: Parimelazhagar's text lacks the usual opening of the விளக்கம் section.
988 and 989: the Parimelazhagar texts cite the same Purananuru line by different numbers (350 and 330).
989: Pope's couplet has 'the fates should fail' for ஊழி பெயரினும, while the commentators read a change of age.

couplet: All goodly things are duties to the men, they say
Who set themselves to walk in virtue's perfect way.
pope.gloss: It is said that those who are conscious of their duty and behave with a perfect goodness will regard as natural all that is good.

reading: For those who know what is fitting and take on fullness of character, all that is good is said to be கடன்.

couplet: The good of inward excellence they claim,
The perfect men; all other good is only good in name.
pope.gloss: The only delight of the perfect is that of their goodness; all other (sensual) delights are not to be included among any (true) delights.

reading: The goodness of the worthy is the goodness of character; any other goodness isn't counted among goodnesses at all.
nuance: Parimelazhagar takes பிறநலம் as bodily good looks, and says it doesn't even appear in the lists of goods such as birth and learning. Kalaignar also has அழகு. The verse's own பிற is open, and a stronger reading dismisses everything other than character.

couplet: Love, modesty, beneficence, benignant grace,
With truth, are pillars five of perfect virtue's resting-place.
pope.gloss: Affection, fear (of sin), benevolence, favour and truthfulness; these are the five pillars on which perfect goodness rests.

reading: Love, shame, fellow-feeling, kindly regard and truthfulness: these five are the pillars planted to bear worth.
nuance: Four of the five are about how one regards other people. Parimelazhagar stretches two of them: love extends beyond kin, and truth holds everywhere. Their absence makes worth fall, not merely diminish.

couplet: The type of 'penitence' is virtuous good that nothing slays;
To speak no ill of other men is perfect virtue's praise.
pope.gloss: Penance consists in the goodness that kills not , and perfection in the goodness that tells not others' faults.

reading: Austerity has the goodness of not killing, and worth has the goodness of not telling others' evil.
nuance: The verse sets speech at the level of the ascetic's non-violence. Talking of another's fault is thus the moral equivalent of what killing is for a tapas. Kalaignar makes the silence cover harm done by others, which leaves open how it fits with exposing wrongdoing.

couplet: Submission is the might of men of mighty acts; the sage
With that same weapon stills his foeman's rage.
pope.gloss: Stooping (to inferiors) is the strength of those who can accomplish (an undertaking); and that is the weapon with which the great avert their foes.

reading: The strength of those who accomplish is to bow; that is the weapon by which the worthy turn foes around.
nuance: படை and மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் use the language of war, and the pun is that a foe (மாற்றார்) gets changed (மாற்றும்), not destroyed. Parimelazhagar makes the bowing concrete and strategic: stooping to gather allies.

couplet: What is perfection's test? The equal mind.
To bear repulse from even meaner men resigned.
pope.gloss: The touch-stone of perfection is to receive a defeat even at the hands of one's inferiors.

reading: If asked what the touchstone of worth is, it is accepting defeat even from those who aren't one's equal.
nuance: Parimelazhagar specifies that one accepts it while able to win. Without that, the verse describes mere loss. The defeat then lifts one above the other person, an inversion of the usual sense of victory.

couplet: What fruit doth your perfection yield you, say!
Unless to men who work you ill good repay?
pope.gloss: Of what avail is perfect goodness if it cannot do pleasing things even to those who have pained (it) ?

reading: If you don't do what is sweet even to those who have done you harm, what has worth brought?
nuance: A demanding test is framed as a question about use: worth is judged by what it produces in the hardest case.

couplet: To soul with perfect virtue's strength endued,
Brings no disgrace the lack of every earthly good.
pope.gloss: Poverty is no disgrace to one who abounds in good qualities.

reading: Poverty is no disgrace for one who has the firmness called worth.
nuance: திண்மை makes worth a hardness able to bear pressure. The verse doesn't call poverty good, only that it doesn't carry the disgrace it otherwise would.

couplet: Call them of perfect virtue's sea the shore,
Who, though the fates should fail, fail not for evermore.
pope.gloss: Those who are said to be the shore of the sea of perfection will never change, though ages may change.

reading: Those called the ஆழி of worth won't shift even when the age shifts.
nuance: ஊழி and ஆழி chime. The cosmic dissolution is a scale reference for constancy.

couplet: The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease,
If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease.
pope.gloss: If there is a defect in the character of the perfect, (even) the great world cannot bear (its) burden.

reading: If the worthy decline in worth, the great earth itself will not bear its load.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says both events are impossible, so this is a thought experiment showing their dependence. He also reports a reading in which the worthy are the earth's helpers in bearing. Kalaignar reads பொறை as the world's forbearance: it won't patiently tolerate their decline.

title: பண்புடைமை
theme: Courtesy of character, பண்பு, is what makes one fully human and keeps the world going. It reaches even to enemies, begins in being approachable, and without it sharp intelligence and great wealth come to nothing.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: how one comes to have it (991-992), the eminence of those who do (993-996), and the lowness of those who don't (997-1000). 1000 also introduces the next chapter on useless wealth.
source_issues: 994: the Tamil in kural.jsonl begins யனொடு, but the commentaries show the opening word is நயனொடு, so the first syllable is missing.

991, 993, 994, 995, 997, 998, 999, 1000: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's gloss, so it may not be independent. It was not used as a separate voice in this chapter.
993: Pope's gloss has 'souls' for மக்கள், a term that is not in the verse.

couplet: Who easy access give to every man, they say,
Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way.
pope.gloss: If one is easy of access to all, it will be easy for one to obtain the virtue called goodness.

reading: They say the practice called courtesy is easy to reach through being accessible to everyone.
nuance: வழக்கு makes courtesy a public custom, not an inner trait. Being available turns out to be the whole method, and யார்மாட்டும் gives it no exception. Parimelazhagar calls it something that wins over the whole world, which adds a strategic note.

couplet: Benevolence and high born dignity,
These two are beaten paths of courtesy.
pope.gloss: Affectionateness and birth in a good family, these two constitute what is called a proper behaviour to all.

reading: Love and being born in a seasoned family: these two are the way called courtesy.
nuance: This puts birth among courtesy's sources. Parimelazhagar softens it, saying குடிப்பிறத்தல் here means the conduct of those so born, and neither factor suffices alone. Kalaignar goes further, asking only that one have the marks of such birth.

couplet: Men are not one because their members seem alike to outward view;
Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true.
pope.gloss: Resemblance of bodies is no resemblance of souls; true resemblance is the resemblance of qualities that attract.

reading: Likeness of limbs isn't likeness among people; true likeness is likeness of settled character.
nuance: வெறுத்தக்க usually means hateful, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as செறியத்தக்க, 'to be drawn close', which is what makes the line work. Pope's gloss, 'qualities that attract', follows him. I can't confirm this sense from the verse alone.

couplet: Of men of fruitful life, who kindly benefits dispense,
The world unites to praise the 'noble excellence.'
pope.gloss: The world applauds the character of those whose usefulness results from their equity and charity.

reading: The world honours the character of those whose useful lives come from doing good with fairness.
nuance: The world honours the பண்பு, not the deeds or their outcome, which makes deeds evidence of character. Parimelazhagar says that it is useful to oneself and to others alike.

couplet: Contempt is evil though in sport. They who man's nature know,
E'en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show.
pope.gloss: Reproach is painful to one even in sport; those (therefore) who know the nature of others exhibit (pleasing) qualities even when they are hated.

reading: Scorn hurts even in jest, so those who know how others feel have courtesy even in enmity.
nuance: Parimelazhagar insists that the two clauses are one argument, and criticizes others who read them apart: knowing that scorn hurts is the reason for courtesy. பாடு here is what another person undergoes.

couplet: The world abides; for 'worthy' men its weight sustain.
Were it not so, 'twould fall to dust again.
pope.gloss: The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good; if not, it would bury itself in the earth and perish.

reading: The world exists by resting upon those of courtesy; otherwise it would enter the earth and perish.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes உலகம் here the way of the world, not the planet. Kalaignar makes it a should: worldly practices ought to depend on such people. A claim about reality becomes a recommendation.

couplet: Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain,
Whose souls are void of 'courtesy humane'.
pope.gloss: He who is destitute of (true) human qualities (only) resembles a tree, though he may possess the sharpness of a file.

reading: Even though sharp as a file, those without human courtesy are like trees.
nuance: The chime of அரம் and மரம் has the point in it. Parimelazhagar says the file wears down what it touches without wearing itself, and the tree has only one sense. Intelligence used without courtesy isn't merely inadequate, it is destructive.

couplet: Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail,
'Tis uttermost disgrace in 'courtesy' to fail.
pope.gloss: It is wrong (for the wise) not to exhibit (good) qualities even towards those who bearing no friendship (for them) do only what is hateful.

reading: Failing in courtesy, even toward those who act without friendship and without kindness, is lowness.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is reflexive: respond in kind and you become like them. The insult harms the character of the one who returns it.

couplet: To him who knows not how to smile in kindly mirth,
Darkness in daytime broods o'er all the vast and mighty earth.
pope.gloss: To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light.

reading: For those who aren't capable of laughing, the great wide world lies in darkness even in the daytime.
nuance: Laughter is treated as a skill (வல்லர்), and the lack of it as blindness. Parimelazhagar makes it the joy of mingling, and says such people don't understand the world because they can't mix with it. He reports a variant reading too.

couplet: Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured,
Is ample wealth in churlish man's unopened coffers stored.
pope.gloss: The great wealth obtained by one who has no goodness will perish like pure milk spoilt by the impurity of the vessel.

reading: Great wealth obtained by one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel.
nuance: Wealth is good milk here, and the fault is the holder's alone. பெற்ற, 'obtained', suggests to Parimelazhagar that he couldn't have created it himself.

title: நன்றியில்செல்வம்
theme: Wealth that is neither enjoyed nor given is effectively no wealth. It does nothing for the holder, the needy or the holder's heirs, and it turns a person into something the world doesn't want. The chapter measures wealth entirely by its use.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: no use to the one who amassed it (1001), no use to others (1002-1004), both failings together (1005-1006), and the faults of such wealth (1007-1010).
source_issues: 1001: Parimelazhagar's text is truncated at the start, with only the last words of the verse's gloss present.
1002: Pope's gloss has 'will be born a demon' from Parimelazhagar; the verse says மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
1004: Pope's gloss has 'in the world to come', which doesn't match the Tamil எச்சம் or his own couplet.
1007: Kalaignar's text has a stray character after ஒருத்தி.

couplet: Who fills his house with ample store, enjoying none,
Is dead. Nought with the useless heap is done.
pope.gloss: He who does not enjoy the immense riches he has heaped up in his house, is (to be reckoned as) dead, (for) there is nothing achieved (by him).

reading: One who has stored up great wealth to the brim and doesn't eat it, is dead: there is nothing left for him to do.
nuance: உண்ணான், 'doesn't eat', treats wealth as food. Parimelazhagar widens it to the five senses.

couplet: Who giving nought, opines from wealth all blessing springs,
Degraded birth that doting miser's folly brings.
pope.gloss: He who knows that wealth yields every pleasure and yet is so blind as to lead miserly life will be born a demon.

reading: Through the delusion of clinging without giving, thinking all things come by wealth, comes a மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
nuance: The delusion isn't the belief that wealth achieves everything, a point the Kural makes elsewhere: it lies in clinging while holding that belief.

couplet: Who lust to heap up wealth, but glory hold not dear,
It burthens earth when on the stage of being they appear.
pope.gloss: A burden to the earth are men bent on the acquisition of riches and not (true) fame.

reading: The appearance on earth of men who cling to accumulation and don't want renown is a burden to the land.
nuance: Parimelazhagar identifies the renown with virtue achieved by giving, so the choice isn't between wealth and vanity. Manakkudavar draws the harshest conclusion: it would be better if they hadn't been born.

couplet: Whom no one loves, when he shall pass away,
What doth he look to leave behind, I pray?
pope.gloss: What will the miser who is not liked (by any one) regard as his own (in the world to come) ?

reading: What does one wanted by no one imagine will remain behind him?
nuance: The issue is what survives a person, and the question implies nothing does, since fame only rests on givers. Pope's gloss moves this to 'the world to come' while his couplet does not. The Tamil says எச்சம், what is left behind.

couplet: Amid accumulated millions they are poor,
Who nothing give and nought enjoy of all they store.
pope.gloss: Those who neither give (to others) nor enjoy (their property) are (truly) destitute, though possessing immense riches.

reading: Those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, even with crores upon crores.
nuance: An ownership paradox: possession is defined by use. Parimelazhagar says giving is named first because virtue outranks pleasure. Kalaignar fuses the two: those not happy in giving.

couplet: Their ample wealth is misery to men of churlish heart,
Who nought themselves enjoy, and nought to worthy men impart.
pope.gloss: He who enjoys not (his riches) nor relieves the wants of the worthy is a disease to his wealth.

reading: One who doesn't use it himself and doesn't naturally give any of it to the deserving is a misfortune with great wealth.

couplet: Like woman fair in lonelihood who aged grows,
Is wealth of him on needy men who nought bestows.
pope.gloss: The wealth of him who never bestows anything on the destitute is like a woman of beauty growing old without a husband.

reading: The wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a woman of exceeding beauty growing old alone.
nuance: The simile mourns what is wasted, and treats a woman's worth as realized through a husband. Parimelazhagar's gloss deepens it: she is unmarried for want of anyone to give her away, a giver being missing in both halves, and she herself loses something too.

couplet: When he whom no man loves exults in great prosperity,
'Tis as when fruits in midmost of the town some p oisonous tree.
pope.gloss: The wealth of him who is disliked (by all) is like the fruit-bearing of the etty tree in the midst of a town.

reading: The wealth of one who isn't wanted is a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of town.
nuance: நச்சப்படாதவன், 'unwanted', and நச்சு, 'poison', chime, and it is what makes the verse work. Being close by is what makes it worse: Parimelazhagar says he is near the needy and still gives nothing. Manakkudavar extends it, saying any who eat out of desire will die.

couplet: Who love abandon, self-afflict, and virtue's way forsake
To heap up glittering wealth, their hoards shall others take.
pope.gloss: Strangers will inherit the riches that have been acquired without regard for friendship, comfort and charity.

reading: Others will take the bright wealth amassed by giving up love, by self-denial and by ignoring virtue.
nuance: The list gives three prices paid, and the last word takes away the prize. Parimelazhagar says பிறர் excludes even his own line. Kalaignar makes ignoring virtue into unethical earning, which is a different charge from not giving.

couplet: 'Tis as when rain cloud in the heaven grows day,
When generous wealthy man endures brief poverty.
pope.gloss: The short-lived poverty of those who are noble and rich is like the clouds becoming poor (for a while).

reading: The சிறுதுனி of the renowned rich has the nature of rain-clouds going dry.
nuance: As a closing verse it gives the positive pole of the chapter's whole contrast: the wealth that does give.

title: நாணுடைமை
theme: Shame over wrongdoing is the distinguishing mark of a human being and the seat of worth. It ranks above life, conduct and the whole earth, and those without it only imitate being alive.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its definition (1011), its excellence (1012-1014), the eminence of those who have it (1015), their deeds (1016-1017), and the lowness of those without it (1018-1020).
source_issues: 1015: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1016: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and nearly identical to Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1017: Kalaignar's text ends with a stray 1018.
1011: Pope's gloss has 'bashfulness of virtuous maids', from Parimelazhagar, a reading that Manakkudavar contradicts.

couplet: To shrink abashed from evil deed is 'generous shame';
Other is that of bright-browed one of virtuous fame.
pope.gloss: True modesty is the fear of (evil) deeds; all other modesty is (simply) the bashfulness of virtuous maids.

reading: Shame is being ashamed through one's actions; anything other is the shame of women of the bright brow.
nuance: The verse separates moral shame from bodily modesty and assigns the second to women. Whichever women are meant, the distinction is gendered.

couplet: Food, clothing, and other things alike all beings own;
By sense of shame the excellence of men is known.
pope.gloss: Food, clothing and the like are common to all men but modesty is peculiar to the good.

reading: Food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and the distinction of humans is having shame.
nuance: The verse seems to separate humans from other life, but the commentators draw the line within humanity. Parimelazhagar contrasts all people with good people, and Manakkudavar contrasts base people with leaders. Parimelazhagar lists the rest of what is shared as sleep, fear and desire.

couplet: All spirits homes of flesh as habitation claim,
And perfect virtue ever dwells with shame.
pope.gloss: As the body is the abode of the spirit, so the excellence of modesty is the abode of perfection.

reading: As all lives are fixed on flesh, worth is fixed on the good called shame.

couplet: And is not shame an ornament to men of dignity?
Without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see.
pope.gloss: Is not the modesty ornament of the noble ? Without it, their haughtiness would be a pain (to others).

reading: Isn't shame an ornament to the worthy? Without it, isn't a proud walk a disease?
nuance: அணி and பிணி rhyme. Parimelazhagar makes this a disease for those who have to watch it. A walk, in other words, is public property and judged by the watcher.

couplet: As home of virtuous shame by all the world the men are known,
Who feel ashamed for others, guilt as for their own.
pope.gloss: The world regards as the abode of modesty him who fear his own and other's guilt.

reading: The world calls those who feel shame for others' disgrace as for their own the dwelling of shame.
nuance: This enlarges shame beyond guilt: one feels it for what one did not do. Moral concern here can't be reduced to self-regard.

couplet: Unless the hedge of shame inviolate remain,
For men of lofty soul the earth's vast realms no charms retain.
pope.gloss: The great make modesty their barrier (of defence) and not the wide world.

reading: The high don't care for the wide world unless they have shame for a fence.
nuance: The verse can mean they would take shame rather than the world, or that they won't want the world without it; Parimelazhagar holds the first and reports the second. Pope's couplet follows the second. Kalaignar has shame as the best of protections, with no choice involved.

couplet: The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make,
But ne'er abandon virtuous shame for life's dear sake.
pope.gloss: The modest would rather lose their life for the sake of modesty than lose modesty for the sake of life.

reading: Those ruled by shame will give up life for shame, and won't give up shame for life.
nuance: The syntax folds on itself like the choice it describes. நாணாள்பவர் can be 'those who wield shame', as a commander does, and not those who are ruled by it. Kalaignar glosses the object as மானம், showing how closely the two virtues run.

couplet: Though know'st no shame, while all around asha med must be:
Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee!
pope.gloss: Virtue is likely to forsake him who shamelessly does what others are ashamed of.

reading: If one is not ashamed of what makes others ashamed, it's a fault that virtue itself would be ashamed of.
nuance: நாண recurs and virtue becomes a person who blushes. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read this as virtue leaving such a man, since virtue doesn't approach the shameless, so shame is a precondition of virtue and not one of its parts.

couplet: 'Twill race consume if right observance fail;
'Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail.
pope.gloss: Want of manners injures one's family; but want of modesty injures one's character.

reading: A lapse in principle burns one's lineage, and lasting shamelessness burns every good thing.
nuance: Parimelazhagar draws the ranking out: destroying shame is worse than destroying conduct, which is significant given the rank chapter 14 gives conduct. Fire (சுடும்) is used for both.

couplet: 'Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life's functions, when
Those void of shame within hold intercourse with men.
pope.gloss: The actions of those who are without modesty at heart are like those of puppet moved by a string.

reading: The movements of those with no shame within are like a wooden puppet feigning life by its string.
nuance: The pun is on நாண், which means both shame and string. The puppet has the one thing the man lacks, as Parimelazhagar notes, in a neat inversion. It leaves a man without shame to be moved from outside.

title: குடிசெயல்வகை
theme: Raising one's people is the highest greatness. It requires ceaseless effort and knowledge, draws divine help and willing kin, ignores season and pride, and costs the one who does it his own bodily ease. A family with no one to carry it falls.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its causes (1021-1022), divine support (1023-1024), the honour it gains (1025-1027), how it is done (1028-1029), and the fate of a family without such a person (1030). Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take குடி as one's own lineage; Kalaignar repeatedly reads it as the people who depend on one, குடிமக்கள், which turns a family ethic into a public one.
source_issues: 1022: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1023: Manakkudavar's text has what appear to be transcription errors: யோபுவன் and படிதற்றல்.
1021: Pope's gloss adds 'to raise my family', from the chapter's theme.
1028: Manakkudavar's gloss takes மானம் as a fault arising from raising the family, and its wording seems unclear, so it wasn't used as a position.

couplet: Who says 'I'll do my work, nor slack my hand',
His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand.
pope.gloss: There is no higher greatness than that of one saying. I will not cease in my effort (to raise my family).

reading: No greatness has more dignity than that of one who says 'I will not stay my hand from the work'.
nuance: The verse says only கருமம், and family comes from the chapter's title. Parimelazhagar rejects two rival readings, one's own work and others' work, the second because serving others isn't leadership. Greatness here sits in the declaration (என்னும்), before any result.

couplet: The manly act and knowledge full, when these combine
In deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race's line.
pope.gloss: One's family is raised by untiring perseverance in both effort and wise contrivances.

reading: By long-continued work in the two things called effort and mature knowledge, the family is extended.
nuance: நீள்வினையால் நீளும் is a chime, in which the long labour lengthens the line.

couplet: 'I'll make my race renowned,' if man shall say,
With vest succinct the goddess leads the way.
pope.gloss: The Deity will clothe itself and appear before him who resolves on raising his family.
