reading: For one who says 'I will raise my people', தெய்வம் tucks up its garment and goes ahead on its own.
nuance: The image of tightened dress is homely and physical: the divine as a worker who gets ready to help.

couplet: Who labours for his race with unremitting pain,
Without a thought spontaneously, his end will gain.
pope.gloss: Those who are prompt in their efforts (to better their family) need no deliberation, such efforts will of themselves succee d.

reading: For those who work without delay for their people, the end arrives by itself, without deliberation.
nuance: The agent is unnamed. Parimelazhagar supplies the deity of 1023, while Manakkudavar supplies the man's good deeds (நல்வினை), and Kalaignar leaves success to come by itself. Each fills the gap to suit his view.

couplet: With blameless life who seeks to build his race's fame,
The world shall circle him, and kindred claim.
pope.gloss: People will eagerly seek the friendship of the prosperous soul who has raised his family without foul means.

reading: The world gathers around one who lives faultlessly raising his people, as kin.
nuance: The chime of சுற்றம் and சுற்றும் turns the noun into what kin do. Parimelazhagar's motive for this is unsentimental: people come for their own benefit.

couplet: Of virtuous manliness the world accords the praise
To him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise.
pope.gloss: A man's true manliness consists in making himself the head and benefactor of his family.

reading: What's called good manliness is making oneself capable of ruling the house one was born to.
nuance: நல்லாண்மை and இல்லாண்மை chime. Parimelazhagar says the adjective நல் is there to exclude the warrior's manliness. Kalaignar reverses the sense: one who rules well brings pride to his birth-family, so it isn't about ruling the family.

couplet: The fearless hero bears the brunt amid the warrior throng;
Amid his kindred so the burthen rests upon the strong.
pope.gloss: Like heroes in the battle-field, the burden (of protection etc.) is borne by those who are the most efficient in a family.

reading: As with the stout-hearted in battle, the burden among kin falls on the capable.
nuance: The commentators stress that many enter the field and many are born in a family: it isn't that others are forbidden, but that it falls to whoever can carry it. A question of ability, not of seniority.

couplet: Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear;
'Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear.
pope.gloss: As a family suffers by (one's) indolence and false dignity there is to be so season (good or bad) to those who strive to raise their family.

reading: Those who raise their people have no season; if they idle and think about மானம், it will be ruined.

couplet: Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill,
Who would his household screen from every ill?
pope.gloss: Is it only to suffering that his body is exposed who undertakes to preserve his family from evil ?

reading: Is the body of one who covers his household against fault only a vessel for suffering?
nuance: Parimelazhagar treats this as a pointed remark and not self-pity: the man accepts it, since the family's rise is his reward.

couplet: When trouble the foundation saps the house must fall,
If no strong hand be nigh to prop the tottering wall.
pope.gloss: If there are none to prop up and maintain a family (in distress), it will fall at the stroke of the axe of misfortune.

reading: When trouble cuts it at the foot, a family with no good person to prop it will fall.
nuance: A tree image is implied: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar supply the axe. They take நல்லாள் as a good man (ஆண்மகன்), while Kalaignar has anyone with the ability. The same word names a personified good woman in 924 and 1040; here it divides as நல் ஆள், 'good person', which doesn't itself specify a man.

title: உழவு
theme: Farming is the world's first occupation because everyone, including kings and renouncers, ends up depending on it. Those who live by it alone owe nothing to anyone, and the land itself responds to attention, as a wife or a mocking woman would.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its excellence (1031), the excellence of those who do it (1032-1036), how it is done (1037-1039), and the fault of not doing it, which also leads into the following chapter on poverty (1040).
source_issues: 1032: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1034: Pope's gloss reads 'patriotic farmers desire to bring all other states under the control of their own king', adding a motive not found in the Tamil.
1036: Pope's gloss says 'ascetic state will fail', dropping the verse's என்பார்.

couplet: Howe'er they roam, the world must follow still the plougher's team;
Though toilsome, culture of the ground as noblest toil esteem.
pope.gloss: Agriculture, though laborious, is the most excellent (form of labour); for people, though they go about (in search of various employments), have at last to resort to the farmer.

reading: Though it whirls about, the world follows the plough; therefore, though toilsome, farming is foremost.
nuance: The verse concedes the toil and doesn't romanticize it (உழந்தும்). Its case is a structural one: all other paths end up at the same place. சுழன்றும் may also suggest the world turning like a wheel behind the plough, and Kalaignar's version keeps this.

couplet: The ploughers are the linch-pin of the world; they bear
Them up who other works perform, too weak its toils to share.
pope.gloss: Agriculturists are (as it were) the linch-pin of the world for they support all other workers who cannot till the soil.

reading: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world's people, for they carry all those who can't do it and rise to other things.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says உழுவார் extends to those who have others plough for them, citing a parallel, which brings landowners into the honour. The verse doesn't say so. He reports a variant, தொழுவாரே, in which those unable to plough cringe to their patrons, which anticipates 1033.

couplet: Who ploughing eat their food, they truly live:
The rest to others bend subservient, eating what they give.
pope.gloss: They alone live who live by agriculture; all others lead a cringing, dependent life.

reading: Only those who live by eating from their own ploughing truly live; all others bow to eat, and walk behind.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's வாழ்வார் are those who belong to themselves (தமக்குரியராய்): the verse is about independence as much as food.

couplet: O'er many a land they 'll see their monarch reign,
Whose fields are shaded by the waving grain.
pope.gloss: Patriotic farmers desire to bring all other states under the control of their own king.

reading: Those with the shade of grain-ears will see many umbrellas' shade under their own umbrella.
nuance: The royal umbrella is set against the grain's shade. Manakkudavar notices a pun: an 'umbrella-less shade'. The verse claims that farming, not armies, underwrites conquest.

couplet: They nothing ask from others, but to askers give,
Who raise with their own hands the food on which they live.
pope.gloss: Those whose nature is to live by manual labour will never beg but give something to those who beg.

reading: Those whose way is to eat what their hands produce don't ask, and give to those who ask without hiding.
nuance: The hand is the verse's key: it labours and it gives, and it never stretches out. Parimelazhagar restricts கைசெய் to ploughing, while Kalaignar makes it any self-earned work. The verse anticipates the chapters on begging, whose word கரவாது it uses.

couplet: For those who 've left what all men love no place is found,
When they with folded hands remain who till the ground.
pope.gloss: If the farmer's hands are slackened, even the ascetic state will fail.

reading: If farmers fold their hands, even those who say they have given up desire won't be able to stay in that state.
nuance: என்பார், 'those who say', carries a slight edge. Parimelazhagar extends the verse to all of this world's aims, the next world's and liberation. He and another reading differ on whether விழைவது is food or desire in general.

couplet: Reduce your soil to that dry state, When ounce is quarter-ounce's weight;
Without one handful of manure, Abundant crops you thus secure.
pope.gloss: If the land is dried so as to reduce one ounce of earth to a quarter, it will grow plentifully even without a handful of manure.

reading: If you dry the soil so that a measure of earth falls to a quarter, it will grow abundantly without even a handful of manure.
nuance: A rare place where the Kural gives technical advice, with exact weights. Kalaignar reads the reduction as coming from repeated ploughing, while Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar have sun-drying. The moral of attention before input is left unstated.

couplet: To cast manure is better than to plough;
Weed well; to guard is more than watering now
pope.gloss: Manuring is better than ploughing; after weeding, watching is better than watering (it).

reading: Manuring is better than ploughing, and after weeding, guarding is better than watering.
nuance: A ladder of care in which each stage beats the previous one, and watchfulness comes out above water, the thing plants most obviously need. Parimelazhagar sets out the sequence of five.

couplet: When master from the field aloof hath stood;
Then land will sulk, like wife in angry mood.
pope.gloss: If the owner does not (personally) attend to his cultivation, his land will behave like an angry wife and yield him no pleasure.

reading: If the owner stays away and doesn't go, the land will resent and sulk like a wife.
nuance: ஊடி is a term from love poetry, used here in farm advice. கிழவன், 'owner', also means husband, a double meaning that makes the comparison work. Parimelazhagar says that the owner must go himself and not send others, which is in some tension with his widening of உழுவார் in 1032.

couplet: The earth, that kindly dame, will laugh to see,
Men seated idle pleading poverty.
pope.gloss: The maiden, Earth, will laug h at the sight of those who plead poverty and lead an idle life.

reading: Seeing those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle, the good woman called Land laughs.
nuance: The Earth doesn't scold but laughs. Parimelazhagar notes this is the bridge to the next chapter on poverty, and he has a variant இரப்பாரை, 'those who beg', which Manakkudavar uses, pointing to the later chapters too.

title: நல்குரவு
theme: Poverty as the worst suffering, one that has no comparison. It strips lineage, speech, learning and even a mother's regard, it returns day after day, and the chapter's last verse asks whether such a person should go on as they are.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the cruelty of poverty (1041-1045), its effects on the poor (1046-1049, including the speech of one poor man in 1048-1049), and what to do when it comes (1050).
source_issues: 1047: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and ends with இது பரிமேலழகருரை, stating that it is Parimelazhagar's commentary. It confirms that [#] entries across this block are not Manakkudavar's own and should not count as an independent voice.
1043: Parimelazhagar's lemma has தல்குரவு where the verse has நல்குரவு, apparently a transcription error.
1047: Pope's gloss has 'absolute poverty', dropping அறஞ்சாரா, though his couplet keeps it.
1050: Pope's gloss has 'renounce their bodies', from Parimelazhagar, and 'salt and water' for உப்பிற்கும் காடிக்கும், which also differs from his couplet's 'salt and vinegar'.

couplet: You ask what sharper pain than poverty is known;
Nothing pains more than poverty, save poverty alone.
pope.gloss: There is nothing that afflicts (one) like poverty.

reading: If asked what is more painful than poverty, what's more painful than poverty is poverty.
nuance: The sentence tries to find a comparison and fails. As Parimelazhagar says, if it has no equal, nothing can exceed it. Tautology is the argument.

couplet: Malefactor matchless! poverty destroys
This world's and the next world's joys.
pope.gloss: When cruel poverty comes on, it deprives one of both the present and future (bliss).

reading: The sinner called poverty comes, with this world and the next both lost.
nuance: பாவி personifies it as an evil actor, although Manakkudavar reads a poor person who has the sin. The next world is lost, in his reason, because one can't afford charity, so poverty denies access to virtue itself. That cuts against the assumption that merit is equally open to all.

couplet: Importunate desire, which poverty men name,
Destroys both old descent and goodly fame.
pope.gloss: Hankering poverty destroys at once the greatness of (one's) ancient descent and (the dignity of one's) speech.

reading: The desire called poverty destroys at once one's ancient descent and தோல்.
nuance: The verse identifies poverty with desire, நசை. Parimelazhagar explains that where there's no craving there's no poverty, which is a remarkable reframing of an economic state as a mental one.

couplet: From penury will spring, 'mid even those of noble race,
Oblivion that gives birth to words that bring disgrace.
pope.gloss: Even in those of high birth, poverty will produce the fault of uttering mean words.

reading: Even in the well-born, poverty brings the lapse from which degrading words are born.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says what the words are: 'you must give to us'. He describes the lapse precisely: at the height of suffering, they forget their birth for a moment. The uncontrolled word is இளிவந்த, degrading, and that is the verdict of chapter 97 on such a person.

couplet: From poverty, that grievous woe,
Attendant sorrows plenteous grow.
pope.gloss: The misery of poverty brings in its train many (more) miseries.

reading: Within the suffering called poverty, many sufferings arrive and settle.
nuance: Parimelazhagar lists a day's humiliations in order: going to the rich man's door, seeing him, being refused, accepting what he gives, and working out how to use it. One of the most vivid passages in his commentary, it is his own and not the verse's.

couplet: Though deepest sense, well understood, the poor man's words convey,
Their sense from memory of mankind will fade away.
pope.gloss: The words of the poor are profitless, though they may be sound in thought and clear in expression.

reading: Even if they speak of good matters, fully understood, the words and meaning of the poor go slack.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a social mechanism and not a cognitive one: nobody listens, in case they come to feel obliged to help. So the meaning fails not in the speaker but in what the listeners are afraid of.

couplet: From indigence devoid of virtue's grace,
The mother e'en that bare, estranged, will turn her face.
pope.gloss: He that is reduced to absolute poverty will be regarded as a stranger even by his own mother.

reading: One in poverty unconnected with virtue is looked at as a stranger, even by the mother who bore him.
nuance: The mother is again the limit case, as in 923. Parimelazhagar's reason is unsentimental: she fears that he would be taking and not giving.

couplet: And will it come today as yesterday,
The grief of want that eats my soul away?
pope.gloss: Is the poverty that almost killed me yesterday, to meet me today too ?

reading: Will it come today too, the poverty that as good as killed me yesterday?
nuance: The verse switches to first-person speech. Parimelazhagar imagines the speaker: someone who with great difficulty filled his belly yesterday. In போலும் he survived what felt like death, which means he will face it again.

couplet: Amid the flames sleep may men's eyelids close,
In poverty the eye knows no repose.
pope.gloss: One may sleep in the midst of fire; but by no means in the midst of poverty.

reading: One can even sleep in the middle of fire, but in the middle of poverty, there is no way of closing the eyes.
nuance: Parimelazhagar explains the sleep in fire as a possibility through mantra and medicine, which rationalizes what looks like hyperbole. He hears the same speaker as in 1048.

couplet: Unless the destitute will utterly themselves deny,
They cause their neighbour's salt and vinegar to die.
pope.gloss: The destitute poor, who do not renounce their bodies, only consume their neighbour's salt and water.

reading: If those without means don't fully renounce, they are death to salt and to gruel.
nuance: The mockery falls on tiny things, salt and sour gruel: the poor person's mere continuing destroys these and nothing more.

title: இரவு
theme: Asking is permitted, even graceful, when the giver is one who can't conceal. The chapter then goes further and says that the world needs askers, since without them giving, fame and even being alive would lose their point. It closes by telling the asker not to be angry at refusal.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar opens by limiting the chapter: this is begging without disgrace, allowed only when poverty brings one to the edge of death (1051-1052). Then the nature of those worth asking (1053-1057), why the world needs askers (1058-1059), and what the asker must be like (1060). The following chapter, on dread of begging, argues nearly the reverse.
source_issues: 1052, 1059: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
1052: Kalaignar's text ends with stray material, ஊ. தெளிவு உரைத் தெளிவுக்கு.
1054: Parimelazhagar's gloss has சுரத்தலை where கரத்தலை is expected, apparently a transcription error.
1056: Pope's gloss has 'evil of begging' for நிரப்பிடும்பை, where his couplet has 'plague of poverty'.
1060: Pope's couplet ('from wrath must stand aloof') is loose; the Tamil is simply that the asker should not be angry.

couplet: When those you find from whom 'tis meet to ask,- for aid apply;
Theirs is the sin, not yours, if they the gift deny.
pope.gloss: If you meet with those that may be begged of, you may beg; (but) if they withhold (their gift) it is their blame and not yours.

reading: Ask if you find those worth asking; if they withhold, the blame is theirs and not yours.
nuance: The chapter starts by moving the moral burden from the asker to the withholder. Parimelazhagar says such givers understand before anything is said, and the blame sticks to them as a stain does on pure white cloth, because they're rare.

couplet: Even to ask an alms may pleasure give,
If what you ask without annoyance you receive.
pope.gloss: Even begging may be pleasant, if what is begged for is obtained without grief (to him that begs).

reading: Even asking is pleasure to a person, if what is asked for comes without suffering.

couplet: The men who nought deny, but know what's due, before their face
To stand as suppliants affords especial grace.
pope.gloss: There is even a beauty in standing before and begging of those who are liberal in their gifts and understand their duty (to beggars).

reading: Even standing and asking before those of unconcealing heart who know கடன் has a certain beauty.
nuance: முன்நின்று is significant: for Parimelazhagar merely standing is enough, and it's the absence of spoken words that keeps the grace.

couplet: Like giving alms, may even asking pleasant seem,
From men who of denial never even dream.
pope.gloss: To beg of such as never think of withholding (their charity) even in their dreams, is in fact the same as giving (it oneself);

reading: Even asking is like giving, from those who don't conceive of concealment even in a dream.
nuance: An extraordinary equivalence that erases the difference in rank. Parimelazhagar tempers it: asking brings no fame, but nor does it damage any you already have, so that is all the likeness. The strong statement is the verse's and the caveat is his.

couplet: Because on earth the men exist, who never say them nay,
Men bear to stand before their eyes for help to pray.
pope.gloss: As there are in the world those that give without refusing, there are (also) those that prefer to beg by simply standing before them.

reading: It's because there are people on earth who don't conceal that askers take up standing before them.
nuance: Parimelazhagar adds the alternative: without such people they would give up their lives, since they can't give up honour. So the existence of generous people is what keeps them alive.

couplet: It those you find from evil of 'denial' free,
At once all plague of poverty will flee.
pope.gloss: All the evil of begging will be removed at the sight of those who are far from the evil of refusing.

reading: If one sees those without the affliction of concealment, every affliction of poverty is destroyed at once.
nuance: Concealing is called இடும்பை, the same word as poverty, so the verse treats the wealthy miser as a sufferer too. The cure comes merely at the sight (காணின்). Manakkudavar concludes one shouldn't ask from those who are merely rich.

couplet: If men are found who give and no harsh words of scorn employ,
The minds of askers, through and through, will thrill with joy.
pope.gloss: Beggars rejoice exceedingly when they behold those who bestow (their alms) with kindness and courtesy.

reading: If one sees those who give without scorn and contempt, the heart is delighted and rejoices deep inside.
nuance: The joy lies in being given to without being lowered. உள்ளுள் உவப்பது goes deeper than the material relief, and it's the manner of the gift that's being measured.

couplet: If askers cease, the mighty earth, where cooling fountains flow,
Will be a stage where wooden puppets come and go.
pope.gloss: If there were no beggars, (the actions done in) the cool wide world would only resemble the movement of a puppet.

reading: If there were no askers, this wide cool world would be wooden puppets coming and going.

couplet: What glory will there be to men of generous soul,
When none are found to love the askers' role?
pope.gloss: What (praise) would there be to givers (of alms) if there were no beggars to ask for and reveive (them).

reading: What renown could givers have, if there were none who want to ask and take?
nuance: The logic has an uncomfortable side: if givers' renown requires askers, a world without poverty would be poorer in virtue. The verse doesn't address this, and it treats askers as a need, not as a problem.

couplet: Askers refused from wrath must stand aloof;
The plague of poverty itself is ample proof.
pope.gloss: He who begs ought not to be angry (at a refusal); for even the misery of (his own) poverty should be a sufficient reason (for so doing).

reading: The one who asks shouldn't be angry; the affliction of his own poverty is proof enough.
nuance: His poverty proves that wealth is hard to come by, so the refuser may have a real reason. This turns the sufferer's own case into a reason for patience. It is a counterweight to 1051, which puts blame on those who withhold.

title: இரவச்சம்
theme: Dread of begging: never asking, even from the best givers, is worth ten million times what asking could bring. The chapter's fury goes so far as a curse on whoever ordered the world so that begging is needed, and it holds the withholder guiltier still.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: the cruelty of begging (1061-1062), it is no way out of poverty (1063), the worthy don't do it (1064), what one's own effort yields (1065), not even for virtue's sake (1066), begging at the cost of honour is forbidden (1067), and the faults of asking and refusing together (1068-1070).
source_issues: 1061: the Manakkudavar text is marked [#] and ends with இது பரிமேலழகருரை, so it is Parimelazhagar's commentary, not Manakkudavar's.
1065, 1067, 1070: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to these verses.
1063: Pope's gloss turns வன்மை, hardness, into 'folly', and adds 'rather than by working' from the commentary.
1070: Pope's couplet says 'the shamefaced asker dies' while the verse says only உயிர் போஒம்; his gloss adds that the word would kill the refuser, which is drawn from commentary.

couplet: Ten million-fold 'tis greater gain, asking no alms to live,
Even from those, like eyes in worth, who nought concealing gladly give.
pope.gloss: Not to beg (at all) even from those excellent persons who cheerfully give without refusing, will do immense good.

reading: Not asking, even from those precious as eyes who give gladly without concealing, is worth ten million times more.
nuance: The verse picks the best case for asking, then refuses it. Parimelazhagar narrows this: it's about not asking even friends who already know of one's poverty, and he concludes one should try to live by hard effort.

couplet: If he that shaped the world desires that men should begging go,
Through life's long course, let him a wanderer be and perish so.
pope.gloss: If the Creator of the world has decreed even begging as a means of livelihood, may he too go abegging and perish.

reading: If even by begging one must live, let the one who made the world wander and perish.
nuance: The Kural's sharpest line against any cosmic order. It doesn't assert that a creator exists, since the curse is conditional. Kalaignar makes that explicit: the one 'said to be' the creator.

couplet: Nothing is harder than the hardness that will say,
'The plague of penury by asking alms we'll drive away.'
pope.gloss: There is no greater folly than the boldness with which one seeks to remedy the evils of poverty by begging (rather than by working).

reading: Nothing is harder than the hardness that says 'we will end the misery of poverty by begging'.
nuance: வன்மை, hardness, is the opposite of what one would expect of an asker's position. Begging isn't weakness here but a kind of obstinate insensitivity. Manakkudavar adds that it doesn't even work, since it won't end poverty.

couplet: Who ne'er consent to beg in utmost need, their worth
Has excellence of greatness that transcends the earth.
pope.gloss: Even the whole world cannot sufficiently praise the dignity that would not beg even in the midst of destitution.

reading: The worth that won't consent to asking even when no means remain is too great for all of space to contain.
nuance: இடம் is used twice: as all of space, and as means or room. A man with no room left holds something that no room can hold.

couplet: Nothing is sweeter than to taste the toil-won cheer,
Though mess of pottage as tasteless as the water clear.
pope.gloss: Even thin gruel is ambrosia to him who has obtained it by labour.

reading: Though it is gruel thin as clear water, nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort brought.
nuance: தாள், literally the foot, stands for effort. Sweetness has become a moral quality here and doesn't describe the taste. Parimelazhagar says it's equal to ambrosia, because it's one's own.

couplet: E'en if a draught of water for a cow you ask,
Nought's so distasteful to the tongue as beggar's task.
pope.gloss: There is nothing more disgraceful to one's tongue than to use it in begging water even for a cow.

reading: Even if one asks for water for a cow, nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking.
nuance: A limit case with the worthiest cause and the smallest request, and it's still degrading. Parimelazhagar: virtue itself should be done by effort, never by begging. He also notes that நாவிற்கு confines the disgrace to the spoken word, and that this still exceeds every other disgrace.

couplet: One thing I beg of beggars all, 'If beg ye may,
Of those who hide their wealth, beg not, I pray.'
pope.gloss: I beseech all beggars and say, "If you need to beg, never beg of those who give unwillingly."

reading: I beg of all who beg: if you must beg, don't beg of those who conceal.
nuance: The poet himself takes on the posture he has just condemned, begging beggars. The repetition of இரப்பன், இரப்பாரை and இரப்பின் is almost a chant.

couplet: The fragile bark of beggary
Wrecked on denial's rock will lie.
pope.gloss: The unsafe raft of begging will split when it strikes on the rock of refusal.

reading: The unsafe boat called asking will split apart when it strikes the rock called concealment.
nuance: The sea of poverty is supplied by both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar. The verse's point isn't the rock alone: the boat itself is flawed, and this is what ஏமாப்பில் says.

couplet: The heart will melt away at thought of beggary,
With thought of stern repulse 'twill perish utterly.
pope.gloss: To think of (the evil of) begging is enough to melt one's heart; but to think of refusal is enough to break it.

reading: Thinking of begging, the heart melts; thinking of concealment, even what remains is gone.
nuance: The heart has two stages: it melts, and then there's nothing left to melt. Concealment is ranked as the worse.

couplet: E'en as he asks, the shamefaced asker dies;
Where shall his spirit hide who help denies?
pope.gloss: Saying "No" to a beggar takes away his life. (but as that very word will kill the refuser) where then would the latter's life hide itself ?

reading: As the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal, where does the life of the one who conceals hide?
nuance: The rhetorical question is a charge: the word that kills the hearer ought to kill the speaker first. Parimelazhagar glosses 'life goes' as being stunned with helplessness, a less literal sense than the verse's own. He reports another reading as a dread-filled man's speech.

title: கயமை
theme: A bitterly ironic portrait of the base: they look perfectly human, are as free as gods, and are happier than the good because nothing troubles them. Only fear and greed move them, and at the first trouble they sell themselves. The chapter ends the whole Book of Wealth.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: excess of their fault (1071), fearless of blame (1072), do as they please (1073), fault of pride in low conduct (1074), their conduct is not natural to them (1075), can't keep a secret (1076), how they give (1077-1078), envy (1079), and they become slaves (1080). Manakkudavar's text marks 1080 as the end of the Book of Wealth.
source_issues: 1075: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
1077: Manakkudavar's text ends with a stray digit 8.
1078: Parimelazhagar's gloss has மறைக் கீழாயினார், which seems garbled; and Pope's gloss adds 'bestow their alms', which is not in the Tamil.
1080: Manakkudavar's text ends with colophons for குடியியல் and பொருட்பால், which aren't commentary on this verse.

couplet: The base resemble men in outward form, I ween;
But counterpart exact to them I've never seen.
pope.gloss: The base resemble men perfectly (as regards form); and we have not seen such (exact) resemblance (among any other species).

reading: The base look just like human beings; we have never seen so close a resemblance.
nuance: Bitter praise opens the portrait. The likeness is complete, and that is the whole problem, since there's no outward way of telling.

couplet: Than those of grateful heart the base must luckier be,
Their minds from every anxious thought are free!
pope.gloss: The low enjoy more felicity than those who know what is good; for the former are not troubled with anxiety (as to the good).

reading: The base are more fortunate than those who know what's good, for they have no anguish in their heart.
nuance: A real observation under the sarcasm: moral knowledge has a psychological cost. Parimelazhagar spells it out: the good worry that they don't do enough, about obstacles to their good deeds, and about what might result. திரு here is mock praise, as he says.

couplet: The base are as the Gods; they too
Do ever what they list to do!
pope.gloss: The base resemble the Gods; for the base ac t as they like.

reading: The base are like the gods, for they too act as they please.
nuance: Having looked like humans in 1071, they now look like gods. Parimelazhagar says the difference between them goes unstated, since the gods act by understanding and the base by lowness. Kalaignar's gloss says 'the gods of the Puranas', which gives the barb a second target.

couplet: When base men those behold of conduct vile,
They straight surpass them, and exulting smile.
pope.gloss: The base feels proud when he sees persons whose acts meaner than his own.

reading: Seeing அகப்பட்டி, the base outdo them and swagger with pride.
nuance: அகப்பட்டி is hard to fix, and I've left it untranslated. The readings below differ so widely that I can't be confident of either.

couplet: Fear is the base man's virtue; if that fail,
Intense desire some little may avail.
pope.gloss: (The principle of) behaviour in the mean is chiefly fear; if not, hope of gain, to some extent.

reading: Fear is the conduct of the base, and beyond that there's some, if there's desire.
nuance: A theory of external motivation: there's no inner source of good conduct in them, so it can only come from fear of punishment and hope of gain. Parimelazhagar names the king as what they fear, and Kalaignar reverses the order and makes it pretence.

couplet: The base are like the beaten drum; for, when they hear
The sound the secret out in every neighbour's ear.
pope.gloss: The base are like a drum that is beaten, for they unburden to others the secrets they have heard.

reading: The base are like a beaten drum, for they carry any secret they hear and proclaim it to others.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that the drum only sounds when beaten, a working likeness. உய்த்து, 'carrying', suggests to him the secret is a heavy burden to such a man, so that he has to go and put it down.

couplet: From off their moistened hands no clinging grain they shake,
Unless to those with clenched fist their jaws who break.
pope.gloss: The mean will not (even) shake off (what sticks to) their hands (soon after a meal) to any but those who would break their jaws with their clenched fists.

reading: The base won't even shake their wet hands for any but those with bent fists who would break their jaws.
nuance: The smallest gift is shaking drops of water off a washed hand. The gift is measured by what it takes to get it. Parimelazhagar sums up: they give nothing to the weak and everything to those who hurt them.

couplet: The good to those will profit yield fair words who use;
The base, like sugar-cane, will profit those who bruise.
pope.gloss: The great bestow (their alms) as soon as they are informed; (but) the mean, like the sugar-cane, only when they are tortured to death.

reading: The worthy are of use at a word, and the base, like sugar-cane, only when crushed.
nuance: A sugar-cane is sweet, so the image concedes that the base do have something to give. But it comes out only under pressure. கொல்ல, 'to kill', is unusually strong.

couplet: If neighbours clothed and fed he see, the base
Is mighty man some hidden fault to trace?
pope.gloss: The base will bring an evil (accusation) against others, as soon as he sees them (enjoying) good food and clothing.

reading: If they see others clothed and fed, the base are able to find a fault in them.
nuance: Ordinary eating and dressing are enough to bring it on; no great success is required.

couplet: For what is base man fit, if griefs assail?
Himself to offer, there and then, for sale!
pope.gloss: The base will hasten to sell themselves as soon as a calamity has befallen them. For what else are they fitted ?

reading: What are the base fit for? When something befalls them, they are fit to sell themselves, quickly.
nuance: The Book of Wealth closes with a person as a thing sold. Parimelazhagar's reading of விரைந்து is grim: they hurry before buyers learn what they are. An answer to the question is the insult: this is the only use they have.

title: தகையணங்குறுத்தல்
theme: The man's first sight of the woman, told as an injury: her beauty and returned gaze attack him like a goddess, an army, Death and a rutting elephant. The chapter treats love's beginning as the defeat of a strong man, and ends by claiming that love, unlike liquor, intoxicates through sight alone.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's headnotes follow what wounds him: her whole form (1081), her returned glance and eyes (1082-1086), her breasts (1087), her forehead (1088), her ornaments (1089). 1090 turns to reading her intent and opens the way to the next chapter.
source_issues: 1085: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.
1083: Parimelazhagar's text has பண்தகையுடனே where பெண்தகையுடனே seems intended, and his gloss has பெண் தகையாள் where the verse has பெண்டகையால்.

couplet: Goddess? or peafowl rare? She whose ears rich jewels wear,
Is she a maid of human kind? All wildered is my mind!
pope.gloss: Is this jewelled female a celestial, a choice peahen, or a human being ? My mind is perplexed.

reading: The man, on first seeing her, cannot tell whether this woman in heavy earrings is a goddess, a rare peahen or a human being, and his heart reels.
nuance: The three guesses aren't mere compliments. Parimelazhagar ties each to evidence: her indescribable form and his distress suggest a goddess, her grace and the grove suggest a peahen, and the way she looks back suggests a woman. Kalaignar's rendering drops the goddess and gives 'beauty that torments me' instead.

couplet: She of the beaming eyes, To my rash look her glance replies,
As if the matchless goddess' hand Led forth an armed band.
pope.gloss: This female beauty returning my looks is like a celestial maiden coming with an army to contend against me.

reading: The man says that when she answers his look with her own, it is as if a goddess who strikes on her own had brought an army with her.
nuance: The returned look is the blow. Parimelazhagar says he has now settled that she is human, so the goddess of 1081 survives only as a figure, and his pain has grown from her beauty to her meaningful glance.

couplet: Death's form I formerly Knew not; but now 'tis plain to me;
He comes in lovely maiden's guise, With soul-subduing eyes.
pope.gloss: I never knew before what is called Yama; I see it now; it is the eyes that carry on a great fight with (the help of) female qualities.

reading: The man says he never knew what Death was, and now he does: it has a woman's grace and large eyes that make war.
nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses the first line as a contrast between hearsay and experience: Death was something known from what the learned say, and only now seen. He adds that the man calls her Death because the suffering outweighs the pleasure.

couplet: In sweet simplicity, A woman's gracious form hath she;
But yet those eyes, that drink my life, Are with the form at strife!
pope.gloss: These eyes that seem to kill those who look at them are as it were in hostilities with this feminine simplicity.

reading: The man says the eyes of this artless, womanly girl have a look that eats the life of those who see them, and he sets those eyes against, or alongside, her gentleness.

couplet: The light that on me gleams, Is it death's dart? or eye's bright beams?
Or fawn's shy glance? All three appear In form of maiden here.
pope.gloss: Is it Yama, (a pair of) eyes or a hind ?- Are not all these three in the looks of this maid ?

reading: The man asks whether it is Death, an eye or a doe, since the young woman's look has the nature of all three.
nuance: The list holds opposites: the look kills, it seeks him out, and it startles like a frightened animal. Parimelazhagar sums this up as pleasure and pain given together, which sets up the double look of 1091.

couplet: If cruel eye-brow's bow, Unbent, would veil those glances now;
The shafts that wound this trembling heart Her eyes no more would dart.
pope.gloss: Her eyes will cause (me) no trembling sorrow, if they are properly hidden by her cruel arched eye-brows.

reading: The man says that if her curved brows would only stop bending and screen her eyes, those eyes could not cause him this trembling pain.
nuance: The conceit turns on the word கோடா, 'unbending'. Parimelazhagar treats the brows as the eyes' close friends, who could restrain them only if they were straight themselves, because anyone who rebukes a friend must be upright. Manakkudavar reads a small scene into it: she has lowered her head and her brows now shade her eyes.

couplet: As veil o'er angry eyes Of raging elephant that lies,
The silken cincture's folds invest This maiden's panting breast.
pope.gloss: The cloth that covers the firm bosom of this maiden is (like) that which covers the eyes of a rutting elephant.

reading: The man says the cloth over her firm breasts is like the face-cloth over the eyes of a rutting elephant.
nuance: A covering usually suggests safety, but this one announces danger. Parimelazhagar makes modesty the reason for the cloth, while the man, seeing strength through it, thinks of what it holds back. Manakkudavar has the man address her directly as மாதரே, while Parimelazhagar has him speak about her.

couplet: Ah! woe is me! my might, That awed my foemen in the fight,
By lustre of that beaming brow Borne down, lies broken now!
pope.gloss: On her bright brow alone is destroyed even th at power of mine that used to terrify the most fearless foes in the battlefield.

reading: The man laments that his might, feared in battle even by enemies who never met him there, has broken before her bright forehead alone.
nuance: The ஓ marks wonder at the mismatch: so great a strength and so small a thing as a forehead. Parimelazhagar is careful to note that this isn't boasting, because the man is grieving for what he has lost.

couplet: Like tender fawn's her eye; Clothed on is she with modesty;
What added beauty can be lent; By alien ornament?
pope.gloss: Of what use are other jewels to her who is adorned with modesty, and the meek looks of a hind ?

reading: The man asks what use foreign ornaments are to one who already has a doe's shy look and modesty.
nuance: It sounds like a pure compliment, but both older commentators hear a complaint. For Parimelazhagar, whoever adorned her lacks sense, because the jewels burden her and harm him; for Manakkudavar, he praises her while seeming to accuse her of cruelty.

couplet: The palm-tree's fragrant wine, To those who taste yields joys divine;
But love hath rare felicity For those that only see!
pope.gloss: Unlike boiled honey which yields delight only when it is drunk, love gives pleasure even when looked at.

reading: Brewed liquor delights only those who drink it, not those who merely see it as love does; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
nuance: Parimelazhagar supplies an unspoken close: love is better than liquor, yet he hasn't obtained it because he hasn't yet read her intent. He also takes காமம் here to mean the person in whom love is enjoyed.

title: குறிப்பறிதல்
theme: Reading desire that won't declare itself. The lovers communicate through lowered eyes, half-smiles and feigned indifference, until spoken words are declared useless.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar assigns the signs to the man (1091-1095), his inference from a rebuff by the friend (1096-1097), his relief at her smile (1098), and the friend's own inference about the couple (1099-1100).
source_issues: 1098: Kalaignar's entry ends with stray text about a rhetorical figure (ஆகியவற்றைக் காணலாம். ஆ. அணி நலம் ...) that is editorial matter from another source, not commentary on this verse. It was not used.
1095: Manakkudavar's gloss implies a different reading, ஒருகால், where the verse has ஒருகண், and its நகா நின்தள் looks like a typo for நகாநின்றாள்.

couplet: A double witchery have glances of her liquid eye;
One glance is glance that brings me pain; the other heals again.
pope.gloss: There are two looks in the dyed eyes of this (fair one); one causes pain, and the other is the cure thereof.

reading: The man sees two looks in her kohl-lined eyes: one gives him the sickness and the other is its cure.

couplet: The furtive glance, that gleams one instant bright,
Is more than half of love's supreme delight.
pope.gloss: A single stolen glance of her eyes is more than half the pleasure (of sexual embrace).

reading: The man says the brief look her eyes steal is not half of love's fulfilment but more than half.
nuance: The arithmetic is odd until you see why it works. Parimelazhagar says the glance guarantees that union will follow, so its value lies in what it promises. Stealing also suits the setting: this is secret love, and the eyes are the first thieves.

couplet: She looked, and looking drooped her head:
On springing shoot of love 'its water shed!
pope.gloss: She has looked (at men) and stooped (her head); and that (sign) waters as it were (the corn of) our love.

reading: The man says she looked, and having looked lowered her head, and that gesture was water poured into the bond between them.
nuance: The verse says only யாப்பு, a binding, and water poured into it. The growing crop of love that makes the image cohere comes from the commentators, and Parimelazhagar notes that the metaphor is only partly stated. Lowering her head is what waters the bond, so modesty here works for desire and not against it.

couplet: I look on her: her eyes are on the ground the while:
I look away: she looks on me with timid smile.
pope.gloss: When I look, she looks down; when I do not, she looks and smiles gently.

reading: The man observes that when he looks she looks at the ground, and when he doesn't she looks at him and smiles softly.
nuance: The whole verse is timing. Their eyes never meet, and that very avoidance tells him she is watching. Parimelazhagar takes மெல்ல நகும் as rejoicing inwardly without showing it, and mentions that others read it as a visible smile.

couplet: She seemed to see me not; but yet the maid
Her love, by smiling side-long glance, betrayed.
pope.gloss: She not only avoids a direct look at me, but looks as it were with a half-closed eye and smiles.

reading: The man says that she doesn't look at him directly, but smiles as though narrowing one eye.

couplet: Though with their lips affection they disown,
Yet, when they hate us not, 'tis quickly known.
pope.gloss: Though they may speak harshly as if they were strangers, the words of the friendly are soon understood.

reading: The man reflects that the words of those without real anger are quickly seen through, even when they speak like strangers.

couplet: The slighting words that anger feign, while eyes their love reveal.
Are signs of those that love, but would their love conceal.
pope.gloss: Little words that are harsh and looks that are hateful are (but) the expressions of lovers who wish to act like strangers.

reading: The man reasons that small harsh words without anger and looks like an enemy's are the signs of those who are close while seeming distant.
nuance: 1096 and 1097 give him a rule for treating refusal as disguise, and the verses rest it entirely on செறாஅ, the absence of real anger. In my reading that condition is doing all the work, and it is exactly what the man can't verify from outside. Parimelazhagar's conclusion is that he needn't fear such signs.

couplet: I gaze, the tender maid relents the while;
And, oh the matchless grace of that soft smile!
pope.gloss: When I look, the pitying maid looks in return and smiles gently; and that is a comforting sign for me.

reading: The man says that when he looks, she softens and smiles gently, and there is something special about the swaying woman at that moment.

couplet: The look indifferent, that would its love disguise,
Is only read aright by lovers' eyes.
pope.gloss: Both the lovers are capable of looking at each other in an ordinary way, as if they were perfect strangers.

reading: Looking at each other with a stranger's common glance is found only in lovers; Parimelazhagar gives this to the friend, who is working out the affair, while the other commentators name no speaker.
nuance: A public pretence of indifference becomes the evidence. The couple's disguise gives them away to the one person placed to notice, so this is close observation from outside the romance.

couplet: When eye to answering eye reveals the tale of love,
All words that lips can say must useless prove.
pope.gloss: The words of the mouths are of no use whatever, when there is perfect agreement between the eyes (of lovers).

reading: Once eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words have no use at all; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the man for Manakkudavar.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes the claim very concrete: the useless words are the couple's cover stories, hers about guarding the millet field and his about hunting. Out of context it reads as a maxim about wordless love.

title: புணர்ச்சிமகிழ்தல்
theme: The man's joy in union, in which one person holds all five senses, cures the sickness she caused, and rivals heaven and the virtuous householder's meal. Its last verse compares this desire to knowledge, which only reveals how much more there is.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's headnotes trace a clandestine narrative: first union (1101), a second meeting (1102), the man's friend objecting (1103), meetings arranged by friends (1104-1106), her friend urging marriage and being put off (1107-1109), and elopement (1110).
source_issues: 1101, 1104: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.
1105: Manakkudavar's gloss assumes the reading தோட்டாழ் கதுப்பு where the verse has தோட்டார் கதுப்பு.
1107: Parimelazhagar's gloss has அரிமை where the verse has அரிவை, apparently a typo.

couplet: All joys that senses five- sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch- can give,
In this resplendent armlets-bearing damsel live!
pope.gloss: The (simultaneous) enjoyment of the five senses of sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch can only be found with bright braceleted (women).

reading: The man says that all five senses, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching, find their objects in this one bright-braceleted woman.
nuance: The claim is about concentration. Parimelazhagar's gloss is that pleasures usually taken from different things at different times are here had at once, from one person. He also folds in the erotic techniques named in Sanskrit treatises, which the verse doesn't mention.

couplet: Disease and medicine antagonists we surely see;
This maid, to pain she gives, herself is remedy.
pope.gloss: The remedy for a disease is always something different (from it); but for the disease caused by this jewelled maid, she is herself the cure.

reading: The man says the cure for a disease is usually something other than its cause, but this jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sharpens பிற: ordinary medicine is opposite in nature to the disease's cause. Love therefore breaks a rule of medicine, not only of common sense.

couplet: Than rest in her soft arms to whom the soul is giv'n,
Is any sweeter joy in his, the Lotus-eyed-one's heaven?
pope.gloss: Can the lotus-eyed Vishnu's heaven be indeed as sweet to those who delight to sleep in the delicate arms of their beloved ?

reading: The man asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one can be sweeter than sleeping on the soft arms of the one you love.
nuance: The question is left open, and the commentators answer it for him. Parimelazhagar has the man's friend object that one fit for supreme bliss shouldn't sink to this small pleasure, and takes the man's point to be that heaven requires hard austerities which this sleep does not.

couplet: Withdraw, it burns; approach, it soothes the pain;
Whence did the maid this wondrous fi re obtain?
pope.gloss: From whence has she got this fire that burns when I withdraw and cools when I approach ?

reading: The man asks where she found this fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he comes near.
nuance: Parimelazhagar observes a small sleight: the fire is the man's own desire, which he attributes to her because she is what draws it out.

couplet: In her embrace, whose locks with flowery wreaths are bound,
Each varied form of joy the soul can wish is found.
pope.gloss: The shoulders of her whose locks are adorned with flowers delight me as if they were the very sweets I have desired (to get).

reading: The man says her shoulders, with flowers in her hair, feel like each thing one craves at the moment of craving it.
nuance: The point is freshness across repetition. For Parimelazhagar, they have already met several times and she still binds him as if new. Manakkudavar's text differs: where the verse has hair adorned with flowers, he has hair fallen loose on her shoulders during love, which changes the picture from adornment to its undoing.

couplet: Ambrosia are the simple maiden's arms; when I attain
Their touch, my withered life puts forth its buds again!
pope.gloss: The shoulders of this fair one are made of ambrosia, for they revive me with pleasure every time I embrace them.

reading: The man says that since her touch makes his life put out fresh shoots each time they meet, this girl's shoulders must be made of ambrosia.
nuance: Ambrosia is inferred from an effect, in the manner of a logical argument. உயிர்தளிர்ப்ப also makes his life a plant, withering between meetings, which Manakkudavar pushes further: without her that life would die.

couplet: As when one eats from household store, with kindly grace
Sharing his meal: such is this golden maid's embrace.
pope.gloss: The embraces of a gold-complexioned beautiful female are as pleasant as to dwell in one's own house and live by one's own (earnings) after distributing (a portion of it in charity).

reading: The man says the embrace of this lovely dark-gold woman is like living in your own home and eating your own food after sharing it.
nuance: A pleasure is measured by a virtue. The comparison brings the whole ethic of the householder into the bedroom, as a kind of satisfaction that has nothing to hide or to owe.

couplet: Sweet is the strict embrace of those whom fond affection binds,
Where no dissevering breath of discord entrance finds.
pope.gloss: To ardent lovers sweet is the embrace that cannot be penetrated even by a breath of breeze.

reading: The man says an embrace so close that not even a breeze can part it is sweet to two who desire each other.
nuance: Parimelazhagar finds an evasion in the word இருவர், 'two'. The friend has urged the uninterrupted union of marriage, and he answers that this holds for two people, whereas they are not two. Manakkudavar sees only the praise.

couplet: The jealous variance, the healing of the strife, reunion gained:
These are the fruits from wedded love obtained.
pope.gloss: Love quarrel, reconciliation and intercourse - these are the advantages reaped by those who marry for lust.

reading: The man names quarrelling, making up and uniting as the rewards of those who have come together in love.
nuance: The verse puts the quarrel inside love's rewards, and first in the list. That is the seed of the book's final chapter.

couplet: The more men learn, the more their lack of learning they detect;
'Tis so when I approach the maid with gleaming jewels decked.
pope.gloss: As (one's) ignorance is discovered the more one learns, so does repeated intercourse with a well-adorned female (only create a desire for more).

reading: The man says that closeness to this red-jewelled woman works like knowledge: each advance shows how much was lacking before.
nuance: Parimelazhagar closes the chapter by noting that the woman feels this joy too, but it shows in her only through signs and never in speech. Nine verses of male voice therefore rest on a convention, and he says so.

title: நலம்புனைந்துரைத்தல்
theme: The man praises her beauty through deliberate hyperbole, defeating the standard comparisons: flowers, the moon, swan's down. As the praise goes on, it becomes a claim of exclusivity, and what is seen by many ceases to compare with what he alone sees.
structure_note: The chapter's movement is by comparison: softness and flowers (1111-1115), the moon (1116-1119), softness again in the feet (1120). Parimelazhagar sets 1116-1119 at a night tryst with the moon overhead.
source_issues: 1113: Parimelazhagar offers two settings for the verse, the man speaking to his own friend or to her friend, so its addressee is open even within one commentary.

couplet: O flower of the sensitive plant! than thee
More tender's the maiden beloved by me.
pope.gloss: May you flourish, O Anicham! you have a delicate nature. But my beloved is more delicate than you.

reading: The man addresses the anicham flower, granting it delicacy and telling it that the woman he loves is more delicate still.
nuance: வாழி sounds like a blessing, but for Parimelazhagar it is a polite way to end the flower's pride: stop thinking you are the softest. He also says the man has just touched her, so the praise comes from touch and not sight.

couplet: You deemed, as you saw the flowers, her eyes were as flowers, my soul,
That many may see; it was surely some folly that over you stole!
pope.gloss: O my soul, fancying that flowers which are seen by many can resemble her eyes, you become confused at the sight of them.

reading: The man scolds his heart for reeling whenever it sees flowers, supposing that her eyes resemble what anyone can look at.

couplet: As tender shoot her frame; teeth, pearls; around her odours blend;
Darts are the eyes of her whose shoulders like the bambu bend.
pope.gloss: The complexion of this bamboo-shouldered one is that of a shoot; her teeth, are pearls; her breath, fragrance; and her dyed eyes, lances.

reading: The man describes her: bamboo shoulders, a body like young shoots, pearl teeth, fragrance, and kohl-lined eyes that are spears.
nuance: Parimelazhagar offers a witty setting as an alternative: her friend claims not to know whom he means, so this list is a description for identifying her. Everything in it is soft except the eyes, the one weapon among the delights, as in chapter 109.

couplet: The lotus, seeing her, with head demiss, the ground would eye,
And say, 'With eyes of her, rich gems who wears, we cannot vie.'
pope.gloss: If the blue lotus could see, it would stoop and look at the ground saying, "I can never resemble the eyes of this excellent jewelled one."

reading: The man says that if blue water-lilies could see, they would bow their heads and look at the ground, saying they can't match the eyes of this finely jewelled woman.
nuance: The lilies would take the posture of a modest woman, which is the very gesture she makes in 1094. Parimelazhagar draws out the unstated corollary: lacking sight and shame, real lilies stand proudly staring at the sky.

couplet: The flowers of the sensitive plant as a girdle around her she placed;
The stems she forgot to nip off; they 'll weigh down the delicate waist.
pope.gloss: No merry drums will be beaten for the (tender) waist of her who has adorned herself with the anicham without having removed its stem.

reading: The man says that she has worn anicham flowers without removing their stems, so no good drums will sound for her waist.
nuance: This is a mock funeral. As Parimelazhagar spells it out, the stems' weight will snap her waist, and then only the drum for the dead will sound. Praise by imagined catastrophe is one of the book's boldest jokes. He glosses கால் as the flower's bud or stalk end, and Manakkudavar as its stems.

couplet: The stars perplexed are rushing wildly from their spheres;
For like another moon this maiden's face appears.
pope.gloss: The stars have become confused in their places not being able to distinguish between the moon and the maid's countenance.

reading: The man says the stars have strayed from their places, unable to tell the moon from the young woman's face.
nuance: This gives a fanciful explanation for why stars move at all: they are lost. Manakkudavar says so directly, that the poet presents their motion as confusion.

couplet: In moon, that waxing waning shines, as sports appear,
Are any spots discerned in face of maiden here?
pope.gloss: Could there be spots in the face of this maid like those in the bright full moon ?

reading: The man asks whether a woman's face has spots, as the bright moon does when it fills out its lost parts.
nuance: This undoes the previous verse. Waning and spots should have told the stars the difference, so Parimelazhagar hears mockery of the stars: they had every means of knowing, and still failed.

couplet: Farewell, O moon! If that thine orb could shine
Bright as her face, thou shouldst be love of mine.
pope.gloss: If you can indeed shine like the face of women, flourish, O moon, for then would you be worth loving ?

reading: The man tells the moon that if it could shine as her face does, it too could be loved.
nuance: வாழி varies in force: Parimelazhagar calls it agreement when spoken to the flower in 1111 and contempt here, because the moon's spots make the condition impossible. Manakkudavar treats it as an empty particle. The tone of the verse depends on that small word.

couplet: If as her face, whose eyes are flowers, thou wou ldst have charms for me,
Shine for my eyes alone, O moon, shine not for all to see!
pope.gloss: O moon, if you wish to resemble the face of her whose eyes are like (these) flowers, do not appear so as to be seen by all.

reading: The man tells the moon that if it wants to resemble the face of the flower-eyed woman, it must not appear where many can see it.
nuance: The criterion has moved from brightness to privacy. For Parimelazhagar, what disqualifies the moon is that it shows itself to everyone, while he alone has fully enjoyed her face. Praise here shades into possession.

couplet: The flower of the sensitive plant, and the down on the swan's white breast,
As the thorn are harsh, by the delicate feet of this maiden pressed.
pope.gloss: The anicham and the feathers of the swan are to the feet of females, like the fruit of the (thorny) Nerunji.

reading: The man says anicham flowers and swan's down are to her feet what the nerunji fruit is.
nuance: The verse says நெருஞ்சிப் பழம், the fruit, and Kalaignar and Pope turn it into a thorn. Parimelazhagar explains the choice of fruit, since it is hard at the tip.

title: காதற்சிறப்புரைத்தல்
theme: Each lover declares what this love is. He makes it a bond of body and life, and she makes it an indwelling so complete that separation is impossible, which leaves the townspeople's talk of an absent, unloving man simply mistaken.
structure_note: Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar divide the chapter by speaker: the man in 1121-1125 and the woman in 1126-1130.
source_issues: 1126: The verse text has பருகுவரா, while Parimelazhagar and Pope read it as பருவரார், 'won't suffer'. பருகுவரா looks like a corruption of the source text.
1130: The verse text has இகந்து, while Parimelazhagar glosses இகழ்ந்து.
1124, 1126, 1130: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: The dew on her white teeth, whose voice is soft and low,
Is as when milk and honey mingled flow.
pope.gloss: The water which oozes from the white teeth of this soft speeched damsel is like a mixture of milk and honey.

reading: The man says the moisture at the white teeth of this soft-spoken woman is like milk mixed with honey.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notices why the comparison is a mixture and not one sweet thing: milk and honey each have a known taste, while their blend has a sweetness you can't name.

couplet: Between this maid and me the friendship kind
Is as the bonds that soul and body bind.
pope.gloss: The love between me and this damsel is like the union of body and soul.

reading: The man says the bond between him and this girl is what the bond between body and life is.
nuance: நட்பு, the word for friendship, is what the verse uses. Parimelazhagar's reading is that these are words for her: she is privately wondering who he is, whether he loves her and whether they will meet again, and he answers what he reads in her face. He files the verse under fear of parting, and Manakkudavar agrees: I can't leave you.

couplet: For her with beauteous brow, the maid I love, there place is none;
To give her image room, O pupil of mine eye, begone!
pope.gloss: O you image in the pupil (of my eye)! depart; there is no room for (my) fair-browed beloved.

reading: The man tells the image in the pupil of his eye to leave, because there is no room there for the fair-browed woman he loves.
nuance: The conceit depends on the Tamil word for the pupil's reflection, பாவை, a little figure living inside the eye. Parimelazhagar sets this at the moment she is leaving him: since he can't bear not seeing her, she must move in.

couplet: Life is she to my very soul when she draws nigh;
Dissevered from the maid with jewels rare, I die!
pope.gloss: My fair-jewelled one resembles the living soul (when she is in union with me), the dying soul when she leaves me.

reading: The man says the finely jewelled woman is to his life what living is when they are together, and what dying is when she goes.
nuance: She isn't compared to life and death as things, but to what happens to a life, its staying in the body and its leaving. Parimelazhagar notes that the ideas of 'for me' and 'in union' have to be supplied, since the verse says only 'when she leaves'.

couplet: I might recall, if I could once forget; but from my heart
Her charms fade not, whose eyes gleam like the warrior's dart.
pope.gloss: If I had forgotten her who has bright battling eyes, I would have remembered (thee); but I never forget her. (Thus says he to her maid).

reading: The man, answering her friend's question whether he remembers them, says he would recall the qualities of the bright-eyed woman if he ever forgot them, but he doesn't know how to forget.
nuance: The answer is a logical joke that turns the friend's question over: remembering presupposes forgetting, so no, he never thinks of her. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both mark this as the end of the man's speech.

couplet: My loved one's subtle form departs not from my eyes;
I wink them not, lest I should pain him where he lies.
pope.gloss: My lover would not depart from mine eyes; even if I wink, he would not suffer (from pain); he is so ethereal.

reading: The woman says her lover won't leave her eyes and isn't hurt even if she blinks, so subtle is he.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives this a strategic setting: she fears her friend will blame the absent man, and speaks to herself so that the friend will overhear. Her defence of him is that he hasn't gone anywhere. The invisible subtle body sounds like metaphysics, but he explains it as ceaseless thinking grown so ripe that the man is always before her.

couplet: My love doth ever in my eyes reside;
I stain them not, fearing his form to hide.
pope.gloss: As my lover abides in my eyes, I will not even paint them, for he would (then) have to conceal himself.

reading: The woman says that since her lover lives in her eyes, she doesn't even line them with kohl, knowing he would be hidden.
nuance: A real sign of separation, an unadorned face, is given a loving explanation. Manakkudavar adds a second one: she is so busy watching him within that she has no time to dress.

couplet: Within my heart my lover dwells; from food I turn
That smacks of heat, lest he should feel it burn.
pope.gloss: As my lover is in my heart, I am afraid of eating (anything) hot, for I know it would pain him.

reading: The woman says that since her lover lives in her heart, she is afraid to eat hot food, knowing he would be burned.
nuance: Manakkudavar supplies the occasion: her friend has asked why she isn't eating. Loss of appetite is one of the visible symptoms, and this is a graceful evasion of the question.

couplet: I fear his form to hide, nor close my eyes:
'Her love estranged is gone!' the village cries.
pope.gloss: I will not wink, knowing that if I did, my lover would hide himself; and for this reason, this town says, he is unloving.

reading: The woman says she won't blink, knowing he would be hidden, and for this much the town calls him loveless.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a quarrel behind 'this town': the friend has criticised the man to help her endure, and she, hurt, refuses to name the friend, calling her the town. Sleeplessness, the very evidence against him, she presents as her own act of care.

couplet: Rejoicing in my very soul he ever lies;
'Her love estranged is gone far off!' the village cries.
pope.gloss: My lover dwells in my heart with perpetual delight; but the town says he is unloving and (therefore) dwells afar.

reading: The woman says he lives joyfully in her heart always, while this town says he is loveless and lives apart.
nuance: The last words are identical to 1129's, and the refrain suggests how worn out she is by this argument. Whether her certainty is comfort or denial, the verse doesn't say.

title: நாணுத்துறவுரைத்தல்
theme: Declaring that shame has been given up. The man threatens to ride the palmyra horse, a public humiliation that forces the issue, while the woman, who may not do so, watches her love go into the streets on its own.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar marks 1131-1137 as the man and 1138-1140 as the woman. He reads the man's verses as one argument with her friend: each verse answers an objection she has raised, about shame, manliness, rafts, timing and whether men should endure better than women.
source_issues: 1135: Parimelazhagar's text is truncated. It starts mid-gloss at மாலை யுழக்குந் துயர் with no headnote. Pope's entry also has a stray '11 35'.
1135: Manakkudavar says these seven are the man's (இவை ஏழும் தலைமகன் கூற்று) at the fifth verse of the chapter, which suggests his order or count differs from this one, or that the note is misplaced.
1139: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: To those who 've proved love's joy, and now afflicted mourn,
Except the helpful 'horse of palm', no other strength remains.
pope.gloss: To those who after enjoyment of sexual pleasure suffer (for want of more), there is no help so efficient as the palmyra horse.

reading: The man says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard and no strength but the palmyra horse.
nuance: ஏமம, 'safeguard', is a surprising word for a public humiliation. The safety he means is pressure: Parimelazhagar explains that the man has given up on the friend's help and intends to get his way as men of old did.

couplet: My body and my soul, that can no more endure,
Will lay reserve aside, and mount the 'horse of palm'.
pope.gloss: Having got rid of shame, the suffering body and soul save themselves on the palmyra horse.

reading: The man says his body and life, unable to bear it any longer, will mount the palmyra horse, once shame has been put aside.
nuance: He says body and life will do this, and not 'I', as though his person had dissolved into what still suffers. Parimelazhagar adds that with the threat, the man is really looking for the friend to see his desperation and grant his plea quickly.

couplet: I once retained reserve and seemly manliness;
To-day I nought possess but lovers' 'horse of palm'.
pope.gloss: Modesty and manliness were once my own; now, my own is the palmyra horse that is ridden by the lustful.

reading: The man says he once had shame and sound manliness, and today he has the palmyra horse that lovers ride.
nuance: The form is an inventory of property, then and now. Parimelazhagar defines the two lost goods: shame keeps one from base acts, and manliness is not giving way to anything. Notably, it is the man who claims shame here; நாண் in the Kural isn't only a woman's virtue.

couplet: Love's rushing tide will sweep away the raft
Of seemly manliness and shame combined.
pope.gloss: The raft of modesty and manliness, is, alas, carried-off by the strong current of lust.

reading: The man says that the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a neat debating context: she objects that shame and manliness are rafts against the flood, and so can't be lost. He concedes that they are rafts, and answers that this flood takes the raft.

couplet: The maid that slender armlets wears, like flowers entwined,
pope.gloss: Has brought me 'horse of palm,' and pangs of eventide!

reading: The man says that the girl with bangles like a garland has given him the palmyra horse and the anguish of evening.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's explanatory note gives the point: love exists at all times but flowers at evening, and the very name for her implies a young girl, who only echoes her friend. So the man tells the friend that what the girl gave, the friend can take away.

couplet: Of climbing 'horse of palm' in midnight hour, I think;
My eyes know no repose for that same simple maid.
pope.gloss: Mine eyes will not close in sleep on your mistress's account; even at midnight will I think of mounting the palmyra horse.

reading: The man says that because of that simple girl his eyes can't close, so even at midnight he will surely think of mounting the palmyra horse.
nuance: Parimelazhagar stresses that பேதை here refers to her foolishness and not her age. Manakkudavar has the friend teasing that he'll forget by morning, and his answer turns his insomnia into a guarantee.

couplet: There's nought of greater worth than woman's long-enduring soul,
Who, vexed by love like ocean waves, climbs not the 'horse of palm'.
pope.gloss: There is nothing so noble as the womanly nature that would not ride the palmyra horse, though plunged a sea of lust.

reading: Nothing has greater worth than womanhood, which suffers a sea of desire and doesn't mount the palmyra horse; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.
nuance: The praise also rests on a restriction: she may not take the only remedy he has been boasting about. Who says it changes its force, since from him it is an excuse, and from the friend it is a demand.

couplet: In virtue hard to move, yet very tender, too, are we;
Love deems not so, would rend the veil, and court publicity!
pope.gloss: Even the Lust (of women) transgresses its secrecy and appears in public, forgetting that they are too chaste and liberal (to be overcome by it).

reading: Love doesn't stop to think that they are firm in restraint or deserving of pity, but breaks through secrecy and comes out in public; the speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a hint under the generalisation: she seems to talk about all women, but means her own love has grown, and that the matter must now be disclosed to the family.

couplet: 'There's no one knows my heart,' so says my love,
And thus, in public ways, perturbed will rove.
pope.gloss: My lust, feeling that it is not known by all, reels confused in the streets (of this town).

reading: The woman says that her love, thinking that not everyone knows, wanders bewildered round the streets.
nuance: Desire is made a separate creature, resentful of her former self-control. She can't ride the horse, so, in effect, her love goes out into the street without her. Parimelazhagar assigns the two verbs to two stages of gossip, அம்பல் and அலர்.

couplet: Before my eyes the foolish make a mock of me,
Because they ne'er endured the pangs I now must drie.
pope.gloss: Even strangers laugh (at us) so as to be seen by us, for they have not suffered.

reading: The woman says fools laugh within her sight because they have not suffered as she has.
nuance: Parimelazhagar names the unnamed fools: it is her friend, who has told her family and now teases her. He also reports, and rejects, a reading in which the man says this to the friend, because a man's speech wouldn't fit here at this point in the chapter.

title: அலரறிவுறுத்தல்
theme: The lovers turn the town's gossip around. Talk meant to shame and stop them feeds the love, keeps the man alive, and can even press for marriage or elopement. The chapter treats public scandal as an unintended gift.
structure_note: On Parimelazhagar's headnotes, the man speaks 1141-1145 and the woman 1146-1149, usually with the man overhearing, and 1150 is the friend's. He says the twenty verses of chapters 114 and 115 belong to the preliminary conditions of union (புணர்தல் நிமித்தம்).
source_issues: 1141: Parimelazhagar's headnote has வந்த தலைமகளை ... அவள் சொல்லியது, but his gloss clearly has a male speaker who can't reach her and says கூறினான். The feminine forms look like errors for தலைமகனை and அவன்.

1141: Manakkudavar's entry ends with களவியல் முற்றிற்று, so his sequence ends the secret-love section at this verse, and his order seems to differ from the one used here. That may also explain why he has no aligned entry for 1144, 1147, 1148 and 1150.

couplet: By this same rumour's rise, my precious life stands fast;
Good fortune grant the many know this not!
pope.gloss: My precious life is saved by the raise of rumour, and this, to my good luck no others are aware of.

reading: A precious life holds on because the gossip has risen, and by good fortune the many don't know this; for Parimelazhagar the man speaks of his own life, while Manakkudavar speaks of her life and leaves the speaker unnamed.
nuance: The joke rests on the second line: if the gossips knew they were helping, they would stop. Commentators differ on the source of luck. Parimelazhagar says தெய்வத்தால் and Manakkudavar says புண்ணியத்தாலே; one is divine and the other is merit, for a verse whose word is the Sanskrit-derived பாக்கியம்.

couplet: The village hath to us this rumour giv'n, that makes her mine;
Unweeting all the rareness of the maid with flower-like eyne.
pope.gloss: Not knowing the value of her whose eyes are like flowers this town has got up a rumour about me.

reading: The man says this town, not knowing how rare the flower-eyed woman is, has made him a present of gossip.
nuance: ஈந்தது is the verb for a generous gift. Parimelazhagar takes it that way, as an ironic thanks. The rarity differs by commentator: for Parimelazhagar, she is hard to reach, and for Manakkudavar, it is her noble birth that the gossips ignore.

couplet: The rumour spread within the town, is it not gain to me?
It is as though that were obtained that may not be.
pope.gloss: Will I not get a rumour that is known to the (whole) town ? For what I have not got is as if I had got it (already).

reading: The man asks whether the gossip the whole town knows isn't his to have, since it feels like having what he hasn't yet obtained.
nuance: The gossip isn't true yet, and that is its use: being talked about as a couple gives a foretaste of being one. Manakkudavar gives a more practical reason, in which the man tells the friend that the talk will bring the families round.

couplet: The rumour rising makes my love to rise;
My love would lose its power and languish otherwise.
pope.gloss: Rumour increases the violence of my passion; without it it would grow weak and waste away.

reading: The man says gossip makes his love flourish, and that without it the love would lose its nature and droop.
nuance: The sound carries the argument: கவ்வை, கவ்விது, தவ்வென்னும். Parimelazhagar explains கவ்விது as a coinage from the noun, and தவ் as a word that imitates sagging. The claim is that love depends in part on being seen.

couplet: The more man drinks, the more he ever drunk would be;
The more my love's revealed, the sweeter 'tis to me!
pope.gloss: As drinking liquor is delightful (to one) whenever one is in mirth, so is lust delightful to me whenever it is the subject of rumour.

reading: Love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking becomes more desired each time one gets drunk; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

couplet: I saw him but one single day: rumour spreads soon
As darkness, when the dragon seizes on the moon.
pope.gloss: It was but a single day that I looked on (my lover); but the rumour thereof has spread like the seizure of the moon by the serpent.
