reading: The woman says she saw him on only one day, and the gossip has spread like the serpent seizing the moon.
nuance: An eclipse is an event no one can miss, and a tiny private act is set against it. Parimelazhagar has her speaking to her friend with the man in earshot, so the complaint is really a demand for marriage. Kalaignar pauses to mark the serpent as an imaginary notion, which the commentators before him don't do.

couplet: My anguish grows apace: the town's report
Manures it; my mother's word doth water it.
pope.gloss: This malady (of lust) is manured by the talk of women and watered by the (harsh) words of my mother.

reading: The woman says this sickness grows long, with the town's gossip as its manure and her mother's words as its water.
nuance: Whatever is meant to shrink the love feeds it, as Parimelazhagar spells out. The one verse in the chapter to name her mother shows where the gossip actually hurts: at home. Parimelazhagar takes ஊரவர் to mean the women of the town.

couplet: With butter-oil extinguish fire! 'Twill prove
Harder by scandal to extinguish love.
pope.gloss: To say that one could extinguish passion by rumour is like extinguishing fire with ghee.

reading: The woman says that to think gossip can put out love is like thinking ghee can put out fire.
nuance: The grammar frames this as an error in thought, 'to say we will extinguish'. Parimelazhagar places it in the same scene as 1147, so it is also her answer to the friend's advice that she should take the talk seriously and bear up.

couplet: When he who said 'Fear not!' hath left me blamed,
While many shrink, can I from rumour hide ashamed?
pope.gloss: When the departure of him who said "fear not" has put me to shame before others, why need I be ashamed of scandal.

reading: The woman asks how she can be ashamed of gossip when the man who told her not to fear has left her, in a way that shames everyone who sees it.
nuance: This verse is the turn in the chapter, with gossip now no longer a game. The promise 'fear not' is quoted against him. Shame has moved from what she feels about the town to what those watching feel on her behalf, so she has none left to spend on rumour.

couplet: If we desire, who loves will grant what we require;
This town sends forth the rumour we desire!
pope.gloss: The rumour I desire is raised by the town (itself); and my lover would if desired consent (to my following him).

reading: The speaker, whom Parimelazhagar identifies as the friend talking to the woman while the man overhears, says the town is raising the very gossip they want, and the lover will grant it if asked or if he wishes.

title: பிரிவாற்றாமை
theme: The inability to bear parting. Mostly in the woman's voice, the chapter argues against his leaving before it happens: promises of a quick return are useless to one who won't survive, and a broken 'fear not' makes trust itself hard.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's headnotes run from the man announcing departure (1151) to her sensing it (1152-1155), hearing of it through her friend (1156-1158), and answering the friend's advice to bear up (1159-1160).
source_issues: Chapter title: the source gives கற்பியல், which names the section beginning here. The chapter's own title, பிரிவாற்றாமை, is missing.

1153: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is word for word the same as Parimelazhagar's gloss, and appears to be borrowed to fill a gap. The same flag appears at 1134 and 1140 and the wording matches there too. It should not be treated as independent witness.
1158: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary, and Parimelazhagar's entry begins மதுவும் அது, an apparent typo for இதுவும் அது.

couplet: If you will say, 'I leave thee not,' then tell me so;
Of quick return tell those that can survive this woe.
pope.gloss: If it is not departure, tell me; but if it is your speedy return, tell it to those who would be alive then.

reading: If you aren't leaving, tell me; if you mean to return quickly, tell that to those who will still be alive by then; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
nuance: One of the book's sharpest lines, a refusal to accept comfort. If the friend is the speaker, then Parimelazhagar's explanation for 'me' matters: she says எனக்கு for the woman because the two aren't distinct. He notes that some give the verse to the woman.

couplet: It once was perfect joy to look upon his face;
But now the fear of parting saddens each embrace.
pope.gloss: His very look was once pleasing; but (now) even intercourse is painful through fear of separation.

reading: The woman says that பார்வல் alone once gave her delight, and now union itself holds the pain of fearing separation.
nuance: The cruelty is that the most that love can give is spoiled by what it anticipates. Parimelazhagar cites Kalittokai for the telling sign: he now fusses over her more than before, which is how she knows he is leaving.

couplet: To trust henceforth is hard, if ever he depart,
E'en he, who knows his promise and my breaking heart.
pope.gloss: As even the lover who understands (everything) may at times depart, confidence is hardly possible.

reading: The woman says trust is hard, since parting sometimes happens even with those who understand.
nuance: அறிவுடையார் isn't a compliment to his learning. Parimelazhagar's gloss is that he knows his own word and knows she can't bear it, which makes his going worse. The verse shifts from this man's fault to the general difficulty of trusting anyone.

couplet: If he depart, who fondly said, 'Fear not,' what blame's incurred
By those who trusted to his reassuring word?
pope.gloss: If he who bestowed his love and said "fear not" should depart, will it be the fault of those who believed in (his) assuring words ?

reading: The woman asks, if the one who was gracious and told her not to fear should leave, whether any fault lies with those who believed his assuring words.
nuance: She refers to herself in the third person as தேறியார், 'those who trusted', which both commentators note. This turns the private complaint into a general moral question about a promise and who answers for it. Parimelazhagar names the fault as the mismatch between his word and deed.

couplet: If you would guard my life, from going him restrain
Who fills my life! If he depart, hardly we meet again.
pope.gloss: If you would save (my life), delay the departure of my destined (husband); for if he departs, intercourse will become impossible.

reading: The woman tells her friend that if she wants to protect her, she must prevent the departure of the one who is fit for her, because once he goes, union will be hard.
nuance: அமைந்தார் is a quiet word: the one who is fitting. Parimelazhagar adds divine ordering, saying he is the one fit by தெய்வம் to be her lord, and Pope follows with 'destined'. The verse itself doesn't mention destiny. He also explains why union would be hard: her life would have gone with him.

couplet: To cherish longing hope that he should ever gracious be,
Is hard, when he could stand, and of departure speak to me.
pope.gloss: If he is so cruel as to mention his departure (to me), the hope that he would bestow (his love) must be given up.

reading: The woman says that if he can be so hard as to speak of leaving, the hope that he would come back and be gracious is pointless.
nuance: The offence is the announcement, even more than the journey. For Parimelazhagar, one who could plan this while still at her side isn't likely to soften at a distance.

couplet: The bracelet slipping from my wrist announced before
Departure of the Prince that rules the ocean shore.
pope.gloss: Do not the rings that begin to slide down my fingers forebode the separation of my lord ?

reading: The woman asks if the bangles slipping past her wrist don't already announce that the lord of the shore has left her.
nuance: தூற்றா is the verb for spreading gossip, so her own body has joined the town. Parimelazhagar sees a rebuke to the friend, who brings the news: 'you too only do what these bangles do', when she should have stopped him. The past tense 'has left' is anticipatory, since the news alone has made her thin.

couplet: 'Tis sad to sojourn in the town where no kind kinsmen dwell;
'Tis sadder still to bid a friend beloved farewell.
pope.gloss: Painful is it to live in a friendless town; but far more painful is it to part from one's lover.

reading: The woman says living in a town without one's own people is painful, and being parted from the one who is dear is more painful still.
nuance: This sounds like a proverb, but Parimelazhagar says it is aimed. Her friend agreed to his leaving instead of preventing it, and so she speaks as if she has no companion here at all, while seeming only to speak about the way of the world.

couplet: Fire burns the hands that touch; but smart of love
Will burn in hearts that far away remove.
pope.gloss: Fire burns when touched; but, like the sickness of love, can it also burn when removed ?

reading: Fire burns only when touched, and can it burn when one moves away, as the sickness of love does? The speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

couplet: Sorrow's sadness meek sustaining, Driving sore distress away,
Separation uncomplaining Many bear the livelong day!
pope.gloss: As if there were many indeed that can consent to the impossible, kill their pain, endure separation and yet continue to live afterwards.

reading: The woman says that many agree to the impossible, remove their pain, endure the parting, and stay on alive afterwards.
nuance: It is all in the tone. Taken flatly, as Pope's couplet takes it, this says many cope; read as Parimelazhagar does, 'many' means no one, and the unstated close is that she too will die. Kalaignar makes the turn explicit by adding, 'but I?'. The three verbs slow down the task of enduring.

title: படர்மெலிந்திரங்கல்
theme: The woman wastes away in grief through the night, caught between a love she can't hide and a shame that forbids telling him. Love is measured against the sea and against the night, and the only company that remains is the night itself.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar sees them mostly as answers to her friend: on concealment and messages (1161-1163), rafts (1164), a rebuke to the friend (1165), the balance of pleasure and pain (1166), and the night (1167-1169). He says 1170 prepares for the next chapter on the eyes.
source_issues: 1162: Kalaignar's entry ends with stray text, எ. சுருக்க விளக்கம் சுருக்க விளக்கத்துக்கு, which is not commentary on this verse. It was not used.
1169: The verse text in the source has a stray leading '>' character.
1170: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It begins at நீந்தல மன்னோவென் கண் with no headnote or complete gloss.
1163, 1165, 1168, 1169: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: I would my pain conceal, but see! it surging swells,
As streams to those that draw from ever-springing wells.
pope.gloss: I would hide this pain from others; but it (only) swells like a spring to those who drain it.

reading: The woman says she would hide this pain, but, as water does in a spring when one draws from it, it only rises.
nuance: The commentators differ quietly over what the drawing out is. Kalaignar makes concealing itself the action, so hiding is what increases it. For Parimelazhagar, the concealment simply fails, as water wells up for one who draws from a spring.

couplet: I cannot hide this pain of mine, yet shame restrains
When I would tell it out to him who caused my pains.
pope.gloss: I cannot conceal this pain, nor can I relate it without shame to him who has caused it.

reading: The woman says she cannot hide this sickness, and telling the one who caused it also brings her shame.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a remarkable reason for the shame: if she sends a messenger, it will imply she is still alive. The grief that is meant to prove love would be disproved by being reported. Her friend has offered her two options, and she refuses both.

couplet: My soul, like porter's pole, within my wearied frame,
Sustains a two-fold burthen poised, of love and shame.
pope.gloss: (Both) lust and shame, with my soul for their shoulder pole balance themselves on a body that cannot bear them.

reading: The woman says love and shame hang from the ends of a carrying pole, which is her life, within her body that can't bear it.
nuance: The verb தூங்கும் conveys the balance: as Parimelazhagar reads it, neither side outweighs the other, so she can't commit to either, and the pole will snap. Kalaignar shifts the image so that the body is the pole; the verse says the life is.

couplet: A sea of love, 'tis true, I see stretched out before,
But not the trusty bark that wafts to yonder shore.
pope.gloss: There is indeed a flood of lust; but there is no raft of safety to cross it with.

reading: The woman says the sea of love certainly exists, and the safe raft for crossing it certainly doesn't.
nuance: Parimelazhagar takes the missing raft as a reproach to the friend, who should have sent word and been the raft. Manakkudavar agrees that she means she has no helper. It is more personal than a cosmic complaint.

couplet: Who work us woe in friendship's trustful hour,
What will they prove when angry tempests lower?
pope.gloss: He who can produce sorrow from friendship, what can he not bring forth out of enmity ?

reading: The woman asks what those who can bring such grief in friendship would do in enmity.

couplet: A happy love 's sea of joy; but mightier sorrows roll
From unpropitious love athwart the troubled soul.
pope.gloss: The pleasure of lust is (as great as) the sea; but the pain of lu st is far greater.

reading: The woman says the pleasure of love is a sea, and when love afflicts her, the pain is greater than the sea.
nuance: This rejects a consoling arithmetic. The friend has said that those who've had the joy should expect the pain, and the woman's point, as Parimelazhagar glosses it, is that an equal measure could be borne, but this isn't equal.

couplet: I swim the cruel tide of love, and can no shore descry,
In watches of the night, too, 'mid the waters, only I!
pope.gloss: I have swam across the terrible flood of lust, but have not seen its shore; even at midnight I am alone; still I live.

reading: The woman says she swims the fierce flood of love and sees no shore, and even at midnight there is only herself.
nuance: யானே உளேன் can mean 'I alone am here', and for Parimelazhagar also 'I am still alive', which he attributes to some evil deed's result. That idea of past deeds is his and isn't in the verse. Pope's prose follows him by adding 'still I live'.

couplet: All living souls in slumber soft she steeps;
But me alone kind night for her companing keeps!
pope.gloss: The night which graciously lulls to sleep all living creatures, has me alone for her companion.

reading: The woman says the night, which puts all living beings to sleep, is to be pitied, as it has no companion but her.
nuance: Everything turns on அளித்து. It is usually a word of pity or grace, and Parimelazhagar marks it as contempt: the night has foolishly chosen as its companion someone about to die. She isn't lamenting her solitude so much as mocking her only companion.

couplet: More cruel than the cruelty of him, the cruel one,
In these sad times are lengthening hours of night I watch alone.
pope.gloss: The long nights of these days are far more cruel than the heartless one who is torturing me.

reading: The woman says these long nights passing now are crueller than the cruelty of that cruel man.
nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses the implicit contrast: nights that were short when they were happy have now grown long. The word கொடியார், 'the cruel one', replaces his name.

couplet: When eye of mine would as my soul go forth to him,
It knows not how through floods of its own tears to swim.
pope.gloss: Could mine eyes travel like my thoughts to the abode (of my absent lord), they would not swim in this flood of tears.

reading: The woman says that if her eyes could go where he is as her heart does, they wouldn't be swimming in a flood of tears.
nuance: For Parimelazhagar, the mind's journey is only thought, while eyes need a body to walk there, so what the heart can do isn't really a substitute for seeing. He says this verse opens the next chapter, and the eyes' complaint begins here.

title: கண்விதுப்பழிதல்
theme: The woman puts her own eyes on trial. They showed her the man, so they caused the sickness; now they weep, can't sleep and betray her secret, and she answers with bitter laughter and a curse. Blaming a body part makes her suffering speakable.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's, almost all spoken to her friend. The eyes are addressed in the third person throughout, and the argument moves from accusation (1171-1173) to satisfaction at their punishment (1174-1177) to their sleeplessness and their betrayal of her (1178-1180).
source_issues: 1174, 1179, 1180: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.
1178: Parimelazhagar reports a variant, கொண்கனை, with a different reading attached.

couplet: They showed me him, and then my endless pain
I saw: why then should weeping eyes complain?
pope.gloss: As this incurable malady has been caused by my eyes which showed (him) to me, why should they now weep for (him).

reading: The woman asks why her eyes weep, when it was they who showed him to her, and so she came to know this unending sickness.
nuance: The verse says 'we saw the sickness' with no mention of him, and the object of 'showed' has to be supplied, as Parimelazhagar says. In her account, seeing him and seeing the sickness are the same act.

couplet: How glancing eyes, that rash unweeting looked that day,
With sorrow measureless are wasting now away!
pope.gloss: The dyed eyes that (then) looked without foresight, why should they now endure sorrow, without feeling sharply (their own fault).

reading: The woman asks why these kohl-lined eyes, which looked as they did, now suffer in misery without coming to terms with it.

couplet: The eyes that threw such eager glances round erewhile
Are weeping now. Such folly surely claims a smile!
pope.gloss: They themselves looked eagerly (on him) and now they weep. Is not this to be laughed at ?

reading: The woman says it's laughable that her eyes looked at him so quickly on their own and now weep on their own.
nuance: The repeated தாம் is the whole charge: they acted of their own accord both times. Manakkudavar pictures real laughter, a distracted woman laughing through her distress and being asked why, which makes this more disturbing than wit.

couplet: Those eyes have wept till all the fount of tears is dry,
That brought upon me pain that knows no remedy.
pope.gloss: These painted eyes have caused me a lasting mortal disease; and now they can weep no more, the tears having dried up.

reading: The woman says her kohl-lined eyes, having fixed in her an inescapable, fatal sickness, have dried up and can no longer even weep.
nuance: Dry eyes come after much weeping. What seems a relief is presented as the eyes' punishment: in Parimelazhagar's words, harm they did her has come back to them by itself.

couplet: The eye that wrought me more than sea could hold of woes,
Is suffering pangs that banish all repose.
pope.gloss: Mine eyes have caused me a lust that is greater than the sea and (they themselves) endure the torture of sleeplessness.

reading: The woman says her eyes, which gave her a sickness too large for the sea, now suffer torments and can't sleep.
nuance: The commentators use the language of moral consequence with some wit: Parimelazhagar says அத் தீவினையால், 'by that evil deed', and Manakkudavar has harm returning to those who harm others. The verse just shows the sequence.

couplet: Oho! how sweet a thing to see! the eye
That wrought this pain, in the same gulf doth lie.
pope.gloss: The eyes that have given me this disease have themselves been seized with this (suffering). Oh! I am much delighted.

reading: The woman exclaims how sweet it is that the eyes that gave her this sickness have fallen into it themselves.
nuance: Vengeance against one's own organ can only hurt the avenger, and that absurdity is the point. Parimelazhagar's gloss, 'as if my suffering had ended', keeps the distance between the delight and any real relief.

couplet: Aching, aching, let those exhaust their stream,
That melting, melting, that day gazed on him.
pope.gloss: The eyes that became tender and gazed intently on him, may they suffer so much as to dry up the fountain of their tears.

reading: The woman curses them: may the eyes that longed and melted and begged to see him suffer on until their inner water is gone.
nuance: The verse echoes itself: உழந்துழந்து against விழைந்திழைந்து, suffering matching longing in the same rhythm. Pay-back is built into the sound.

couplet: Who loved me once, onloving now doth here remain;
Not seeing him, my eye no rest can gain.
pope.gloss: He is indeed here who loved me with his lips but not with his heart but mine eyes suffer from not seeing him.

reading: The woman says there is one who desired without cherishing, and her eyes can't be at peace without seeing him.
nuance: The syntax allows several readings, and the second one Parimelazhagar gives rests on a different text, கொண்கனை. I'm unsure which is best. The steady part is the last clause: whatever he is, the eyes can't do without him.

couplet: When he comes not, all slumber flies; no sleep when he is there;
Thus every way my eyes have troubles hard to bear.
pope.gloss: When he is away they do not sleep; when he is present they do not sleep; in either case, mine eyes endure unbearable agony.

reading: The woman says that when he doesn't come her eyes don't sleep, and when he does they still don't sleep, so either way they suffer terribly.
nuance: Parimelazhagar supplies the two reasons: they stay up watching for him, and when he is there they stay up for fear he'll leave. Kalaignar's gloss reads this more generally, as the lot of all lovers' eyes.

couplet: It is not hard for all the town the knowledge to obtain,
When eyes, as mine, like beaten tambours, make the mystery plain.
pope.gloss: It is not difficult for the people of this place to understand the secret of those whose eyes, like mine, are as it were beaten drums.

reading: The woman says it isn't hard for the town to learn the secret in the hearts of those like her, whose eyes are beaten drums.
nuance: The eyes' final offence is treason. The friend has asked her to hide his cruelty so the town won't blame him, and she answers that the eyes make that impossible. Parimelazhagar notes the variant reading அறைபறைக் கண்ணார், which removes the poetic strain.

title: பசப்புறுபருவரல்
theme: The pallor of longing (பசலை), the woman's most visible symptom, personified as a creature that rides her body, moves in the instant he moves away, and earns her the town's blame while he escapes it. She ends by offering her body as the price of his good name.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar has her first alone (1181), then answering her friend: on why it came (1182-1187), and then with growing irritation at the friend's blame of her and of him (1188-1190).
source_issues: 1187-1188: Parimelazhagar's commentary on 1188 is merged into his 1187 entry, including the verse text, while 1188 shows no aligned Parimelazhagar. The 1188 commentary was read and summarised in the nuance, but can't be quoted under the check.
1188: Manakkudavar also has no aligned commentary.
1182: Pope's entry places his prose inside the couplet field with a stray '< br>', leaving the prose field empty.
1184: Pope's prose is cut off mid-sentence ('and this is').
1190: Parimelazhagar's headnote has தரைமகள், a typo for தலைமகள்.

couplet: I willed my lover absent should remain;
Of pining's sickly hue to whom shall I complain?
pope.gloss: I who (then) consented to the absence of my loving lord, to whom can I (now) relate the fact of my having turned sallow.

reading: The woman, to herself, asks to whom she can describe her pallor, since she herself agreed to the absence of the man who loves her.
nuance: Consent has closed off complaint. Parimelazhagar reads every word of this as her logic: having agreed, she feels it would be a further wrong even to tell anyone. 1181 is the first verse of the chapter, so the book's most visible symptom starts with her taking responsibility for it.

couplet: 'He gave': this sickly hue thus proudly speaks,
Then climbs, and all my frame its chariot makes. < br> Sallowness, as if proud of having been caused by him, would now ride on my person.

reading: The woman says the pallor climbs on and rides over her body, proud that he is the one who gave it.
nuance: Parimelazhagar uses the chariot-and-rider sense of இவர்தல் and adds that this is a claim of right, like a retainer's, which she can't resist because it comes from him. By his reading she is also comforting her friend: it's riding me by right, so don't worry. For Manakkudavar, she is saying that it isn't her doing, so take it up with him.

couplet: Of comeliness and shame he me bereft,
While pain and sickly hue, in recompense, he left.
pope.gloss: He has taken (away) my beauty and modesty, and given me instead disease and sallowness.

reading: The woman says he took away her grace and modesty, and gave her sickness and pallor in exchange.
nuance: The language is commercial: கைம்மாறா, 'in exchange'. Parimelazhagar notices the crossed pairing, in which sickness replaces modesty, since the more she tries to suppress it, the more it grows, and pallor replaces grace. He takes சாயல் as bodily beauty, and Manakkudavar as femininity (பெண்மை).

couplet: I meditate his words, his worth is theme of all I say,
This sickly hue is false that would my trust betray.
pope.gloss: I think (of him); and what I speak about is but his excellence; still is there sallowness; and this is

reading: The woman says she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits, and still the pallor comes, a kind of cheating.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes this a small argument: body follows mind and speech, and both are faithfully his, so the body shouldn't have paled. The verse never accuses her of faithlessness; the pallor is the deceiver.

couplet: My lover there went forth to roam;
This pallor of my frame usurps his place at home.
pope.gloss: Just as my lover departed then, did not sallowness spread here on my person ?

reading: The woman says: look there, her lover is going, and look here, the pallor is spreading over her body.
nuance: The verse is built only from the pointing words உவக்காண் and இவக்காண், which turn distance into simultaneity. Parimelazhagar compares his leaving and the pallor's coming to the changing of day and night. He treats it as a memory of a past parting, and Manakkudavar as happening right now.

couplet: As darkness waits till lamp expires, to fill the place,
This pallor waits till I enjoy no more my lord's embrace.
pope.gloss: Just as darkness waits for the failing light; so does sallowness wait for the laxity of my husband's intercourse.

reading: The woman says pallor watches for her lover's embrace to weaken, as darkness watches for a lamp to falter.
nuance: Darkness isn't an enemy that attacks; it is simply what is there when the lamp fails. Read so, pallor is her natural state, and his embrace is what holds it off. Parimelazhagar's conclusion: if it waits for this tiny opening, what won't it do in a real separation?

couplet: I lay in his embrace, I turned unwittingly;
Forthwith this hue, as you might grasp it, came on me.
pope.gloss: I who was in close embrace just turned aside and the moment I did so, sallowness came on me like something to be seized on.

reading: The woman says she lay in his embrace and turned slightly, and at that the pallor was on her so thick it could be scooped up.
nuance: This is the chapter's most vivid hyperbole, and it is almost comic in its domesticity. Manakkudavar's setting makes it sad: he has left without telling her, and the friend sees the change in her next morning and is told this.

couplet: On me, because I pine, they cast a slur;
But no one says, 'He first deserted her.'
pope.gloss: Besides those who say "she has turned sallow" there are none who say "he has forsaken her".

reading: The woman says people will say she has grown pale, and no one says he has left her.
nuance: A flat remark about how blame is apportioned. The cause is invisible and the symptom is on her skin, so she bears the talk. Parimelazhagar reads the plural 'people' as aimed at the friend, whom she refuses to name in her anger.

couplet: Well! let my frame, as now, be sicklied o'er with pain,
If he who won my heart's consent, in good estate remain!
pope.gloss: If he is clear of guilt who has conciliated me (to his departure) let my body suffer its due and turn sallow.

reading: The woman says let her body go pale as it will, if the man who persuaded her is in a good state.

couplet: 'Tis well, though men deride me for my sickly hue of pain;
If they from calling him unkind, who won my love, refrain.
pope.gloss: It would be good to be said of me that I have turned sallow, if friends do not reproach with unkindness him who pleased me (then).

reading: The woman says that being called pale is good, if they won't spread talk of how unkind the man who won her has been.
nuance: Parimelazhagar pushes பசப்பெனப் பேர் to its limit: not 'she has pallor' but 'she is pallor', a loss of identity she says she will welcome. He also says she speaks in scorn at the friend, who has criticised him to help her. Her good name is what she is ready to give for his.

title: தனிப்படர்மிகுதி
theme: The surfeit of lonely grief turns into an argument about reciprocity. Mutual love is the seedless fruit and the timely rain; one-sided love is a carrying pole weighted at one end. The chapter asks what love is worth if it isn't returned.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. She starts with a run on mutuality (1191-1196), blames the love god (1197), and then turns to the absence of any word from him (1198-1200). Parimelazhagar's headnotes treat 1198 and 1200 as about a message that doesn't come.
source_issues: 1191: Manakkudavar's entry has பாலில்லாத where the sense requires பரலில்லாத, 'stoneless'.
1198: Parimelazhagar's entry ends without the usual '---' and its note isn't marked விளக்கம் as elsewhere. This is only a formatting difference.
1200: Parimelazhagar's note has கேட்பார் உறவினராகலானும், where the logic needs கேட்பார் உறவிலராகலானும். It looks like a corruption.
1196, 1199: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: The bliss to be beloved by those they love who gains,
Of love the stoneless, luscious fruit obtains.
pope.gloss: The women who are beloved by those whom they love, have they have not got the stone-less fruit of sexual delight ?

reading: The woman says those who are loved by the ones they love have obtained the stoneless fruit of love.
nuance: A fruit without a stone is enjoyment with nothing to spit out. The verse is general and ungendered, while Parimelazhagar makes it 'women loved by husbands', adds that this needs good deeds from before, and supplies the unstated close that she hasn't got this fruit.

couplet: As heaven on living men showers blessings from above,
Is tender grace by lovers shown to those they love.
pope.gloss: The bestowal of love by the beloved on those who love them is like the rain raining (at the proper season) on those who live by it.

reading: The woman says the grace shown by the beloved to the one who loves them is like the rain to those who live by it.
nuance: The grace here is measured and timely, as rain is, and Parimelazhagar takes that to include a man who returns from duty when he should. He brings out the shadow: if the rain fails, those dependent on it die.

couplet: Who love and are beloved to them alone
Belongs the boast, 'We've made life's very joys our own.'
pope.gloss: The pride that says "we shall live" suits only those who are loved by their beloved (husbands).

reading: The woman says the pride of saying 'we shall live' suits only those who are loved by those they love.
nuance: செருக்கு, 'pride', is usually a vice in the Kural, and here it is a privilege she envies. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar agree on the corollary: what suits her is death.

couplet: Those well-beloved will luckless prove,
Unless beloved by those they love.
pope.gloss: Even those who are esteemed (by other women) are devoid of excellence, if they are not loved by their beloved.

reading: The woman says that those who are esteemed are still without something, if they aren't loved by the one they love.
nuance: Manakkudavar ends with a proverb, கொண்டான் கயிற் கண்டான் காயும்: if the husband is angry at her, all who see her will be too. That gives a social reason why public esteem can't survive this loss.

couplet: From him I love to me what gain can be,
Unless, as I love him, he loveth me?
pope.gloss: He who is beloved by me, what will he do to me, if I am not beloved by him ?

reading: The woman asks what those she loves can do for her if they themselves don't love her.
nuance: It answers a compliment. Parimelazhagar has the friend say that she bore this well because of her love; the reply is that love has brought her only pain.

couplet: Love on one side is bad; like balanced load
By porter borne, love on both sides is good.
pope.gloss: Lust, like the weight of the KAVADI, pains if it lies in one end only but pleases if it is in both.

reading: The woman says love is painful when it is on one side only, and sweet on both sides, like the load of a carrying pole.
nuance: It is a physical fact that a load at both ends is easier than half that load at one. The verse therefore doesn't claim only that shared love is pleasant; shared love is also lighter to carry.

couplet: While Kaman rushes straight at me alone,
Is all my pain and wasting grief unknown?
pope.gloss: Would not cupid who abides and contends in one party (only) witness the pain and sorrow (in that party)?

reading: The woman asks whether Kaman, who works on one side alone, doesn't see her misery and grief.
nuance: A rare appearance of a named love god in the Kural, and the verse makes him a partial combatant. The older commentators take the theology seriously: for Parimelazhagar, a god should know all and be impartial, and for Manakkudavar, he wouldn't hurt her if he saw, being a god. Kalaignar's version has him as simply indifferent.

couplet: Who hear from lover's lips no pleasant word from day to day,
Yet in the world live out their life,- no braver souls than they!
pope.gloss: There is no one in the world so hard-hearted as those who can live without receiving (even) a kind word from their beloved.

reading: The woman says that no one in the world is harder than those who go on living without receiving a kind word from their beloved.
nuance: வன்கண் is ambiguous between hardness and courage, and Pope chooses 'braver'. The commentators read it as an accusation she makes against herself. Parimelazhagar notes that any word at all from him would count as sweet.

couplet: Though he my heart desires no grace accords to me,
Yet every accent of his voice is melody.
pope.gloss: Though my beloved bestows no love on one, still are his words sweet to my ears.

reading: The woman says that though the man she longs for gives no grace, even இசை from him is sweet to her ears.

couplet: Tell him thy pain that loves not thee?
Farewell, my soul, fill up the sea!
pope.gloss: Live, O my soul, would you who relate your great sorrow to strangers, try rather to fill up your own sea (of sorrow).

reading: The woman tells her heart that it wants to tell its pain to one who is not close, and that it may as well try to fill up the sea.
nuance: வாழிய, 'may you live', is sarcasm here for Parimelazhagar. The chapter ends with her declining what she spent the chapter wanting, and the sea from 1137 and 1164 comes back as a job to be done with a basket. It is an image of utter futility.

title: நினைந்தவர்புலம்பல்
theme: Remembering the absent lover as both the only thing keeping one alive and a burning pain. The chapter starts with a man's claim that memory itself gives joy, and turns to a woman who wonders whether she exists in his thoughts at all.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1201-1202 to the man, speaking to the friend who carried his message, and 1203-1210 to the woman. Manakkudavar gives 1202 to the woman.
source_issues: 1201: Manakkudavar's entry has நாமம் where the verse has காமம், a typo.
1202: The verse text has எனைத்தொனறு ஏனிதேகாண் where other sources read எனைத்தொன்று இனிதேகாண், apparently corrupt.
1204: Parimelazhagar's entry starts with the fragment தோஒ வுளரே யவர், the end of the verse text.
1205: Parimelazhagar's gloss ends with என்றான், the masculine form, for a verse spoken by the woman, apparently a typo; Manakkudavar's entry has several garbled words, such as எர்மை and காணாபோ.
1210: Parimelazhagar reports a variant, படாது, that yields the reading Manakkudavar gives.
1204, 1206, 1207: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: From thought of her unfailing gladness springs,
Sweeter than palm-rice wine the joy love brings.
pope.gloss: Sexuality is sweeter than liquor, because when remembered, it creates a most rapturous delight.

reading: The man says love is sweeter than liquor, because even thinking of it brings a great joy that doesn't fade.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's headnote has him speaking to the friend who has carried his message: his claim is also a report of loneliness and faithfulness. The older comparison with liquor gains a new term here, since liquor needs drinking while love needs only memory.

couplet: How great is love! Behold its sweetness past belief!
Think on the lover, and the spirit knows no grief.
pope.gloss: Even to think of one's beloved gives one no pain. Sexuality, in any degree, is always delightful.

reading: Love is sweet in every way, since thinking of the beloved brings no pain; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.

couplet: A fit of sneezing threatened, but it passed away;
He seemed to think of me, but do his fancies stray?
pope.gloss: I feel as if I am going to sneeze but do not, and (therefore) my beloved is about to think (of me) but does not.

reading: The woman wonders if he seems about to think of her and doesn't, since a sneeze seems to come and then dies away.
nuance: She reads her own body for evidence about his mind, using a folk belief that a sneeze means a distant loved one is thinking of you. Manakkudavar notes that she is repeating what ordinary women say, a rare moment of commentary on popular custom. An aborted sneeze makes for deflating, near-comic evidence.

couplet: Have I a place within his heart!
From mine, alas! he never doth depart.
pope.gloss: He continues to abide in my soul, do I likewise abide in his ?

reading: The woman asks whether she too has a place in his heart, for, ah, he is always in hers.
nuance: The verse uses the same indwelling that she argued for with such confidence in chapter 113, but now with doubt. Parimelazhagar extends the doubt into a tender either-or: is he kept away by unfinished work, or does he not remember her?

couplet: Me from his heart he jealously excludes:
Hath he no shame who ceaseless on my heart intrudes?
pope.gloss: He who has imprisoned me in his soul, is he ashamed to enter incessantly into mine.

reading: The woman asks whether he, who has barred her from his heart, isn't ashamed to keep coming into hers.
nuance: Her thoughts of him are treated as his actions, so she can rebuke him for trespassing. கடிகொண்டார் means he has guarded his heart against her; Pope's prose, 'imprisoned me in his soul', gets this backwards, though his couplet has it right.

couplet: How live I yet? I live to ponder o'er
The days of bliss with him that are no more.
pope.gloss: I live by remembering my (former) intercourse with him; if it were not so, how could I live ?

reading: The woman asks what else she could live by, since she lives only by remembering the days she shared with him.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sets it as a reply to the friend's advice to forget. He lists the things she lacks that would otherwise sustain her: his messenger, sending her own. Memory is what is left.

couplet: If I remembered not what were I then? And yet,
The fiery smart of what my spirit knows not to forget!
pope.gloss: I have never forgotten (the pleasure); even to think of it burns my soul; could I live, if I should ever forget it ?

reading: The woman asks what would become of her if she forgot, since she doesn't know forgetting, and even remembering burns.
nuance: A precise bind: remembering burns her, and forgetting would kill her, as Parimelazhagar supplies. Compare 1206, where memory is what keeps her alive.

couplet: My frequent thought no wrath excites. It is not so?
This honour doth my love on me bestow.
pope.gloss: He will not be angry however much I may think of him; is it not so much the delight my beloved affords me ?

reading: The woman says that however much she thinks of him, he doesn't get angry; that much is the honour her lover does her.
nuance: All she can claim is that he doesn't object to being thought of. Parimelazhagar hears the sarcasm directed at her friend's promise that he will come and bring her joy. Manakkudavar defines grace as not getting angry even at a fault, so the 'honour' is very small.

couplet: Dear life departs, when his ungracious deeds I ponder o'er,
Who said erewhile, 'We're one for evermore'.
pope.gloss: My precious life is wasting away by thinking too much on the cruelty of him who said we were not different.

reading: The woman says her dear life is ending, as she thinks too much about the lack of grace in one who said they weren't separate.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a key distinction: in her own words, it's not the parting that is killing her, but his lack of love.

couplet: Set not; so may'st thou prosper, moon! that eyes may see
My love who went away, but ever bides with me.
pope.gloss: May you live, O Moon! Do not set, that I mine see him who has departed without quitting my soul.

reading: The woman speaks to the moon, blessing it and asking about seeing with her eyes the man who went away without leaving her.
nuance: விடாஅது சென்றாரை, 'who left without leaving', packs the whole chapter's paradox into two words.

title: கனவுநிலையுரைத்தல்
theme: Dreams as the woman's way of staying alive. She argues that a lover who won't come when she is awake comes when she sleeps, and so waking life is the villain and the gossips are simply people who have never dreamed of a beloved.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's in Parimelazhagar's reading, except that Manakkudavar gives 1211 to the friend. Parimelazhagar sees her first praising the dream and using it to reassure her friend (1211-1216), then pained on waking (1217), and finally defending the man against the friend's blame (1218-1220).
source_issues: 1216: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is essentially the same as Parimelazhagar's gloss, including the word பாவி, so it isn't independent.
1212: Manakkudavar's entry has கடலுண்கண் where the verse has கயலுண்கண், apparently a typo.
1213, 1220: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: It came and brought to me, that nightly vision rare,
A message from my love,- what feast shall I prepare?
pope.gloss: Where with shall I feast the dream which has brought me my dear one's messenger ?

reading: What feast can be given to the dream that came with a message from the lover? The speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.
nuance: The Kural's great social duty of hospitality is turned on a dream guest. Parimelazhagar's little note gets the joke exactly: it is a guest for which one can find nothing to serve.

couplet: If my dark, carp-like eye will close in sleep, as I implore,
The tale of my long-suffering life I'll tell my loved one o'er.
pope.gloss: If my fish-like painted eyes should, at my begging, close in sleep, I could fully relate my sufferings to my lord.

reading: The woman says that if her carp-like kohl-lined eyes would sleep when she begs them to, she would tell the one who joined with her that she is surviving.
nuance: She must beg her eyes for sleep, after cursing them in chapter 118. Parimelazhagar notes her reason for preferring this to a messenger: there are things kept back from messengers, or shortened, which she could tell him in full.

couplet: Him, who in waking hour no kindness shows,
In dreams I see; and so my lifetime goes!
pope.gloss: My life lasts because in my dream I behold him who does not favour me in my waking hours.

reading: The woman says her life continues because she sees in her dreams the man who gives no grace in waking life.
nuance: Parimelazhagar takes it as a reassurance to the friend who worries: 'don't worry, I'm bearing up'. It may comfort the friend, but what it actually says is hardly comforting.

couplet: Some pleasure I enjoy when him who loves not me
In waking hours, the vision searches out and makes me see.
pope.gloss: There is pleasure in my dream, because in it I seek and obtain him who does not visit me in my wakefulness.

reading: The woman says there is pleasure in dreams, since they seek out and bring her the man who gives no grace in waking life.
nuance: The dream becomes an agent, a go-between travelling to where he is. That is what she wanted from her friend. Manakkudavar has the friend ask what use a dream is without real enjoyment, and the verse is her answer.

couplet: As what I then beheld in waking hour was sweet,
So pleasant dreams in hour of sleep my spirit greet.
pope.gloss: I saw him in my waking hours, and then it was pleasant; I see him just now in my dream, and it is (equally) pleasant.

reading: The woman says that what she saw in waking life was sweet only then, and likewise the dream is sweet at the time it is seen.
nuance: A strong philosophical move: both are equally over when over. Waking joy has no special standing in memory. Parimelazhagar's gloss is plain: 'the two are equal for me', and what she had before was no more than this.

couplet: And if there were no waking hour, my love
In d reams would never from my side remove.
pope.gloss: Were there no such thing as wakefulness, my beloved (who visited me) in my dream would not depart from me.

reading: The woman says that if there were no such thing as waking, her lover in the dream wouldn't leave.
nuance: Parimelazhagar supplies a charged word, பாவி, 'sinner', for waking, and reads ஒன்று as pointing up its cruelty. Waking is what barges in and parts them, so the person responsible for leaving is no longer him but waking itself.

couplet: The cruel one, in waking hour, who all ungracious seems,
Why should he thus torment my soul in nightly dreams?
pope.gloss: The cruel one who would not favour me in my wakefulness, what right has he to torture me in my dreams?

reading: The woman asks why the cruel one who gives no grace in waking life torments her in dreams.
nuance: A flat reversal of the last six verses, with the comfort now a torment. Parimelazhagar explains: on waking she doesn't find him, and because he vanishes from her shoulder, that too brings pain. He also tests a proverb against her case, that what isn't in waking isn't in dreams.

couplet: And when I sleep he holds my form embraced;
And when I wake to fill my heart makes haste!
pope.gloss: When I am asleep he rests on my shoulders, (but) when I awake he hastens into my soul.

reading: The woman says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder, and when she wakes he quickly moves into her heart.
nuance: In Parimelazhagar's reading she is defending him against her friend: he never leaves her at all. விரைந்து, 'quickly', gives the speed of a fugitive, and Manakkudavar hears the friend's tease that prompted it: where does he go when sleep ends?

couplet: In dreams who ne'er their lover's form perceive,
For those in waking hours who show no love will grieve.
pope.gloss: They who have no dear ones to behold in their dreams blame him who visits me not in my waking hours.

reading: The woman says those who haven't seen their lovers in dreams are the ones who blame the man for not being gracious in waking life.
nuance: This is an attack by pretending to speak about outsiders, as both commentators note. For Parimelazhagar she is hinting that the friend has no lover, which is a harsh thing to imply, and marks how angry the blaming makes her.

couplet: They say, that he in waking hours has left me lone;
In dreams they surely see him not,- these people of the town;
pope.gloss: The women of this place say he has forsaken me in my wakefulness. I think they have not seen him visit me in my dreams.

reading: The woman says that the people of this town say he has left her in waking life, and asks if they don't see him in dreams.
nuance: A surreal question, since no one else could see her dream. Parimelazhagar makes sense of it by way of the unity between her and her friend: if they are truly one, what the woman saw, the friend has seen too, and in not seeing she has become an outsider, 'this town'.

title: பொழுதுகண்டிரங்கல்
theme: Evening, once a friend, returns as an executioner. The woman speaks to the hour, quarrels with it and maps her sickness through the day, ending on the man whose nature, she says, has become wealth itself.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar has her addressing evening itself (1221-1222), answering her friend (1223-1227), and describing its signs and effects (1228-1230). The chapter's main contrast is between evening as it was when they were together and evening as it is now.
source_issues: 1229: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts at மாலை படர்தரும் போழ்து, so his headnote and main gloss are missing.
1230: Pope's prose is cut off mid-sentence ('at the thought of him who').
1222: Parimelazhagar's entry has மருள் வாலை - மயங்கிய மாலாய், typos for மாலை and மாலாய்/மாலையே.
1226: Parimelazhagar's note has a closing parenthesis with no opening one, which suggests that a word விளக்கம் has been lost.

couplet: Thou art not evening, but a spear that doth devour
The souls of brides; farewell, thou evening hour!
pope.gloss: Live, O you evening are you (the former) evening? No, you are the season that slays (married) women.

reading: The woman tells the hour, with a bitter blessing, that it isn't evening at all but வேலை, which eats the life of those once wed.

couplet: Thine eye is sad; Hail, doubtful hour of eventide!
Of cruel eye, as is my spouse, is too thy bride?
pope.gloss: A long life to you, O dark evening! You are sightless. Is your help-mate (also) as hard-hearted as mine.

reading: The woman says to the bewildered evening, may you live, you look sad-eyed; is your partner as hard-eyed as mine?
nuance: The tender moment of the chapter: she stops fighting the hour and sees it as a fellow sufferer. Parimelazhagar explains that the pale evening's fading of light is what suggests its grief, and says she has put her own inner state onto it. The word மருள் means both the mixing of day and night and being confused.

couplet: With buds of chilly dew wan evening's shade enclose;
My anguish buds space and all my sorrow grows.
pope.gloss: The evening that (once) came in with trembling and dimness (now) brings me an aversion for life and increasing sorrow.

reading: The woman says that evening, which comes with chill and pale, now comes with revulsion budding and sorrow growing.
nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses துனி strongly, as disgust with living. Evening used to tremble and pale before her when she was happy; now she trembles before it. Manakkudavar keeps the reversal smaller, with today's evening following yesterday's.

couplet: When absent is my love, the evening hour descends,
As when an alien host to field of battle wends.
pope.gloss: In the absence of my lover, evening comes in like slayers on the field of slaughter.

reading: The woman says that when her lover is absent, evening comes like enemies coming to a killing ground.
nuance: ஏதிலர் is the word she has been using of the town and of the man's accusers; Parimelazhagar glosses it here as 'those with no grace at all', executioners. That evening was once her friend is part of the pain.

couplet: O morn, how have I won thy grace? thou bring'st relief
O eve, why art thou foe! thou dost renew my grief.
pope.gloss: What good have I done to morning (and) what evil to evening?

reading: The woman asks what good she has done to morning and what enmity she has shown to evening.
nuance: It is framed as a legal puzzle about reward and punishment. Both commentators note a hidden reversal: morning used to be the hated hour, when they feared his leaving, and now it's the shore at the end of the flood of night. Evening made the opposite change.

couplet: The pangs that evening brings I never knew,
Till he, my wedded spouse, from me withdrew.
pope.gloss: Previous to my husband's departure, I know not the painful nature of evening.

reading: The woman says she didn't know that evening brings sickness, while he who wed her had not yet left.
nuance: It answers the most painful question: why did you consent? Parimelazhagar spells out that she would have refused had she known this. So 1181's self-accusation gets its answer: she agreed in ignorance.

couplet: My grief at morn a bud, all day an opening flower,
Full-blown expands in evening hour.
pope.gloss: This malady buds forth in the morning, expands all day long and blossoms in the evening.

reading: The woman says this sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and opens in the evening.
nuance: A flower is made a sickness, in a lovely, cruel inversion. Parimelazhagar's reasons are as vivid as the verse: at morning she is still comforted by a dream, by day memory thins, and at evening she watches creatures and people returning to their mates.

couplet: The shepherd's pipe is like a murderous weapon, to my ear,
For it proclaims the hour of ev'ning's fiery anguish near.
pope.gloss: The shepherd's flute now sounds as a fiery forerunner of night, and is become a weapon that slays (me).

reading: The woman says the herdsman's flute is a messenger for the burning evening and a weapon that kills.
nuance: The one sound in the chapter, pastoral and sweet in itself. Parimelazhagar reads it as a change from 'pleasant before' to deadly now. Evening has its own envoy and arms, like a king making war.

couplet: If evening's shades, that darken all my soul, extend;
From this afflicted town will would of grief ascend.
pope.gloss: When night comes on confusing (everyone's) mind, the (whole) town will lose its sense and be plunged in sorrow.

reading: The woman says that when evening spreads, bewildering the mind, the whole town is bewildered and suffers.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss is missing in this source, but his note says the unstated thought is 'I shall die', and he treats evening as Death, implying that the town grieves for her. He adds that others read it as her own mind reeling, and with so little of his comment left, I can't say which he preferred in full.

couplet: This darkening eve, my darkling soul must perish utterly;
Remembering him who seeks for wealth, but seeks not me.
pope.gloss: My (hitherto) unextinguished life is now lost in this bewildering night at the thought of him who

reading: The woman says that thinking of the one whose nature is wealth, in this confused evening, her life that wouldn't die is dying.
nuance: The wordplay does much of the work: பொருள்மாலை, 'wealth-natured', against மருள்மாலை, 'confused evening', and மாயும் against மாயா. For Parimelazhagar, he has broken his word to keep to wealth, so he has lost his nature to it. Manakkudavar says she takes him to have neither love nor virtue.

title: உறுப்புநலனழிதல்
theme: The woman's body as a public record of his absence. Eyes, shoulders and forehead lose their beauty, and each speaker reads that record differently: the friend sees an accusation, the woman refuses to let it be one, and the man, far away and turning for home, sees a reason to hurry.
structure_note: On Parimelazhagar's headnotes, the friend speaks to her in 1231-1235, the woman replies in 1236-1237, and the man, remembering on his way back, speaks in 1238-1240. Manakkudavar gives 1233 and 1234 to the woman, and places the start of the man's speech at 1239, saying three verses begin there.
source_issues: 1231: Pope's prose is cut off mid-word ('and shun (the').
1233: Parimelazhagar's entry ends with a stray underscore before ---.

1239: Manakkudavar's count of 'three verses from here' for the man doesn't match the chapter's end at 1240, unless his order differs from this one. 1238 is also in the man's voice in his gloss, which suggests a misplaced note.
1240: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: Thine eyes grown dim are now ashamed the fragrant flow'rs to see,
Thinking on him, who wand'ring far, leaves us in misery.
pope.gloss: While we endure the unbearable sorrow, your eyes weep for him who is gone afar, and shun (the

reading: The friend tells her that as she thinks of the man gone far away, leaving them this misery, her eyes are ashamed before fragrant flowers.

couplet: The eye, with sorrow wan, all wet with dew of tears,
As witness of the lover's lack of love appears.
pope.gloss: The discoloured eyes that shed tears p rofusely seem to betray the unkindness of our beloved.

reading: The friend says that her eyes, pale and running with tears, seem to be telling others of the unkindness of the one they desired.
nuance: போலும், 'seem', is doing precise work. Parimelazhagar calls it inference: others deduce what the eyes don't actually say. For the friend, the point is that weeping exposes him, so stop.

couplet: These withered arms, desertion's pangs abundantly display,
That swelled with joy on that glad nuptial day.
pope.gloss: The shoulders that swelled on the day of our union (now) seem to announce our separation clearly (to the public).

reading: Her shoulders, which swelled on the day of union, seem to announce loudly that he has left; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
nuance: The record needs both moments. Parimelazhagar says those who saw the swelling and now the wasting will quickly work out what happened. It is a before-and-after that is hard to explain away.

couplet: When lover went, then faded all their wonted charms,
And armlets' golden round slips off from these poor wasted arms.
pope.gloss: In the absence of your consort, your shoulders having lost their former beauty and fulness, your bracelets of pure gold have become loose.

reading: Her shoulders, their old beauty faded with her partner gone, have lost their fullness, and her bright bangles slip; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
nuance: தொல்கவின், 'old beauty', matters: for Parimelazhagar she has lost both the beauty he gave and the beauty she had before him. Commentators also differ over the bangle, gold for Parimelazhagar, emerald for Manakkudavar.

couplet: These wasted arms, the bracelet with their wonted beauty gone,
The cruelty declare of that most cruel one.
pope.gloss: The (loosened) bracelets, and the shoulders from which the old beauty has faded, relate the cruelty of the pitiless one.

reading: The friend says the shoulders, with bangles lost and old beauty faded, are declaring the cruelty of the cruel one.
nuance: The friend now says openly what 1232-1234 only implied, with both commentators attributing it to her. Manakkudavar gives the purpose: she blames him to help the woman bear up. That prepares the next verse.

couplet: I grieve, 'tis pain to me to hear him cruel chid,
Because the armlet from my wasted arm has slid.
pope.gloss: I am greatly pained to hear you call him a cruel man, just because your shoulders are reduced and your bracelets loosened.

reading: The woman tells her friend that with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts is hearing him called cruel.
nuance: The friend's strategy has backfired. Parimelazhagar spells out the claim: it's not his absence I can't bear, but what you say. Kalaignar widens the accusers from the friend to anyone who sees her. It's the same defence as in 1190.

couplet: My heart! say ought of glory wilt thou gain,
If to that cruel one thou of thy wasted arms complain?
pope.gloss: Can you O my soul! gain glory by relating to the (so-called) cruel one the clamour of my fading shoulders?

reading: The woman asks her heart if it could win any glory by telling the 'cruel' one of the uproar over her wasting shoulders.
nuance: A sardonic challenge. For Parimelazhagar, she says கொடியார் only in quotation, as in 'the one they call cruel'. He reads பூசல் as the friend's blame and her own distress, while Manakkudavar reads it as the town's gossip.

couplet: One day the fervent pressure of embracing arms I checked,
Grew wan the forehead of the maid with golden armlet decked.
pope.gloss: When I once loosened the arms that were in embrace, the forehead of the gold-braceleted women turned sallow.

reading: The man remembers that when he once loosened the arms that held her, the forehead of the girl with bright bangles turned pale.
nuance: The voice changes suddenly: we have been with her, and now he is far away and remembering. The conclusion, as Parimelazhagar gives it: if that much did this, what will this absence do? I must go quickly.

couplet: As we embraced a breath of wind found entrance there;
The maid's large liquid eyes were dimmed with care.
pope.gloss: When but a breath of breeze penetrated our embrace, her large cool eyes became sallow.

reading: The man remembers that when a cool breeze slipped between them in their embrace, the girl's large cool eyes grew pale.
nuance: Parimelazhagar draws the arithmetic: if a breeze could do this, what about mountains, forests and whole countries now between them? Manakkudavar says three verses of the man's speech begin here, which is a different division from Parimelazhagar's.

couplet: The dimness of her eye felt sorrow now,
Beholding what was done by that bright brow.
pope.gloss: Was it at the sight of what the bright forehead had done that the sallowness of her eyes became sad?

reading: The man asks whether the pallor in her eyes itself grew distressed on seeing what her bright forehead had done.
nuance: An odd and very ingenious image, and the commentary has to work hard. For Parimelazhagar, the eye's pallor is ashamed because the forehead paled faster, so her parts are competing to lose their beauty, and he should hurry. I find this plausible but can't be sure the verse means that much.

title: நெஞ்சொடுகிளத்தல்
theme: The woman argues with her own heart about what to do: find a remedy, stop suffering, go to him, or forget him. The heart is a separate party that can be scolded, sent away and accused, and the chapter ends without any option having won.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's, addressed to her heart. Parimelazhagar finds a plot: she urges her heart to go to him (1242-1246), shame stops her (1247), she scolds the heart for going ahead (1248-1249), and she tells it to forget (1250). Manakkudavar reads the verses as independent utterances.
source_issues: 1248: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts at பின்செல்வாய் பேதையென் னெஞ்சு, so the headnote and gloss are missing.
1243: Pope's prose has 'lewd thoughts' where the Tamil and his own couplet concern pity.
1242: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary. Parimelazhagar's gloss has அவா where அவர் seems intended.

couplet: My heart, canst thou not thinking of some med'cine tell,
Not any one, to drive away this grief incurable?
pope.gloss: O my soul, will you not think and tell me some medicine be it what it may, that can cure this incurable malady?

reading: The woman asks her heart to think and tell her of some medicine, of whatever kind, for this incurable sickness.
nuance: Parimelazhagar takes எனைத்தொன்றும், 'of any kind', very far: even a remedy that means giving up shame, which is dearer than life. The heart is asked because she herself no longer has the power to know.

couplet: Since he loves not, thy smart
Is folly, fare thee well my heart!
pope.gloss: May you live, O my soul! While he is without love, for you to suffer is (simple) folly.

reading: The woman tells her heart, with a mocking blessing, that it's folly for it to suffer when he has no love.
nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a surprising purpose in this: it isn't telling the heart to give up, but to stop waiting and go, since going would be wise. On this reading, it's the first move towards a woman going after a man.

couplet: What comes of sitting here in pining thought, O heart? He knows
No pitying thought, the cause of all these wasting woes.
pope.gloss: O my soul! why remain (here) and suffer thinking (of him)? There are no lewd thoughts (of you) in him who has caused you this disease of sorrow.

reading: The woman asks her heart why it sits and suffers, thinking of him, when the one who caused this sickness has no thought of pity.
nuance: இருந்து, 'sitting here', is the barb, because the alternatives are stated in Parimelazhagar's gloss: neither going to him nor dying. Waiting has become the worst option.

couplet: O rid me of these eyes, my heart; for they,
Longing to see him, wear my life away.
pope.gloss: O my soul! take my eyes also with you, (if not), these would eat me up (in their desire) to see him.

reading: The woman tells her heart to take the eyes with it if it goes, since they are eating her alive with longing to see him.
nuance: A practical request and one of the book's most physical: the body has parts she wants to send away. By Parimelazhagar's reading, this is a way to mean that she herself will go, since she can't part with her eyes.

couplet: O heart, as a foe, can I abandon utterly
Him who, though I long for him, longs not for me?
pope.gloss: O my soul! can he who loves not though he is beloved, be forsaken saying he hates me (now)?

reading: The woman asks her heart if one can really abandon him as an enemy, simply because he doesn't respond when she draws close.
nuance: The commentators shift the emphasis subtly. For Parimelazhagar, she lacks the strength to abandon him; for Manakkudavar, the issue is whether it would be proper. One treats loyalty as weakness, and the other treats it as what's right.

couplet: My heart, false is the fire that burns; thou canst not wrath maintain,
If thou thy love behold, embracing, soothing all thy pain.
pope.gloss: O my soul! when you see the dear one who remove dislike by intercourse, you are displeased and continue to be so. Nay, your displeasure is (simply) false.

reading: The woman tells her heart that when it sees the man who ends quarrels by union, it can't stay angry, and so its present anger is false.
nuance: She exposes her own anger as fake, calling it பொய்க்காய்வு. The heart is angry only while he's absent, and is no use when it would count.

couplet: Or bid thy love, or bid thy shame depart;
For me, I cannot bear them both, my worthy heart!
pope.gloss: O my good soul, give up either lust or honour, as for me I can endure neither.

reading: The woman tells her good heart to give up either desire or shame, since she can't bear both.
nuance: நன்னெஞ்சே, 'good heart', isn't flattery alone. For Parimelazhagar, the heart is good because holding on to both keeps her womanhood intact, but she can't afford that goodness, as her life is at stake. யானோ implies a split: 'you may be able to, I can't.'

couplet: Thou art befooled, my heart, thou followest him who flees from thee;
And still thou yearning criest: 'He will nor pity show nor love to me.'
pope.gloss: You are a fool, O my soul! to go after my departed one, while you mourn that he is not kind enough to favour you.

reading: The woman calls her heart a fool for following the man who has left, while lamenting that he isn't gracious.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's surviving note gives the logic: he saw her distress and left anyway, so how would telling him at a distance change anything? This reverses 1242-1244, where she was urging the heart to go.

couplet: My heart! my lover lives within my mind;
Roaming, whom dost thou think to find?
pope.gloss: O my soul! to whom would you repair, while the dear one is within yourself?

reading: The woman asks her heart whom it goes looking for, since her lover is within it.
nuance: Parimelazhagar says it's laughable to go looking outside for one who is inside. To me, this resembles the later devotional complaint about seeking God outside, though this resemblance isn't something the verse or its commentators claim.

couplet: If I should keep in mind the man who utterly renounces me,
My soul must suffer further loss of dignity.
pope.gloss: If I retain in my heart him who has left me without befriending me, I shall lose even the (inward) beauty that remains.

reading: The woman says that if she keeps in her heart the man who left without coming close, she will lose still more of her கவின்.

title: நிறையழிதல்
theme: The breaking of self-containment (நிறை). Desire is an axe against a door, a sneeze that can't be held back, a tyrant working her at midnight. The chapter ends with a woman who sets out to sulk and finds her heart has already gone over to him.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar has her reply to her friend's appeals for restraint (1251-1256), and then account for how she has yielded after he returned, in his setting from the courtesans (1257-1260).
source_issues: 1260: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts at புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல், so his headnote and gloss are missing.
1252: Parimelazhagar's note has a stray question mark and a garbled phrase, தொழிலின்கண்ணேயாடல் ?- ... தாயைப் பணி கோடல், where தன்னைப் பணி கோடல் seems intended.
1253, 1254: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption in வௌ¢ப்பட்டே and வௌ¢ப்படா.

couplet: Of womanly reserve love's axe breaks through the door,
Barred by the bolt of shame before.
pope.gloss: The axe of lust can break the door of chastity which is bolted with the bolt of modesty.

reading: The woman says that the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint, bolted with the bar of shame.
nuance: The architecture is exact, as Parimelazhagar explains: restraint is the door that keeps what is inside from being taken, shame is the bolt, since restraint holds as long as shame does. Manakkudavar has அறிவு, 'understanding', as the door, though the verse says நிறை.

couplet: What men call love is the one thing of merciless power;
It gives my soul no rest, e'en in the midnight hour.
pope.gloss: Even at midnight is my mind worried by lust, and this one thing, alas! is without mercy.

reading: The woman says that this thing called desire has no pity, for it puts her heart to work even at midnight.
nuance: The image is forced labour: everyone else's work stops at midnight, and hers doesn't. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar identify the task as sending the heart to him, which, Parimelazhagar notes, isn't a proper task for a woman, and is why she says 'this thing called desire'.

couplet: I would my love conceal, but like a sneeze
It shows itself, and gives no warning sign.
pope.gloss: I would conceal my lust, but alas, it yields not to my will but breaks out like a sneeze.

reading: The woman says she would hide her desire, but like a sneeze it comes out without her intending it.
nuance: The comparison is deliberately undignified. குறிப்பின்றி means without intent, using a word that in chapter 110 named her coded signs, which were deliberate. Now the sign sends itself.

couplet: In womanly reserve I deemed myself beyond assail;
But love will come abroad, and casts away the veil.
pope.gloss: I say I would be firm, but alas, my malady breaks out from its concealment and appears in public.

reading: The woman says she used to say she had restraint, yet her desire passes beyond concealment and comes out in public.
nuance: The tense matters, on Parimelazhagar's gloss: 'until today I thought of myself as restrained'. She has lost not only the restraint but also a belief about who she is.

couplet: The dignity that seeks not him who acts as foe,
Is the one thing that loving heart can never know.
pope.gloss: The dignity that would not go after an absent lover is not known to those who are sticken by love.

reading: The woman says the greatness of not going after one who has turned hostile is something those who are sick with love can't know.
nuance: Honour isn't rejected, but it's placed out of reach. Parimelazhagar gives the other half: those who don't have the sickness can know it, and he calls them the people of honour (மானம் உடையார்). He also softens going after to continual thought, and softens செற்றார், 'enemy', as one who has made time painful.

couplet: My grief how full of grace, I pray you see!
It seeks to follow him that hateth me.
pope.gloss: The sorrow I have endured by desiring to go after my absent lover, in what way is it excellent?

reading: The woman exclaims, in irony, how fine is the grief that has come to her, making her want to go after one who has turned hostile.
nuance: Both older commentators hear sarcasm in அளித்து, 'sweet', as they did in the night verse 1168, meaning the opposite. Her comment on her own condition has become a dry detachment.

couplet: No sense of shame my gladdened mind shall prove,
When he returns my longing heart to bless with love.
pope.gloss: I know nothing like shame when my beloved does from love (just) what is desired (by me).

reading: The woman says she knows nothing of shame when the man she loves does in desire what she longs for.

couplet: The words of that deceiver, versed in every wily art,
Are instruments that break through every guard of woman's heart!
pope.gloss: Are not the enticing words of my trick-abounding roguish lover the weapon that breaks away my feminine firmness?

reading: The woman says that the soft speech of that thief of many deceptions is the weapon that breaks her womanhood.
nuance: The chapter's picture of siege ends here, with Parimelazhagar glossing பெண்மை as restraint, a fortress taken by words. She knows them to be deceptive, and that doesn't protect her. பணிமொழி was how he praised her, in 1121.

couplet: 'I 'll shun his greeting'; saying thus with pride away I went:
I held him in my arms, for straight I felt my heart relent.
pope.gloss: I said I would feign dislike and so went (away); (but) I embraced him the moment I say my mind began to unite with him!

reading: The woman says she went away meaning to sulk, and embraced him when she saw her heart beginning to join with him.
nuance: She didn't yield to him but to her heart, and embracing is what's left when her instrument defects. Parimelazhagar says it exactly: the heart that is the means of sulking has itself turned into the means of joining.

couplet: 'We 'll stand aloof and then embrace': is this for them to say,
Whose hearts are as the fat that in the blaze dissolves away?
pope.gloss: Is it possible for those whose hearts melt like fat in the fire to say they can feign a strong dislike and remain so?

reading: The woman asks whether those whose hearts are like fat thrown in a fire can ever say 'we will join and then hold out in a sulk'.
nuance: An extraordinary image of unlovely and total melting: not wax or butter, but animal fat.

title: அவர்வயின்விதும்பல்
theme: Impatience for reunion on both sides of the distance. She has worn down her fingers counting days and rehearses how she will greet him, and, on Parimelazhagar's reading, he is stuck on campaign and starting to fear he may come back too late.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1261-1267 to the woman and 1268-1270 to the man, arguing against earlier commentators who give 1268 to the woman. Manakkudavar does give 1268 and 1270 to the woman.
source_issues: 1261: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts mid-gloss, without a headnote.
1267: The verse text has விரன் where the commentators and meaning require வரின். Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is the same as Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1268: Pope's prose has 'my wife', while his couplet is unclear about the speaker.
1263, 1266: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: My eyes have lost their brightness, sight is dimmed; my fingers worn,
With nothing on the wall the days since I was left forlorn.
pope.gloss: My finger has worn away by marking (on the wall) the days he has been absent while my eyes have lost their lustre and begin to fail.

reading: The woman says her eyes have lost their light and her fingers have worn down from marking the days since he left.
nuance: Fingers wear down from touching marks on a wall, in Parimelazhagar's and Kalaignar's picture, and from folding to count, in Manakkudavar's. The verse itself just says they marked the days. Either way, this is the book's most concrete image of waiting.

couplet: O thou with gleaming jewels decked, could I forget for this one day,
Henceforth these bracelets from my arms will slip, my beauty worn away.
pope.gloss: O you bright-jewelled maid, if I forget (him) today, my shoulders will lose their beauty even in the other life and make my bracelets loose.

reading: The woman tells her bright-jewelled friend that if she forgets him today, her beauty will leave and the bangles will slip from her shoulders thereafter.

couplet: On victory intent, His mind sole company he went;
And I yet life sustain! And long to see his face again!
pope.gloss: I still live by longing for the arrival of him who has gone out of love for victory and with valour as his guide.

reading: The woman says she still lives by longing for the return of the man who left, longing for victory, with his own resolve as his companion.
nuance: The pointed word is துணை, 'companion'. Parimelazhagar spells it out: he has scorned her as a partner and taken resolve instead. There are two longings set side by side, நசைஇ in each line, for victory and for him.

couplet: 'He comes again, who left my side, and I shall taste love's joy,'-
My heart with rapture swells, when thoughts like these my mind employ.
pope.gloss: My heart is rid of its sorrow and swells with rapture to think of my absent lover returning with his love.

reading: The woman says that thinking of the return of the man who left with the love they shared, her heart கோடுகொடேறும்.

couplet: O let me see my spouse again and sate these longing eyes!
That instant from my wasted frame all pallor flies.
pope.gloss: May I look on my lover till I am satisfied and thereafter will vanish the sallowness of my slender shoulders.

reading: The woman says may she see her husband till her eyes are full, and after that the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes what this is answering: the friend brings news that he's coming, and asks why she still pales. Her answer is that hearing won't do it, since the eyes must see. The news of the cure isn't the cure.

couplet: O let my spouse but come again to me one day!
I'll drink that nectar: wasting grief shall flee away.
pope.gloss: May my husband return some day; and then will I enjoy (him) so as to destroy all this agonizing sorrow.

reading: The woman says may her husband come one day, and she'll drink him in so that all this agonising sickness is destroyed.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes பருகுவன் drinking through all five senses, recalling 1101, and says that in that single day she'll destroy not only all past pain but all that might still come. That one day is asked to carry a lot.
