couplet: Shall I draw back, or yield myself, or shall both mingled be,
When he returns, my spouse, dear as these eyes to me.
pope.gloss: On the return of him who is as dear as my eyes, am I displeased or am I to embrace (him); or am I to do both?

reading: The woman asks, should he who is dear as her eyes return, whether she will sulk, embrace him or do both.
nuance: The chapter's real interest here is the planning, with him not yet home. Parimelazhagar sets aside an alternative, that the third means to behave as if nothing happened: she wants to do all three, and that's her impatience.

couplet: O would my king would fight, o'ercome, devide the spoil;
At home, to-night, the banquet spread should crown the toil.
pope.gloss: Let the king fight and gain (victories); (but) let me be united to my wife and feast the evening.

reading: Let the king fight and win, and let there be a home-joined feast for the evening; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and Kalaignar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
nuance: Parimelazhagar rejects the woman's reading at length, on the grounds that she wouldn't name the king rather than the husband. But Manakkudavar gives a reason for that: the king's unfinished war is what holds him back. Evening, the woman's executioner, is for the man a feast to come.

couplet: One day will seem like seven to those who watch and yearn
For that glad day when wanderers from afar return.
pope.gloss: To those who suffer waiting for the day of return of their distant lovers one day is as long as seven days.

reading: One day passes like seven for those who pine with an eye on the day when those far away return; Parimelazhagar gives it to the man, projecting her pain, and the other commentators name no speaker.
nuance: Parimelazhagar uses the general phrasing as proof that it can't be the woman: she would say 'me', so the man is imagining how it is for her. If he's right, it's a rare moment in the book when a man grasps the other side of his absence. He takes 'seven' as meaning many.

couplet: What's my return, the meeting hour, the wished-for greeting worth,
If she heart-broken lie, with all her life poured forth?
pope.gloss: After (my wife) has died of a broken heart, what good will there be if she is to receive me, has received me, or has even embraced me?

reading: What use is it if she gets, or has got, or even touches, once the heart has broken and spilled? The speaker is the man, of her, for Parimelazhagar, and the woman, of herself, for Manakkudavar.

title: குறிப்பறிவுறுத்தல்
theme: Communicating what can't be said. Thread within crystal, scent within a bud, and the movement of her gaze from bangles to shoulders to feet: unspoken signs carry the fear of a new parting and the resolve to go with him. It is the book's mature counterpart to the first signs of chapter 110.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar sets this after a reunion, when the man's new tenderness makes her fear another departure. In his plan, the man speaks in 1271-1275, the woman in 1276-1278, her friend in 1279, and the man in 1280. Manakkudavar gives 1275 and 1280 to the friend and often reads the verses as belonging to courtship.
source_issues: 1271: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is close to word for word Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1271, 1275-1277, 1279, 1280: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption in தௌ¢ where தெளி is intended.
1275: Pope's prose reads கள்ளம் as 'well-meant departure', with no support from the commentators.

couplet: Thou hid'st it, yet thine eye, disdaining all restraint,
Something, I know not, what, would utter of complaint.
pope.gloss: Though you would conceal (your feelings), your painted eyes would not, for, transgressing (their bounds), they tell (me) something.

reading: The man tells her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes have gone beyond her control and have something they want to say.
nuance: In Parimelazhagar's setting the man has returned and is lavishing affection on her, and she takes fright, which makes this a kind of tragic misunderstanding. Kalaignar has the eyes declare love that resists separation. The verse only says there is something.

couplet: The simple one whose beauty fills mine eye, whose shoulders curve
Like bambu stem, hath all a woman's modest sweet reserve.
pope.gloss: Unusually great is the female simplicity of your maid whose beauty fills my eyes and whose shoulders resemble the bamboo.

reading: The man says this artless girl who fills his eyes, with her bamboo shoulders, has a great measure of womanly nature.
nuance: The compliment may be a rebuke. Parimelazhagar glosses நீர்மை as மடமை, 'naivety', and has him complain to her friend that she fears a separation he has no thought of. Kalaignar takes it as simple praise.

couplet: As through the crystal beads is seen the thread on which they 're strung
So in her beauty gleams some thought cannot find a tongue.
pope.gloss: There is something that is implied in the beauty of this woman, like the thread that is visible in a garland of gems.

reading: The man says that, like the thread that shows in strung gems, there is something that shows through this young woman's beauty.
nuance: The gem image needs transparent stones, and Parimelazhagar says crystal: inside but visible. What is inside isn't compatible with the outer beauty, he says, but appears with it.

couplet: As fragrance in the opening bud, some secret lies
Concealed in budding smile of this dear damsel's eyes.
pope.gloss: There is something in the unmatured smile of this maid like the fragrance that is contained in an unblossomed bud.

reading: The man says there is something within the bud of this girl's smile, like the scent within a closed bud.
nuance: It's a companion to 1273, except that here nothing shows: scent inside a bud can't be perceived, so his certainty about it is a matter of faith. Manakkudavar sets it in courtship, with the man telling his own heart that her smile promises joy, and Kalaignar says the smile holds the memory of her lover.

couplet: The secret wiles of her with thronging armlets decked,
Are medicines by which my raising grief is checked.
pope.gloss: The well-meant departure of her whose bangles are tight-fitting contains a remedy that can cure my great sorrow.

reading: The stealth with which the tight-bangled woman slipped away holds a medicine for great sorrow; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

couplet: While lovingly embracing me, his heart is only grieved:
It makes me think that I again shall live of love bereaved.
pope.gloss: The embrace that fills me with comfort and gladness is capable of enduring (my former) sorrow and meditating on his want of love.

reading: The woman tells her friend that his great comfort and eager lovemaking contains in it her having to endure hardship again and to think about his lack of love.
nuance: A sad piece of reading. His tenderness is the very thing that gives him away, since she reasons from excess of kindness to a coming parting. Both older commentators give it to her, speaking to the friend.

couplet: My severance from the lord of this cool shore,
My very armlets told me long before.
pope.gloss: My bracelets have understood before me the (mental) separation of him who rules the cool seashore.

reading: The woman says her bangles knew before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted from her.
nuance: Parimelazhagar makes the separation inward: he is still physically with her but has left in his mind. Her body has registered this before her understanding did. So bangles, the book's most public symptom, are here her private source of knowledge.

couplet: My loved one left me, was it yesterday?
Days seven my pallid body wastes away!
pope.gloss: It was but yesterday my lover departed (from me); and it is seven days since my complexion turned sallow.

reading: The woman says that her lover left only yesterday, and her body has been pale for seven days.
nuance: The sum doesn't add up, on purpose. The pain started before the event, because she read it coming.

couplet: She viewed her tender arms, she viewed the armlets from them slid;
She viewed her feet: all this the lady did.
pope.gloss: She looked at her bracelets, her tender shoulders, and her feet; this was what she did there (significantly).

reading: Parimelazhagar's speaker, the friend, tells the man that she looked at her bangles, looked at her soft shoulders and looked at her feet: this is what she did there.
nuance: The whole verse is a silent gesture, and the commentators read it as a sentence: 'these will slip if you leave me; these will thin; so I'll go with you on these'. The verse itself doesn't state the conclusion. This is perhaps the most purely dramatic thing in the Kural, and the friend's 'that's what she did' leaves him to work it out.

couplet: To show by eye the pain of love, and for relief to pray,
Is womanhood's most womanly device, men say.
pope.gloss: To express their love-sickness by their eyes and resort to begging bespeaks more than ordinary female excellence.

reading: Those who know say that telling love's sickness with the eyes and begging adds more womanhood to womanhood; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

title: புணர்ச்சிவிதும்பல்
theme: The eagerness for union overrides every plan to sulk. She can't see his faults once he is in view, and sets out to quarrel but her heart betrays her. The chapter's most quoted verse states why: love is more delicate than a flower, and few catch its moment.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1281-1287 to the woman speaking to her friend, 1288 to the friend speaking to the man, and 1289-1290 to the man, faced with a sulk that won't end. Manakkudavar gives 1288 and 1289 to the woman.
source_issues: 1283: Pope's prose makes the eyes disregard the speaker, which conflicts with his couplet and with the commentators.
1288: Parimelazhagar's headnote has a stray question mark, புணர்ச்சி? விதுப்பு.

couplet: Gladness at the thought, rejoicing at the sight,
Not palm-tree wine, but love, yields such delight.
pope.gloss: To please by thought and cheer by sight is peculiar, not to liquor but lust.

reading: The woman says that being intoxicated at a thought and delighted at a look belong not to liquor but to love.
nuance: Parimelazhagar's setting is pointed: the friend teases her about why she isn't angry at a man planning to leave. So the famous line is an excuse. He also distinguishes the words: களித்தல், with awareness intact, and மகிழ்தல், with awareness lost.

couplet: When as palmyra tall, fulness of perfect love we gain,
Distrust can find no place small as the millet grain.
pope.gloss: If women have a lust that exceeds even the measure of the palmyra fruit, they will not desire (to feign) dislike even as much as the millet.

reading: The woman says that when love fills to the size of a palmyra tree, there should be no sulking, not even the size of a millet seed.
nuance: The huge and tiny are the proverbial measures. Parimelazhagar says she seems to be giving others good advice, and is in fact describing her own eagerness. Manakkudavar has her say this to her own heart, which is thinking of sulking.

couplet: Although his will his only law, he lightly value me,
My heart knows no repose unless my lord I see.
pope.gloss: Though my eyes disregard me and do what is pleasing to my husband, still will they not be satisfied unless they see him.

reading: The woman says that though he disregards her and does only what pleases him, her eyes won't rest without seeing him.
nuance: It's a clear admission, with no self-deception. He is at fault, she knows it, and the eyes don't care. Pope's prose wrongly makes the eyes the ones who disregard her; the commentators and his couplet agree it is the man.

couplet: My friend, I went prepared to show a cool disdain;
My heart, forgetting all, could not its love restrain.
pope.gloss: O my friend! I was prepared to feign displeasure but my mind forgetting it was ready to embrace him.

reading: The woman tells her friend that she went there to sulk, but her heart forgot that and went there to unite.
nuance: The same verb, சென்றேன் and சென்றது, is used for both: she and her heart set out together and went to different places. Parimelazhagar's word for this is அறைபோக, treason in a military sense.

couplet: The eye sees not the rod that paints it; nor can I
See any fault, when I behold my husband nigh.
pope.gloss: Like the eyes which see not the pencil that paints it, I cannot see my husband's fault (just) when I meet him.

reading: The woman says that, as the eye can't see the stick that lines it at the moment of lining, she doesn't see her husband's fault when she sees him.
nuance: A wonderfully precise image: the object is at its closest and most intimate exactly when it can't be seen. Parimelazhagar notes that the eye knows the stick well enough at other times, and so she too knows his faults.

couplet: When him I see, to all his faults I 'm blind;
But when I see him not, nothing but faults I find.
pope.gloss: When I see my husband, I do not see any faults; but when I do not see him, I do not see anything but faults.

reading: The woman says that when she sees him she doesn't see his faults, and when she doesn't see him she sees nothing but his faults.
nuance: A perfectly symmetrical verse about what presence does to judgement. As with the previous verse, this isn't presented as an illusion that she can see through and correct; it's just how it is. Sight is what removes her power to judge him.

couplet: As those of rescue sure, who plunge into the stream,
So did I anger feign, though it must falsehood seem?
pope.gloss: Like those who leap into a stream which they know will carry them off, why should a wife feign dislike which she knows cannot hold out long?

reading: The woman asks what use it is to sulk, knowing it will fail, like those who jump into a stream knowing it will carry them off.
nuance: Parimelazhagar registers a strain in the syntax, and offers an alternate shape: 'I learned by trying once that sulking fails; I won't do it again'. Pope's couplet is rather different in having a rescue. The swimmer who knows she'll be swept away jumps in anyway, and the verse doesn't deny that this might be the fun of it.

couplet: Though shameful ill it works, dear is the palm-tree wine
To drunkards; traitor, so to me that breast of thine!
pope.gloss: O you rogue! your breast is to me what liquor is to those who rejoice in it, though it only gives them an unpleasant disgrace.

reading: Thief, your chest is to us as liquor is to those who drink it, though it does them shameful harm; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.

couplet: Love is tender as an opening flower. In season due
To gain its perfect bliss is rapture known to few.
pope.gloss: Sexual delight is more delicate than a flower, and few are those who understand its real nature.

reading: Love is softer than a flower, and few attain its moment; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman, to her heart, for Manakkudavar.
nuance: The famous line has a practical use. Parimelazhagar lists what makes this moment rare: two people need to share intent, desire, enjoyment and pleasure at one time, in a fit place, moment and setting. He has the man saying this to end her sulk, so the maxim is also a plea.

couplet: Her eye, as I drew nigh one day, with anger shone:
By love o'erpowered, her tenderness surpassed my own.
pope.gloss: She once feigned dislike in her eyes, but the warmth of her embrace exceeded my own.

reading: The man recalls that she sulked with her eyes alone and then, more eager than he for the embrace, was undone.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives this an edge: spoken during her present sulk, it means 'the woman who gave up so quickly was not this one'. Manakkudavar has him simply observing her now. A rare moment of him looking back on her eagerness, and one that might flatter him.

title: நெஞ்சொடுபுலத்தல்
theme: Quarrelling with one's own heart for taking the other side. The woman charges it with disloyalty for loving him when she wants to sulk, and the chapter ends in the man's voice, on Parimelazhagar's reading, with both lovers facing the same discovery: one's own heart may not be on one's side.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1291-1298 to the woman, addressing or describing her heart, and 1299-1300 to the man, in a sulk he can't end. Manakkudavar gives 1299 to the woman.
source_issues: 1295, 1298: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.
1299: Parimelazhagar's gloss has பணை அல் வழி where the verse has துணையல் வழி, a typo.
1293: Parimelazhagar's note has a misplaced விளக்கம் inside the Kalittokai citation.

couplet: You see his heart is his alone
O heart, why not be all my own?
pope.gloss: O my soul! although you have seen how his soul stands by him, how is it you do not stand by me?

reading: The woman asks her heart why it isn't hers, when it has seen how his heart belongs to him.
nuance: An elegantly sharp opening. Two hearts are compared as servants, and his has a better idea of loyalty. Parimelazhagar adds the sting: even those who can't figure out what to do can copy someone else, and the heart won't do even that.

couplet: 'Tis plain, my heart, that he 's estranged from thee;
Why go to him as though he were not enemy?
pope.gloss: O my soul! although you have known him who does not love me, still do you go to him, saying "he will not be displeased."

reading: The woman says that her heart, even after seeing that he isn't close to her, goes to him as if he weren't hostile.
nuance: The heart's reason is the small hope, that he won't be angry. Parimelazhagar says it's relying on old familiarity, which is a thin basis, and calls it the greatest folly.

couplet: 'The ruined have no friends, 'they say; and so, my heart,
To follow him, at thy desire, from me thou dost depart.
pope.gloss: O my soul! do you follow him at pleasure under the belief that the ruined have no friends?

reading: The woman asks her heart if it follows him as it pleases, on the principle that the ruined have no friends.
nuance: A piece of proverbial wisdom about false friends, turned against the heart. By using it she also admits that she is the one ruined. Parimelazhagar glosses கெட்டார் as her loss of honour, and the verse casts her heart as a fair-weather friend.

couplet: 'See, thou first show offended pride, and then submit,' I bade;
Henceforth such council who will share with thee my heart?
pope.gloss: O my soul! you would not first seem sulky and then enjoy (him); who then would in future consult you about such things?

reading: The woman tells her heart that it won't first sulk and then enjoy, so no one will plan such things with it any more.
nuance: It's almost comic: she drops the heart from her team as an unreliable accomplice. Sulking here is a strategy with a sequence to it, sulk first and enjoy later, and the heart can't wait.

couplet: I fear I shall not gain, I fear to lose him when I gain;
And thus my heart endures unceasing pain.
pope.gloss: My soul fears when it is without him; it also fears when it is with him; it is sub ject to incessant sorrow.

reading: The woman says her heart fears not having him and, on having him, fears parting, so it is in endless grief.
nuance: In Parimelazhagar's setting she says this within the hearing of a friend who has come as an envoy, so it also means she will let him in. He observes that there is no third state, which makes this grief complete.

couplet: My heart consumes me when I ponder lone,
And all my lover's cruelty bemoan.
pope.gloss: My mind has been (here) in order to eat me up (as it were) whenever I think of him in my solitude.

reading: The woman says that when she sits alone and thinks of him, her heart is there only to eat her.
nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the irony: it stays with her only to work on her, not to help her quarrel. Manakkudavar gives this a small domestic turn: she tells the friend, 'you've come now, and so I've escaped it'.

couplet: Fall'n 'neath the sway of this ignoble foolish heart,
Which will not him forget, I have forgotten shame.
pope.gloss: I have even forgotten my modesty, having been caught in my foolish mind which is not dignified enough to forget him.

reading: The woman says that, stuck with this worthless, foolish heart that can't forget him, she has even forgotten shame.
nuance: There are two forgettings in tension. Parimelazhagar's definition of shame is one of the finest things in his commentary: however long two have been together, to shrink as if seeing the other for the first time. His definition of the heart's foolishness: remembering when he's away, forgetting when he's there.

couplet: If I contemn him, then disgrace awaits me evermore;
My soul that seeks to live his virtues numbers o'er.
pope.gloss: My soul which clings to life thinks only of his (own) gain in the belief that it would be disgraceful for it to despise him.

reading: The woman says her heart, thinking it would be disgraceful to despise him, keeps thinking of what pertains to him, out of உயிர்க்காதல்.

couplet: And who will aid me in my hour of grief,
If my own heart comes not to my relief?
pope.gloss: Who would help me out of one's distress, when one's own soul refuses help to one?

reading: Who will be a companion in grief, when one's own heart is no companion? The speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
nuance: If it's the man, then he has come to the state she has been in for ten verses. His heart is doing to him what hers did: urging union when he should be standing firm.

couplet: A trifle is unfriendliness by aliens shown,
When our own heart itself is not our own!
pope.gloss: It is hardly possible for strangers to behave like relations, when one's own soul acts like a stranger.

reading: The man, for Parimelazhagar, says that it's no wonder if strangers aren't one's own, when one's own heart isn't.
nuance: Parimelazhagar gives a witty aim: 'stranger' here is the sulking woman, who no longer seems his beloved, so if his own heart pains him for her sake, it's a small thing if she, a stranger, sulks. The other commentators don't name a speaker, and read it as a maxim.

title: புலவி
theme: Sulking and its right measure. The quarrel is salt: just enough makes love tasty and a little more spoils it. Nothing holds it in check except that the other person cares, as the chapter's closing verses, in which the man finds her sulk has gone too far, make clear.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar has the friend tease and advise (1301-1302), the woman send the man back to the courtesans with sarcasm (1303-1304), the man reflect on sulking after making up (1305-1307), and the man again, in a sulk he can't end (1308-1310). Manakkudavar differs on 1305, 1306 and 1308.
source_issues: 1305: Kalaignar's entry ends with stray text, உ. இடைமிடை சொல்நலம் ..., editorial matter about reading the Kural that is not commentary on this verse. It was not used.
1303: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], repeats Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1302: Parimelazhagar's headnote has அவர் சொல்லியது where அவள் seems intended, given the friend's voice.
1310: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: Be still reserved, decline his profferred love;
A little while his sore distress we 'll prove.
pope.gloss: Let us witness awhile his keen suffering; just feign dislike and embrace him not.

reading: The friend tells the woman not to embrace him but to sulk, so that they may watch his sharp pain for a little while.
nuance: It's mischief with a purpose. Parimelazhagar says the friend has actually come as his envoy, and sides with the woman, teasing, as a way of bringing her round. சிறிது, 'a little', is the word that matters: the quarrel mustn't go on long.

couplet: A cool reserve is like the salt that seasons well the mess,
Too long maintained, 'tis like the salt's excess.
pope.gloss: A little dislike is like salt in proportion; to prolong it a little is like salt a little too much.

reading: The friend says that sulking is like the right amount of salt, and letting it go on a little too long is like a little too much salt.
nuance: The image puts sulking in the kitchen, as an everyday and necessary ingredient without any drama. The second line is exact: just a little too much is enough to spoil it. Kalaignar makes the measure a time span, and Parimelazhagar makes it knowing when desire is about to fade.

couplet: 'Tis heaping griefs on those whose hearts are grieved;
To leave the grieving one without a fond embrace.
pope.gloss: For men not to embrace those who have feigned dislike is like torturing those already in agony.

reading: The woman says that not embracing those who have sulked with you is like adding sharp pain to those already in distress.

couplet: To use no kind conciliating art when lover grieves,
Is cutting out the root of tender winding plant that droops.
pope.gloss: Not to reconcile those who have feigned dislike is like cutting a faded creeper at its root.

reading: The woman says that not reconciling those who have sulked is like cutting a withered creeper at its root.

couplet: Even to men of good and worthy mind, the petulance
Of wives with flowery eyes lacks not a lovely grace.
pope.gloss: An increased shyness in those whose eyes are like flowers is beautiful even to good and virtuous husbands.

reading: The grace of those good in their virtues is the depth of sulking in flower-eyed women; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

couplet: Love without hatred is ripened fruit;
Without some lesser strife, fruit immature.
pope.gloss: Sexual pleasure, without prolonged and short-lived dislike, is like too ripe, and unripe fruit.

reading: Without serious and light quarrels, love is like over-ripe fruit and unripe fruit; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
nuance: There are two kinds of quarrels for two kinds of failure, and the verse uses them in order: no deep quarrel, and love is fruit going off; no light quarrel, and love is unripe. Manakkudavar supplies the tastes, sour and astringent. Pope's couplet reads 'ripened fruit' as a good thing, and the commentators don't.

couplet: A lovers' quarrel brings its pain, when mind afraid
Asks doubtful, 'Will reunion sweet be long delayed?'
pope.gloss: The doubt as to whether intercourse would take place soon or not, creates a sorrow (even) in feigned dislike.

reading: The man says there is one pain even within sulking: the worry about whether union will be delayed or not.
nuance: This is where the game has its risk. Parimelazhagar takes it as the worry that union will be put off, and Kalaignar as a worry that the time for union will shrink. In either case, the player can't be sure the quarrel will end in time.

couplet: What good can grieving do, when none who love
Are there to know the grief thy soul endures?
pope.gloss: What avails sorrow when I am without a wife who can understand the cause of my sorrow?

reading: What use is it to suffer, when there is no lover who knows that this person is suffering? The speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar, and the friend, speaking to him, for Manakkudavar.

couplet: Water is pleasant in the cooling shade;
So coolness for a time with those we love.
pope.gloss: Like water in the shade, dislike is delicious only in those who love.

reading: The man says water is sweet in the shade, and sulking too is sweet only with those who love.
nuance: It's a reciprocal theory of sulking. A quarrel is a pleasure only inside a shared love, and without it there is only heat. Parimelazhagar applies this pointedly: she doesn't feel this for him, and so her sulk is unpleasant.

couplet: Of her who leaves me thus in variance languishing,
To think within my heart with love is fond desire.
pope.gloss: It is nothing but strong desire that makes her mind unite with me who can leave her to her own dislike.

reading: The man, in Parimelazhagar's reading, says that his heart's wish to join with someone who leaves a sulk to wither is simply craving.
nuance: அவா, 'craving', is a strong word to use on one's own heart, with a long negative history in the Kural's ethics. He diagnoses himself exactly as the ascetic chapter might, and it doesn't stop him.

title: புலவி நுணுக்கம்
theme: The fine points of sulking, a comedy of jealous logic. Every word he says, every sneeze, whether he hides it or not, whether he pleads or looks, is turned into evidence. It is the most purely entertaining chapter in the Kural, and it also shows how love trains two people in close reading.
structure_note: The woman speaks in 1311-1312. The man speaks in 1313-1320, telling her friend about it on Parimelazhagar's reading, with the woman's words quoted in each verse. The chapter's last line in several verses is what she said.
source_issues: 1318, 1319: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.
1320: Manakkudavar's entry ends with கரியது, a typo for கூறியது.
1315, 1319: Parimelazhagar's notes have a character corruption, வௌ¢ப்படு and தௌ¢.
1311: Parimelazhagar's note has நுணக்கமாயிற்று, a typo for நுணுக்கமாயிற்று.

couplet: From thy regard all womankind Enjoys an equal grace;
O thou of wandering fickle mind, I shrink from thine embrace!
pope.gloss: You are given to prostitution; all those who are born as womankind enjoy you with their eyes in an ordinary way. I will not embrace you.

reading: The woman calls him a philanderer and refuses his chest, because all women feast on him in common with their eyes.
nuance: The offence is only that he was seen, and being seen is a form of being consumed. பரத்த is applied to him in the vocative, and is the verse's own word for his straying.

couplet: One day we silent sulked; he sneezed: The reason well I knew;
He thought that I, to speak well pleased, Would say, 'Long life to you!'
pope.gloss: When I continued to be sulky he sneezed and thought I would (then) wish him a long life.

reading: The woman tells her friend that while she was sulking he sneezed, knowing she would then say 'long life' and so break her silence.
nuance: A real gem of observed domestic strategy. Parimelazhagar says what makes this a 'fine point': she takes a natural sneeze for a deliberate sign. We can't tell if he meant it, and that is the fun.

couplet: I wreathed with flowers one day my brow, The angry tempest lowers;
She cries, 'Pray, for what woman now Do you put on your flowers?'
pope.gloss: Even if I were adorned with a garland of branch-flowers, she would say I did so to show it to another woman.

reading: The man tells her friend that even if he wears a wreath of bent flowers, she is angry and says he wore it to show some other woman.
nuance: The word கோட்டுப்பூ is a puzzle. Parimelazhagar offers flowers woven in a curve or flowers from another landscape, Manakkudavar offers side-worn flowers, and Kalaignar flowers from a tree-branch. The offence doesn't depend on the answer, which is the point.

couplet: 'I love you more than all beside,' 'T was thus I gently spoke;
'What all, what all?' she instant cried; And all her anger woke.
pope.gloss: When I said I loved her more than any other woman, she said "more than others, yes, more than others," and remained sulky.

reading: The man says he told her he loved more than anyone, and she sulked: 'than whom, than whom?'
nuance: A grammatical quarrel. He meant 'we love more than any other couple', and she took it to mean 'more than the other women I love'. The commentators spell this out, and the verse gives only her repeated words, one of the most natural bits of speech in the book.

couplet: 'While here I live, I leave you not,' I said to calm her fears.
She cried, 'There, then, I read your thought'; And straight dissolved in tears.
pope.gloss: When I said I would never part from her in this life her eyes were filled with tears.

reading: The man says he told her they wouldn't part in this birth, and her eyes filled with tears.
nuance: A promise made in the language of rebirth backfires on its own qualifier: 'in this birth' implies 'not in the next'. Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar explain it so. Kalaignar has her ask 'is there a next birth, then?', which is a modern touch that isn't in the verse. Rebirth is taken for granted, as material for a joke.

couplet: 'Each day I called to mind your charms,' 'O, then, you had forgot,'
She cried, and then her opened arms, Forthwith embraced me not.
pope.gloss: When I said I had remembered her, she said I had forgotten her and relaxing her embrace, began to feign dislike.

reading: The man says he told her he had thought of her, and she said 'why did you forget?', and wouldn't embrace him, and went into a sulk.
nuance: A strict logical inference, and Parimelazhagar uses a term from Indian logic for it, அருத்தாபத்தி: remembering presupposes forgetting. She is using the man's own argument from 1125.

couplet: She hailed me when I sneezed one day; But straight with anger seized,
She cried; 'Who was the woman, pray, Thinking of whom you sneezed?'
pope.gloss: When I sneezed she blessed me, but at once changed (her mind) and wept, asking, "At the thought of whom did you sneeze?"

reading: The man says that when he sneezed she blessed him, and then undid it and wept: 'who were you thinking of, that you sneezed?'
nuance: The blessing comes automatically and the suspicion comes a second later, and the verse catches that interval. Parimelazhagar notes that the belief behind this is a women's usage (மகளிர் வழக்கு) and that she's taking it as literal fact.

couplet: And so next time I checked my sneeze; She forthwith wept and cried,
(That woman difficult to please), 'Your thoughts from me you hide'.
pope.gloss: When I suppressed my sneezing, she wept saying, "I suppose you (did so) to hide from me your own people's remembrance of you".

reading: The man says that when he suppressed a sneeze, she wept: 'are you hiding from me that your people are thinking of you?'
nuance: It's the next stage of the farce. He has learned from 1317, and that's now the crime. Parimelazhagar sums it up: it's a fault to sneeze and a fault not to. So what is there to do?

couplet: I then began to soothe and coax, To calm her jealous mind;
'I see', quoth she, 'to other folks How you are wondrous kind'
pope.gloss: Even when I try to remove her dislike, she is displeased and says, "This is the way you behave towards (other women)."

reading: The man says that even when he tries to appease her, she is angry and says that this is how he behaves with other women too.
nuance: The cure has become evidence. Parimelazhagar notes the extra detail: he has even admitted to faults he didn't commit in order to placate her, and that confession is what now counts against him.

couplet: I silent sat, but thought the more, And gazed on her. Then she
Cried out, 'While thus you eye me o'er, Tell me whose form you see'.
pope.gloss: Even when I look on her contemplating (her beauty), she is displeased and says, "With whose thought have you (thus) looked on my person?"

reading: The man says that even when he just sits and gazes at her in thought, she is angry: 'whom are you thinking of as you look me over?'
nuance: Silence and adoration are his last resort, and they fail too. For Parimelazhagar, her logic is very neat: as no one woman could match all her parts, he must be comparing each part with a different woman, so there must be several. So she wants them named.

title: ஊடலுவகை
theme: The joy of the quarrel, and the end of the Kural. Sulking is here set above heaven, and above union itself as digestion is above eating; the loser wins, and a man prays for the night to last. The whole work ends not on virtue or God but on a condition about an embrace.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar gives 1321-1324 to the woman and 1325-1330 to the man, each explaining their delight. Manakkudavar's commentary ends the entire Kural at 1323 and marks the book's completion there, and calls the group at 1324 the man's eight, so his order of these last verses differs.
source_issues: 1323: Manakkudavar's entry ends with கற்பியல் முற்றிற்று ... திருக்குறள் மூலமும் உரையும் முற்றுப்பெற்றன, which marks this verse as the last of the work in his order, unlike the 1330 of the received order. The closing verse of the Kural therefore differs across traditions.
1324: Manakkudavar's note இவையெட்டும் தலைமகன் கூற்று, 'these eight are the man's', doesn't fit its position here and depends on his different order.
1322: Manakkudavar's entry has உடலிற் where ஊடலிற் is required.
1328: Parimelazhagar's gloss has சொல்லோ for கொல்லோ, and his note has the feminine என்றாள் for a verse whose gloss has a male speaker (இவள் நுதல்).
1326: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary.

couplet: Although there be no fault in him, the sweetness of his love
Hath power in me a fretful jealousy to move.
pope.gloss: Although my husband is free from defects, the way in which he embraces me is such as to make me feign dislike.

reading: The woman says that even though he has no fault, the way he shows his grace has the power to bring on a sulk.

couplet: My 'anger feigned' gives but a little pain;
And when affection droops, it makes it bloom again.
pope.gloss: His love will increase though it may (at first seem to) fade through the short-lived distress caused by (my) dislike.

reading: The woman says that even if his fine grace droops a little through the small misery sulking brings, it rises to greatness.
nuance: She is justifying the risk to a friend who has pointed out she could have his kindness without quarrelling. வாடினும், 'though it droop', uses a word for a plant that comes back stronger. Parimelazhagar keeps the concession small: a quarrel with no real fault passes quickly.

couplet: Is there a bliss in any world more utterly divine,
Than 'coyness' gives, when hearts as earth and water join?
pope.gloss: Is there a celestial land that can please like the feigned dislike of those whose union resembles that of earth and water?

reading: The woman asks if there is any heaven to compare with sulking with one to whom one is joined as water to earth.
nuance: Readers of Tamil poetry will recall Kuruntokai 40 here, with its rain and red earth. I offer that as an echo. In the sequence Manakkudavar's text gives, these are the last words of the Kural.

couplet: 'Within the anger feigned' that close love's tie doth bind,
A weapon lurks, which quite breaks down my mind.
pope.gloss: In prolonged dislike after an embrace there is a weapon that can break my heart.

reading: Within the sulk that follows an embrace and won't let go arises the weapon that breaks 'my' heart; the speaker is the woman for Parimelazhagar and the man for Manakkudavar.
nuance: Both identify the weapon: his bows and soft words for Parimelazhagar, and soft words (பணிமொழி) for Manakkudavar. Being broken is exactly what she is after, so the battle imagery here is pure pleasure. Compare the same weapon in 1258.

couplet: Though free from fault, from loved one's tender arms
To be estranged a while hath its own special charms.
pope.gloss: Though free from defects, men feel pleased when they cannot embrace the delicate shoulders of those whom they love.

reading: The man, delighted after making up, says that though men may be faultless, being kept from the soft arms of those they love has a certain something.
nuance: ஆங்கொன்று, 'a certain something', is an honest refusal to name it, and Parimelazhagar takes it that way: the pleasure is beyond words. Even the wrongly accused gets something from this. It matches 1321, in which she sulks at a man with no fault.

couplet: 'Tis sweeter to digest your food than 'tis to eat;
In love, than union's self is anger feigned more sweet.
pope.gloss: To digest what has been eaten is more delightful than to eat more; likewise love is more delightful in dislike than intercourse.

reading: The man says digesting what you have eaten is sweeter than eating, and for love sulking is sweeter than union.
nuance: Earthy and unusual, as digestion rarely comes into love poetry. The thought behind it is appetite: as Parimelazhagar says, hunger makes food better, and distance makes union better.

couplet: In lovers' quarrels, 'tis the one that first gives way,
That in re-union's joy is s een to win the day.
pope.gloss: Those are conquerors whose dislike has been defeated and that is proved by the love (which follows).

reading: The man says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses wins, as can be seen when they come together.
nuance: A paradox with a precise explanation in Parimelazhagar: the one who gives way first gets the great joy, and only later learns this. He adds the first-person point: I gave way, and so I got this joy.

couplet: And shall we ever more the sweetness know of that embrace
With dewy brow; to which 'feigned anger' lent its piquant grace.
pope.gloss: Will I enjoy once more through her dislike, the pleasure of that love that makes her forehead perspire?

reading: The man asks whether by sulking they might again win that savour which appeared in union, with her forehead wet with sweat.
nuance: உப்பு, 'salt', stands for sweetness here, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as இனிமை, which he explains as all five senses at once, recalling 1101. It's a frankly physical detail near the end of the Kural, and Manakkudavar notes that sulking belongs to both of them.

couplet: Let her, whose jewels brightly shine, aversion feign!
That I may still plead on, O night, prolong thy reign!
pope.gloss: May the bright-jewelled one feign dislike, and may the night be prolonged for me to implore her!

reading: The man wishes that the bright-jewelled woman would keep on sulking, and that the night would last, so that he may go on pleading.
nuance: The pleading has become what he wants, and not merely a way to get to what he wants. யாமிரப்ப, 'that we may plead': the man who began the book with his might broken now prays for the chance to beg.

couplet: A 'feigned aversion' coy to pleasure gives a zest;
The pleasure's crowned when breast is clasped to breast.
pope.gloss: Dislike adds delight to love; and a hearty embrace (thereafter) will add delight to dislike.

reading: The man says sulking is love's pleasure, and the pleasure of sulking is being able to come together and embrace.
nuance: In the received order, the last verse of the entire work ends on பெறின், 'if one gets to'. So 1,330 verses on virtue, wealth and love close with a chained definition and an open condition. Parimelazhagar explains the condition: knowing how far to go is the hard part, so that the union will still be possible.

title: Which wealth is the true wealth?
claim: Several verses award the title of true or only wealth to different things: grace, hearing, not wanting, and learning, and 751 says nothing but wealth counts. Commentators read each against material wealth, so these may be a rhetorical form rather than one ranking.

title: Superlatives that compete
claim: The formula recurs beyond wealth and sometimes collides: nothing surpasses virtue, yet nothing surpasses apt speech; nothing beats truth, yet not killing is ranked above it; poverty is unmatched pain, yet wealth under a tyrant hurts more. Commentators reconcile the first two, and 323 is a deliberate ranking, so these superlatives need case-by-case reading.

title: Absolute ethics and the needs of the state
claim: Five rules stated without exception in the Book of Virtue meet specific verses in the Book of Wealth that suspend or limit them: killing, anger, hypocrisy, generosity and purity of mind. The verses do not acknowledge this; Parimelazhagar reconciles some by adding limits such as royal duty and enemies only. The Book of Wealth elsewhere upholds ethics (546, 657).

title: Echoes of the earlier books in the Book of Love
claim: A few lover-speakers reuse the earlier books' language against its grain: shame worth dying for is set aside to save life (1132/1017), the body-soul bond called flimsy in 338 becomes the image of union (1122), and honour's ban on following those who slight you is called unavailable to the lovesick (1255/966). These are dramatised speeches and do not overturn the earlier teaching.

title: Where the man and woman differ
claim: On Parimelazhagar's speaker assignments, the man and woman differ over shame (1132/1163) and memory (1202/1207), and 1137 states the first contrast outright. Manakkudavar assigns some speakers differently, and most other differences in the Book of Love follow union and separation rather than gender.

title: Truth defined by what it does
claim: On Parimelazhagar's reading, chapter 30 defines truthfulness by harmlessness of effect and explicitly sets aside mere statement of what happened, though 293 still treats lying as going against what one knows. That definition carries real weight: without it, 297's unbroken not-lying and 292's blameless falsehood would conflict.

title: Is the world's moral order just?
claim: The Kural says the upright do not fall (170, 210), yet treats the prosperity of the crooked and ruin of the upright as a puzzle (169), and it both accepts the apportioner (377) and curses the world's maker if begging was decreed (1062). The verses leave this open; Parimelazhagar resolves it through past deeds.

title: Fate and agency, across the whole book
claim: Chapter 38 makes effort and sloth products of fate, while other verses treat effort and heedlessness as within a person's power and say persistence puts fate behind you. Commentators narrow the conflict, but the verses pull apart. The phrase தான் முந்துறும் at 380 and 1023 is an echo, not a conflict.

title: Poverty: a discipline and a catastrophe
claim: The Kural disagrees with itself on whether worth survives poverty (988 against 1044) and on whether the world despises the poor (752 against 841). இன்மை also names the ascetic's chosen possessionlessness, but that is a different condition from destitution.

title: Birth: denied in one verse, assumed in many
claim: Besides denials of birth's rank (972; also 409 for learning), the book also treats birth as a real factor: integrity is natural to the well-born (951), friends are screened by family (793, 794) and birth is named as a source of courtesy (992). Quoting 972 alone gives a partial picture.

title: Where does understanding come from?
claim: The book names at least three sources of understanding that do not sit easily together: study (396), one's own or fated nature (373) and company (454). Parimelazhagar reconciles study with fate by limiting study's reach to where fate does not oppose it. Separately, it is divided on whether a speaker's standing matters (423, 415, 850).

title: Can signs be trusted?
claim: The face is said to show the heart (706), yet enemies' smiles are said to hide hostility even from the face (824) while their words are soon seen through (826). Tears publish love in 71 and may conceal a weapon in 828, but those verses concern different people and do not conflict.

title: Giving and asking
claim: Giving is valued for itself and for its returns. Asking is permitted from the right person and also called the worst thing a tongue can do. Consecutive chapters open in direct opposition.

title: What can friendship survive?
claim: The book says those devoted to friendship do not leave a friend (791) yet leaving a fool's friendship is gain (797), and says friendship grows with practice (783) yet does not need it (785). Parimelazhagar supplies the limit: exit is for what one took on unknowingly (800). Old friends who harm you are kept (807), which he treats as a separate case.
